title: The Prerequisite for Revival — A Change of Mindset

sections.heading: Introduction: On the Wrong Road, Going Forward Won’t Bring You Closer
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Let me begin by asking a very everyday question.

Have you ever had this experience? You head out in the car, set the satnav, and drive on with your foot on the accelerator. Half an hour later, your phone suddenly gives a cold little announcement: “You have left the route. Recalculating.” Only at that moment do you realise that for the past half hour you have been driving very conscientiously, very diligently — but in the wrong direction. The harder you tried, the further you got from where you were going.

At that moment you have only two choices. The first is to pretend you didn’t hear it and keep your foot on the accelerator; the second is to admit you have gone wrong and turn round at once.

Brothers and sisters, the Bible calls the second choice “repentance”; it calls it “turning back”.

The English writer and apologist C. S. Lewis, in Mere Christianity, says something that cuts deep. We all want progress, he says; but progress means getting nearer to the place you want to be. And if you have taken a wrong turning, then going forward does not get you any nearer to your goal — it takes you further away. In that case, the most progressive person is the one who turns back soonest.

Those words state the heart of this lesson: change is not going backwards; change is the only real progress.

The title of our lesson is “A Change of Mindset Is Necessary.” Please notice those last words — “is necessary”. The lesson makes it very clear from the start: revival is not a chance gift of grace; it is the result of people being willing to respond to God with “change”. No change, no revival; no turning back, no healing.

Brothers and sisters, God has never put revival in the place of “waiting”; he has put it in the place of “turning”.

On 31 October 1517, Martin Luther nailed his Ninety-five Theses to the door of the church in Wittenberg and set the whole Reformation ablaze. Many people assume the first thesis must have been a fierce attack on indulgences, but it wasn’t. The first of the ninety-five reads like this: When our Lord and Master Jesus Christ said, “Repent,” he willed that the entire life of believers should be one of repentance.

The first brick of the Reformation was not protest; it was repentance. The first brick of revival is not excitement; it is turning back.

So this morning, I want to invite you, brothers and sisters, to face together a question that is very uncomfortable but very precious: in my life, is there a stretch of road I have been driving very hard for a long time, but in the wrong direction?

May the Holy Spirit speak to us this morning.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Two Verses, One Call
sections.html: For the key passage of this lesson we have chosen 2 Corinthians 5:17, read alongside Romans 12:2. Of these two verses, one speaks of “a change of identity” and the other of “a change of mindset”; one sets out what God has already done for us, the other what we must respond with every day. Put together, they form the very skeleton of this lesson.

sections.heading: (1) 2 Corinthians: Author, Date and Recipients
sections.html:
The author of 2 Corinthians is the apostle Paul. It was written around AD 56, generally thought to be from Macedonia, and it was addressed to the church in Corinth.

Corinth was the capital of the province of Achaia, set on the isthmus of the Greek peninsula; its two harbours, east and west, made it a hub of trade for the Mediterranean world. Wealth flowed through the city, ideas of every kind mingled there, and morals were loose — so much so that in the Greek of the day, “to live like a Corinthian” even became a byword for sexual immorality. The church that grew up in a city like this carried a strong whiff of the world: factions, quarrels, lawsuits, misuse of spiritual gifts, contempt for the apostle’s authority.

In other words, the Corinthian church’s biggest problem was not that they had not been saved; it was that after they were saved, their mindset had not changed. Their identity had changed, but their thinking still lived in the old city.

2 Corinthians is a “letter after reconciliation”, and every line of it is full of a shepherd’s tenderness and a shepherd’s scars. Chapter 5 is the summit of the whole letter: here Paul speaks of the judgment seat to come, of the love of Christ that compels us, of no longer living for ourselves — and only then does he bring out the stirring declaration of verse 17.

“Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.” (2 Corinthians 5:17)

The verse just before it is the key: “Therefore we know no one after the flesh from now on. Even though we have known Christ after the flesh, yet now we know him so no more.” (2 Corinthians 5:16) What Paul means is this: since the new creation has already happened, the way I look at people must change, and the way I look at Christ must change too. The new creation brings a new perspective — and that is exactly what this lesson is about.

sections.heading: (2) The Setting of Romans
sections.html:
Romans was written around AD 57; Paul wrote it from Corinth to the church in Rome. Rome was the heart of the empire, the centre of the world’s power, wealth and idols in that day. The first eleven chapters of Romans set out doctrine, and from chapter 12 on Paul turns to daily living, beginning with these words: “Therefore I urge you, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service.” (Romans 12:1) Immediately after comes verse 2:

“Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” (Romans 12:2)

“Be conformed to this world” is συσχηματίζω (syschēmatizō) in the original, meaning “to share the same mould with…”, like something poured into a mould and shaped to its form. The “transformed” of “be transformed by the renewing of your mind” is μεταμορφόω (metamorphoō), meaning “to undergo metamorphosis, to change in substance”. In Matthew 17:2 this word describes Jesus being transfigured on the mountain, and in 2 Corinthians 3:18 it describes our being transformed into the Lord’s image.

Brothers and sisters, see this contrast clearly: one is “a mould pressed on you from outside”; the other is “a metamorphosis that grows from within”. The world wants to squeeze you into its mould; the Holy Spirit wants to renew you from the inside out. And where is the switch for all of this? Paul says it plainly — in the “mind”, νοῦς (nous) in the original: our thinking, our thoughts, our mindset.

Wherever the mindset goes, life follows. That is why this lesson says: a change of mindset is necessary.

sections.heading: 1. Change Is God’s Call to Revival
sections.html:
The lesson says: in the Bible, God again and again calls his people to turn back; and when Jesus preached on earth, he opened his message with the very same words.

1. Hosea’s call: return to Yahweh, and you will be healed

“Come! Let’s return to Yahweh; for he has torn us to pieces, and he will heal us; he has injured us, and he will bind up our wounds. After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him. Let’s acknowledge Yahweh. Let’s press on to know Yahweh. As surely as the sun rises, Yahweh will appear. He will come to us like the rain, like the spring rain that waters the earth.” (Hosea 6:1–3)

Hosea was a prophet to the northern kingdom of Israel in the eighth century BC, serving at a time when the nation was in steep decline. On the surface the northern kingdom prospered, but underneath it worshipped idols and lived in immorality. God told Hosea to marry Gomer, an unfaithful woman, and used his marriage as a living lesson, acting out before the whole nation Israel’s unfaithfulness and God’s faithfulness.

In the midst of such darkness, chapter 6 opens up a way to life — not political reform, not a military alliance, but “return to Yahweh”.

“Return” in Hebrew is שׁוּב (shuv), the most important word for repentance in the Old Testament, appearing more than a thousand times across the whole Old Testament. Its basic meaning is very concrete: to turn round, to turn back, to come home. It is not “to feel sorry”, nor “to be sad inside”; it is “to turn a hundred and eighty degrees and walk back”.

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully to the order in Hosea’s words: first “return”, then “heal”; first “turning back”, then “revive” and “raise up”. God’s healing is not hung up in the sky for us to grab; it hangs right behind the word “return”.

And how beautiful the promise of verse 3 is: “As surely as the sun rises, Yahweh will appear. He will come to us like the rain, like the spring rain that waters the earth.” This is a morning devotion, so these words fit especially well. God has never been stingy; the only question is — has our field been ploughed?

2. Jesus’ first message: the Kingdom is at hand — repent

“From that time, Jesus began to preach, and to say, ‘Repent! For the Kingdom of Heaven is at hand.’” (Matthew 4:17)

This was the first message of Jesus’ public ministry. Notice the order: not “repent, and then the Kingdom will come near”, but “the Kingdom is at hand, therefore repent”. Grace comes first, our response after; it is not our repentance that buys the Kingdom, but the nearness of the Kingdom that presses us to repent.

“Repent” in Greek is μετανοέω (metanoeō), formed from μετά (change) plus νοέω (to think, to perceive); its literal meaning is “change your thinking”, “take on a different mind”.

Brothers and sisters, fix this word firmly in your memory. The Chinese word for repentance easily makes people think of emotions — regret, sorrow, tears. But the weight of the biblical original lies not in tears but in thinking. The heart of repentance is this: from today on, the way I see this matter is going to be the way God sees it.

So Jesus’ first message is the title of this lesson: a change of mindset is necessary.

After Pentecost, Peter preached the same message: “Repent therefore, and turn again, that your sins may be blotted out, so that there may come times of refreshing from the presence of the Lord.” (Acts 3:19) From John the Baptist, to Jesus, to Peter, to Paul, the first call of the New Testament never changed.

3. The end-time call: come out of that city

“I heard another voice from heaven, saying, ‘Come out of her, my people, that you have no participation in her sins, and that you don’t receive of her plagues.’” (Revelation 18:4)

The city meant in Revelation 18 is “Babylon the great”, described in chapter 17. In the Bible, Babylon has never been only a city; it is a system — a system with man at the centre, self as king, and wealth and power as god. Starting with the tower of Babel in Genesis 11, people wanted to make a name for themselves and build a tower that reached to heaven. That was humanity’s first collective declaration: we don’t need God.

Brothers and sisters, what does “come out” mean? Moving house geographically? No. “Coming out” means changing systems, migrating in our mindset — walking out of that self-centred system of values.

John puts it even more directly in his letter: “Don’t love the world or the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the Father’s love isn’t in him. For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, isn’t the Father’s, but is the world’s.” (1 John 2:15–16)

The lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, the pride of life — these three are the three pillars of the Babylonian system. You can be in church in body while your heart is still in Babylon. You can attend on Sundays while your values are still rankings, comparison, face and possessions.

The lesson puts it well: if we still cling to old ways of thinking and old ways of living, we will be trapped in the currents of Babylon’s thinking, losing both our discernment and the blessing of God’s presence.

4. The conditions for revival have never changed

“If my people, who are called by my name, will humble themselves, pray, seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then I will hear from heaven, will forgive their sin, and will heal their land.” (2 Chronicles 7:14)

These are the words Yahweh spoke when he appeared to Solomon by night after the dedication of the temple. Count the four conditions God sets out: humble themselves, pray, seek my face, turn from their wicked ways. Four conditions, and every one of them is a “change”. Only then come the three promises: I will hear, I will forgive, I will heal.

In the great Welsh Revival of 1904–1905, God used a twenty-six-year-old young man, Evan Roberts. The message he preached was startlingly simple, just four points: confess every sin not yet confessed; put away everything doubtful from your life; obey the Holy Spirit’s leading completely; confess Christ publicly.

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? Not one of them is about methods, techniques or programmes. All four are about “change”. Revival has never been God changing his mind; revival is people changing their direction.

5. Psychology bears witness: change happens in stages

In 1983 the American psychologists James Prochaska and Carlo DiClemente put forward the Transtheoretical Model. Studying how people overcome addictive behaviours, they found that real change is not a decision made in an instant but a process with stages: precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action and maintenance.

This bears out the order of the Bible exactly. Why did Jesus open his mouth by saying “Repent”? Because unless we see that we need to change, none of God’s grace can get in. That is also why, in 2 Chronicles 7:14, God puts “humble themselves” as the first condition — to humble ourselves is to admit that I need to be changed.

6. Applying 321: shifting the focus

Brothers and sisters, the 321 vision has a very practical exercise here: a shift of perspective.

From man’s perspective to God’s; from an earthly perspective to a heavenly one; from a temporary perspective to an eternal one; from a worldly perspective to a godly one.

These four shifts are what “coming out of that city” concretely means. Babylon doesn’t need to tie your feet; it is enough to tie your eyes. If you measure yourself with an earthly ruler, you will live for ever in comparison; if you look at loss with temporary eyes, you will live for ever in fear.

So 321 says: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. The first step of change is not to change our behaviour first but to change our focus first. Where the eyes look, the feet will go.

sections.heading: 2. 321 Is the Direction and the Standard for Change
sections.html:
The lesson says: God’s intention is not for us to “change for the sake of change”, but for us to return to his original blueprint for creation. 321 is exactly the standard and direction God gives us for change.

A ship on the open sea without a compass only gets further from port the faster it sails. So the question we must ask is not “Have I changed?” but “Which way am I changing?”

1. The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model

“Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus,” (Philippians 2:5)

“Have this in your mind” is φρονέω (phroneō) in the original, meaning “to think, to set great store by, to keep in mind”. In other words, what Paul is saying is: think the same way Jesus thinks.

Jesus himself also said, “For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you.” (John 13:15) He said this after he had finished washing his disciples’ feet. A role model is not a portrait hanging on the wall; it is the act of bending down.

2. The Three Foundations: the Bible is my standard

“Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path.” (Psalm 119:105)

“Every Scripture is God-breathed and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness, that each person who belongs to God may be complete, thoroughly equipped for every good work.” (2 Timothy 3:16–17)

Notice the four uses in this passage from 2 Timothy: teaching (telling you what is right), reproof (telling you what is wrong), correction (helping you back from wrong to right), and instruction in righteousness (training you to keep walking on the right road).

Brothers and sisters, these four uses are exactly one complete cycle of “change”. The Bible is not only a book of comfort; even more, it is a book of calibration.

Freedom is not having no standard; freedom is living within the right standard. A train only runs fast on its rails; a derailed train is not called free, it is called a disaster. A fish is only at ease in water; leaping out of the water is not called liberation, it is called death.

3. The Three Foundations: the Holy Spirit is my guide

“However when he, the Spirit of truth, has come, he will guide you into all truth, for he will not speak from himself; but whatever he hears, he will speak. He will declare to you things that are coming.” (John 16:13)

“For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are children of God.” (Romans 8:14)

Brothers and sisters, if a change of mindset relies only on willpower, it won’t hold for long. You can force yourself not to lose your temper for a week, but you can’t change a heart that is easily provoked. Real change needs a Teacher who lives within us.

The prophet Ezekiel foretold this long ago: “I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you. I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh.” (Ezekiel 36:26)

A heart of stone does not soften because you try hard; a heart of stone has to be replaced. This is God’s work, not ours. Our work is only one thing — to be willing.

321 has a very precious saying: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled, rely on the heart and you’ll be glad. Solomon says, “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23) The mindset lives in the heart; change the heart, and the wellspring of your whole life changes.

4. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory

“The seventh angel sounded, and great voices in heaven followed, saying, ‘The kingdom of the world has become the Kingdom of our Lord, and of his Christ. He will reign forever and ever!’” (Revelation 11:15)

“Whether therefore you eat, or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.” (1 Corinthians 10:31)

Brothers and sisters, what does it mean to “let Jesus be King”? It’s very simple: there is only one King, and only one throne. The question has never been “Is Jesus qualified to be King?” The question is “Am I willing to get down from that seat?”

Here is the core insight of 321: the problem of the old self is the self-centred life; the road of the new self is selflessness. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of every problem. What is pride? Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place. What is humility? Humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.

“But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’” (James 4:6)

Notice the word “resists”. In the original it is ἀντιτάσσομαι (antitassomai), a military term meaning “to draw up in battle array against”. The proud person’s problem is not that there isn’t enough grace; it is that God himself stands against him. How serious that is!

And John the Baptist summed up the Two Core Values in a single sentence: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” (John 3:30)

This is not low self-esteem; this is clear-sightedness. The sky doesn’t need two suns.

5. The Goal: establish God’s system

“Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.” (Matthew 6:10)

“to an administration of the fullness of the times, to sum up all things in Christ, the things in the heavens and the things on the earth, in him.” (Ephesians 1:10)

Brothers and sisters, earlier we said that Babylon is “a system with man at the centre”. God’s answer is not to turn us into a scattered band with no system at all, but to establish on earth “a system with God at the centre” — so that his will is done on earth as it is in heaven.

That is why 321 speaks of the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal. The Three Foundations are the roots, the Two Core Values are the trunk, and the Goal is the fruit. If the roots are wrong, the tree can’t grow tall; if the trunk isn’t straight, no fruit will come.

6. An illustration: Copernicus and his revolution in mindset

In 1543 the Polish astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus published On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres, arguing that the sun, not the earth, is the centre around which the planets move. At the time this was considered absurd, because everyone “saw with their own eyes” the sun rise in the east and set in the west every day.

Where was the problem? Not a lack of data, but the centre in the wrong place. In the earth-centred model, astronomers had to keep adding one circle after another — “epicycles” — to force an explanation of the planets’ retrograde motion; once the centre was switched to the sun, all that tangled complexity at once became simple and elegant.

Brothers and sisters, this is the power of a change of mindset. Change the centre, and everything falls into place.

321 says: let Jesus be King. This is not a religious slogan; it is a Copernican revolution. Change the centre, and the formula of life becomes simple.

7. Psychology bears witness: change first needs “unfreezing”

In 1947 the social psychologist Kurt Lewin put forward a three-stage model of change: unfreezing, changing and refreezing. He pointed out that real change must begin with “unfreezing” — loosening the existing structure of perceptions and habits; skip the unfreezing, and the old structure will snap everything back to how it was.

8. Applying 321: life first, then relationships, then ministry

Brothers and sisters, 321 has an order that must not be reversed: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

And relationships have an order too: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things.

The lesson asks “which areas have strayed from 321”, and in fact what we stray from most often is this very order. When we are willing to put the order right again — first letting God reign as King in my heart, then being at peace with myself, then being at peace with others, and only last of all talking about tasks — you will find that the tasks actually go more smoothly.

321 also lays out the Path of Serving in full: Spirit (the Holy Spirit is my guide), Understanding (the Bible is my standard), Life (Jesus is my role model), Service (let Jesus be King), God (let Jesus receive all the glory). From Spirit to God, every step on this path calls for a change of mindset.

sections.heading: 3. Change Is the Key to Growth and Renewal
sections.html:
The lesson says: the life we live after coming to faith ought to be renewed every day and changed every day. God does not only change our identity; he means for our thinking and our behaviour to be renewed as well.

1. The new creation: an accomplished fact

“Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.” (2 Corinthians 5:17)

“A new creation” in the original is καινὴ κτίσις (kainē ktisis). The word for “new” is καινός (kainos), not νέος (neos). The difference between these two words matters a great deal: νέος is new in time, new as in fresh out of the factory; καινός is new in kind, new as in altogether different.

So Paul is not saying “You’ve been repaired”; he is saying “You’ve been remade”. It’s not an old car given a coat of wax; it’s a brand-new engine.

Brothers and sisters, this is a fact already accomplished, not a goal to strive towards. You are not “in the process of becoming” a new creation; in Christ you “already are” a new creation.

Then why do we still fail? Because our identity is accomplished once for all, but our mindset is renewed day by day. This is what Paul says in Ephesians:

“that you put away, as concerning your former way of life, the old man that grows corrupt after the lusts of deceit, and that you be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who in the likeness of God has been created in righteousness and holiness of truth.” (Ephesians 4:22–24)

Put away, be renewed, put on — three actions. And the one in the middle, “be renewed in the spirit of your mind”, is the very title of this lesson: a change of mindset is necessary.

2. True change is returning to God’s original intention

The lesson puts it superbly: “change” is not about chasing the latest trend or fitting in with the world, but about “returning to God’s original intention”. True change is not an outward makeover but an inward renewal. Every change is a homecoming.

“But when he came to himself he said, ‘How many hired servants of my father’s have bread enough to spare, and I’m dying with hunger! I will get up and go to my father, and will tell him, “Father, I have sinned against heaven, and in your sight.”’” (Luke 15:17–18)

Which sentence is the prodigal son’s turning point? “He came to himself.” In the original it means “he came back into himself” — at last he recovered a clear-headed mindset. Only then does the action follow: “I will get up.”

Brothers and sisters, see this order: first coming to himself, then getting up. First the mindset, then the action. If the mindset hasn’t changed, the action is just forcing yourself to keep going; once the mindset changes, the action flows out naturally.

So repentance is not being frogmarched home; it is seeing things clearly at last and walking home of your own accord. From beginning to end the father never changed; what changed was the son’s way of seeing.

3. Metamorphosis: the most beautiful picture in science

We mentioned earlier that the “transformed” of “be transformed by the renewing of your mind” is μεταμορφόω — the English word metamorphosis, the very term biology uses for an insect’s complete change of form.

A caterpillar becoming a butterfly is one of the most astonishing changes in the natural world. It doesn’t simply grow wings. Inside the chrysalis, most of the caterpillar’s tissue is broken down by enzymes into an almost liquid state, and then clusters of cells that were hidden in its body all along, called “imaginal discs”, build wings, compound eyes and a new body.

Brothers and sisters, notice two things. First, metamorphosis does not produce an upgraded caterpillar; it produces a new creature. Second, the blueprint for that “new” was already placed inside it while it was still a caterpillar.

Isn’t this the gospel? The life of Christ has already been placed within us, waiting only for us to be willing to enter that process of breaking and remaking. “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)

4. Science bears witness: the brain really does change

Science used to think that the adult brain was fixed. But research over recent decades has overturned that view and confirmed “neuroplasticity” — the brain changes its structure through repeated experience and practice.

One of the best-known studies was published in 2000 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) by Eleanor Maguire’s team at University College London. They scanned the brains of London taxi drivers and found that these drivers, who must memorise the streets of the entire city, had noticeably more grey matter in the rear part of the hippocampus than the control group — and the longer they had been driving, the greater the difference.

Another study, directly related to practice, is the finding published in 2010 in the European Journal of Social Psychology by Phillippa Lally’s team, also at University College London: for a new habit to become automatic takes on average sixty-six days, with individual cases ranging from eighteen days to two hundred and fifty-four.

Brothers and sisters, these two studies bring us comfort, and also a reminder. The comfort is this: change is genuinely possible; when God made us, he wove “changeability” into our very bodies. The reminder is this: change takes time.

So please don’t give up on day three. What God gives is not a burst of fireworks but a season of spring rain.

5. Falling is not the frightening thing; refusing to get up is

The lesson says: change is not easy, because old habits and old mindsets often hold us back; but if we are willing to repent and willing to get up again, the Holy Spirit will help us. Failure is not the frightening thing; the frightening thing is refusing to change. Falling is not the frightening thing; the frightening thing is being unwilling to stand up again.

“for a righteous man falls seven times and rises up again; but the wicked are overthrown by calamity.” (Proverbs 24:16)

Notice that the Bible does not say the righteous never fall; it says that when the righteous fall, they rise up again. The difference between the righteous and the wicked lies not in how many times they fall, but in the power to get up.

Paul himself walked this way: “Brothers, I don’t regard myself as yet having taken hold, but one thing I do: forgetting the things which are behind, and stretching forward to the things which are before, I press on toward the goal for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.” (Philippians 3:13–14)

And the source of strength is never in ourselves: “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5)

6. Applying 321: the fivefold change

Brothers and sisters, 321 describes change as one complete chain: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry.

Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; change daily living and you change relationships; change relationships and you change ministry.

Where does this chain begin? With the mindset. That is why this lesson is not titled “A Change of Behaviour Is Necessary”, but “A Change of Mindset Is Necessary”.

Water doesn’t flow where it does because it is pushed; it flows according to the lie of the land. Change the lie of the land, and the water flows there by itself. The mindset is the lie of the land of our life.

And where does this chain end? “But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord, the Spirit.” (2 Corinthians 3:18) “Transformed into the same image” — and this “transformed” is that same word again, μεταμορφόω.

Brothers and sisters, the end point of change is not becoming a better version of ourselves; it is being transformed into the image of the Lord.

sections.heading: 4. Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s draw together the whole thread of this lesson.

The Three Foundations are the content of change: Jesus is my role model — whom I change to be like; the Bible is my standard — what I change by; the Holy Spirit is my guide — on whom I rely to change.

The Two Core Values are the direction of change: let Jesus be King — I come down from the throne; let Jesus receive all the glory — I don’t steal his glory.

The Goal is the result of change: establish God’s system — coming out of Babylon and entering the order of God’s kingdom.

And the main thread running through all of this is a single word: selflessness.

The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of our problems. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

I want to make one thing especially clear: selflessness is not having nothing; it is not erasing yourself and becoming a person with no thoughts and no worth. Selflessness is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living it out — “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (see Galatians 2:20). We are emptied in order to be filled; we make room in order to be inhabited by something greater.

Brothers and sisters, 321 gives us two very concrete practices that fit this lesson exactly.

The 920 practice: living out change in our relationships

The 920 practice means this: everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”; in every relationship we practise living out a selfless (0) life, and let the Holy Spirit bear his fruit in all nine (9) of its expressions.

“But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.” (Galatians 5:22–23)

Why must a change of mindset land in our relationships? Because the most honest test of whether our mindset has changed is not the quiet of the morning, but the heat of a conflict. The reply you give your spouse, the look you give a colleague, the moment you lose patience with your child — that is your real mindset.

Notice that the fruit of the Spirit is “fruit”, not “fruits” — in the original it is singular. Love, joy, peace… are not nine products to pick and choose from; they are nine facets of one and the same fruit. Wherever a facet is missing, that is where the mindset has not yet been renewed.

The 235 relationships: letting change multiply

The 235 relationships mean this: with a selfless person you become a “2”, establishing spiritual companions; you build a “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children; and finally you become a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades working in harmony with one another.

If change stops with ourselves, it is only self-improvement; only when change is passed on is it revival.

That is also why the last of the eight stages of changing our mindset is “Multiplication”. A person who has truly been changed will always bring forth another person who is changed.

Brothers and sisters, the three key points of this lesson are really one road from the heart to the community: the first point is God’s call coming to me; the second is 321 correcting my direction; the third is the Holy Spirit completing the renewal within me. And 920 and 235 are how this renewal flows outward and becomes God’s system.

sections.heading: 5. Putting It into Practice
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. Let’s take them deeper using the eight stages of changing our mindset in 321 — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice 1: Examine your daily living and your service — which areas have strayed from 321?

Information: take a sheet of paper and draw three columns; at the top of each, write the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal. This step simply sets the standard in front of your eyes.

Revelation: be still and ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light on you. This is not you picking faults with yourself; it is asking God to illuminate. “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.” (Psalm 139:23–24)

Conviction: when the Holy Spirit points something out, don’t argue, don’t explain, don’t compare yourself with others. Conviction is saying: Lord, you are right.

Implementation: pick just one thing and start changing it this week. Changing ten things at once is the same as changing none.

Evaluation: every evening, spend three minutes looking back at how you did with that one thing today.

Correction: if you can’t manage it, adjust the method; don’t abandon the goal. The method can change; the direction can’t.

Repetition: remember the research of Lally’s team — sixty-six days on average. Please give yourself at least two months.

Multiplication: find a spiritual companion and tell him the one thing you are changing, and listen as he tells you his. This is your “2”.

Practice 2: Write the Three Foundations in your notebook, meditate on them daily, and ask the Holy Spirit to adjust your focus

I suggest beginning each morning with three sentences, one minute for each, quietly asking yourself:

Jesus is my role model — in what one thing today will I do as Jesus did?

The Bible is my standard — what decision today will I bring before the Bible to check?

The Holy Spirit is my guide — at what moment today am I willing to stop first and listen to the Holy Spirit speak?

These three sentences are short enough not to become a burden, yet deep enough to change a day. Look back after thirty days, and you will find that your focus really has shifted.

Practice 3: When you find your thoughts or behaviour out of step with the truth, repent at once, and ask God to give you the power to change

Please notice the word the lesson uses: “at once”.

Why at once? Because our perceptions protect themselves. In 1957 the social psychologist Leon Festinger put forward the theory of “cognitive dissonance”: when people’s behaviour is out of step with their beliefs, they feel uncomfortable inside, and the way they most often resolve it is not by changing their behaviour but by changing their beliefs — finding themselves a reason that makes what is wrong look right.

Brothers and sisters, that is why it must be “at once”. The longer we put it off, the more excuses we find; the more excuses we find, the harder our hearts become.

“Create in me a clean heart, O God. Renew a right spirit within me.” (Psalm 51:10) This is the prayer David wrote after his deepest failure. What he asked for was not good luck, but a clean heart.

And God’s promise is always greater than our failure: “Behold, I will do a new thing. It springs out now. Don’t you know it? I will even make a way in the wilderness, and rivers in the desert.” (Isaiah 43:19)

sections.heading: 6. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, the lesson’s gentle reminder puts it very tenderly: God does not require us to be perfect, but he longs for us to be “willing to change”. As long as you are willing, he can begin to work in your life, making the old new, raising the dead to life, and making the impossible possible.

Please take these words to heart. What God wants from you this morning is not your perfection but your willingness.

“The Lord is not slow concerning his promise, as some count slowness; but he is patient with us, not wishing that anyone should perish, but that all should come to repentance.” (2 Peter 3:9)

We often think God is waiting for us to get better before he is willing to use us; in fact God is waiting for us to be willing to turn around.

The lesson’s closing words say: change is not an optional extra; it is the road revival must travel. When we are willing to change, Jesus reigns as King; when Jesus reigns as King, his glory comes.

So this morning, on the Lord’s behalf, I want to extend three invitations to you, brothers and sisters.

First, please hand over the steering wheel. Not inviting Jesus into the passenger seat, but asking him to take the driver’s seat. Let Jesus be King.

Second, please come out of that city. Not by moving house, but by changing how you see — from man’s perspective, the earthly, the temporary and the worldly, to God’s perspective, the heavenly, the eternal and the godly.

Third, please begin today with one small thing. Don’t wait for a great revival to arrive before you change, because revival begins with one person who is willing to change today.

“Therefore let’s also, seeing we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, lay aside every weight and the sin which so easily entangles us, and let’s run with perseverance the race that is set before us, looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith.” (Hebrews 12:1–2)

Lay aside the weight, lay aside the sin, run, look to Jesus. Brothers and sisters, may every change we make make us more like Christ; and may all the glory go to Jesus, who sits upon the throne.

keyVerses: “Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.” (2 Corinthians 5:17)
“Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” (Romans 12:2)
practices: Examine your daily living and service: which areas have strayed from 321?
Write the Three Foundations in your notebook, meditate daily, and ask the Holy Spirit to adjust your focus
When your thoughts or actions are out of step with the truth, repent at once and ask God for the power to change
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we thank you for shining the light of your word on us this morning.
Lord, we confess that we often try very hard yet travel in the wrong direction; we often ask for revival yet refuse to turn back. Have mercy on us.
Lord Jesus, I am willing to be changed by you. Shine your light on every thought in my life that is not after your heart; take away my heart of stone and give me a heart of flesh.
Holy Spirit, lead me back into the truth of 321: let Jesus be my role model, let the Bible be my standard, and let you be my guide.
Help me come down from the throne and let Jesus be King; help me come out of the currents of Babylon’s thinking and live out a selfless life.
Lord, I do not ask to be perfect; I ask only to be willing. Let this willingness, beginning today, be renewed day by day.
May revival be kindled in my heart, and may all the glory go to Jesus. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” (Romans 12:2) In your life right now, which mindset has been shaped by the world’s mould rather than by God’s word? Please name one specific thing.

“Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.” (2 Corinthians 5:17) Looking back over your life since you came to faith, which mindset of yours has God already changed? How did that change affect your daily living and your relationships? Please share with your group, and pray for one another.
l038.title: A Change of Mindset Is Necessary
l038.subtitle: Revival Begins with a Renewed Mind
l038.partTitle: Unit 4 · The Prerequisite for Revival — A Change of Mindset

sections.heading: Introduction: Why “Wanting to Change” Is So Easy and “Truly Changing” So Hard
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning.

Every year on 1 January, there are queues in front of the treadmills at the gym. By February the queue is half as long; by March there are often only one or two people left beside those machines. John C. Norcross, a clinical psychologist at the University of Scranton in the United States, published a follow-up study with his colleagues in the Journal of Clinical Psychology (2002). It found that of those who made New Year’s resolutions to change themselves, only about 46 per cent were still keeping them six months later. More than half had gone back to square one within half a year.

That number is not far away from us. It lives in the daily living of every one of us.

A sister once said to me through her tears, “Pastor, every single year I repent of the same thing — my temper. At every prayer meeting I weep and tell God I’m going to change. But when I get home and my child knocks the milk onto the floor, the words still come flying out first, and only afterwards do I remember that I prayed. What is wrong with me? I really do want to change.”

Brothers and sisters, she meant it. The problem wasn’t her sincerity. The problem was that she was changing her “actions”, not her “mindset”; she was trimming the “fruit”, not healing the “root”.

We often misunderstand change. We think it is a contest of willpower: if we just grit our teeth, if we just get more disciplined, we can become new people. So we copy other people’s methods and imitate other people’s practices. After a while we find we can’t keep it up, and we start to suspect we aren’t spiritual enough.

Many people long for a breakthrough in their life, renewal in their family, growth in their service, yet they often stay at the level of “wanting to change the outside” and overlook the real key, which is the “mindset within”. If outward behaviour isn’t built on the renewal of the heart within, it is only a temporary action and cannot last. It is like someone picking up fallen leaves one by one without noticing that the tree has long since withered from the root.

Real change doesn’t come from straining to imitate others. It comes from letting God’s truth enter our thinking so that our heart is renewed. When the heart changes, everything in life changes with it.

This is exactly what Paul says in Romans 12:2: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind.” Notice the order of that sentence. Paul didn’t say, “Don’t do what the world does.” He said, “Don’t be conformed to this world.” Nor did he say, “Be improved by the correcting of your behaviour.” He said, “Be transformed by the renewing of your mind.” The battlefield of change has never been our hands and feet; it has always been our thoughts. It is not outward behaviour but the mindset within.

In the 321 vision we call this the “fivefold change”: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. All change begins with the first link, and that first link is “mindset”. If the mindset hasn’t changed, the life won’t change; and if the life hasn’t changed, every change in daily living is just a performance.

In today’s message we will see three things together. First, the starting point of change is a turning of the “heart”. Second, real change begins with the mindset. Third, let God renew our minds.

May the Holy Spirit himself be our guide this morning.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Romans 12 Is a Watershed
sections.html:
To grasp the weight of the words “be transformed by the renewing of your mind”, we first need to know the situation in which Paul wrote them.

The author of Romans is the apostle Paul. Most scholars hold that the letter was written between AD 56 and 58 in Corinth in Greece. Paul was then finishing his third missionary journey and preparing to take the churches’ offering up to Jerusalem (Romans 15:25–26). He planned to pass through Rome afterwards on his way to Spain (Romans 15:24), so he wrote this letter first, setting out in full the gospel he preached to a group of believers most of whom he had never met.

The church in Rome that received the letter was not one Paul had founded. It was a mixture of Jewish and Gentile believers, living in the capital of the Roman Empire — a great city of perhaps more than a million people, full of idol worship and emperor worship. In AD 49 the emperor Claudius ordered the Jews expelled from Rome (Acts 18:2 mentions that Aquila and Priscilla left because of it). A few years later the Jewish believers began drifting back, only to find that the church was now led by Gentile believers, and the two groups judged one another over their different mindsets on the law, food and festivals. That is exactly the problem Romans 14 deals with.

So Romans is not a cold theological treatise. It is a pastoral letter. In the first eleven chapters Paul sets out the gospel: all have sinned (Romans 3:23); we are justified by faith (Romans 5:1); we die and live with Christ (Romans 6); the law of the Spirit sets us free (Romans 8). When he reaches the end of chapter 11, Paul can’t help bursting into praise: “Oh the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and the knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past tracing out!” (Romans 11:33)

Then the very first sentence of chapter 12 is: “Therefore I urge you, brothers, by the mercies of God…”

That “therefore” is the watershed of the whole letter. Before it, what God has done for us; after it, how we should respond. Before it, doctrine; after it, daily living. Before it, God’s grace; after it, our offering. Paul’s order is always grace first and demand second — not “change first, and then God will love you”, but “God already loves you, so you are able to change.”

Brothers and sisters, many people’s change doesn’t last because the motive is wrong. They change to make God satisfied; they practise to win people’s praise. As soon as they fail, they live in shame, and then they give up. Paul says our change is a response that stands on “the mercies of God”. You don’t change in order to be loved. You change because you are already loved.

Then Paul says two contrasting things, and in the original language these two sentences form a beautiful pair.

The first is “Don’t be conformed to this world.” The Greek for “be conformed” is syschēmatizō (συσχηματίζω), from the root schēma, which means an outward shape, a visible pattern, an appearance that keeps changing. Paul uses the same root in 1 Corinthians 7:31: “For the mode of this world passes away.” So “be conformed to this world” means squeezing yourself into the world’s mould and letting the world’s values decide your shape.

The second is “be transformed by the renewing of your mind.” The Greek for “be transformed” is metamorphoō (μεταμορφόω), from the root morphē, which means the inward, essential form.

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? What is outside is called schēma; what is inside is called morphē. The world wants to change your schēma; God wants to change your morphē. The world wants to give you a change of clothes; God wants to give you a change of heart.

Even more worth noticing, both verbs in the original are present imperatives in the passive voice: don’t keep being shaped by this world; keep being transformed. We don’t fashion a new self by our own effort. We hand ourselves over and let the Holy Spirit work, one day at a time. This is an ongoing process, not a once-for-all event.

And where does the renewing happen? Paul says it is the “mind” — in Greek nous (νοῦς), meaning a person’s thoughts, understanding, the machinery of thinking — in other words, what we call “mindset”. When God renews us, he begins by renewing our mindset.

In the last phrase, Paul tells us the purpose of the renewing: “so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” The Greek for “prove” is dokimazō (δοκιμάζω), which originally meant to test, discern and verify, the way metal is assayed for purity. Only someone whose mindset has been renewed is able to discern what God’s will is.

We can’t skip the mindset and go straight to behaviour. The mindset is the eyes; behaviour is the feet. If the eyes haven’t seen clearly, the faster the feet move, the further off course they go.

sections.heading: 1. The Starting Point of Change Is a Turning of the “Heart”
sections.html:
1. Five layers in an old saying

People often say, “If the mountain won’t turn, the road turns; if the road won’t turn, the person turns; if the person won’t turn, the heart turns; if the heart won’t turn, God turns.” These aren’t the words of the Bible; it is an old folk saying. But it expresses a very deep truth.

The saying has five layers. The “mountain” is the difficulty in front of us — that unreasonable boss, that body that never seems to heal, that marriage that has gone cold. Mountains usually can’t be moved. When the mountain won’t turn, what do you do? “The road turns” — you adjust your method and take another route. But sometimes even the road won’t turn; there are walls on every side. What then? “The person turns” — you let yourself be adjusted, and change your own attitude and approach. But people are the hardest thing of all to change. What if even the person won’t turn? “The heart turns” — let the heart turn towards God. And the moment our heart turns towards God, the last line comes true: “God turns” — God himself goes to work and turns the whole situation around.

Brothers and sisters, notice the direction of these five layers: from circumstances to methods, from methods to ourselves, from ourselves to the heart, from the heart to God. Most people spend their whole lives stuck on the first layer, using all their strength to shift the mountain. But God wants us to reach the fourth layer — the heart turning. Because once the heart turns, God turns.

2. What Jesus said: a fruit problem is a tree problem

The Lord Jesus used trees and fruit as a picture of human life. Luke 6:43–45 records: “For there is no good tree that produces rotten fruit; nor again a rotten tree that produces good fruit. For each tree is known by its own fruit. For people don’t gather figs from thorns, nor do they gather grapes from a bramble bush. The good man out of the good treasure of his heart brings out that which is good, and the evil man out of the evil treasure of his heart brings out that which is evil, for out of the abundance of the heart, his mouth speaks.”

Here the Lord speaks of three layers: fruit, tree and heart. The fruit is the words and actions we can see; the tree is the essence of the life; and the heart is the storehouse of the fruit — “out of the good treasure of his heart”, literally “bringing it out of the storeroom of the heart”.

Matthew 7:17 records the same principle: “Even so, every good tree produces good fruit; but the corrupt tree produces evil fruit.”

Brothers and sisters, the Lord’s logic is very clear. Don’t worry about the fruit; tend the tree. Don’t worry about your words and deeds; tend your heart. Our words and actions are the natural overflow of the thoughts in our hearts. To see the fruit change, we must begin at the source — our “heart”. If our heart is filled with truth and love, our life will bear the fruit of love, joy and peace.

We often think a wrong word was just “a slip of the tongue”. It wasn’t. A slip of the tongue proves precisely that the word was already in the heart. When someone bumps your cup, what spills out depends on what was in the cup to begin with; the bump only brings what is inside into view. I once heard a brother say, “I’m not that kind of person. I was just under too much pressure that day.” I asked him gently, “When you’re under pressure, is the one who comes out the real you, or the pretend you?” He was silent for a long time.

3. What the Bible means by “heart”

In the Old Testament, the Hebrew word for “heart” is lēb (לֵב), and it appears more than eight hundred times. The Chinese word for heart mostly refers to feelings, but the Hebrew “heart” means the centre of a person’s thinking, will, judgement and decisions — something much closer to what we today call “mindset”.

That is why Proverbs 23:7, in the Chinese Union Version’s wording, says, “As he thinks in his heart, so is he.” Not how you talk, not how you put on a show, but how you think in your heart when no one is watching.

And so Proverbs 4:23 urges us: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.”

Brothers and sisters, hear the weight of this verse. “With all diligence” — above everything else you guard. A person can guard his reputation, his property, his health and his position, but if he loses his heart, he has nothing at all. “Out of it is the wellspring of life” — what kind of fruit you bear in your lifetime isn’t decided by your circumstances or by your background. It is decided by your heart.

After David sinned, he didn’t ask God to change his behaviour. He prayed, “Create in me a clean heart, O God. Renew a right spirit within me.” (Psalm 51:10) The word “create” in the original is bārā’ (בָּרָא), the same “create” as in Genesis 1:1, “God created the heavens and the earth” — a word used specifically for God’s work of making something out of nothing. David understood: a clean heart doesn’t come from a bit of patching up. God has to create it anew.

4. Corroboration from psychology: it isn’t things that disturb you, but your view of them

Modern psychology has offered corroboration of the Bible.

In 1955 the American clinical psychologist Albert Ellis (1913–2007) proposed Rational Emotive Behaviour Therapy (REBT). At its core is his well-known ABC model: A is the Activating event; B is the person’s Belief about and interpretation of the event; C is the resulting emotional and behavioural Consequence. Ellis’s point was that A doesn’t directly cause C; B determines C. The same event happens to two people with completely different results, and the difference lies not in the event but in the belief.

Around the same time, Aaron T. Beck (1921–2021), a psychiatrist at the University of Pennsylvania, developed cognitive therapy. He found that people with depression have a great many “automatic thoughts” — ideas that pop up without any reflection, such as “I’m worthless” or “It’s bound to go wrong.” The key to treatment wasn’t forcing people to grit their teeth and do cheerful things. It was catching those automatic thoughts and examining, challenging and replacing them one sentence at a time.

Ellis himself said his theory could be traced back to the first-century Stoic philosopher Epictetus, whose famous saying runs: “People are disturbed not by things, but by the views they take of them.”

Brothers and sisters, psychology has walked for two thousand years and arrived where the Lord Jesus had already been: “For out of the abundance of the heart, his mouth speaks.” Let us be clear: psychology is not our standard; the Bible is. Psychology is only corroboration, evidence that people made by God really do work this way. What can truly exchange a heart of stone for a heart of flesh isn’t a therapy; it is God: “I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you. I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh.” (Ezekiel 36:26)

5. Applying the 321 vision: Jesus is the focal point; rely on the heart, not the brain

In the 321 vision we often remind ourselves of one sentence: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances.

Have you noticed that most of our worries come from putting our focus in the wrong place? Focus on your circumstances, and you are dragged along by them. Focus on other people, and you live in comparison and judgement. Focus on yourself, and you swing back and forth between self-reproach and self-pity. Only when Jesus is the focal point can the heart be at rest.

When Peter was walking on the water, the Bible says: “But when he saw that the wind was strong, he was afraid, and beginning to sink.” (Matthew 14:30) The wind had been strong all along; the wind hadn’t changed. What changed was Peter’s eyes — he went from looking at the Lord to looking at the wind. The mountain may not turn, the road may not turn, but as long as the heart turns to the Lord, a person can stand on the waves.

We also often say: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll have joy, rely on the brain and you’ll have worry. The wellspring of life flows out of the heart, not out of the brain. Relying on the brain means I do my own calculating, my own analysing, my own carrying. Relying on the heart means handing things over to God and listening for how the Holy Spirit guides. Brothers and sisters, this morning, where is your focus? Are you relying on your brain or on your heart?

In 321’s priority of relationships we say: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. A heart that turns puts the first priority back in its place. When our relationship with God is right, the way we see ourselves becomes right; when the way we see ourselves is right, our relationships with others become right. Many people spend their whole lives going round in circles over “things”, yet never return to the first link — “with God”. That is why the busier they get, the emptier they feel, and the harder they try, the drier they become.

sections.heading: 2. Real Change Begins with the Mindset
sections.html:
1. Hanging good fruit on a bad tree

Imagine a farmer with a sick tree in his orchard. The fruit it bears is small and sour. He gets anxious, so he goes to the market, buys a basket of big red apples, and ties them one by one with fine string onto the branches of that sick tree. From a distance the tree looks laden with fruit. But three days later the apples on the strings begin to wrinkle and blacken, and one by one they drop to the ground. And the tree is still sick.

Brothers and sisters, have we ever done that? A change of outward behaviour without a foundation of inward thinking is like hanging good fruit on a bad tree — it looks lovely, but there is no life in it. To bear good fruit you must first plant a good tree; to have a healthy life, you must first have the right mindset.

The greatest danger of hanging fruit isn’t that the fruit falls off. It is that after it has hung there long enough, you start to believe you grew it yourself. A person can learn every spiritual phrase and every proper response in church without a single mindset ever being truly changed by God. This is why the Lord Jesus rebuked the Pharisees most severely of all: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you are like whitened tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful, but inwardly are full of dead men’s bones, and of all uncleanness.” (Matthew 23:27) Whitewash is the quickest change there is, and also the falsest.

2. The seed is the word of God

Where does the right mindset come from? The Lord Jesus gives us the answer in the parable of the sower.

Luke 8:11 records the Lord’s own explanation: “Now the parable is this: The seed is the word of God.”

Brothers and sisters, the Lord didn’t say the seed is a method, an experience or an emotional stirring. The Lord said: the seed is the word of God. Once God’s word enters the heart, it is like a seed falling into the soil — it isn’t stuck onto the surface; it is buried deep. It makes no noise and no fuss, yet in the darkness it splits its shell, puts down roots and grows upwards.

Then the Lord said: “Those in the good ground, these are those who with an honest and good heart, having heard the word, hold it tightly, and produce fruit with perseverance.” (Luke 8:15) Notice the three verbs: having heard, hold it tightly, produce fruit with perseverance. Many people today do only the first — they hear. You can listen to three messages in one morning without a single sentence being held tightly in your heart. If the seed is scattered only on the surface, the birds come and snatch it away.

If we let the world’s thinking and people’s words become the seeds in our hearts, our life will grow the world’s fruit. But if we take God’s word as the seed of our thinking, the truth will change our mindset and bring new life.

What are the seeds the world sows? “You have to rely on yourself.” “Without money there’s no security.” “What other people think of you decides who you are.” Nobody formally taught us these words, yet we swallowed them one by one from advertisements and from years of being rejected since childhood. They grew into mindsets, and then bore the fruit of anxiety, comparison, envy and anger.

But the seeds God sows are these: “But seek first God’s Kingdom, and his righteousness; and all these things will be given to you as well.” (Matthew 6:33) “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” (2 Corinthians 12:9)

Thinking determines behaviour; mindset determines direction. If we don’t change the content of our thinking, we will go round and round in the wrong patterns for ever.

3. Our mindset determines how we see God

The twentieth-century pastor A. W. Tozer (1897–1963), on the first page of “The Knowledge of the Holy” (1961), wrote a sentence that shakes the heart: “What comes into our minds when we think about God is the most important thing about us.”

Brothers and sisters, that sentence is worth meditating on for a whole morning. What God is like in your heart determines what kind of Christian you are.

If the God in your heart is a harsh taskmaster, your faith will be full of fear and performance. If the God in your heart is a cash machine, your faith will be full of bargaining and complaining. But if the God in your heart is the Father who has “loved you with an everlasting love” (Jeremiah 31:3), the Lord who laid down his life for you, then your faith will grow rest, confidence and passion.

So “mindset” isn’t a philosophical question; it is a spiritual question of life and death. Satan never needs to wreck your behaviour. He only needs to twist one mindset you hold about God, and the rest collapses by itself. In the Garden of Eden he didn’t push Adam and Eve over. He asked just one question: “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden’?” (Genesis 3:1) With one sentence he planted a mindset in the human heart: God is stingy, God holds things back, God can’t be fully trusted. Once that seed sprouted, they reached out and took the fruit.

So where does Paul say our battle is fought? “For the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh, but mighty before God to the throwing down of strongholds, throwing down imaginations and every high thing that is exalted against the knowledge of God and bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ.” (2 Corinthians 10:4–5)

Where are these “strongholds”? In our thinking. Every wrong mindset must be taken captive, brought before Christ, and redefined by him.

4. Corroboration from science: mindsets carve roads in the brain

The brain God made bears wonderful witness to this truth.

The Canadian psychologist Donald O. Hebb (1904–1985), in “The Organization of Behavior”, published in 1949, put forward the famous Hebbian theory, which later generations boiled down to one sentence: neurons that fire together wire together. In other words, repeated thoughts make particular neural pathways stronger and stronger. Every time you think “I can’t do it”, that road is trodden a little deeper; tread it for thirty years and it becomes a motorway you could drive with your eyes shut.

Research by the team of neuroscientist Eleanor Maguire at University College London, published in 2000 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, is even more astonishing. To pass their extremely demanding test, London taxi drivers must memorise tens of thousands of streets across the city. The study found that the grey matter in the hippocampus at the back of their brains was markedly larger than in the control group, and that it grew in proportion to their years of driving. In other words, thinking that is used repeatedly over a long time really does change the structure of the brain.

Scientists call this phenomenon “neuroplasticity”. It gives us enormous hope: old roads of thinking can be replaced by new ones. It doesn’t happen overnight, but it really does happen.

The Stanford psychologist Carol S. Dweck, in “Mindset” (2006), also points out that people who believe their abilities can be changed through effort (a growth mindset) and people who believe their abilities are fixed (a fixed mindset) differ enormously in how they respond to failure and in the course their lives take — all from the difference of this one mindset.

Brothers and sisters, if a change in one secular mindset can make such a difference, how great a turnaround will the word of the living God bring when it enters a person’s heart?

That is why Paul tells us to choose deliberately what we think about: “Finally, brothers, whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are just, whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report: if there is any virtue and if there is any praise, think about these things.” (Philippians 4:8) “Think about” doesn’t mean a passing thought. It means deliberately and repeatedly letting your mind rest there.

5. Applying the 321 vision: from the self-centred life to selflessness

In the 321 vision we say that the root of humanity’s fall is the self-centred life, and the core of the self-centred life is pride. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

Brothers and sisters, underneath our most stubborn mindsets there is always a “self” hiding. “I can’t let people look down on me” — that is the “self” guarding its face. “This has to be done my way” — that is the “self” guarding its rights. “I can’t fail” — that is the “self” guarding its sense of worth. In the end, the renewing of our mindset is a journey from the self-centred life to selflessness.

And selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out. “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. Paul could not have put it more clearly: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20)

321 also teaches us four shifts of perspective: from man’s perspective to God’s perspective; from an earthly perspective to a heavenly perspective; from a temporary perspective to an eternal perspective; from a worldly perspective to a godly perspective. Joseph was sold, falsely accused and forgotten, and in the end he said to his brothers: “As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to save many people alive, as is happening today.” (Genesis 50:20) The events didn’t change; Joseph’s perspective changed, and so the whole family was saved.

Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. A person whose mindset has been renewed discovers he doesn’t need to win, because in Christ he already has everything.

sections.heading: 3. Let God Renew Our Minds
sections.html:
1. “Transformed” means metamorphosis

In Romans 12:2 Paul teaches us: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.”

The word “transformed” here is metamorphoō (μεταμορφόω) in the original, meaning “to undergo metamorphosis”. The word we use in biology today, metamorphosis, comes straight from it.

Brothers and sisters, Paul could easily have used a gentler word, such as “improve” or “make progress”. But the Holy Spirit moved him to use this one — metamorphosis. Metamorphosis isn’t polishing up the old thing. The old form passes away completely, and a new form grows.

This word is used only four times in the New Testament. Twice it is used of the Lord Jesus: “He was changed before them. His face shone like the sun, and his garments became as white as the light.” (Matthew 17:2) The other two times it is used of us — Romans 12:2 and 2 Corinthians 3:18: “But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord, the Spirit.”

This verse tells us the secret of metamorphosis. It isn’t straining to change ourselves; it is “with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord”. Whoever you gaze at, you become like. Moses spoke with God on the mountain for forty days and forty nights, and when he came down he “didn’t know that the skin of his face shone by reason of his speaking with him” (Exodus 34:29).

2. What happens inside the chrysalis

Metamorphosis is like a caterpillar becoming a butterfly — from crawling to flying, from confinement to freedom. It is a process that takes time, and it comes at a cost.

Picture that caterpillar. It only ever does two things: eat and crawl. Its world is the size of one leaf; it has never seen the sky. One day it crawls to the underside of a branch, spins silk around itself, and enters a state of complete darkness, complete stillness and complete defencelessness.

In the “chrysalis” stage of metamorphosis, the caterpillar is wrapped in a dark outer shell. It looks lonely and helpless, but inside an enormous reorganisation and renewal is taking place. Biologists tell us that most of the larva’s tissue is broken down by enzymes. Only certain clusters of cells are kept, cells that were already there during the larval stage, called “imaginal discs”; the butterfly’s wings, antennae and compound eyes grow from these imaginal discs.

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully — the blueprint for those wings was placed inside it while it was still crawling on the ground. It doesn’t turn into a different species. It becomes what it was created to be all along.

Paul says: “Don’t you know that you are a temple of God, and that God’s Spirit lives in you?” (1 Corinthians 3:16) Renewal doesn’t turn us into someone else. It lets the new self, created in the likeness of God, grow out (Ephesians 4:24).

In a study published in PLoS ONE in 2008, the biologist Martha Weiss of Georgetown University in the United States and her colleagues trained tobacco hornworm caterpillars to avoid a certain smell. After those caterpillars went through the pupal stage and emerged as moths, they still remembered to avoid that smell. Even though their bodies had been almost completely taken apart and rebuilt, the memory was preserved.

This gives us a beautiful reminder: metamorphosis is not amnesia; it is not starting from zero. God doesn’t wipe out the road you have walked. He weaves your past anew into your future. Those tears, that waiting, those nights in the dark chrysalis counting the days — none of it will be wasted.

3. The chrysalis stage is necessary

Brothers and sisters, when we are inside the chrysalis, the prayer we pray most often is, “Lord, let me out quickly.” But sometimes God’s answer is, “Child, wait a little longer. Your wings haven’t hardened yet.”

James 1:2–4 says: “Count it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various temptations, knowing that the testing of your faith produces endurance. Let endurance have its perfect work, that you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing.”

Are you inside a chrysalis right now? Is your work at a standstill, a relationship stuck, your prayers seemingly unanswered? Brothers and sisters, darkness doesn’t mean God is absent, and silence doesn’t mean God isn’t moving. Inside the chrysalis is where God is busiest.

4. Three gifts God gives us

In the same way, when we let God’s word into our hearts, he tears down the old frameworks of our thinking and reshapes our values and beliefs, so that we are no longer held hostage by the world’s mindsets and can live out a heavenly life.

And he hasn’t told us to undergo metamorphosis on our own. The lesson text reminds us that God has given us three things, and they are precisely the Three Foundations of 321.

First, he has given his word — the Bible is my standard. “Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path.” (Psalm 119:105) The renewing of a mindset needs a measuring rule. Without one, we can only measure ourselves by our own feelings, and however much we measure, we are still the same old self.

Second, he has given the power of the Holy Spirit — the Holy Spirit is my guide. “But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you. You will be witnesses to me in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth.” (Acts 1:8) Brothers and sisters, between knowing you need to change and having the power to change there lies a deep chasm, and only the Holy Spirit can cross it. Paul says, “For desire is present with me, but I don’t find it doing that which is good.” (Romans 7:18) And the answer comes in the next chapter: “For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus made me free from the law of sin and of death.” (Romans 8:2)

Third, he has given Jesus as our role model — Jesus is my role model. “For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you.” (John 13:15) When the Lord said this, he had just knelt down and washed the feet of the twelve disciples — including Judas, who was about to betray him. He didn’t change the disciples’ mindset with a sermon. He used a basin of water and a towel.

Brothers and sisters, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide, Jesus is my role model — these Three Foundations are the three pillars of a renewed mind. Without the standard, renewal goes off course; without the guide, renewal has no power; without the role model, renewal becomes abstract.

5. Renewal is continual, not once-for-all

Ephesians 4:22–24 describes this process very fully: “that you put away, as concerning your former way of life, the old man that grows corrupt after the lusts of deceit, and that you be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who in the likeness of God has been created in righteousness and holiness of truth.”

Put away, be renewed, put on — and the middle link is “be renewed in the spirit of your mind”. Many people only do the “putting away”: they give up a few bad habits, but their mind is never renewed, and before long the old clothes are back on.

And this is an ongoing work. Paul says: “being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ.” (Philippians 1:6) It is God who begins the work, and God who completes it; our responsibility is to hand ourselves over to him every day.

6. Applying the 321 vision: life first, then relationships, then ministry

In the 321 vision we say: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

Why this order? Because if the chrysalis stage isn’t completed, you can’t fly once you’re out. When someone whose life hasn’t been renewed goes into ministry, the ministry becomes a stage on which he proves himself.

We also practise “920”: everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”; before every “2” we practise living out the “0” — the selfless life — and that bears the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23)

Brothers and sisters, notice that Galatians speaks of “fruit”, not “products”. Products are manufactured; fruit is grown. You can’t manufacture gentleness by effort; you can only grow gentleness by life. And the renewal of life begins with the mindset.

We also practise “235” in our relationships: finding a selfless person to be our “2”, a spiritual companion with whom we hold each other up; building the “3”, spiritual parents and spiritual children; and going on to become the “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades, establishing God’s system together.
