Changing a person’s mindset is very hard to do as a lone fighter. A chrysalis may be spun alone, but no butterfly grows up in a vacuum. Brothers and sisters, who is your “2”? This morning, can you think of one name and pass on to that person what you have received today?

sections.heading: 4. Integrating the 321 Vision: A Map of Change
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, if we place today’s message within the 321 vision, we will see a complete map of change.

The Three Foundations: the bedrock of renewal

Jesus is my role model — he washed his disciples’ feet and showed us what the selfless life looks like (John 13:15). The Bible is my standard — God’s word is the seed, and it is also the measuring rule (Luke 8:11). The Holy Spirit is my guide — he gives the power, so that we don’t just know but are able to do (Acts 1:8). God not only gives us his word; he also gives the power of the Holy Spirit and sets Jesus before us as our role model, walking with us and helping us on the journey of renewal. These three aren’t three options. They are three pillars, and not one can be missing.

The Two Core Values: the direction of renewal

Let Jesus be King — the end point of a renewed mindset is not that I become a better version of me, but that I step down from the throne and let Jesus reign as King in my thinking. Let Jesus receive all the glory — when others see us change, our first words are not “I worked really hard” but “The Lord did this.”

Someone whose mindset has truly been renewed bears one mark: he needs less and less for other people to notice him.

The Goal: establish God’s system

Why do we want to change our mindset? Not to feel good about ourselves, but because God wants to establish his system on this earth, fulfilling what the Lord’s Prayer says: “Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.” (Matthew 6:10) God’s system isn’t built by piling up institutions. It is built out of people whose mindsets have been renewed, one by one.

The fivefold change: the order of renewal

Mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry — change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; change daily living and you change relationships; change relationships and you change ministry.

Brothers and sisters, please don’t reverse this order. We often want to start from the last link: do a bit more ministry, look a bit more spiritual — and the more ministry we do, the drier our life becomes. Others try desperately to patch up their relationships, only to find that their mindset hasn’t changed, so the same conflict carries on with a different person. The real shortcut is to go back to the first link — change begins with the mindset.

The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless

The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of the problem. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

And selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out. “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me (Galatians 2:20). The caterpillar lost its old body, and gained the sky.

Shifts of perspective

From man’s perspective to God’s perspective; from an earthly perspective to a heavenly perspective; from a temporary perspective to an eternal perspective; from a worldly perspective to a godly perspective.

“If then you were raised together with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated on the right hand of God. Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth.” (Colossians 3:1–2)

The word Paul uses here for “set your mind” (phroneō) is the same word as “have this in your mind” in Philippians 2:5. In the end, renewing our mindset means turning the direction of our thoughts from the earth to the things above.

sections.heading: 5. Putting It into Practice: Let Truth Become the New Seed
sections.html:
This lesson gives us three practices. We will use 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to take them deeper.

Practice 1: Write down your three most frequent negative thoughts and replace them with biblical truth

This week, get a small notebook and write down the three negative thoughts that come to you most often.

Information: first, gather the data. Don’t go by impressions; actually write them down. You’ll find that although countless thoughts pop up in a day, the ones that hurt you usually come down to the same three or four sentences, over and over: “I’m not good enough.” “Nobody really cares about me.” “I’m bound to mess it up again.”

Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light. When did this thought first enter your heart? Who said it? How long have you treated it as fact? “Yahweh’s words are flawless words, as silver refined in a clay furnace, purified seven times.” (Psalm 12:6)

Conviction: find the verse that replaces it, and say “Amen” to it. For example, replace “I’m not good enough” with Psalm 139:14, “I am fearfully and wonderfully made”; replace “There’s definitely no way” with Psalm 23:1, “Yahweh is my shepherd: I shall lack nothing”; replace “I can’t hold on any longer” with 2 Corinthians 12:9, “My grace is sufficient for you.”

Implementation: when that thought pops up again, don’t argue with it; just read the verse out loud. Argue with a lie and you will never win; but the moment truth is spoken, darkness retreats. When the Lord Jesus was tempted in the wilderness, all three times he said only one thing: “It is written…” (Matthew 4:4, 7, 10)

Evaluation: every evening, take three minutes to look back. How many times did this thought appear today? How many times did I answer it with truth?

Correction: if the verse doesn’t fit well enough, swap it for another. If you discover that the real root isn’t “I’m not good enough” but “I’m not loved”, adjust accordingly.

Repetition: this is the most crucial step. A road of thinking trodden for thirty years won’t disappear after three days of walking a new one. Hebb’s research reminds us that new neural pathways only grow strong through repetition. Truth has to be repeated until it becomes more automatic than the lie.

Multiplication: once you have experienced change, go and tell your “2”. If a change of mindset isn’t passed on, it stops with you; pass it on, and it becomes a living stone in God’s system.

Practice 2: Spend ten minutes each day meditating on one verse of God’s word

Not reading ten chapters — meditating on one verse.

“But his delight is in Yahweh’s law. On his law he meditates day and night. He will be like a tree planted by the streams of water, that produces its fruit in its season, whose leaf also does not wither. Whatever he does shall prosper.” (Psalm 1:2–3) The Hebrew for “meditates” is hāgāh (הָגָה), which carries the sense of murmuring under one’s breath, over and over. Meditation isn’t emptying the mind. It is like a cow chewing the cud: turning one verse over and over in your heart and chewing on it.

How do you actually do it? Ten minutes, four actions: read it three times; ask, “Lord, what do you want to say to me in this sentence?”; be still for one minute; write it down and carry it out of the door with you. The size of the seed is never the key. The key is whether it has truly been buried in the soil.

Practice 3: When facing circumstances you cannot change, turn your focus back to God

When facing circumstances you cannot change, stop complaining or running away; learn to change your own attitude and turn your focus back to God.

Complaining puts the focus on our circumstances; running away puts the focus on ourselves. The Israelites walked both roads in the wilderness, and after forty years they were still where they started.

Paul and Silas were in the prison at Philippi, their backs wounded and their feet fastened in the stocks. Did their circumstances change? No. Yet the Bible says: “But about midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them.” (Acts 16:25) They couldn’t change that prison, but they changed what they did inside it. And then there was a great earthquake, all the doors flew open, and the jailer and his whole household were saved.

If the mountain won’t turn, the road turns; if the road won’t turn, the person turns; if the person won’t turn, the heart turns; if the heart won’t turn, God turns.

This week, when that immovable mountain stands in front of you again, do one small thing: exchange the complaining sentence for a sentence of thanks. You aren’t hypnotising yourself. You are practising turning your focus from your circumstances back to the God who sits enthroned as King.

sections.heading: 6. A Gentle Reminder
sections.html:
You can’t change every “mountain”, but you can change your “heart”. When your heart is renewed by the truth, difficulties are no longer obstacles; they become the tools God uses to transform your life.

Brothers and sisters, we have spent too many years trying to move mountains, while God has been waiting all along for us to give him our hearts. That mountain may still be standing in the same place on the day we leave this world, but it can become a chisel in God’s hand, carving us into the shape he wants.

“We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, for those who are called according to his purpose.” (Romans 8:28)

sections.heading: 7. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, we began today with an old saying: if the mountain won’t turn, the road turns; if the road won’t turn, the person turns; if the person won’t turn, the heart turns; if the heart won’t turn, God turns. We saw the Lord Jesus say that a fruit problem is a tree problem, and a tree problem is a heart problem. We heard Paul say, don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind. And we watched that caterpillar, inside its dark chrysalis, grow wings it had never once used.

Change doesn’t come from outside forces; it begins with the renewal of the heart within. God is not only the God who changes circumstances; even more, he is the Lord who changes hearts. When we let his word sink deep into our thinking, he can make us like a caterpillar becoming a butterfly — leaving the old self behind and flying into new life.

Starting today, let change begin in your heart. Let the truth take root and sprout within you and bring forth the wellspring of a whole life.

So this morning I want to give you three calls.

First, let Jesus reign as King in your thinking. Not only on Sundays — let him reign in the three seconds when someone cuts you up on the road, in the minute when you read that message and everything in you churns. Wherever there is a mindset that hasn’t yet let Jesus be King, there is still a patch of ground that is Satan’s stronghold.

Second, let Jesus receive all the glory. When your temper really has changed, when your worries really have shrunk, please don’t say, “I finally did it.” Say, “The Lord did it.” A butterfly never boasts about its wings, because it knows those wings were created, not earned.

Third, bring someone along to change with you. Who is your “2”? Send them a message today: I heard something this morning — change begins with the mindset.

Brothers and sisters, today isn’t about making a new resolution. Today is about handing over an old mindset. Are you willing?

keyVerses: Romans 12:1–2: “Therefore I urge you, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service. Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.”
Proverbs 4:23: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.”
declarations: Lord, I am willing to let your truth renew my thinking and to let my mind be changed by you. May your word become the seed of my life; change me from the inside out, and let me bear good spiritual fruit.

Brothers and sisters, this declaration is short, but every sentence is a decision. “I am willing” — that is the surrender of the will. “May your word become the seed of my life” — that is choosing what to sow. “From the inside out” — that is acknowledging the order. This morning, please read these words again, slowly, saying them to the Lord one sentence at a time.
practices: Write down your three most frequent negative thoughts and replace them with biblical truth
Spend ten minutes each day meditating on one verse of God’s word
When facing circumstances you cannot change, turn your focus back to God
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you.

Lord, we confess that we have spent far too much strength trying to change the outside, and have seldom let you change the inside. We have pruned the branches many times, but we have never handed the root over to you. Have mercy on us.

Lord, create in us a clean heart, and renew a right spirit within us. Plant your word deep in our hearts like a seed. By the power of the Holy Spirit, throw down every stronghold within us that does not agree with your truth, and bring every thought of ours captive to the obedience of Christ.
Lord, we hand over to you that mountain we cannot move. We will no longer complain, no longer run away. We ask you to change our hearts, and, in your own time, to change that mountain as well.
Lord, let us wait patiently in your hands through the chrysalis stage, until the wings you give have grown, until we can fly, until we are like you.
Reign as King in our thinking, and may all the glory be yours.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Luke 6:45: “The good man out of the good treasure of his heart brings out that which is good, and the evil man out of the evil treasure of his heart brings out that which is evil, for out of the abundance of the heart, his mouth speaks.” Think back to the last time words came flying out of your mouth that you regretted afterwards. What mindset in your heart did those words reveal? Which mindset are you willing to let God replace?

Romans 12:2: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” What “immovable mountain” is there in your life right now? If you look at this mountain from God’s perspective, a heavenly perspective, an eternal perspective and a godly perspective, what do you see that you didn’t see before?
l039.title: Change Begins with the Mindset
l039.subtitle: Transformed by the Renewing of the Mind, Life Turned Around at the Root
l039.partTitle: Unit 4 · The Prerequisite for Revival — A Change of Mindset

sections.heading: Introduction: The Barrel of New Wine That Would Not Fit
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I’d like to begin by asking you to close your eyes and picture a scene.

It is early on an autumn morning, and the vineyards of the Judean hill country have just been harvested. A farmer pours the freshly pressed grape juice into a skin, ties the neck tight, and hangs it against a cool, shaded wall. A few days later the skin begins to swell ever so slightly, its walls stretched little by little by an unseen force inside. If it is a newly made goatskin, it will soften and swell along with the wine. But if it is an old skin, used for years and now dry, hard and brittle, there is only one ending — a sharp crack, the skin splits, the wine runs all over the ground, and the skin is good for nothing.

Both are ruined. The wine is gone, and so is the skin.

With this everyday picture that every Jew understood, Jesus spoke a spiritual principle that shakes us to the core: the problem is not the wine; the problem is the skin.

Brothers and sisters, let me ask you a very honest question. In your life, could it be that God has not stopped pouring the wine at all — it’s just that your skin can no longer hold it?

We often pray like this: “Lord, revive me; Lord, fill me with your Holy Spirit.” That is a prayer after God’s own heart. But in this parable Jesus turns the question round the other way. It is as though he is saying, “My child, I have been pouring the wine all along. I have never held back. The real question is this — have you made ready a new wineskin?”

God’s work is always new. What he does goes beyond human thinking, and beyond human experience. The Holy Spirit is constantly renewing us, wanting to lead us into deeper truth and a richer life. Yet if we still try to understand the Holy Spirit through old mindsets, human rules and past experience, we cannot receive his new wine. It is not that there isn’t enough wine; it is that the skin is wrong.

That is the heart of today’s lesson: only a change of mindset can receive the work of the Holy Spirit.

In my years of ministry I have seen this scene far too many times. A sister earnestly asks God to open a way. God really does open one — but it looks nothing like what she imagined. So she turns it down and says, “This can’t possibly be God’s will.” That is the tragedy of the old wineskin. It is not that God isn’t working; it is that our mindset cannot hold what God is doing.

So this morning we are not asking for a new experience. First, we are asking for a new wineskin.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Three Parables Sparked by a Dinner Party
sections.html:
To understand this parable rightly, we must first go back to its setting.

The Gospel of Luke was written by Luke. He was a physician (Colossians 4:14 calls him “Luke the beloved physician”), a co-worker of Paul on his missionary journeys, and the only Gentile author in the New Testament. Luke wrote around the AD 60s to a distinguished man named Theophilus, and he states his purpose plainly: “that you might know the certainty concerning the things in which you were instructed” (Luke 1:4). Luke has a special concern for the people the religious system shut out — tax collectors, sinners, women, the poor. That concern is the very backdrop to the parable of the new wine.

The parable comes at the end of Luke chapter 5, and chapter 5 is a string of signs that something new has come. Jesus calls Peter and gives him a catch of fish so great the nets can hardly hold it; Jesus reaches out and touches a man with leprosy; four friends tear open a roof to lower a paralysed man, and Jesus forgives his sins; and finally Jesus calls Levi the tax collector to follow him.

Levi (that is, Matthew) throws a great banquet and invites Jesus to sit at table with a whole crowd of tax collectors. The text says: “Their scribes and the Pharisees murmured against his disciples, saying, ‘Why do you eat and drink with the tax collectors and sinners?’” (Luke 5:30). Then they press him further: “Why do John’s disciples often fast and pray, likewise also the disciples of the Pharisees, but yours eat and drink?” (Luke 5:33).

Brothers and sisters, notice where the conflict lies. They are not arguing about theological doctrine; they are arguing about “the rules” — who may share a table, and when one ought to fast. They held in their hands a whole, tightly woven set of religious customs, and what Jesus was doing did not follow that set of customs at all.

Jesus answers first with the image of the bridegroom: “Can you make the friends of the bridegroom fast while the bridegroom is with them?” (Luke 5:34). The bridegroom has come; this is a wedding feast, not a funeral. Then, in one breath, Jesus tells two parables: you don’t tear a piece from a new garment to patch an old one, and you don’t put new wine into old wineskins. In other words, what Jesus brings is not a patched-up edition of Judaism but a wholly new covenant, a wholly new life, a wholly new system. He has not come to sew a patch onto the Pharisees’ old robe; he has come to give a new garment.

In Jesus’ day, wine was kept in skins sewn from a whole goatskin or sheepskin. A new skin was soft and supple; an old skin, after years of use, of drying out and soaking again, of sun and smoke, had long since lost its ability to stretch. The book of Joshua records that when the Gibeonites came to deceive the Israelites, they “took old sacks on their donkeys, and old, torn-up and bound up wine skins” (Joshua 9:4), and pointed to them, saying, “These wine skins, which we filled, were new; and behold, they are torn” (Joshua 9:13). The psalmist, too, uses this image to describe his own dryness: “For I have become like a wineskin in the smoke. I don’t forget your statutes” (Psalm 119:83).

So the people listening to Jesus knew exactly what he meant: you never put new wine into old wineskins. That’s common sense. And Jesus used that very common sense, which everyone understood, to lay bare a truth that no one wanted to face — your problem is not me; it is your own wineskin.

As for the second theme passage of this lesson, it comes from 2 Corinthians chapter 3. The author is the apostle Paul, writing around AD 55–56 to the church in Corinth. At the time, some people came bearing letters of recommendation and held up the letter of the law of Moses to call Paul’s ministry into question. So in this chapter Paul contrasts two kinds of ministry: one “of the letter” and one “of the Spirit”. He says: God “also made us sufficient as servants of a new covenant, not of the letter, but of the Spirit. For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Corinthians 3:6). Close on its heels comes that stunning sentence: “Now the Lord is the Spirit and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty” (2 Corinthians 3:17).

Brothers and sisters, put these two passages side by side and the theme becomes very clear. The old wineskin is the system of “the letter” — rules, frameworks, human traditions. The new wineskin is the system of “the Spirit” — liberty, life, God’s own guidance.

Now let us go together into the three key points of this lesson.

sections.heading: 1. New Wine Needs New Wineskins
sections.html:
1. Jesus’ declaration

“No one puts new wine into old wine skins, or else the new wine will burst the skins, and it will be spilled, and the skins will be destroyed. But new wine must be put into fresh wine skins” (Luke 5:37–38).

In this parable the “new wine” stands for the work of the Holy Spirit, and the “wineskin” stands for our human mindset and attitude.

The work of the Holy Spirit is alive and expansive, like new wine still fermenting. Put it into an old skin that cannot stretch, and it is hemmed in — it may even cause the skin to burst.

Notice how serious the consequences are that Jesus describes: not only is the wine spilled, but the skin is ruined as well. Both sides lose. That is the most common ending when an old mindset meets a new work — God’s work is hindered, and human lives are wounded too.

2. A light from the original: two different kinds of “new”

In the original, this passage uses two different Greek words for “new” — a treasure that is hard to see in our translations.

The “new” in “new wine” is νέος (neos): new in time, something just produced, just appeared.

The “new” in “new wineskins” is καινός (kainos): new in kind, something whose very nature has changed, wholly renewed.

Brothers and sisters, this distinction matters enormously. What God wants to pour out is a work that has “just appeared”; what God wants us to become is a vessel whose “very nature has changed”. In other words, it is not enough to wash the old skin, wipe it down and patch it up. We must become a new skin of an altogether different kind.

Scripture uses this very word, καινός, to describe who we are in Christ: “Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new” (2 Corinthians 5:17). God’s intention has never been repair; it has always been renewal.

3. Scripture interpreting Scripture: a renewed mindset is the Bible’s constant call

This truth does not appear in this one parable alone; it runs through the whole Bible.

Paul says: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God” (Romans 12:2). “The renewing of your mind” in the original is ἀνακαίνωσις τοῦ νοός — “the renewal of the mind (νοῦς)”. Notice that Paul does not say, “be transformed by the renewing of your behaviour.” He speaks of the mind — of our mindset. The mindset is the source; behaviour is the outlet. If the source does not change, the outlet cannot change either.

There is another word worth noticing. In the New Testament, “repent” is μετανοέω (metanoeō), made up of μετά (change) and νοῦς (mind); its literal meaning is “a change of mind”. The very first words Jesus preached when he began his ministry were “Repent! For the Kingdom of Heaven is at hand” (Matthew 4:17). So the first step of the gospel is to change wineskins.

The prophets had long proclaimed the same thing: “I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you. I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh” (Ezekiel 36:26). The Hebrew speaks of a “new heart” (לֵב חָדָשׁ) and a “new spirit” (רוּחַ חֲדָשָׁה). What God takes away is a “stony heart”; what he gives is “a heart of flesh”. Stone does not stretch; flesh does. The old wineskin is like the heart of stone; the new wineskin is like the heart of flesh.

Brothers and sisters, what God wants to give us has never been a repaired heart of stone, but a brand-new heart of flesh.

4. Supporting evidence from science: how great the pressure of fermentation is

Why must new wine go into new wineskins? This isn’t religious fussiness; it’s physics.

When grape juice ferments, yeast breaks sugar down into alcohol and carbon dioxide. The gas needs room, and if fermentation happens in a sealed container, the pressure climbs quickly. Take the champagne we know today: it undergoes a second fermentation in the bottle, and the pressure inside can reach about six atmospheres — roughly three times the pressure of an ordinary car tyre. That’s why champagne bottles must be made of thick glass, and why the cork is held down with a wire cage.

Now you understand: an old skin that has already hardened, faced with pressure like that, has only one fate.

And why does leather harden? Because over time, through repeated drying and wetting, oxidation and cross-linking, the collagen fibres in the leather gradually lose their elasticity and become stiff and brittle. That skin was once new. It was once soft. It once held fine wine. It isn’t a villain; it has simply grown old and hard.

Brothers and sisters, this is what breaks the heart most. The Pharisees did not oppose God from the start. Their forerunners were the devout men of the Maccabean era who would rather die than forsake the law; they were once a new wineskin. But as the years went by, zeal turned into routine, devotion turned into rules, and softness turned into hardness.

So please hear me: the old wineskin is not someone else. The old wineskin may very well be the you of twenty years ago who burned the brightest.

5. Confirmation from psychology: why we resist new things

In 1957 the American psychologist Leon Festinger put forward the theory of “cognitive dissonance”. He found that when people receive new information that conflicts with what they already believe, they feel a deeply uncomfortable tension inside. And the easiest way to relieve that tension is often not to change the belief, but to reinterpret, belittle or even reject the new information.

In other words, our instinct is to protect the old wineskin, not to change it.

Brothers and sisters, this finding matches Luke 5:39 exactly. After speaking about the wineskins, Jesus added a strikingly true-to-life sentence: “No man having drunk old wine immediately desires new, for he says, ‘The old is better’” (Luke 5:39).

He says the old is better. Not because the old really is better, but because the old is more familiar. The familiar makes us feel safe, and feeling safe makes us not want to change.

That is why a change of mindset is so hard — and also why a change of mindset matters so much.

6. An example from life: the old water jar that could not be mended

Out in the countryside I once saw an old water jar. There was a fine crack down its side, and the owner couldn’t bear to throw it away, so year after year he patched it with mud and stuck it with glue. Usually it held half a jar of water and was fine. But every time a heavy rain came and the water rose to the brim, the crack burst open again. The owner’s problem was never a shortage of rain; it was a jar that could not bear the overflowing rain.

Brothers and sisters, we often ask God to “pour out abundantly”, yet forget to ask first: can my jar hold it?

The Pharisees clung to tradition and human rules, meeting Jesus’ new work with an old wineskin. The result was that they not only failed to receive the grace of the Holy Spirit but became the very people who stood in the way of revival. What a solemn warning this is — those who hinder revival are often not the most rebellious, but the most devout who most refuse to change their mindset. Jesus rebuked them: “For you set aside the commandment of God, and hold tightly to the tradition of men” (Mark 7:8). And again: “making void the word of God by your tradition, which you have handed down” (Mark 7:13).

Brothers and sisters, are we the same today? Are we still insisting on our own ideas, experiences and methods, so that we cannot make room for the Holy Spirit’s new leading? The Holy Spirit does not act according to our frameworks. He wants to create new life and new thinking within us. Only when we are willing to be renewed and become “new wineskins” can we receive God’s new wine.

7. Applying the 321 vision: Jesus is the focal point, not ourselves

In the 321 vision, the third of the Three Foundations is “the Holy Spirit is my guide”. That’s easy to say, but living it costs something — because its premise is this: I do not guide myself.

At its core, the old wineskin is the self-centred life: “I feel”, “I’m used to”, “we’ve always done it this way”. Self-centred people measure God by their own ruler; selfless people let God measure them anew. The 321 vision says: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not others, not our circumstances. When the focus is on myself, however much wine God pours, all I worry about is whether the skin’s shape looks good. When the focus is on Jesus, I will say, “Lord, as long as your wine can be poured in, however the skin has to change, you have the final say.”

In his book Humility, Andrew Murray says that true humility is the self vanishing completely in the vision that God is all. That is selflessness. Brothers and sisters, a new wineskin is a selfless life; its suppleness comes from having no shape of its own inside.

sections.heading: 2. A Worldly Mindset Hinders the Work of the Holy Spirit
sections.html:
1. The challenge facing the church in the last days

The church of the last days is facing the challenge of the Babylonian system.

In the Bible, Babylon has never been just a city. It began with a tower in the land of Shinar: “Come, let’s build ourselves a city, and a tower whose top reaches to the sky, and let’s make a name for ourselves, lest we be scattered abroad on the surface of the whole earth” (Genesis 11:4). Notice the crucial phrase — “let’s make a name for ourselves”. That is the soul of Babylon: self-centred, living for self, relying on self, glorifying self. By the book of Revelation, Babylon has become the code name for the whole Worldly system of the end times, and God’s call to his people is: “Come out of her, my people, that you have no participation in her sins, and that you don’t receive of her plagues” (Revelation 18:4).

Brothers and sisters, Babylon represents a worldly way of thinking — with self-centredness at its core, stressing living for self, relying on self and satisfying oneself. This mindset permeates society and culture, and even quietly slips into the church, so that people serve God by the world’s logic without realising it.

What does it mean to serve God by the world’s logic? It means measuring anointing by numbers, replacing prayer with efficiency, replacing life with image, replacing the cross with applause. The outward form of the service belongs to God, but the operating system inside belongs to Babylon. That is the most dangerous old wineskin of all — it hangs on the wall of the temple with the word “Ministry” written on the outside.

2. The natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit

Paul explains this principle with great clarity: “Now the natural man doesn’t receive the things of God’s Spirit, for they are foolishness to him, and he can’t know them, because they are spiritually discerned” (1 Corinthians 2:14).

“Natural” in the original is ψυχικός (psychikos), whose root is “soul”; it describes a life run on human thinking, emotion and will. Such a life is not powerless; the trouble is that its power points the wrong way. It judges the work of the Holy Spirit to be “foolishness”, and then hinders it with a perfectly clear conscience.

On the day of Pentecost, when the Holy Spirit came down, how did some people respond? “Others, mocking, said, ‘They are filled with new wine’” (Acts 2:13). The new wine really had come — yet the old wineskin’s first reaction was to mock.

Brothers and sisters, faced with the same event, the spiritual person sees revival and the natural person sees chaos. The difference is not in the event; the difference is in the wineskin.

3. Confirmation from psychology: how strong the pressure of the majority is

In 1951 the American psychologist Solomon Asch carried out his famous conformity experiments at Swarthmore College. Participants simply had to judge which line was the same length as a standard line — an extremely simple task on which almost no one goes wrong. But when the other “participants” in the room (actually research assistants) all gave the same obviously wrong answer, the result was startling: about three in four of the real participants went along with the majority at least once, giving an answer they knew was wrong.

Brothers and sisters, if people will deny what their own eyes see about the length of a line just to fit in, how much more will they do so over their stand of faith, the order of their values, the direction of their lives?

What makes a worldly mindset so frightening is not that it makes sense, but that it has the numbers. It is the air — you breathe it every day without noticing. It is the water — the fish lives in it and has no idea what “wet” means. So we need a standard stronger than the air.

4. Back to the Three Foundations and the Two Core Values

We must return to the Three Foundations and the Two Core Values God has given us.

The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model; the Bible is my standard; the Holy Spirit is my guide.

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.

The Goal: establish God’s system.

Notice how these Three Foundations confront the three pillars of Babylon head-on.

Babylon says, “Live for self.” But Jesus says: “For the Son of Man also came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). He denied himself, so I learn to deny myself.

Babylon says, “Rely on self.” But the Bible says: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit” (Zechariah 4:6). I don’t go by my feelings; I go by God’s word.

Babylon says, “Satisfy yourself.” But the Holy Spirit wants to lead us towards God’s will: “For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are children of God” (Romans 8:14). It is not I who lead myself.

And the Two Core Values are the most thorough reversal of “let’s make a name for ourselves”. Babylon wants man to be king and man to receive the glory; the 321 vision says, let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory.

Brothers and sisters, the battlefield of the mindset is the battlefield of the throne. Whoever sits on the throne of my heart decides whether my wineskin is new or old.

5. The fourfold shift of perspective

The 321 vision reminds us that a renewed mindset shows itself concretely in four shifts:

From a human perspective to God’s perspective.

From an earthly perspective to a heavenly perspective.

From a temporary perspective to an eternal perspective.

From a worldly perspective to a godly perspective.

These four shifts are the four steps of the process that exchanges an old wineskin for a new one.

Here’s an example. A co-worker misunderstands you. The worldly perspective says, “I’ve got to stand up for myself”; the godly perspective says, “This is a lesson the Lord is giving me.” The temporary perspective says, “This is so hard right now”; but the eternal perspective says, “For our light affliction, which is for the moment, works for us more and more exceedingly an eternal weight of glory” (2 Corinthians 4:17). The same event, four shifts — and a completely different outcome.

The 321 vision puts it well: pride stirs up pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. When an old wineskin meets new wine, the wine spills and the skin is ruined — both lose. When a new wineskin meets new wine, the wine is kept and the skin is kept — both are gained.

Jesus himself said exactly this: “No, they put new wine into fresh wine skins, and both are preserved” (Matthew 9:17).

6. From the individual to the church, from the church to the kingdom

When we replace worldly thinking with a godly mindset, we can establish God’s system.

A renewed mindset in the individual brings personal revival.

A renewed mindset in the church brings revival to the church.

If the church is renewed, God’s kingdom can be established on earth, ready to welcome the end time revival.

Church history confirms this order again and again. In 1517 Martin Luther saw afresh that “the righteous shall live by faith” (Romans 1:17); one man’s mindset was renewed, and the spiritual map of all Europe was redrawn. On the evening of 24 May 1738, in a small meeting in Aldersgate Street, London, John Wesley heard someone reading Luther’s preface to the Epistle to the Romans. He later wrote that he felt his heart “strangely warmed”. One man’s mindset was renewed, and the spiritual revival of eighteenth-century England began.

The following year George Whitefield invited Wesley to preach in the open air in the mining district near Bristol. At first Wesley was deeply reluctant — in his Anglican training, preaching outside the walls of a church was almost an impropriety. But he obeyed. He went out into the fields and preached salvation to the miners, and tens of thousands of them wept and repented.

Brothers and sisters, if Wesley had clung to his old wineskin that day, what would England’s revival have looked like? There has never been a shortage of new wine; what is lacking is skins willing to change.

7. Applying the 321 vision: life first, then relationships, then ministry

The 321 vision has a very important order: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. What the Babylonian system does best is turn that order upside down. And so we work ourselves to the bone, yet our life lies desolate; we build organisations, yet lose our brothers.

The first mark of a new wineskin is putting the order right. The same goes for the priority of relationships: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things.

Brothers and sisters, if you feel today that serving is exhausting, dry and hard, please don’t rush to try twice as hard. First ask yourself: has my order been turned upside down?

sections.heading: 3. Let the Holy Spirit Change Our Mindset
sections.html:
1. The Holy Spirit’s work is inward renewal

The work of the Holy Spirit is not outward ritual but inward renewal.

If our minds are still bound by tradition, by reason or by self, the Holy Spirit cannot move freely. Paul reminds us: “Now the Lord is the Spirit and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty” (2 Corinthians 3:17).

“Liberty” in the original is ἐλευθερία (eleutheria), the freedom of someone released from slavery. Notice Paul’s logic: freedom does not come from circumstances loosening their grip; it comes from the presence of the Spirit of the Lord. Where there is no freedom, it is usually because the Spirit of the Lord is being hindered.

Paul goes on: “But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord, the Spirit” (2 Corinthians 3:18). “With unveiled face” — that is the posture of a new wineskin. When Moses had finished speaking God’s words to the people, he put a veil over his face (Exodus 34:33), but we may come with unveiled faces. And what is the veil? The veil is all those old mindsets that cover us and keep us from seeing.

To receive the work of the Holy Spirit, we must first let the Holy Spirit change our mindset. The lesson gives us three very concrete shifts.

2. The first shift: from control to obedience

No longer analysing God’s works with our reason, but simply obeying his leading.

Jesus said: “The wind blows where it wants to, and you hear its sound, but don’t know where it comes from and where it is going. So is everyone who is born of the Spirit” (John 3:8).

The Hebrew רוּחַ (ruach) and the Greek πνεῦμα (pneuma) both carry the meanings “wind”, “breath” and “spirit” at once. When Jesus uses the wind to describe the Holy Spirit, he is telling us one thing: you can move with the wind, but you can never hold it in your hand.

We can raise the sail, but we cannot command the wind. A true sailor is not someone who controls the wind; he is someone who reads it.

Brothers and sisters, we often harbour a subtle urge to control God. We pray, and then we quietly draw up the list of possible answers for him in advance, marking in our hearts which one is “more reasonable”. That is not faith; that is vetting.

When the Israelites crossed the Jordan, God commanded: “Yet there shall be a space between you and it of about two thousand cubits by measure—don’t come closer to it—that you may know the way by which you must go; for you have not passed this way before” (Joshua 3:4).

“For you have not passed this way before.” That sentence is a lesson every new wineskin has to learn.

Peter is a good example. In Acts chapter 10, God gives him a vision and tells him to eat things he had considered unclean all his life. Peter’s reaction is very honest: “Not so, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean” (Acts 10:14). In one breath he says “Lord”, and in the same breath he says “Not so” — that is the old wineskin’s standard sentence pattern: confessing him as Lord with the mouth, while keeping the right of veto in the heart.

How does God answer? “What God has cleansed, you must not call unclean” (Acts 10:15). And it happens three times over. God knows that a change of mindset is not accomplished in one go.

Later, in Jerusalem, Peter gives an account of all this to the believers and says a remarkable thing: “If then God gave to them the same gift as us, when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I, that I could withstand God?” (Acts 11:17).

Brothers and sisters, “Who was I, that I could withstand God?” — that sentence is the very moment an old wineskin becomes a new one. The gospel could reach the Gentiles, could reach you and me, because one man was willing to let God change his mindset.

3. The second shift: from doubt to trust

Believing that the work of the Holy Spirit comes from love and is for our good.

Jesus said: “However when he, the Spirit of truth, has come, he will guide you into all truth, for he will not speak from himself; but whatever he hears, he will speak. He will declare to you things that are coming” (John 16:13).

The Holy Spirit is called the “Counsellor”; in the original it is παράκλητος (paraklētos), meaning “the one called alongside to help”. He is not an exam invigilator; he is a fellow traveller.

Our trust in God determines how far we open ourselves to him. At the opening of his book The Knowledge of the Holy, the theologian A. W. Tozer wrote a line that has been quoted far and wide: what comes into our minds when we think about God is the most important thing about us.

Brothers and sisters, if the God in your heart is a harsh creditor, you will spend your whole life anxiously paying off a debt. Only if the God in your heart is a loving Father will you dare to place your whole self in his hands.

Paul says: “He who didn’t spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how would he not also with him freely give us all things?” (Romans 8:32). Since he has already given the greatest gift, what could he possibly begrudge us? So when the Holy Spirit wants to renew your mindset, he isn’t trying to take something from you; he wants to give you something better. The one doing the pruning is not an enemy; he is the gardener.

Paul also says: “Don’t quench the Spirit” (1 Thessalonians 5:19). The original means “don’t put out the Spirit’s fire”. Brothers and sisters, doubt is the bucket of water.

4. The third shift: from the past to the present

Not being bound by past experience, but being willing to welcome what God is newly doing today.

In Isaiah, Yahweh says: “Don’t remember the former things, and don’t consider the things of old. Behold, I will do a new thing. It springs out now. Don’t you know it? I will even make a way in the wilderness, and rivers in the desert” (Isaiah 43:18–19).

Notice the setting of this passage. God says, “Don’t remember the former things” — yet just before, in verses 16 and 17, he has only just brought up the Red Sea. God is not asking us to be ungrateful; he is asking us not to mistake the shape of grace for grace itself. When Israel came out of Egypt, God parted the Red Sea; when they entered Canaan, God instead told the priests to set their feet in the Jordan first. Had the Israelites of that day insisted, “The way God opens a path is by parting the sea,” they would have stood on the bank of the Jordan waiting for the rest of their lives.

Brothers and sisters, have you turned one wonderful experience into a contract that God is obliged to keep?

Here’s some good news: the brain itself was made to change. In 2000 a research team led by Eleanor Maguire at University College London published a study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, finding that London taxi drivers, after years of memorising the city’s complex street network, had noticeably more grey matter in the rear of the hippocampus than a control group. This is “neuroplasticity” — the structure of the brain changes with sustained practice.

Brothers and sisters, when God made us, he wrote “capable of renewal” into our very make-up. So when we say, “That’s just how I am; I can’t change,” it is usually not a fact. It is an excuse.

In 1947 the psychologist Kurt Lewin proposed three stages of change: unfreezing, changing and refreezing. He pointed out that unless existing mindsets are first “unfrozen”, no new way of doing things can get moving. Often the first thing the Holy Spirit does is precisely to unfreeze. The process can be uncomfortable at times, but it is grace.

I know an older gentleman who has been driving for thirty years and knows every road in the city. Once his satnav suggested a newly opened expressway. He shook his head and said, “I’ve never driven that road.” So he took the old route and sat in traffic for more than an hour. It wasn’t that he couldn’t drive; he was simply too good at driving that old road. Old experience is not a sin. Treating old experience as the only way — that is the old wineskin.

5. Applying the 321 vision: the fivefold change, and relying on the heart and the Holy Spirit

The 321 vision speaks of a fivefold change — mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; change daily living and you change relationships; change relationships and you change ministry.

Notice that the first link in this fivefold change is the mindset. The theme of this lesson stands right at the entrance to the whole 321 life system. If the mindset doesn’t move, none of the four links after it can move; once the mindset moves, the other four move with it.

The 321 vision also says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you will be glad, rely on the brain and you will be troubled. Solomon said it long ago: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23).

“Relying on the brain and ourselves” means control, doubt, and clinging to the past. “Relying on the heart and the Holy Spirit” means obedience, trust, and openness to what God is doing today.

When we let the Holy Spirit change our minds, we can be led by him and filled by him, and become vessels that receive his new work.

sections.heading: 4. Integrating the 321 Vision: The Full Picture of the New Wineskin
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s set this lesson back within the whole panorama of the 321 vision.

1. The Three Foundations are the three steps of making a new wineskin

Jesus is my role model — this is the “pattern”. A wineskin has to be sewn to a pattern, and Jesus is that pattern: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 2:5). He existed in the form of God, yet emptied himself and took the form of a servant. He is the softest, most supple new wineskin of all.

The Bible is my standard — this is the “measurements”. Without a measuring rule you cannot cut a skin. The renewal of our mindset is not renewal in any direction we please; it is renewal according to God’s word. Any so-called leading of the Holy Spirit that contradicts Scripture is not the Holy Spirit.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — this is “the breath of life”. Even with the pattern and the measurements, we still need the Spirit who gives life to do the work himself. The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life (see 2 Corinthians 3:6).

The Three Foundations are not three slogans; they are three real steps of the process. Leave one out and the skin is useless.

2. The Two Core Values: who sits on the throne, who receives the glory

Let Jesus be King — the stubbornness of the old wineskin is, in the end, a question of sovereignty. When I say, “I can’t accept this,” what I’m really saying is, “I want to be in charge of this.” To let Jesus be King is to hand the right of veto back to him.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — when a person no longer needs to use ministry to prove himself, his skin becomes soft.

3. The Goal: establish God’s system

God renews our mindset not so that we can know more than others, but so that God’s system may be established on earth, fulfilling what the Lord’s Prayer says: “Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven” (Matthew 6:10). The end point of a renewed mindset is not personal satisfaction; it is the establishing of the kingdom.

4. The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless

The 321 vision says: the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

Where exactly had the Pharisees’ old wineskin gone hard? In putting themselves in the judge’s seat. It wasn’t that they lacked devotion; they were far too sure they were right.

Paul says: “that you put away, as concerning your former way of life, the old man that grows corrupt after the lusts of deceit, and that you be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who in the likeness of God has been created in righteousness and holiness of truth” (Ephesians 4:22–24).

Notice the phrase in the middle — “be renewed in the spirit of your mind”. Between putting off the old self and putting on the new self stands a door, and that door is the renewal of the mind — the renewal of our mindset.

Peter says: “Yes, all of you clothe yourselves with humility, to subject yourselves to one another; for ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble’” (1 Peter 5:5). The humble receive grace, because the humble have room. The proud receive nothing, because they are already full of themselves.

Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the infinite and living out the infinite. “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20).

Brothers and sisters, a new wineskin can hold new wine not because it is stronger, but because it is empty inside.

5. The 920 practice: letting the new wine flow into our relationships

The 321 vision’s 920 practice reminds us that every person we are in a relationship with is our “2”; with that person we practise living out a selfless (0) life and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions.

“But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23).

Notice that the fruit of the Spirit isn’t grown in a cave; it is grown in relationships. Patience needs someone who is hard to get along with; gentleness needs someone who provokes you.

Brothers and sisters, how can you tell whether your wineskin is new or old? The most accurate test is not in the words of your prayers, but in your relationships with others. If the new wine has really come in, the first to taste it will be the “2” right beside you.

6. 235 relationships and the Path of Serving

The 321 vision also speaks of 235 relationships: becoming a “2” with a selfless person — a spiritual companion; establishing a “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children; and becoming a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.

A renewed mindset is hard to achieve alone, because I can’t see my own blind spots, just as an eye cannot see itself. Even after Peter’s mindset was renewed, he still needed the six brothers who went with him to bear witness (see Acts 11:12). New wine has never been poured into just one skin.

The Path of Serving that the 321 vision describes is: Spirit (the Holy Spirit is my guide), Understanding (the Bible is my standard), Life (Jesus is my role model), Service (let Jesus be King), God (let Jesus receive all the glory). Notice that the path begins with “Spirit”, not “Service”. So often, as soon as we come to faith, we rush to serve, skipping Spirit, Understanding and Life and charging straight to Service. The result is new wine in an old wineskin: we wear ourselves out, and we spoil the work too.

Life first, then relationships, then ministry. This is not a matter of efficiency; it is a matter of order. When the order is right, God works; when the order is wrong, we end up doing God’s worrying for him.

sections.heading: 5. Practice for Daily Living
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three very practical exercises. I want to deepen each of them, one by one, using the 321 vision’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Exercise 1: Ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light on my old wineskins

Please quieten yourself and ask: what “old wineskins” are there in my life — stubborn ideas, past hurts, or habits I don’t want to change?

Information: first take in the truth of today’s lesson — God does not pour new wine into old wineskins. This is the first step, at the level of knowledge.

Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to carry this truth from your head into your heart. Pray as David prayed: “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts” (Psalm 139:23).

Conviction: when the light comes, don’t argue your case. The old wineskin’s most typical reaction is to explain. Simply say, “Lord, you are right.”

Implementation: write down on paper the one thing the Holy Spirit points out, specific enough to be one matter, one person, one sentence.

Evaluation: after a week, look back. On this matter, did I respond differently even once?

Correction: if not, don’t condemn yourself; just adjust. Perhaps the scope was too big — narrow it down. Perhaps the timing was wrong — try a different setting.

Repetition: renewing the mindset is not a one-off event; it is an ongoing practice. God spoke to Peter three times, and he will speak to us many times too.

Multiplication: when you have truly experienced change, go and tell someone. A testimony spoken aloud will turn round and strengthen you yourself.

Exercise 2: Pray one sentence every day

Please pray this sentence every day: “Lord, renew my mindset, so that I can receive your new wine.”

Brothers and sisters, don’t underestimate a one-sentence prayer. A study published in 2002 by the psychologist Wendy Wood and her colleagues found that a substantial proportion of our everyday behaviour consists of habits repeated automatically in fixed settings. Since old mindsets were built through daily repetition, new mindsets must be built through daily repetition too. So please attach this prayer to a fixed “trigger” — for example, make it the first thing you say each morning when you open your eyes. A fixed setting will nail the new mindset into your daily living.

Here is how the eight stages work in this exercise: Information is the content of the prayer; Revelation is the day you suddenly find yourself in tears over these words; Conviction is when you begin to believe God really will renew you; Implementation is thirty days in a row without a break; Evaluation is looking back at the end of each week for a time when “I would have done the same old thing, but I didn’t”; Correction is adjusting the time and place of the prayer; Repetition is letting it become the breath of a lifetime; Multiplication is teaching your family to pray this way with you.

The psalm says: “Create in me a clean heart, O God. Renew a right spirit within me” (Psalm 51:10). David uses the word “create” (Hebrew בָּרָא, bara) — the same word used for God creating the heavens and the earth in Genesis chapter 1. Brothers and sisters, renewing our mindset is not self-improvement; it is God’s work of creation. That is why we must pray — because only the Creator can do it.

Exercise 3: See challenges with new eyes

In your service and in daily living, try seeing challenges with new eyes, believing that the Holy Spirit is at work in them.

The next time something goes wrong, don’t start by asking, “Why me?” Ask these three questions instead:

Lord, what do you want me to see in this? (From a human perspective to God’s perspective.)

Lord, will this still matter ten years from now? (From a temporary perspective to an eternal perspective.)

Lord, in this matter, how can I let you reign as King? (From a worldly perspective to a godly perspective.)

Here is how the eight stages work in this exercise: from Information and Revelation through to Conviction that “all things work together for good” (see Romans 8:28); Implementation is deliberately using these questions in your next conflict; in Evaluation and Correction, find out which question is hardest to ask — that is often where you are hardest; Repetition is letting it become a reflex; Multiplication is teaching these three questions to others when they come to you with their troubles.

Brothers and sisters, this is how a renewed mindset is formed — one day at a time, one situation at a time.

sections.heading: 6. A Gentle Reminder
sections.html:
God is doing a new thing, but he never pours new wine into old wineskins.

If you long to be filled with the Holy Spirit, you must first let him renew your mind and your mindset.

Brothers and sisters, please hold this sentence in your heart: God’s supply is always greater than our capacity, so what we need to enlarge is not God’s hand, but our heart.

sections.heading: 7. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, we are coming to the end of this morning’s devotion. Let’s gather this lesson up into a single sentence:

The renewal of the Holy Spirit is never an outward form; it is the inward transformation of our mindset.

When we are willing to put off the old self, to have our minds renewed and to let the Holy Spirit move freely, we can receive God’s “new wine” and see him bring real revival — in us personally, in the church and in this generation.

If our mindset does not change, the work of the Holy Spirit is limited; but when our mindset is renewed, the tide of revival will surely come.

So this morning I want to put three calls before you.

First, confess. Confess that you are holding an old wineskin. It may be a hurt you refuse to let go of; it may be the words “we’ve always done it this way”; it may be a prejudice you grew used to long ago but have never brought before God. Confession is where renewal begins.

Second, surrender. Hand the right of veto back to Jesus. Letting Jesus be King does not mean letting him be your consultant; a consultant only offers advice, but a king holds the power to decide. Brothers and sisters, are you willing this morning to say to the Lord, “Lord, from today on, in this matter, you have the final say”?

Third, open up. With unveiled face, open yourself to what he is doing today. You don’t have to understand it first; just say “yes” first. For you have not passed this way before — but the ark goes on ahead.

Paul says: “Don’t be drunken with wine, in which is dissipation, but be filled with the Spirit” (Ephesians 5:18). In the original the verb is in the continuous tense — keep on being filled with the Spirit. God’s new wine has never stopped; he is still pouring. Only one question remains: have you changed your wineskin?

May each one of us become a soft new wineskin; may our church become a new wineskin able to receive the great revival. And may all this renewal and all its fruit be credited not to our methods, our gifts or our reputation, but to the One who sits on the throne alone — let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory.

keyVerses: “No one puts new wine into old wine skins, or else the new wine will burst the skins, and it will be spilled, and the skins will be destroyed. But new wine must be put into fresh wine skins” (Luke 5:37–38).
“Now the Lord is the Spirit and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty” (2 Corinthians 3:17).
declarations: Please declare with me:
Lord, I am willing to be your new wineskin!
Renew my thinking, and take away all my old frameworks,
so that I can receive your new wine and experience the Holy Spirit’s new work,
and live out your glorious will.
practices: Ask the Holy Spirit to shine on my old wineskins
Pray one sentence every day
See challenges with new eyes
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we thank you.
Lord, you have never stopped pouring the wine; it is our skins that have grown old and hard. This morning we come before you asking not for more experiences, but only for a new heart.

Lord Jesus, you are our role model. You existed in the form of God, yet you emptied yourself and became obedient to the point of death. Give us your soft heart, and take away our hardness and our self-righteousness.

Holy Spirit, shine your light on us and show us every corner within us that refuses to change. Loosen our clenched hands; bring us from control to obedience, from doubt to trust, from clinging to the past to embracing what you are newly doing today. Take away our heart of stone and give us a heart of flesh; create in us a clean heart, and renew a right spirit within us.

We are willing to be your new wineskins and to receive your new wine. May we be renewed personally, may our families be renewed, may our church be renewed, and may the end time revival come upon this land.
Not by might, nor by power, but by your Spirit.
May all the glory go to you alone. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “No one puts new wine into old wine skins, or else the new wine will burst the skins, and it will be spilled, and the skins will be destroyed. But new wine must be put into fresh wine skins” (Luke 5:37–38). Please share: in your present life or ministry, what “old wineskin” has the Holy Spirit shown you? Is it a stubborn idea, a past hurt, or a habit you don’t want to change? How do you plan, in concrete terms, to hand it over to the Lord?

“Now the Lord is the Spirit and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty” (2 Corinthians 3:17). Think back to a time when God did something beyond what you expected. Was your first reaction control, doubt or obedience? If the same thing happened again today, how would you respond by shifting “from a human perspective to God’s perspective, from a temporary perspective to an eternal perspective”?
l040.title: A Renewed Mindset Holds New Wine
l040.subtitle: Only a Change of Mindset Can Receive the Work of the Holy Spirit
l040.partTitle: Unit 4 · The Prerequisite for Revival — A Change of Mindset

sections.heading: Introduction: Change Starts Not with Our Circumstances but with Our Mindset
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, peace be with you this morning. Let’s begin with a very ordinary picture.

There was a sister who had been coming to church for more than ten years, and she always sat in the back row. When the choir was short of singers, she didn’t go. When a small group needed a leader, she shook her head. When someone asked her to share her testimony, she waved her hands again and again: “I can’t. I’m no good with words. I don’t have any gifts.” One day a pastor sat down with her and asked, “You say you can’t. Who told you that?” She sat stunned for a long time, and then the tears suddenly came. When she was ten years old, a teacher had called her stupid in front of the whole class. That one sentence was like a nail, and it had been driven into her heart for forty years. For forty years, it wasn’t her circumstances that held her back. It was a mindset.

Brothers and sisters, we often think a changed life needs a great miracle, a dramatic turnaround in our circumstances, a big opportunity coming our way. But we so often forget: what really holds us back is usually not a wall outside us but a sentence inside us; not the hardness of our circumstances but a mindset that has set hard.

The introduction to our lesson puts it with great precision: a person’s whole life is directed by their thinking. Mindset determines direction, and direction determines destiny. If we long for our lives to be renewed and our daily living to be changed, the key is not our outward circumstances or how many miracles we see, but whether our mindset has been renewed by the truth.

The twentieth-century American pastor A. W. Tozer opened his book “The Knowledge of the Holy” (1961) with a sentence that shakes the heart: “What comes into our minds when we think about God is the most important thing about us.” Why the most important? Because the picture of God we carry in our hearts decides how we pray, how we suffer, how we love and how we face tomorrow. The bigger God is in your heart, the bigger your life will be; the smaller God is in your heart, the bigger your fear will be.

So the Bible does not tell us to change our circumstances first. The Bible tells us to change our minds first. Paul says, “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind” (Romans 12:2). This verse is the key to today’s lesson, and it is also the starting point of the “fivefold change” in the 321 vision: when the mindset changes, the life changes; when the life changes, daily living changes; when daily living changes, relationships change; when relationships change, ministry changes.

In this morning’s devotion we will look at three things: first, mindset shapes every dimension of life; second, the mindset of Jesus produced compassion and action; third, God longs to change our mindset even more than he longs simply to work miracles. May the Lord this morning perform a kind of “lens replacement” surgery inside each of us.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: The Setting and Original Language of Romans 12:2
sections.html:
To understand a verse, we first need to know its author, its readers and its setting.

Romans was written by the apostle Paul. It is generally thought that Paul wrote this letter toward the end of his third missionary journey, around AD 57, in the Greek city of Corinth, and sent it to the imperial capital, Rome (see Romans 15:25–28: he was about to take the gift from the believers of Macedonia and Achaia to Jerusalem). Paul had not founded the church in Rome himself. Its readers were brothers and sisters most of whom he had never met — believers from a Jewish background and believers from a Gentile background — and between these two groups there was a good deal of tension over the law, food and festivals (Romans 14 deals with exactly this).

Rome was the heart of the world in those days: statues of Caesar in the streets, idols of every kind in the temples, bloody entertainment in the arena. A believer living in such a city opened his eyes every day to a whole society that was “shaping” him, telling him what success was and what honour was. Paul knew the power of that force only too well, and so he wrote 12:1–2.

“Therefore I urge you, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service. Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” (Romans 12:1–2)

Notice the first word of verse 1: “Therefore.” Romans 1–11 sets out the gospel of God — human corruption, justification by faith, union with Christ, the life of the Spirit, God’s plan for Israel. From chapter 12 on, Paul turns to daily practice. “Therefore” is a bridge: first the truth, then the living; first a changed mindset, then changed behaviour. Christian ethics has never been moral effort; it is the response to grace.

Now look at the original. “Conformed” in Greek is συσχηματίζω (syschēmatizō), from the root σχῆμα (schēma), meaning “outward form, mould.” The word paints a picture of dough pressed into a mould: whatever shape the outside presses it into, that is the shape it takes. The world is that mould. It doesn’t change your nature; it just keeps squeezing your outside.

“Transformed” in Greek is μεταμορφόω (metamorphoō), the source of the English word “metamorphosis.” The word has one very important use in the Gospels: “He was changed before them” (Matthew 17:2). When Jesus was transfigured on the mountain, this is exactly the word used. It describes a change that comes from within, like a caterpillar becoming a butterfly — not wings glued onto the caterpillar’s back, but a whole life remade.

“Mind” is the Greek νοῦς (nous), meaning a person’s thinking, understanding, the inner system by which we judge things — in today’s language, our “mindset.” “Renewing” is ἀνακαίνωσις (anakainōsis), meaning “made new, renewed in its very fabric.” And the verb “be transformed” is, in the original, present tense, passive voice, imperative mood: not done once, but continuously; not by your own straining, but by letting God transform you; and yet it is a command — every day you must hand yourself over to be renewed.

Brothers and sisters, this one verse sets two forces in front of us: on one side the world presses from outside; on the other the Spirit changes us from within. And where is the battlefield? The battlefield is your nous — your mindset.

Paul goes on to say that the result of a renewed mind is to “prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” “Prove” is δοκιμάζω (dokimazō) in the original, the word used for testing the purity of gold. Only a person whose mindset has been renewed has the discerning eye to recognise which road is God’s road. Very often we ask God for direction and hear nothing — not because God isn’t speaking, but because we haven’t changed our lenses yet.

sections.heading: Key Point 1: Mindset Shapes Every Dimension of Life
sections.html:
Our lesson says that a mindset is not merely a product of thought; it is the root of how we respond to life. Mindset shapes principles, and principles shape choices; mindset shapes feelings, and feelings shape attitudes; mindset shapes strategies, and strategies shape actions.

These three chains are exactly what the Bible made plain long ago.

sections.heading: 1. What the Bible Says
sections.html:
“For as he thinks about the cost, so he is.” (Proverbs 23:7; the Chinese Union Version reads, “For as he thinks in his heart, so is he.”)

The word for “thinks” here is the Hebrew שָׁעַר (sha’ar), whose basic meaning is “to reckon, to measure,” like someone quietly weighing in their heart how heavy a matter is. However a person weighs things inside, that is how they will live outside. Whatever you count as weighty in your heart, that is where your time, your money and your emotions will flow.

Solomon also said, “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23). Notice — not the wellspring of a moment, but the wellspring of life; not flowing out of our circumstances, but “out of it,” out of the heart. The heart is the source; daily living is the river. People are forever fishing rubbish out of the river downstream, but God wants us to go back upstream and deal with the source.

Paul says too, “For the mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace” (Romans 8:6). The word “mind” here is φρόνημα (phronēma) in the original, which refers precisely to the set of our thinking, the leaning of our mindset. Wherever our thinking is set, that is where we end up: on one side death, on the other life and peace. Brothers and sisters, mindset is no small matter. Mindset is a matter of life and death.

sections.heading: 2. A Striking Example: Twelve Spies, Two Mindsets
sections.html:
The clearest example in the Bible is Numbers 13. Moses sent twelve spies to explore the land of Canaan. Forty days later they came back. Notice this: they walked the same road, saw the same land, measured the same cluster of grapes and met the same sons of Anak. The information was exactly the same, yet their conclusions were worlds apart.

Ten of the spies said, “There we saw the Nephilim, the sons of Anak, who come from the Nephilim. We were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight” (Numbers 13:33).

Listen carefully to that sentence. “We were in our own sight as grasshoppers” — that is a mindset. “And so we were in their sight” — that is a guess. When did they ever ask the sons of Anak what they thought? They didn’t. But once a person sees himself as a grasshopper in his heart, he automatically assumes the whole world sees him as a grasshopper too. This is called “projecting our self-image.” Caleb’s mindset was completely different: “Let’s go up at once, and possess it; for we are well able to overcome it!” (Numbers 13:30).

And the result? The same generation, the same promise — but because of two mindsets, two destinies: the ten spies and the people who followed them fell dead in the wilderness, while Caleb and Joshua entered Canaan. Brothers and sisters, what held Israel back was never the size of the sons of Anak; it was the size of the grasshopper in their hearts. And what holds us back is often not the size of our difficulty, but the size of God in our hearts.

sections.heading: 3. What Psychology Confirms
sections.html:
In the twentieth century two psychologists, each through clinical work of his own, discovered principles the Bible had stated long before.

The first was Albert Ellis. In 1955 he put forward Rational Emotive Behaviour Therapy (REBT), whose core is the famous “ABC model”: A is the Activating event, B is the Belief, and C is the emotional and behavioural Consequence. Most people think A causes C — the event upsets me. Ellis pointed out that what really causes C is B — my interpretation of the event upsets me.

The second was Aaron T. Beck. In the 1960s he developed cognitive therapy and found that people with depression had certain “automatic thoughts” running through their minds again and again, such as “I’m worthless” or “Nothing will ever get better.” The way to healing was not to change their situation but to identify, test and correct those thoughts.

There is also Carol S. Dweck of Stanford University. In her 2006 book “Mindset” she distinguished between a “fixed mindset” and a “growth mindset.” People with a fixed mindset believe ability is fixed, so failure means rejection of who they are, and they avoid challenges. People with a growth mindset believe ability can grow through effort, so failure simply means they haven’t learned it yet, and they rise to meet challenges. The same report card, read through two mindsets, produces two different lives.

Brothers and sisters, these studies are not meant to replace the Bible; the Bible is our standard. But they reflect how true God’s word is. Three thousand years ago Solomon said, “As he thinks in his heart, so is he”; today’s psychology is simply adding footnotes to that sentence in the laboratory.

sections.heading: 4. From “I Can’t” to “There Is a Great God in Me”
sections.html:
Our lesson gives an example very close to home. If someone believes deep down, “I can’t,” then when he is invited to serve, he shrinks back — that is mindset shaping choices. When he fails, he is crushed — that is mindset shaping feelings. When he faces a challenge, he runs from it — that is mindset shaping strategy and action.

But if this person begins to believe, “There is a great God in me,” he sees himself differently. It isn’t that he has suddenly become capable; it’s that he no longer faces things alone. Moses said of himself, “I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue” (Exodus 4:10). God did not argue with him about his eloquence. He simply said, “I will be with your mouth, and teach you what you shall speak” (Exodus 4:12). Gideon considered himself the least in his father’s house, yet the angel called him “you mighty man of valor” (Judges 6:12). God never uses us according to our own self-assessment; he reshapes how we see ourselves according to his own word.

I often use a picture: a mindset is like the lens in a pair of glasses. The lens doesn’t change the world outside, but it decides the world you see. Wear grey lenses, and even a sunny day looks overcast; look at a problem through a magnifying glass, and even an ant looks like an elephant. When the disciples on the Sea of Galilee saw Jesus walking on the water, they thought he was a ghost and cried out (see Matthew 14:26). The same Lord, the same night — but with the wrong lens, grace was mistaken for terror. Brothers and sisters, what we most need to ask for this morning may not be a change of circumstances but a change of lenses.
