sections.heading: 5. Applying the 321 Vision
sections.html:
One of the core elements of the 321 vision is the “fivefold change”: when the mindset changes, the life changes; when the life changes, daily living changes; when daily living changes, relationships change; when relationships change, ministry changes. Notice that this order cannot be reversed. Many people do it backwards: first they struggle desperately to change their behaviour (daily living); when that doesn’t work, they blame their relationships; when their relationships break down, they change churches or change ministries. They go round in a big circle, and the mindset at the source never moves. It’s like constantly pruning the branches while refusing to deal with the root.

“The Three Foundations” tell us whose pattern our mindset must be changed by: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. The role model gives me direction, the standard gives me content, the guide gives me power. We cannot do without any of the three. A role model without a standard, and we follow a Jesus of our own imagination; a standard without a guide, and we slide into legalism; a guide without a standard, and we are easily led around by our feelings.

So today’s first lesson is simple, yet very deep: stop and ask yourself one question — “What mindset lies behind the way I’m reacting right now?” Pull that mindset out, put it in the light of Scripture, and let the Holy Spirit tell you: is this truth, or is it a lie?

sections.heading: Key Point 2: The Mindset of Jesus Produced Compassion and Action
sections.html: Second, we turn to the Lord Jesus himself. He didn’t only teach the renewing of the mind; he lived out the power of a renewed mindset.

sections.heading: 1. The Background: The Moment You Least Want to Serve
sections.html:
Our lesson points us to Mark 6. Let’s set out the whole picture.

Mark’s Gospel is generally thought to have been written by Mark (John Mark) in Rome in the AD 60s, for Gentile believers under persecution. The early church father Papias records that Mark was the interpreter of the apostle Peter. That is why Mark moves at such a fast pace, often using “immediately” and “straightway.” It is a Gospel of action.

The setting of chapter 6 is one of the heaviest passages in all four Gospels. Earlier in this very chapter, John the Baptist has just been killed by Herod, and his disciples have taken his body and buried it (see Mark 6:14–29). Jesus’ forerunner, his relative, the man who had pointed to him and said, “Behold, the Lamb of God,” is dead. At the same time, the twelve disciples have just come back from their first mission trip, tired and excited, wanting to report to Jesus everything they had done.

“The apostles gathered themselves together to Jesus, and they told him all things, whatever they had done, and whatever they had taught. He said to them, ‘You come apart into a deserted place, and rest awhile.’ For there were many coming and going, and they had no leisure so much as to eat.” (Mark 6:30–31)

See how considerate the Lord is. He didn’t say, “Keep pushing on.” He said, “Rest awhile.” He knew the disciples didn’t even have time to eat. And so “they went away in the boat to a deserted place by themselves” (Mark 6:32).

And what happened? “They saw them going, and many recognized him and ran there on foot from all the cities. They arrived before them and came together to him” (Mark 6:33).

Brothers and sisters, imagine the moment they landed. You have just lost someone very close to you. You are exhausted in body and soul. You have rowed all that way across the water to a lonely shore, wanting a little quiet — and as soon as the boat touches land, there is a vast crowd on the shore, and they got there before you. If it were us, what thoughts would spring up? Probably: “Can’t these people take a hint?” “We’re human too, you know!” “Can’t you just leave me alone today?”

But this is what Scripture records:

sections.heading: 2. The Mindset of Jesus: Like Sheep Without a Shepherd
sections.html:
“Jesus came out, saw a great multitude, and he had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd, and he began to teach them many things.” (Mark 6:34)

Notice the order of cause and effect in the verse: first he “saw,” then he “had compassion,” and finally he began “to teach.” And between “compassion” and “teach” there is a “because” — because in Jesus’ mindset, these people were not “the people disturbing my rest” but people who were “like sheep without a shepherd.”

The word “compassion” in Greek is σπλαγχνίζομαι (splanchnizomai), from the root σπλάγχνα (splanchna), meaning a person’s inner organs, the bowels, the gut. The Greeks believed the deepest feelings came from the inner organs. So this word is not polite sympathy; it is the kind of deep feeling that churns your insides and stirs you to your very core. The same word appears in Luke 15:20, where the father sees his prodigal son a long way off and is “moved with compassion” — a phrase that captures it beautifully.

And the phrase “like sheep without a shepherd” was not a picture Jesus made up on the spot. It was a mindset he had drawn from reading the Old Testament. Moses once asked God to appoint another leader for Israel, “that the congregation of Yahweh may not be as sheep which have no shepherd” (Numbers 27:17). Ezekiel rebuked Israel’s shepherds for feeding only themselves: “They were scattered, because there was no shepherd” (Ezekiel 34:5). Jeremiah said, “My people have been lost sheep. Their shepherds have caused them to go astray” (Jeremiah 50:6).

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? The reason Jesus was moved with compassion even in his most exhausted moment is that he was already full of God’s word. When his eyes saw the crowd, what rose in his heart at once was not “trouble” but that flock from the Old Testament prophets — sheep without a shepherd, scattered, helpless, close to death. A mindset is not formed in the moment of crisis; a mindset is put in day by day. A crisis only squeezes out what is already inside. If what’s inside is God’s word, what comes out is compassion; if what’s inside is our own grievances, what comes out is complaint.

sections.heading: 3. How a Mindset Brings Change to Every Dimension
sections.html:
Our lesson analyses this very well, so let’s follow it through.

Jesus’ mindset was, “These people are like sheep about to die.” That mindset shaped his feelings — compassion; it changed his choices — he gave up his rest; and it determined his actions — he stayed and taught them.

And that mindset carried all the way through. When evening came, the disciples said, “Send them away, that they may go into the surrounding country and villages, and buy themselves bread” (Mark 6:36). The disciples’ mindset was, “These people are a problem we can’t afford,” so their strategy was, “Send them away.” Jesus’ mindset was, “These people are sheep my Father wants to feed,” so his action was, “You give them something to eat” (Mark 6:37). The same crowd, the same evening, the same situation — two mindsets, two strategies, two outcomes. Had the disciples acted on their mindset, five thousand people would have gone away hungry. Jesus acted on his, and five thousand ate their fill, with twelve baskets left over.

Brothers and sisters, in the church and in our families we are constantly choosing between these two mindsets. That brother who keeps on stumbling — in your eyes, is he a “nuisance” or a “sheep”? That co-worker who never seems to learn — in your eyes, is she a “burden” or a “sheep God has entrusted to you”? That family member who is so hard to live with — in your eyes, an “enemy” or “a sheep God wants to shepherd through me”? How you see them decides how you treat them.

sections.heading: 4. Where Did Jesus’ Mindset Come From?
sections.html:
Let’s go a level deeper and ask: where did Jesus’ mindset come from? The Lord himself answers:

“Most certainly, I tell you, the Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing. For whatever things he does, these the Son also does likewise.” (John 5:19)

Jesus’ mindset came from his unbroken connection with the Father. He went out to a deserted place to pray before daybreak (see Mark 1:35); he overcame temptation with the words of Scripture (see Matthew 4:4, 7, 10). So when the moment of crisis came, he didn’t need to squeeze out love on the spot; he only needed to let flow what was already within.

God says, “‘For my thoughts are not your thoughts, and your ways are not my ways,’ says Yahweh. ‘For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways, and my thoughts than your thoughts’” (Isaiah 55:8–9). Brothers and sisters, the essence of a renewed mindset is exchanging our low thoughts for God’s high thoughts. And the way to make that exchange is not to figure it out ourselves; it is to come before him again and again.

The Austrian psychiatrist Viktor E. Frankl lost his parents, his wife and almost everything in the Nazi concentration camps. In “Man’s Search for Meaning” (1946) he wrote down what he had discovered: everything can be taken from a person but one thing — the freedom to choose one’s attitude in any given set of circumstances. Even in the extremity of a concentration camp, there remained within a person a space no one could seize. Frankl was speaking of human freedom; the Bible tells us something even more beautiful: that space is not only free, it can be filled by the Holy Spirit and renewed by the truth.

sections.heading: 5. Applying the 321 Vision
sections.html:
“Jesus is my role model” — here that becomes concrete. A role model is not a distant idol; it is a mind we can imitate. Paul says, “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 2:5). And verses 6–8, which follow straight on, explain that the mind of Christ is to empty himself, to take the form of a servant, and to humble himself in obedience to the point of death.

This is exactly what 321 says: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred person, when exhausted, sees only his own needs, and so he says, “I need rest too.” The selfless person, when exhausted, still sees the needs of others, and so he says, “They are like sheep without a shepherd.” Please note: selflessness is not having no self, it is not repression, it is not gritting your teeth and pushing through. Selflessness is “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (see Galatians 2:20) — it is entering into the fullness of Jesus and living out that fullness. Jesus didn’t grit his teeth that day; he was overflowing from the abundance within.

321 also says: life first, then relationships, then ministry; people matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things. Jesus could easily have said that day, “My schedule says rest.” But he put people before the schedule. He did not cancel the value of rest; he let the love in his life decide the order of his ministry.

And one more thing: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. The disciples’ focus was on their circumstances (it’s late, this place is remote) and on themselves (where would we find that much money?). Jesus’ focus was on the Father. Change the focus, and five loaves and two fish are enough.

sections.heading: Key Point 3: God Longs to Change Our Mindset Even More Than to Work Miracles
sections.html: The third point is the one in this lesson that cuts deepest. We often ask God to change our circumstances, but God wants to change our mindset first.

sections.heading: 1. Three Days: A Startling Number
sections.html:
Exodus records one of the most spectacular miracles in human history. The Israelites saw with their own eyes the Red Sea part, walked through the middle of the sea on dry ground, and then watched Pharaoh’s army drown in the waters.

“Israel saw the great work which Yahweh did to the Egyptians, and the people feared Yahweh; and they believed in Yahweh and in his servant Moses.” (Exodus 14:31)

Then comes the first great song in the Bible: “Then Moses and the children of Israel sang this song to Yahweh, and said, ‘I will sing to Yahweh, for he has triumphed gloriously. He has thrown the horse and his rider into the sea’” (Exodus 15:1). Miriam took up her tambourine, all the women danced, and the sound of worship rang through the wilderness. If you had been there that day, you would surely have said: these people’s faith will never waver again.

And then? Look at the very next passage:

“Moses led Israel onward from the Red Sea, and they went out into the wilderness of Shur; and they went three days in the wilderness, and found no water. When they came to Marah, they couldn’t drink from the waters of Marah, for they were bitter. Therefore its name was called Marah. The people murmured against Moses, saying, ‘What shall we drink?’” (Exodus 15:22–24)

Brothers and sisters, how long was it from “singing” to “murmuring”? Three days. Three days! The last notes of that song had hardly faded, the tambourines were still ringing in their ears, and already they had started to complain.

“Marah” in Hebrew is מָרָה (marah), which simply means “bitter.” When Naomi returned to Bethlehem, she said to the people, “Don’t call me Naomi. Call me Mara, for the Almighty has dealt very bitterly with me” (Ruth 1:20). It is the same root. Brothers and sisters, what was truly bitter that day was not only the water of Marah but the hearts of the Israelites. Bitter water is a problem of circumstances; a bitter heart is a problem of mindset. God could fix the bitter water with a single piece of wood, but he would take forty years to deal with the bitter heart.

sections.heading: 2. Where Moses and the People Parted Ways
sections.html:
The same wilderness, the same thirst, the same bitter water — yet Moses responded completely differently:

“Then he cried to Yahweh. Yahweh showed him a tree, and he threw it into the waters, and the waters were made sweet.” (Exodus 15:25)

The people murmured against Moses; Moses cried out to Yahweh. One looked sideways for someone to blame; the other looked up and called on God. What made the difference? Our lesson puts it precisely: the mindset Moses had learned from the miracle was, “God can make a way where there is no way.” The people saw what God had done; Moses knew what kind of God he is.

Scripture spells out this difference very clearly:

“He made known his ways to Moses, his deeds to the children of Israel.” (Psalm 103:7)

Brothers and sisters, please engrave this verse on your heart. It was the same exodus, but Moses knew God’s “ways” — his character, his principles, the way he works — while the Israelites knew only God’s “deeds,” the things he had done. The one who knows his ways still has a way forward the next time he meets bitter water; the one who knows only his deeds has nothing left but complaint the next time he meets bitter water.

This is also why the Israelites fell again and again. After the Red Sea, they complained there was no water; after Marah, they complained there was no meat: “when we sat by the meat pots, when we ate our fill of bread” (Exodus 16:3). At Kadesh, when the twelve spies returned, they preferred to believe the grasshopper mindset rather than the God who had parted the Red Sea. Looking back on this history, the psalmist sighs, “They forgot his doings, his wondrous deeds that he had shown them” (Psalm 78:11).

sections.heading: 3. A Miracle Changes Us for a Moment; a Mindset Changes Us for Life
sections.html:
Our lesson has a sentence that lands with real weight: a miracle can change a person for a moment; a mindset can change a person for a lifetime.

The Lord Jesus himself confirmed this. The day after the five loaves and two fish, the crowd crossed the lake to find him, and the Lord said, “Most certainly I tell you, you seek me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves, and were filled” (John 6:26). Five thousand had eaten the bread, but few stayed to hear the truth; by the end of chapter 6: “At this, many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him” (John 6:66).

Then there were the ten lepers. All ten were healed, but only one came back to give glory to God. The Lord said, “Weren’t the ten cleansed? But where are the nine?” (Luke 17:17). All ten were cured of their disease, but only one had his mindset changed. To that one the Lord said, “Get up, and go your way. Your faith has healed you” (Luke 17:19) — the Chinese Union Version reads, “Your faith has saved you.” Nine received healing; one received salvation.

Brothers and sisters, this is not to say miracles don’t matter. Miracles are God’s grace, signs of his compassion, and we should give thanks for every one of them. But a miracle is like a firework — brilliant, breathtaking, and then gone. A mindset is like a streetlamp — not dazzling, but it lights your way down the whole dark road. God knows better than we do what we need. We ask for a firework; he wants to give us a lamp.

sections.heading: 4. What Science Says: The Shock Fades, but the Pathways Can Be Rewired
sections.html:
Psychology has a name for a certain phenomenon: “hedonic adaptation.” Brickman and Campbell (Brickman & Campbell, 1971) put forward the concept; in 1978 Brickman, Coates and Janoff-Bulman (Brickman, Coates & Janoff-Bulman) published a famous study interviewing major lottery winners and patients paralysed in accidents. They found that after a while the lottery winners’ overall happiness was not much higher than anyone else’s. The emotional impact of an outward event drifts back, over time, to somewhere near where it started.

Brothers and sisters, this is a modern footnote to “complaining after three days.” The shock fades; that is how we are made. So God does not build our faith on shocks. He wants to build our faith on knowing him.

But science also tells us the other side, and it is good news: the human brain has “neuroplasticity.” In 2000 a team at University College London led by Eleanor A. Maguire studied brain scans of London taxi drivers. They found that these drivers, who must carry the street map of the whole of London in their heads, had significantly more grey matter in the posterior hippocampus than the control group, and that it correlated positively with the number of years they had been driving. In other words: the mental pathways you use again and again are physically thickened.

This gives us tremendous hope. An old pathway of thought that you’ve walked for forty years can be replaced by a new one — not through one great shock, but through repeated practice. This is exactly why the eight stages of changing our mindset in 321 include the stage of Repetition. Neuroscience says, “Use it or lose it”; the Bible said long ago, “This book of the law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night” (Joshua 1:8). Meditating day and night is spiritual neuroplasticity.

In 1967 Martin E. P. Seligman and Steven F. Maier described “learned helplessness”: after animals had failed again and again to escape electric shocks they could not avoid, they stopped trying even when the door to escape was left open. It wasn’t that they couldn’t escape; they had learned to believe they couldn’t. Brothers and sisters, isn’t that a portrait of the Israelites? God could bring Israel out of Egypt in a single night, but it took him forty years to bring Egypt out of Israel.

sections.heading: 5. Applying the 321 Vision
sections.html:
“The Bible is my standard” — this is where the content of a renewed mindset comes from. Our mindset is not adjusted by our feelings; it is corrected by the word of God.

Paul says, “For the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh, but mighty before God to the throwing down of strongholds, throwing down imaginations and every high thing that is exalted against the knowledge of God and bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ” (2 Corinthians 10:4–5). Notice what these “strongholds” are — not enemies outside us, but systems of thought within us that are “exalted against the knowledge of God.” The main battlefield of spiritual warfare is our mindset.

321 speaks of a shift in perspective: from man’s perspective to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. The Israelites’ perspective was human, earthly, temporary and worldly — so all they asked was, “What shall we drink?” Moses’ perspective was God’s, heavenly, eternal and godly — so he cried out to Yahweh.

321 also says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. At Marah the people were relying on the brain and themselves — counting the water, counting the miles, counting the days, and the more they counted, the more troubled they became. Moses relied on the heart and the Holy Spirit — crying out, looking up, obeying — and God showed him a tree. Brothers and sisters, this morning, are you counting, or are you calling out to God?

Integrating the 321 Vision

Let’s set what we have received today within the whole picture of 321.

The Three Foundations, the Two Core Values, the Goal

The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide.

The three key points of this lesson line up exactly with the Three Foundations. Key Point 1, on mindset shaping every dimension of life, reminds us that we need an absolute standard — the Bible is my standard. Key Point 2, on Jesus’ compassion even in exhaustion, is a living demonstration — Jesus is my role model. Key Point 3, on the renewal of our mindset coming not from shocks but only from an inward work — the Holy Spirit is my guide. For when Paul says “be transformed by the renewing of your mind,” the verb in the original is passive: we do not renew ourselves; we let the Holy Spirit renew us.

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory.

The destination of a renewed mindset is not “I become a better version of me,” but “I let Jesus reign as King in every corner of my thinking.” A mindset not yet surrendered is a piece of territory not yet handed over to the Lord. While the lie “I can’t” still lives in my heart, fear sits enthroned on that ground; while the prejudice “he’s such a nuisance” still lives in my heart, my old self sits enthroned on that ground. Only when we let Jesus be King does that ground truly become his.

The Goal: establish God’s system.

The world has its system, and it presses on us from outside and moulds us; God has his system, and he renews us from within and remakes us. Every person whose mindset has been renewed is a living stone in God’s system.

The Fivefold Change

Mindset changes, life changes, daily living changes, relationships change, ministry changes.

The title of this lesson is the first three of the five changes. Look at how it really works out:

A brother’s old mindset was, “Everyone else is better than me; I’m completely useless.” When the Holy Spirit renewed him with the truth, “You are made in the image of God,” his life began to find security. With that security, he no longer protected himself by withdrawing; he began to come early to church to set out chairs and take out the rubbish — that is daily living changing. When he stopped comparing himself with others, his relationships with his brothers and sisters loosened up. And once his relationships were open, God put a few young people into his hands, and he became their spiritual father.

The order cannot be reversed. Much of people’s frustration comes from trying to skip over life and go straight into ministry, until ministry becomes a mask to cover the life underneath. 321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry; people matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things. The priority of relationships has an order too: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. This lesson reminds us that the first layers a renewed mindset must reach are precisely these two: “me and God” and “me and myself.”

The Self-Centred Life and Selflessness

The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem.

Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

Look back over this lesson. When the Israelites murmured at Marah, on the surface it was about a lack of water, but underneath it was the self-centred life: my needs haven’t been met, so I have the right to complain; I want God to act on my timetable — that is leaving our originally intended position and wanting to take God’s place. When Moses cried out to Yahweh, he returned to his originally intended position: he let God be God.

When the disciples said, “Send them away,” that too was the self-centred life: my strength is limited, my purse is limited, my time is limited — every sentence is about “me.” When Jesus said, “You give them something to eat,” that was selflessness: not looking at how much we have, but only at what the Father wants to do.

Let me say it once more: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living that fullness out. “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). When this small container called “I” is moved aside, the boundless life of Christ can flow out from within us. Five loaves and two fish are not enough by the arithmetic of the self-centred life; placed in selfless hands, they fed five thousand.

The 920 Practice and the 235 Relationships

The 920 practice is this: every person we are in relationship with is our “2”; with that person we practise living a selfless (0) life and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions — “the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23).

This lesson gives the 920 practice a very practical key: your mindset toward that “2” decides what fruit you will bear toward them. If you see them as “a nuisance,” what you squeeze out is an imitation of patience; if you see them as “like sheep without a shepherd,” what flows out is real kindness. This morning, name one person in your heart — the “2” who gives you the hardest time. Ask the Lord for a new pair of lenses, and let him help you see that person again.

The 235 relationships are these: with someone who is selfless, become a “2” — spiritual companions; build a “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children; become a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. The renewal of a mindset is very rarely accomplished by one person behind a closed door. The Bible’s way is to have companions who remind each other, spiritual parents who point out our blind spots, and a team that moves forward together. The spiritual companion beside you who dares to tell you the truth is often the very hand God uses to change your lenses.

The Path of Serving runs the same way: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God. From Spirit to Understanding is precisely the process of a mindset being renewed; from Understanding to Life is precisely the process of a life being changed.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Going Deeper with the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset
sections.html:
Our lesson gives us three practices for daily living. Let’s combine them with the eight stages of changing our mindset in 321 — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — so that the practices take root in real life.

Practice 1: Recall the last time you felt anxious or shrank back, ask yourself, “What is my mindset here?” and renew it with God’s truth

Stage 1, Information: take a sheet of paper and write down plainly what happened — the time, the place, what took place, what you said and did at the time. Write only the facts, with no commentary.

Stage 2, Revelation: become quiet and ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light: “In that moment, what did I really believe in my heart?” Perhaps it was, “I’m bound to be rejected.” Perhaps it was, “Nobody really cares about me.” Perhaps it was, “God won’t bother with small things like mine.” Write that sentence down. This stage is not self-analysis; it is asking the Lord to open your eyes — “For the word of God is living and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword … and is able to discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart” (Hebrews 4:12).

Stage 3, Conviction: find in Scripture the truth that stands squarely against that lie. Not a nice-sounding sentence, but a word you are willing to stake your whole self on. Then read it out loud until your heart says, “Amen.” Conviction is not understanding; it is surrender.

Practice 2: Meditate on one verse each day, especially a truth that can change your old ways of thinking, and let the Holy Spirit renew your mind

Stage 4, Implementation: each morning choose one verse — just one. Copy it onto a card, stick it beside the mirror, make it your phone’s wallpaper. Throughout the day — waiting at a red light, washing the dishes, before a meeting — say it over quietly once more. “This book of the law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, that you may observe to do according to all that is written in it” (Joshua 1:8).

Stage 5, Evaluation: in the evening, take three minutes to ask yourself: at what moment today did this verse really help me? At what moment did I slip back into my old mindset? Don’t condemn yourself; just be honest. Evaluation is not judgment; it is bringing things into focus.

Stage 6, Correction: if you find the verse doesn’t fit the problem, choose another; if you find the old mindset is especially strong in one particular situation, prepare a word aimed at that situation. Correction is grace, not failure.

Practice 3: When you meet difficulties, don’t first ask for a miracle; ask God to change your mindset and the way you see

Stage 7, Repetition: this is the least impressive stage, yet the most crucial. An old pathway of thought walked for decades won’t vanish because you’ve heard one message. The London taxi drivers’ hippocampi didn’t thicken from one day of memorising streets. So repeat — read the same sentence a hundred times; pray the same prayer for forty days. The psalmist says, “I have hidden your word in my heart, that I might not sin against you” (Psalm 119:11). “Hidden” is an ongoing action.

Try changing the words of your prayer. Don’t only say, “Lord, please take this difficulty away.” Try adding: “Lord, if you don’t take it away just yet, please first take away the wrong mindset in my heart; let me see in this situation what you want me to see.” This is not giving up on asking for a miracle; it is asking for a greater miracle — a renewed heart.

Stage 8, Multiplication: when you truly experience a mindset being renewed, please don’t keep it to yourself. Go and tell someone. Say to your “2”: “I always used to think … and then God showed me …” Your testimony will become someone else’s Information and set off their own eight stages. The goal of 321 is to establish God’s system, and a system is established by multiplication, not by gathering.

A Gentle Reminder

Our lesson has a very precious gentle reminder: when you ask God to change your circumstances, God often changes you first. For your circumstances are a mirror, reflecting your heart and your mindset. Let God change your thinking first, and you will see your circumstances change along with it.

Brothers and sisters, what a precious reminder this is. We often get angry at the mirror, forgetting that the mirror is only being honest. In the same office, one person complains every day and another gives thanks every day; in the same family, one person sees only lack and another sees grace. The circumstances are no different, but the face in the mirror is. Of course God can change our circumstances — he parted the Red Sea. But he loves us more than that, so he often changes us first. Because if your circumstances change and you are still the old you, the next set of circumstances will knock you right back to where you were; but if you change, the same circumstances can never trap you again.

sections.heading: Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s go back to where we began: change does not start on the outside; it starts with our mindset.

The life of Jesus bears witness that when our thinking is in line with God’s heart, our lives will express love and power. In his most exhausted moment, he saw not a nuisance but sheep without a shepherd; when he had every reason to step back, he chose to stay and teach. That was not willpower; it was what flowed naturally from a mind filled with truth.

So don’t just ask for a miracle to come; let the truth renew you. A miracle changes your situation for a moment; the truth changes the direction of your whole life. When your mindset changes, your life will change; when your life changes, your daily living will be made completely new. This is where revival begins, and it is the key to spiritual growth.

This morning the Lord is knocking at the door of every mind. Perhaps what he wants to knock on is a lie you have believed for a long time — “I can’t,” “I’m not worthy,” “I’m useless,” “God won’t use me.” Brothers and sisters, those words did not come from God. God says, “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them” (Ephesians 2:10).

Perhaps what he wants to knock on is your prejudice against a particular person. Ask the Lord today to give you a new pair of lenses, so that in that person you see a sheep without a shepherd.

Perhaps what he wants to knock on is the way you know him. You have always treated him as a stern judge, as an elder who smiles only when you perform well. Brothers and sisters, he is the Shepherd who laid down his life for you.

Let Jesus reign as King in your mind. Place every mindset, every word you say to yourself, every judgment you make about others, into his hands. When he reigns as King in our minds, our lives, our daily living, our relationships and our ministry will all be turned around, and all the glory will go to him.

“But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord, the Spirit” (2 Corinthians 3:18). Notice that “transformed” here is exactly the same word as “transformed” in Romans 12:2 — μεταμορφόω. And how does it happen? By looking at him with unveiled face. Brothers and sisters, what you look at, you become. This morning, let us look at him with unveiled face.

keyVerses: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” (Romans 12:2)
declarations: Let us make together the declaration of faith from our lesson:

Lord, please renew my thinking, so that I see the world through your eyes. May my mindset be aligned with yours, so that my life is changed and my daily living is turned around, and I live out your truth and your glory.
practices: Recall the last time you felt anxious or shrank back, ask yourself, “What is my mindset here?” and renew it with God’s truth
Meditate on one verse each day, especially a truth that can change your old ways of thinking, and let the Holy Spirit renew your mind
When you meet difficulties, don’t first ask for a miracle; ask God to change your mindset and the way you see
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we thank you.

Thank you for reminding us this morning that change does not start on the outside but on the inside. Lord, we confess that we often ask you to change our circumstances but refuse to let you change us; we often long for the thrill of miracles but refuse to pay the price of a renewed mindset. Have mercy on us.

Lord Jesus, you are our role model. In your most exhausted moment, you still saw sheep without a shepherd. Give us your heart, so that we see people through your eyes and love them with your compassion.

Holy Spirit, please do your work of renewal. Shine the light of truth into every corner of our minds, show us the strongholds, and tear down the thoughts that keep us from knowing you. Take every thought of ours captive, and bring us all into obedience to Christ.
Make us like Moses — not only knowing your deeds but knowing your ways; not murmuring beside the bitter water, but crying out to you beside the bitter water.
May my mindset be renewed, my life changed, my daily living turned around, my relationships restored, and my ministry used by you. May Jesus reign as King in my mind, and may all the glory go to you.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “For as he thinks about the cost, so he is” (Proverbs 23:7). Recall the last time something made you anxious, made you shrink back or made you angry. In that moment, what sentence did you really believe in your heart? Where did that sentence come from? How does the Bible answer it?

“Jesus came out, saw a great multitude, and he had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd, and he began to teach them many things” (Mark 6:34). Is there someone near you whom you have always treated as a “nuisance”? If you asked the Lord for a new pair of lenses so that you could see them as “like sheep without a shepherd,” what one concrete thing would you do for them this week?
l041.title: Change the Mindset, Change the Life
l041.subtitle: Transformed by the Renewing of the Mind, Daily Living Is Made New
l041.partTitle: Unit 4 · The Prerequisite for Revival — A Change of Mindset

sections.heading: 1. Introduction: Where One Seed Falls Decides a Whole Forest
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning.

Let me begin with a simple question that very few people ever answer seriously: yesterday, over the whole day, how many things did your eyes look at? How many sounds did your ears take in?

We couldn’t put a number on it. But deep down we all know this: what we’ve seen and heard hasn’t disappeared. Like rain soaking into the ground, it seeps, drop by drop, into our hearts. The thoughts in our hearts today are simply the information we fed our hearts yesterday, sprouting and growing up.

A mother once told me that her child had never used foul language growing up — until one summer holiday when he played online games with his classmates every single day. Less than two months into the new school year, his tone, his vocabulary, his whole attitude toward people had changed. The mother asked, heartbroken, “He’s the same child — how could he turn into a different person?” In fact the child hadn’t turned into a different person. He had simply fed himself two months of new information; that information had grown into new mindsets, and the new mindsets had grown into a new way of speaking.

We often imagine that a changed life is some sudden, dramatic event, striking like a bolt of lightning. It isn’t. A changed life is much more like a tree: first a seed falls to the ground, and then it sprouts, puts down roots, grows a stem, flowers and bears fruit. From the outside, the tree grows slowly; from the inside, its whole direction was already decided the moment that seed hit the ground.

The theme of this lesson is a single word — information. It sounds very ordinary, almost as if we were talking about computers or the internet. But brothers and sisters, please don’t underestimate this word. In the message of 321 we keep stressing the fivefold change: when the mindset changes, the life changes; when the life changes, daily living changes; when daily living changes, relationships change; when relationships change, ministry changes. This whole chain of change begins with the very first link — the mindset. And where does a change of mindset begin? The answer is: information.

There are eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Today we look at the first stage. Get the first step wrong, and the next seven will all veer off course; get the first step right, and the next seven have a true starting point. It’s like the first reference line when you build a house: be one centimetre out at the bottom, and by the tenth floor you’re a metre out.

We also have to face something honestly: the generation that hears the most sermons is not necessarily the generation that changes the most. Information is not revelation; knowing is not believing; having heard is not having received. Information is the doorway, not the living room; it is the starting point, not the destination. But turn that around: no one can skip the doorway and walk straight into the living room. When God wants to shine his light on us, he always begins by setting his word in front of us.

So this morning let’s look together at three things: first, information is the starting point of a change of mindset; second, information sets the direction — right information produces a right mindset; third, information needs filtering — we must be selective about what we look at and what we listen to.

May the Holy Spirit, this early morning, plant his word in our hearts himself.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Background: Two Verses, One Lesson in Keeping the Gate
sections.html:
Today’s two theme verses — one in the Old Testament and one in the New; one about the “heart” and one about the “ear” — together make up the whole message of this lesson.

First, Proverbs 4:23.

The main author of Proverbs is Solomon. 1 Kings 4:32 records, “He spoke three thousand proverbs; and his songs numbered one thousand five.” Solomon reigned roughly between 970 and 930 BC. The contents of Proverbs gradually took shape in his court and were later edited again in the days of King Hezekiah (Proverbs 25:1: “These also are proverbs of Solomon, which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied out”). Proverbs is not a law book but wisdom literature. It is not telling us, “Here’s what you must not do,” but, “Here’s how a person who fears God looks at life.”

The form of Proverbs 4 is very special: it is a father’s charge to his son. Verse 1 says, “Listen, sons, to a father’s instruction. Pay attention and know understanding.” In verse 4 the father recalls how his own father taught him. In other words, this is something handed down across three generations. And as this long charge draws to a close, the father places his most important sentence in verse 23: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” The Chinese Union Version reads, “Keep your heart above all that you guard,” and adds a marginal alternative, “Keep your heart diligently” — which is just how the WEB renders it — meaning to guard it doubly, urgently.

The word “keep” here is the Hebrew nātsar, whose basic meaning is “to watch, to guard, to keep watch over” — the action of a sentry guarding a city gate or a watchman guarding a vineyard. And “heart” is the Hebrew lēb, which in the Old Testament does not mean only our emotions or feelings but the centre of a person’s thinking, will, judgment and decisions — in today’s language, our “mindset system.”

So the picture in this verse is this: your heart is a city, and at the city gate stands a guard. People come and go outside the city — merchants, and enemy soldiers too. The guard’s job is not to seal the gate shut but to discern who may come in and who may not. Straight afterward, in verses 24–27, the father speaks in one breath about the mouth, the eyes and the feet: “Put away from yourself a perverse mouth. Put corrupt lips far from you. Let your eyes look straight ahead. Fix your gaze directly before you. Make the path of your feet level. Let all of your ways be established.” Mouth, eyes, feet — all of them are gateways to the “heart.” So keeping the heart means, in concrete terms, keeping watch over what we look at, what we listen to, what we say and where we go.

Next, Romans 10:17.

Romans was written by the apostle Paul, generally thought to be around AD 57, most likely in Corinth, when Paul was about to take the gift from the churches of Macedonia and Achaia to Jerusalem (Romans 15:25–26). It was addressed to the church in Rome, a group of believers Paul had not yet met, both Jews and Gentiles.

Chapters 9–11 are a long and anguished plea Paul writes for his own flesh and blood — the people of Israel. In 10:14 he fires off three questions in a row: “How then will they call on him in whom they have not believed? How will they believe in him whom they have not heard? How will they hear without a preacher?” Paul is reasoning backwards: to call on him, you must first believe; to believe, you must first hear; to hear, someone must first proclaim. Link by link, he traces it back to the very root, which is the conclusion of verse 17: “So faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.”

The word for “hearing” here is the Greek akoē, a very interesting word: it can mean “the act of hearing,” and it can also mean “the message that is heard.” And “the word of God” — in the original Greek text Paul’s phrase is rhēma Christou, “the word of Christ,” as the Chinese Union Version renders it. Rhēma means “a word that is spoken,” carrying the sense of something present, living, addressed to someone. In other words, faith doesn’t arise out of nothing, and we don’t think it up ourselves; faith is a response — a response to the message that comes from Christ, is proclaimed by people, and is heard and taken in by us.

Brothers and sisters, see how beautiful these two verses are side by side. Romans tells us that a changed life begins with “hearing”; Proverbs tells us that our “hearing” needs a gatekeeper. One is the point of entry; the other is customs. God’s word must come in first before our hearts can be renewed; but not every word may come in, so our hearts must have a guard.

And that is the order of this lesson’s three key points: starting point, direction, filtering.

sections.heading: 3. Key Point 1: Information Is the Starting Point of a Change of Mindset
sections.html:
“So faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.” (Romans 10:17)

1. God Always Begins by Speaking

Brothers and sisters, please notice something: every great change in the Bible begins with God speaking.

Genesis 1:3: “God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light.” The universe began with a word. Abraham’s story began with a word: “Leave your country, and your relatives, and your father’s house, and go to the land that I will show you” (Genesis 12:1). Moses’ story began with a word from a burning bush; Samuel’s began with a call in the night, three times over; and Saul’s story on the road to Damascus began with a word too: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” (Acts 9:4).

God could simply move our wills directly, yet he chooses to speak to us first. Why? Because what God values is not controlling a person but renewing a person. He wants our hearts to be persuaded by the truth, not overpowered by force. This is exactly what 321 says: God has given us free will. He does not seize; he waits. He does not take our place; he walks with us.

That’s why the very first sentence of the Lord Jesus’ parable of the sower is, “Behold, a farmer went out to sow” (Matthew 13:3). He didn’t say, “A farmer went out to change the soil,” but “to sow.” And what is the seed? Luke 8:11 says plainly: “Now the parable is this: The seed is the word of God.”

The seed is information. When God’s word enters a human heart, a piece of information carrying life has fallen into the ground.

2. Between “Knowing” and “Believing” Stands a Threshold

But a seed of information falling into the ground is not the same thing as a changed life.

Our lesson says it straight: the Information stage is still only “knowing”; it isn’t yet “believing.” We may be touched by a certain sentence or moved by a certain testimony, and feel in our hearts, “That’s right.” But if we stop at “I get it” or “I’ve heard that,” it remains intellectual understanding; it hasn’t yet reached the heart.

Psychology agrees with the Bible’s observation here to a remarkable degree. In 1885 the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus carried out his famous memory experiments and drew the “forgetting curve”: after we learn something, our memory of it drops sharply over the first few hours to a day, and only then levels off. In other words, most information we have simply “heard once” is gone before the next day. That explains an experience we all know well: Sunday’s sermon moves us deeply, and by Tuesday we can’t remember what it was about.

In the 1960s the American psychologist Aaron T. Beck developed cognitive therapy and put forward a central observation: our emotions and behaviour are not determined directly by events but by our “automatic thoughts” and “core beliefs” about those events. In other words, what really governs our daily living is not what happens outside us but what we believe inside. Only when information settles into “belief” does it begin to govern our lives.

Brothers and sisters, this is the dividing line between Information and Revelation. Information is the mind receiving something; Revelation is the Holy Spirit lighting up that word so that it suddenly becomes “spoken to me.” You can read the same verse thirty times and feel nothing, and then one early morning you read it again and the tears come — in that moment, information has become revelation.

The Lord Jesus himself drew this distinction. After Peter’s confession, “Jesus answered him, ‘Blessed are you, Simon Bar Jonah, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven’” (Matthew 16:17). Everyone had heard the same information, but only Peter, in that moment, received revelation.

3. Why Years of Sermons Bring No Change

Our lesson points out a sobering fact: many Christians hear sermons for years and yet do not change, precisely because they stay stuck at the Information stage. If knowledge is not transformed into revelation, it only piles up as data in the head and never becomes power in the heart.

James 1:22 says, “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.” The word “deluding,” paralogizomai in the original, means “to mislead yourself with false reasoning.” Those who only hear the word quietly do a false sum in their hearts: I’ve heard it, so I’ve probably done it too. It is a very subtle kind of self-deception.

The Lord Jesus puts it even more seriously. Luke 8:18: “Be careful therefore how you hear. For whoever has, to him will be given; and whoever doesn’t have, from him will be taken away even that which he thinks he has.” Notice that the Lord didn’t say, “Be careful what you hear”; he said, “Be careful how you hear.” From the same message, some people receive more and more, and others less and less. The difference isn’t in the preacher; it’s in the attitude of the listener.

I often use a picture: information is like the dishes a restaurant brings to your table. A dish placed on the table doesn’t mean you’ve eaten it; eating it doesn’t mean you’ve digested it; only when it’s digested does it become your flesh and blood and strength. People who hear sermons for years without changing are like people who go to restaurants every day to photograph the food and post it online, but rarely actually eat the meal. In Jeremiah 15:16 the prophet describes it like this: “Your words were found, and I ate them. Your words were to me a joy and the rejoicing of my heart, for I am called by your name, Yahweh, God of Armies.” The prophet didn’t “look at” God’s words; he “ate” them.

Neuroscience offers a lovely confirmation too. In his 1949 book “The Organization of Behavior,” the Canadian psychologist Donald Hebb proposed a neural mechanism for learning, which later scholars often sum up in one sentence: neurons that fire together wire together. This is the basis of “neuroplasticity”: think a thought once, and it’s a small footpath; think it a thousand times, and it becomes a highway. This shows why, among the eight stages, Repetition has to come after Implementation, Evaluation and Correction. The truth needs repetition — not because God’s word lacks power, but because a new road needs to be worn into our hearts.

4. Applying the 321 Vision: Life First, Then Relationships, Then Ministry

Brothers and sisters, 321 keeps stressing: life first, then relationships, then ministry. The renewal of life begins with mindset, and the renewal of mindset begins with information.

That is why, among the Three Foundations of 321, the second foundation is this: the Bible is my standard. A standard means I don’t treat the Bible as one reference book among many but as my only measure. The world supplies us with a flood of information every day, but only God’s word can serve as the standard; every other piece of information must be brought before this ruler and measured.

At the same time we must remember the third foundation: the Holy Spirit is my guide. Without the Holy Spirit, information will only ever be information. In John 16:13 the Lord promises, “However when he, the Spirit of truth, has come, he will guide you into all truth.” Our part is to put God’s word into our hearts; the Holy Spirit’s part is to light that word up. As 321 puts it: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled.

If all that happens this morning is that we know one more lesson, it is still only information. May the Lord make this morning’s devotion a moment of revelation.

sections.heading: 4. Key Point 2: Information Sets the Direction — Right Information Produces a Right Mindset
sections.html:
“Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23)

1. What We Take In Is What We Come to Believe

Our lesson says that although information is only the starting point, it is an absolutely crucial starting point. For if a person takes in wrong information, it forms a wrong mindset, which in turn leads to wrong choices and wrong behaviour.

This is an invisible but extremely strong chain: information determines mindset, mindset determines choices, choices determine behaviour, and behaviour determines destiny. The fivefold change of 321 — mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry — runs along exactly this chain. The trouble is that the chain runs both ways. Feed in truth, and it grows life; feed in lies, and it will just as faithfully grow bondage.

Humanity’s first fall was an accident of information. Genesis 3:1: “Now the serpent was more subtle than any animal of the field which Yahweh God had made. He said to the woman, ‘Has God really said, “You shall not eat of any tree of the garden”?’” Satan didn’t lift a hand first; he opened his mouth first. The first thing he did was put out a piece of twisted information — turning the generosity of God’s “You may freely eat of every tree of the garden” (Genesis 2:16) into the stinginess of “You shall not eat of any tree of the garden.”

Eve took in that information, and her mindset was knocked off course; once her mindset was off course, the way she saw things changed. Genesis 3:6: “When the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took some of its fruit, and ate. Then she gave some to her husband with her, and he ate it, too.” Notice the order — first “hearing,” then “seeing,” and only then “taking” and “eating.” The whole fall of the human race began with one piece of false information.

In the language of 321: Satan’s work is to push people from selflessness toward the self-centred life. The information he feeds us always circles around the same theme — you don’t have to stay in your originally intended position; you can be like God; you can be your own master. The self-centred life is the root of the fall, and pride is the root of the problem. And pride never grows up in a day; it is fed, one piece of information at a time.

2. David’s Fall Began with “Seeing” and “Inquiring”

Our lesson gives a very weighty example: the root of David’s sin did not begin with an action; it began with “information.”

2 Samuel 11:2–3: “At evening, David arose from his bed and walked on the roof of the king’s house. From the roof, he saw a woman bathing, and the woman was very beautiful to look at. David sent and inquired after the woman. One said, ‘Isn’t this Bathsheba, the daughter of Eliam, Uriah the Hittite’s wife?’”

Put these actions in order: he arose, he walked, he saw, he inquired. Four actions: the first two are neutral; the third is information coming in; the fourth is actively going out to gather more information. The sin hasn’t happened yet, but the direction is already set.

The word “saw” in verse 2 is the Hebrew rā’āh, which can mean a glance or a fixed gaze. That is exactly where the difference lies: the first look is usually not sin; the second look is a choice. There is a widely quoted saying generally attributed to Martin Luther: you cannot stop the birds from flying over your head, but you can stop them from building a nest on it. David didn’t stop the first bird flying over; he reached out and built it a nest — he sent someone to inquire.

Even more chilling is verse 3. The information brought back to David was in fact one brake after another: she had a father’s house; she had a husband; and Uriah was one of David’s thirty-seven mighty men (2 Samuel 23:39), a brother who had faced death at his side. God set three “stop” signs in front of David. But the wrong information had already taken root in his heart, and even when the right information came in, it could no longer turn him.

Brothers and sisters, here is a solemn warning: when we allow wrong information to settle in our hearts, however many reminders God gives us, we’ll hear them as background noise.

By contrast, Job took a different road. Job 31:1: “I made a covenant with my eyes, how then should I look lustfully at a young woman?” Job didn’t rely on gritting his teeth with willpower; he made a “covenant” — he decided beforehand, instead of waiting to struggle in the moment. So did the psalmist. Psalm 101:3: “I will set no vile thing before my eyes. I hate the deeds of faithless men. They will not cling to me.” “Set no vile thing before my eyes” is a lesson for the preparation stage, not for the moment itself.

3. The Twelve Spies: One Land, Two Reports, Two Destinies

If David’s story is a personal one, the story in Numbers 13–14 belongs to a whole generation.

Twelve spies went together, saw the same things and came back together. The “facts” they brought back were exactly the same: the land flowed with milk and honey; its people were tall; its cities were fortified. Yet the “information” they brought back was utterly different.

Numbers 13:32–33: “They brought up an evil report of the land which they had spied out to the children of Israel, saying, ‘The land, through which we have gone to spy it out, is a land that eats up its inhabitants; and all the people who we saw in it are men of great stature. There we saw the Nephilim, the sons of Anak, who come from the Nephilim. We were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight.’”

But Caleb said, “Let’s go up at once, and possess it; for we are well able to overcome it!” (Numbers 13:30).

Notice the ten spies’ confession: “We were in our own sight as grasshoppers.” First they saw themselves as grasshoppers in their own hearts, and only then did they conclude that the enemy saw them that way too. That wasn’t intelligence; it was the mindset in their hearts, walking out dressed as intelligence.

And the result? One evil report spread, the whole congregation wept all night (Numbers 14:1), and a whole generation fell dead in the wilderness over forty years. But God’s verdict on Caleb was this: “But my servant Caleb, because he had another spirit with him, and has followed me fully, him I will bring into the land into which he went” (Numbers 14:24). “Another spirit” — that is the literal Hebrew: “there was another spirit in him”; the Chinese Union Version renders it “a different resolve.” The difference was not in their eyes but in their hearts; not in what they saw but in the perspective they saw it from.

This is exactly the shift in perspective 321 speaks of: from man’s perspective to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. The ten spies measured the giants with a human, earthly, temporary eye; Caleb and Joshua measured God with a divine, heavenly, eternal eye. One land, two reports, two destinies.

4. Supporting Evidence from Psychology: We Are Shaped by What We Take In

Psychology has produced a good deal of solid research on this point.

In 1961 the Canadian psychologist Albert Bandura conducted the famous “Bobo doll experiment.” One group of children watched an adult punching and kicking an inflatable doll; another group did not. Afterward, each child was left alone in the same room, and the children who had seen the violent model were clearly more likely to show the same aggressive behaviour — even imitating the adult’s particular movements. From this Bandura developed his social learning theory: people don’t need to be rewarded or punished; simply “seeing” is enough for them to learn.

In 1968 the American psychologist Robert Zajonc described the “mere exposure effect”: simply by being exposed to something repeatedly, people grow to like it more, even without any persuasion at all. This reveals something frightening: we can move from distaste for a set of values, to getting used to it, to accepting it, often without any reason at all — just by “seeing it all the time.”

In a 1960 study the British psychologist Peter Wason described “confirmation bias”: when we look for information, we tend to seek evidence that supports what we already think and to ignore evidence to the contrary. Once a wrong mindset has formed, it actively goes looking for more wrong information to feed itself. That is why the first step is so crucial — a wrong starting point automatically reproduces itself.

5. Applying the 321 Vision: Discern First, Then Receive

So our lesson says: we must learn to discern information. “So faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Romans 10:17). Only information that comes from God can bring true faith and the renewal of life. On the other hand, if we let the voices of the world and the values of the media fill us, we will be shaped into a worldly mould and drift far from God’s heart.

Paul says in Romans 12:2, “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” “Conformed,” syschēmatizō in the original, means “pressed into the same mould as …”; “transformed,” metamorphoō in the original, means a change of form from within — the very word used when the Lord was transfigured on the mountain. One is a mould clamped on from outside; the other is a life exchanged from within. What decides which force shapes us is the information we feed our hearts every day.

The Bereans left us the best example. Acts 17:11: “Now these were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, examining the Scriptures daily to see whether these things were so.” Notice: on the one hand they “received the word with all readiness”; on the other they were “examining the Scriptures daily.” Open, but not gullible; teachable, but with a standard. That is what 321 means by “the Bible is my standard” — not shutting up the heart, but setting a ruler at the heart’s gate.

1 Thessalonians 5:21: “Test all things, and hold firmly that which is good.” Test, and then hold firmly. First discernment, then receiving.

sections.heading: 5. Key Point 3: Information Needs Filtering — Be Selective About What You See and Hear
sections.html:
“The lamp of the body is the eye. If therefore your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light. But if your eye is evil, your whole body will be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in you is darkness, how great is the darkness!” (Matthew 6:22–23)

1. The Eyes — the Windows of the Soul

Our lesson says: the eyes are the windows of the soul. We should “look often” at heavenly things — at God’s works, at the truth of Scripture, at the testimony of people’s lives. When we focus on what is good and true, our hearts are naturally filled with light.

The Lord Jesus says the eye is “the lamp of the body.” A lamp here is not the source of the light; it is what lets the light in. The eye doesn’t manufacture light; the eye decides which light enters our whole body. When the Lord says, “If your eye is sound,” the original word is haplous, whose basic meaning is “single, undivided, not forked”; its opposite, “evil” (the Chinese Union Version has “dim”), is ponēros in the original, meaning “wicked.” The context of these words is treasure and service (Matthew 6:19–24): if the eye is fixed on God alone, the whole body is full of light; if the eye is split in two by other things, the whole body is full of darkness.

What are these “heavenly things”?

First, look at God’s works. Psalm 103:2: “Praise Yahweh, my soul, and don’t forget all his benefits.” Write down what God has done in your life and look at it often; that is the most powerful spiritual information there is.

Second, look at the truth of Scripture. Psalm 119:105: “Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path.” The lamp shines at your feet, the light shines along your path; one takes care of the step you’re on now, the other of the direction ahead.

Third, look at the testimony of people’s lives. Hebrews 12:1–2: “Therefore let’s also, seeing we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, lay aside every weight and the sin which so easily entangles us, and let’s run with perseverance the race that is set before us, looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith.” We look at the witnesses so that, in the end, we may look to Jesus. This is exactly what 321 says: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances.

In Philippians 4:8 Paul simply hands us a list: “Finally, brothers, whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are just, whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report: if there is any virtue and if there is any praise, think about these things.” This is not passive avoidance but an active choice. The heart is not made clean by “not thinking about things”; it is filled by “thinking more about the right things.”

2. The Ears — the Entrance to Faith

Our lesson says: the ears are the entrance to faith. We should choose to listen to God’s word, to words that build people up, to the sharing of truth. As for negative, complaining, critical and judgmental words, we must learn to “hear without taking them in.”

In Mark 4:24 the Lord Jesus says, “Take heed what you hear. With whatever measure you measure, it will be measured to you, and more will be given to you who hear.” He compares listening to a measuring vessel. However large the vessel you bring to listening, that is the size of the vessel God measures out to you. Those who mark down the message in their hearts as they listen receive a marked-down life.

So what does it look like to “listen well”? Isaiah 50:4 gives us a beautiful picture: “The Lord Yahweh has given me the tongue of those who are taught, that I may know how to sustain with words him who is weary. He awakens morning by morning, he awakens my ear to hear as those who are taught.” See the connection here: the tongue that sustains others comes from a taught ear — and it is “morning by morning.” This verse might almost have been written for 321 Morning Devotion.

The boy Samuel shows us the way too. 1 Samuel 3:10: “Yahweh came, and stood, and called as at other times, ‘Samuel! Samuel!’ Then Samuel said, ‘Speak; for your servant hears.’” That sentence, “Speak; for your servant hears,” is worth saying every morning before we open our Bibles. So often our prayers turn it upside down: “Listen, Lord, for your servant is speaking.”

As for “hearing without taking it in,” this is not indifference; it is spiritual discipline. Proverbs 26:20 says, “For lack of wood a fire goes out. Without gossip, a quarrel dies down.” If a piece of gossip has no next stop after you, it goes out. 321 speaks of the 235 relationships — spiritual companions, spiritual parents and spiritual children, a fivefold-ministry team — and the quickest way to damage a team is to let judgmental words circulate freely. Guard your ears, and you guard the team.

Modern psychology offers some intriguing support for “selective listening.” In 1953 the British cognitive scientist Colin Cherry carried out his famous “dichotic listening” experiments and described the “cocktail party effect”: at a noisy party, people can focus on one person’s voice and push all the other voices into the background; but the moment someone nearby says their name, their attention is instantly pulled away. This shows two things: first, we really are able to choose what we listen to; second, the things we care about most will automatically break through every filter we have.

Brothers and sisters, what kind of voice instantly grabs your attention amid all the noise? Other people’s opinions of you, or God’s word? Whatever you care about most is what you will automatically hear.

3. Keep Your Heart — Post a Guard at the Heart’s Gate

Our lesson says: we cannot control every voice we hear, but we can choose what we let into our hearts.

This sentence is very important, because it protects us from falling into two extremes. One extreme is laxity: since I can’t avoid it anyway, I’ll watch everything and listen to everything. The other is escape: I’ll just cut myself off from the world and have contact with nothing. The Lord Jesus prayed for us, “I pray not that you would take them from the world, but that you would keep them from the evil one” (John 17:15). We are not called out of the world; we are called to be gatekeepers.

That is why our theme verse says, “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23).

“With all diligence” — the Chinese Union Version says “above all that you guard”: of everything you have to guard, the heart comes first. We put passcodes on our phones and locks on our houses, yet we often leave our hearts wide open all day long.

“Out of it is the wellspring of life” — the word for “wellspring” here is the Hebrew tôts’āôt, whose basic meaning is “outlets, the place where a source flows out.” Your heart is the source; if the source is clean, the river will be clean. The Lord Jesus says it even more directly: “For out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks” (Matthew 12:34).

The father of American psychology, William James, wrote a famous sentence in “The Principles of Psychology” (1890): “My experience is what I agree to attend to.” Brothers and sisters, your experience of life is not determined by what happens, but by what you agree to pay attention to. Two people walk down the same street: one sees only rubbish, the other sees flowers. The same street, two worlds.

At the opening of his “Confessions,” Augustine says, “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.” Our hearts are made with a God-shaped space. If we don’t fill it with God’s word, the world will certainly fill it with something else. The heart is never left empty.

4. Applying the 321 Vision: Living Out the Lesson of Keeping the Gate

Brothers and sisters, this third key point lands right at the heart of the 920 practice in 321.

The 920 practice says: every person we are in relationship with is our “2”; in these relationships we practise living a selfless (0) life and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions. And notice: of the fruits listed in Galatians 5:22–23 — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control — the last one is precisely “self-control.” Self-control is not only about controlling our appetite and temper; it also means controlling our eyes and our ears.

Why is keeping the gate so hard? Because the self-centred life always wants everything. Self-centred people are afraid of missing out, afraid of falling behind, afraid of being left out of the conversation, so they have to watch everything, hear everything, know everything. Selfless people are secure, because they know their worth isn’t given to them by information; it is given by Jesus.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. Only someone who has returned to their originally intended position can keep watch over their eyes and ears, because they don’t need to prove themselves by being on top of every piece of information.

Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. In our chat groups, our families and our teams, let one judgmental word in and it sets off another; let one word that builds up in and it draws out another. Every one of us is someone else’s source of information. Brothers and sisters, please remember: you are not only filtering the information others give you; you are also producing the information others have to filter.

Proverbs 18:21 says, “Death and life are in the power of the tongue; those who love it will eat its fruit.” Our mouths are other people’s entrances.

sections.heading: 6. Integrating the 321 Vision: From One Piece of Information to God’s System
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s put today’s three key points back into the big picture of 321.

1. The Three Foundations Are Three Floodgates for Information

Jesus is my role model — he determines what counts as “right” for me to take in. When the Lord Jesus was tempted in the wilderness, all three times he answered, “It is written” (Matthew 4:4, 7, 10). Satan fed him information, and the Lord turned that information back with the word of God. The Lord himself said, “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds out of God’s mouth” (Matthew 4:4). He is our role model in keeping the gate.

The Bible is my standard — it determines the ruler I measure with. 2 Timothy 3:16–17: “Every Scripture is God-breathed and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness, that each person who belongs to God may be complete, thoroughly equipped for every good work.” All the information in the world needs a ruler, and that ruler is the Bible.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — he determines when information becomes revelation. Hebrews 4:12: “For the word of God is living and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing even to the dividing of soul and spirit, of both joints and marrow, and is able to discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart.” God’s word can discern the thoughts of our hearts — that is the power of information once the Holy Spirit has lit it up.

2. The Two Core Values: Let Jesus Reign as King over My Eyes and Ears

“Let Jesus be King” sounds grand, but it always lands somewhere very concrete. This morning it lands somewhere very small: who is in charge of my eyes and my ears?

2 Corinthians 10:5 says, “throwing down imaginations and every high thing that is exalted against the knowledge of God and bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ.” The verb “bringing into captivity,” aichmalōtizō in the original, is the word for taking prisoners on the battlefield. Our thoughts had been carried off captive by wrong information; now we must take them back and bring them into obedience to Christ.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — when a person’s mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry have all changed, what others see is not that this person has become impressive, but that Jesus is in this person. That is what it means for the glory to go to Jesus.

3. The Goal: Establish God’s System

When one person’s mindset changes, one person is saved; when a whole group’s mindset changes, it becomes a system. 321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things. The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. Today’s lesson begins precisely with “with God” — every morning, let God’s word come in first.

The 235 relationships are built the same way. The “2” is a spiritual companion, two selfless people walking alongside each other; the “3” is the passing on from spiritual parents to spiritual children; the “5” is a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. And what is the common language of all of this? One and the same source of information — the word of God. If everyone in a team feeds themselves on different information, sooner or later their relationships will fork apart; if every day they share the same bread of the word, their relationships will naturally become one.

4. The Fivefold Change Is Right Here in This Lesson

Mindset changes: I no longer think that “having heard it” means “having received it.”

Life changes: every day I let God’s word take the lead in my thinking.

Daily living changes: I begin to be selective about what I look at, what I listen to and what I say.

Relationships change: I no longer pass on judgmental words; I become a source of information through which others are blessed.

Ministry changes: the people I serve are built up by the information I pass on.

These five changes are not five separate things; they are five stretches of one river. If the source is clean, the whole river is clean.

5. A Shift in Perspective

From man’s perspective to God’s: not asking, “Is this piece of news interesting?” but, “Does this piece of news glorify God?”

From the earthly perspective to the heavenly: not asking, “What do other people think of me?” but, “What does God think of me?”

From the temporary perspective to the eternal: not asking, “Will this make me happy today?” but, “Does this have value for eternity?”

From the worldly perspective to the godly: not asking, “What is everybody watching?” but, “What does my Lord want me to look at?”
