Ephesians 4:22–24 says, “that you put away, as concerning your former way of life, the old man that grows corrupt after the lusts of deceit, and that you be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who in the likeness of God has been created in righteousness and holiness of truth.” Notice the sentence in the middle — “be renewed in the spirit of your mind.” Between putting off the old self and putting on the new self stands precisely the renewal of the mind.

And the pattern of the new self is what Galatians 2:20 describes: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living that fullness out — “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me.

sections.heading: 7. Putting It into Practice: Walking Through the Three Lessons with the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset
sections.html:
Our lesson gives us three practices for daily living. Let’s set them within the eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — so that they are not just three good suggestions but a road we can actually walk to the end.

Practice 1: Spend Fifteen Minutes a Day Listening to God’s Word

The practice in our lesson: spend fifteen minutes a day listening to God’s word — for example, reading the Bible or listening to a sermon — and let right information renew your thinking.

Information: fix the time, fix the place, fix the reading plan. Don’t wait until you “feel moved” to read; keep to it like mealtimes. Joshua 1:8: “This book of the law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, that you may observe to do according to all that is written in it; for then you shall make your way prosperous, and then you shall have good success.”

Revelation: when you’ve finished reading, be quiet for one minute and ask the Holy Spirit one question: “Lord, which sentence are you speaking to me today?” Copy that sentence onto a small card. Information often becomes revelation in exactly that one minute.

Conviction: move that word from “this is true” to “this is truth spoken to me.” Try making a sentence: “Because God says …, today I will ….”

Implementation: put it to use that same day. A truth needs to be used at least once within twenty-four hours if it is going to stay.

Evaluation: in the last minute before you sleep, ask yourself: did I use today’s word? Where did I get stuck?

Correction: not self-blame, but adjustment. If the time isn’t working, change the time; if the method isn’t working, change the method.

Repetition: forty days in a row. According to the law of learning Hebb proposed in 1949, a new pathway of thought has to be walked again and again before a footpath becomes a road.

Multiplication: find someone, share with them what you’ve received over these forty days, and invite them to do it with you. Psalm 119:11 says, “I have hidden your word in my heart, that I might not sin against you.” What is hidden in our hearts must in the end flow into other people’s hearts.

Practice 2: List three pieces of negative information you’ve taken in recently, and deliberately move away from them or stop taking them in

The practice in our lesson: list three pieces of negative information you’ve taken in recently (for example, from the media, social media or conversations), and deliberately move away from them or stop taking them in.

Information: take a sheet of paper and write honestly. Which account? Which group chat? Which conversation? Which time of day? The more specific, the better.

Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light — which kind of self-centred life inside me are these three things feeding? The pride that fears being outdone? The anxiety that fears being left out? Or the desire to control other people?

Conviction: admit one thing: I’m not being forced; I’m being drawn. The real battle isn’t in my phone; it’s in my heart.

Implementation: take one concrete action right away. Unfollow, turn off notifications, charge your phone in another room, set a certain time of day as “no screens.” Don’t just decide; act.

Evaluation: after a week, look at how much time you’ve gained, and how much quieter your heart has become.

Correction: if there’s one thing you really can’t give up, don’t fight alone; find a spiritual companion to walk with you — that is the “2” of 321.

Repetition: make the list again a month later. Keeping the gate is a lifelong work, not a one-off activity.

Multiplication: when someone asks you, “How did you become so much more at peace?” share with them what you did with this list.

Practice 3: Practise listening attentively for God’s voice, and when facing a choice, first ask, “Does this come from God’s word?”

The practice in our lesson: in daily life, practise “listening attentively for God’s voice,” and whenever you face a choice, first ask yourself: does this come from God’s word?

Information: write this question down and stick it somewhere you’re sure to see every day — beside your computer screen, in your car, on your mirror.

Revelation: in John 10:27 the Lord says, “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.” Hearing the Lord’s voice is not a privilege reserved for special conferences; it is the instinct of a sheep. You are a sheep; you can hear.

Conviction: believe that God still speaks, and that what he says never contradicts the Bible.

Implementation: before you make a decision today, pause for thirty seconds and ask this question — even if it’s only replying to a message.

Evaluation: in the evening, look back: how many times today did I ask first, and how many times didn’t I?

Correction: the times you didn’t ask usually share a pattern — being in a hurry, emotions running high, or caring what others think. Find the pattern, and you’ve found the breach in the wall.

Repetition: 1 Thessalonians 5:21 says, “Test all things, and hold firmly that which is good.” Testing all things means asking, again and again.

Multiplication: teach this question to your family and to your small group. When everyone in a family asks this one question, that family begins to become God’s system.

sections.heading: 8. Closing and Call: Begin with Information, and Let Revival Come
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, the conclusion of our lesson puts it well: information is the beginning of a change of mindset, and the starting point of a renewed life. If we are willing to let right information — the word of God — keep flowing into our hearts, the Holy Spirit can work within us, bringing old thinking into the light and building up new life. Begin with information, and the mindset will be renewed; when the mindset is renewed, the life changes; when the life changes, revival comes.

Our lesson also gives us a gentle reminder: what you look at, listen to and think about every day determines your future. Wrong information throws the heart into confusion; right information fills the heart with light. Choose every day to let God’s word take the lead in your thinking.

In Isaiah 55:11 God promises, “so is my word that goes out of my mouth: it will not return to me void, but it will accomplish that which I please, and it will prosper in the thing I sent it to do.” Brothers and sisters, not one word of God that we have received this morning will return empty; it will go on working in us, day by day, week by week, year by year.

Psalm 1:2–3 paints the outcome: “but his delight is in Yahweh’s law. On his law he meditates day and night. He will be like a tree planted by the streams of water, that produces its fruit in its season, whose leaf also does not wither. Whatever he does shall prosper.” A tree bears fruit not because it strains, but because it stands by the streams of water. Our responsibility is not to struggle to bear fruit; it is to sink our roots into living water every day.

So this morning, let us answer this call together:

Let Jesus reign as King over my eyes — I choose to look at what he wants me to look at.

Let Jesus reign as King over my ears — I choose to listen to what he wants me to hear.

Let Jesus reign as King over my mind — I take back my thoughts and bring them into obedience to Christ.

May all the glory go to Jesus.

keyVerses: Proverbs 4:23
“Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.”
Romans 10:17
“So faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.”
practices: Spend fifteen minutes a day listening to God’s word
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,
We come before you this early morning. Thank you that you are the God who speaks; thank you that your word is a lamp to our feet and a light for our path.

Lord, forgive us. So often we hear a great deal and change very little; we pile your words up in our heads but never plant them in our hearts. And so often we look carelessly and listen carelessly, letting the voices of the world quietly shape us.

Today, please be the guard at the gate of our hearts yourself. Help us to keep our hearts above all else. Holy Spirit, turn the information we have received today into real revelation; turn revelation into conviction, conviction into practice, and practice into a lifelong habit — and let us pass it on to the next person.
Lord, I give you my eyes, I give you my ears, I give you my mind. Reign as King within me, so that it is no longer I who live, but you who live in me.
May our mindsets be renewed, our lives changed, our families built up and our teams raised up; may revival begin in the heart of every one of us.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Proverbs 4:23: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” Think back over the past month: which piece of information (a video, a remark, a news story) clearly affected your emotions or decisions? If you could go back, how would you stand guard at the gate of your heart?

Romans 10:17: “So faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.” At present, how and when do you take in God’s word each day? What one concrete adjustment will you make this week so that “information” has a chance to become “revelation”? Say it out loud in your small group, and ask a spiritual companion to remind you next week.

l042.subtitle: The First Stage of Changing Our Mindset: Information
l042.partTitle: Unit 4 · The Prerequisite for Revival — A Change of Mindset

sections.heading: Introduction: Information Lets Us Know; Revelation Lets Us See
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, peace to you this morning. Let’s begin today’s devotion with an experience a great many of us have had.

There was a brother who had been a believer for twenty-three years and had never once missed a Sunday service. His Bible was worn soft at the edges, his notebooks filled one after another, and a whole row of commentaries stood on the bookshelf at home. Someone asked him, “You’ve believed for so long — what has been your greatest struggle?” He was silent for a long while. Then he said quietly, “I know everything. I just can’t live it.”

Brothers and sisters, haven’t those words echoed in your heart and mine at some point? We know we should forgive, and we still hold grudges; we know we should be humble, and we still compete; we know God is love, and yet we toss and turn in the middle of the night, feeling that God is far away. Our heads are full of Bible knowledge, but our lives haven’t changed to match. So where exactly is the problem?

The lesson’s introduction puts its finger right on it: information lets us “know”, but revelation lets us “see”. Without the help of the Holy Spirit, our mindset stays forever at the level of head knowledge and never becomes power for living.

In 1885 the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus carried out the first systematic memory experiment in human history. Using himself as the subject, he measured again and again how much of what he had learned he could still recall. He found that twenty minutes after learning something, less than sixty per cent of it remained; after a day, only about a third. This is the famous “forgetting curve”.

Brothers and sisters, that is exactly the fate of “information”. While we’re listening our hearts are warm; once we walk out the door it fades; a few days later it’s forgotten; a few months later we can’t even remember what the speaker’s topic was. With information alone, we will never outrun the speed of forgetting. That’s why some people hear a thousand sermons and their lives stay right where they were; some read the whole Bible through and their temper hasn’t changed one bit.

But brothers and sisters, have you noticed that there is a kind of “knowing” you never forget as long as you live? That day, that morning, that sentence that suddenly pierced your heart — you may even remember the weather, the seat you were in, the cup in your hand. From that day on, something was different. That wasn’t information. That was revelation.

The revelation of the Holy Spirit is like light. It shines into our hearts, so that the truth is no longer mere words on a page but a light that can change a life. When information passes through revelation, it becomes the power that sets a life in motion, carrying us from “hearing” to “understanding”, and from “understanding” to “living it out”.

In the 321 teaching, the eight stages of changing our mindset are Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition and Multiplication. In the last lesson we learned the first stage, “Information”. Today we move into the second — “Revelation”. This stage is the decisive turning point in the whole process of changing our mindset: information stays in the head, revelation goes into the heart; information is what someone else tells me, revelation is what God himself says to me.

Today we’ll follow the lesson’s three key points: first, revelation is the key to the transformation of our mindset; second, the revelation of the Holy Spirit turns us from discouragement to strength; third, humility is the door to revelation.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: An Opening on an Easter Evening
sections.html:
To understand a verse, we first need to know its author, its audience and its setting.

The author of the Gospel of Luke is Luke. He was Paul’s co-worker, and in his letters Paul calls him “Luke the beloved physician” (Colossians 4:14). He is generally thought to have been a Gentile, the only Gentile author in the New Testament. He wrote the Gospel of Luke and the Acts of the Apostles, and together those two books are longer than all of Paul’s letters combined. They are generally dated between AD 60 and 65, and were written for a man of rank named Theophilus.

At the start of his book Luke explains his purpose: “having traced the course of all things accurately from the first, to write to you in order, most excellent Theophilus; that you might know the certainty concerning the things in which you were instructed” (Luke 1:3–4). Notice the word “certainty”. In the Greek it is ἀσφάλεια (asphaleia), meaning firm, reliable, unshakeable. In other words, what Luke offers is first-hand, solid, utterly reliable “information”.

But brothers and sisters, here is something startling: the disciples had all of this solid information. They had heard Jesus preach with their own ears, seen the five loaves and two fish with their own eyes, touched the Lord with their own hands before the resurrection. At least three times Jesus told them in plain words that he would suffer, be killed and rise on the third day. And still they didn’t understand. Luke himself records it: “But they didn’t understand this saying. It was concealed from them, that they should not perceive it, and they were afraid to ask him about this saying” (Luke 9:45). And again: “They understood none of these things. This saying was hidden from them, and they didn’t understand the things that were said” (Luke 18:34).

And so we come to Luke 24. It is the day Jesus rose from the dead. In the early morning the women find the empty tomb and come back with the news, and the apostles’ response is this: “These words seemed to them to be nonsense, and they didn’t believe them” (Luke 24:11). In the afternoon two disciples are on the road to Emmaus, walking along and “sad” (Luke 24:17). The risen Lord himself comes near and walks with them, and Scripture says, “But their eyes were kept from recognizing him” (Luke 24:16).

Brothers and sisters, look closely at this picture: the Truth was walking right beside them, and they could not recognise him. The problem wasn’t too little information. The problem was that their eyes had not been opened.

Then the Lord did two things. The first was that he explained: “Beginning from Moses and from all the prophets, he explained to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luke 24:27). The second was that he opened: as he broke the bread, “Their eyes were opened and they recognized him” (Luke 24:31). Only at that moment did it dawn on them, and they said to one another, “Weren’t our hearts burning within us, while he spoke to us along the way, and while he opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24:32).

That same evening the Lord appeared to the Eleven and did the very same two things again. First he explained the Scriptures, and then — and this is our theme verse today — “Then he opened their minds, that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24:45).

The word “opened” in Greek is διανοίγω (dianoigō), formed from two roots meaning “thoroughly” and “open”. It means to open completely, to prise open, to throw wide something that was shut. Interestingly, Luke uses this word three times in the same chapter: the Lord “opened” their eyes (verse 31), the Lord “opened” the Scriptures — in the original, laying the truth open to them (verse 32), and the Lord “opened” their minds (verse 45). The same word appears again in Acts 16:14: “The Lord opened her heart to listen to the things which were spoken by Paul.” That was the moment Lydia came to faith.

The word translated “minds” is νοῦς (nous) in Greek. It refers to a person’s thinking, their understanding, the whole inner system by which they make sense of things. In today’s language, that is our “mindset”. Brothers and sisters, notice this: the Lord Jesus didn’t change their circumstances first or their status first. He opened their nous first — he changed their mindset first. This is exactly what 321 calls the fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. The starting point of everything is a mindset that has been opened.

And there is an order here we must not miss: the Lord explained first and opened their minds afterwards. Information first, then revelation. Without information, revelation has no content, and people easily slip into reading the Bible by their feelings and making it say whatever they like. Without revelation, information has no power, and the more people hear, the colder they grow. Brothers and sisters, we cannot do without either one.

sections.heading: Key Point 1: Revelation Is the Key to the Transformation of Our Mindset
sections.html:
The lesson says that without the revelation of the Holy Spirit, our knowledge remains dead. The Pharisees knew the Law inside out, yet they could not recognise the Messiah standing right before their eyes, because they had only “information” and no “revelation”.

In fact it was not only the Pharisees. When the Lord Jesus taught the crowds in parables, he said something very weighty about those who heard and yet did not understand, recorded in Matthew 13: “In them the prophecy of Isaiah is fulfilled, which says, ‘By hearing you will hear, and will in no way understand; Seeing you will see, and will in no way perceive’” (Matthew 13:14).

These words were first spoken by God to Isaiah at his calling (Isaiah 6:9). More than seven hundred years later, the Lord Jesus pointed to the crowds of his day who heard him with hardened hearts and said the words had been fulfilled in them. There was nothing wrong with their ears, and nothing wrong with their eyes; the trouble was in the heart. The next verse goes on: “for this people’s heart has grown callous, their ears are dull of hearing, they have closed their eyes; or else perhaps they might perceive with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and would turn again; and I would heal them” (Matthew 13:15).

The Greek word for “understand” here is συνίημι (syniēmi), which literally means “to put things together”. Brothers and sisters, what a vivid word that is. Understanding isn’t knowing a lot; understanding is when scattered fragments suddenly fit together, when it all suddenly “clicks”. You might have a hundred jigsaw pieces in your hands and see every one of them perfectly clearly, but if you can’t fit them together, you’ll never see the picture. Revelation is the moment the Holy Spirit fits the pieces together.

Let Scripture interpret Scripture. The Lord Jesus said to people who knew the Bible thoroughly, “You search the Scriptures, because you think that in them you have eternal life; and these are they which testify about me. Yet you will not come to me, that you may have life” (John 5:39–40). Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: they searched the Scriptures, yet would not come to the Lord; they held the finest information in the world, yet walked straight past life. Paul says too, “Now the natural man doesn’t receive the things of God’s Spirit, for they are foolishness to him, and he can’t know them, because they are spiritually discerned” (1 Corinthians 2:14). “He can’t know them” — not that he won’t, but that he can’t. It is a question of ability, not of willingness.

Paul also says, “But to us, God revealed them through the Spirit. For the Spirit searches all things, yes, the deep things of God” (1 Corinthians 2:10). Brothers and sisters, that is the definition of revelation: not man climbing up to discover God, but God stooping down to make himself known to man.

Let’s look at a scientific illustration. In 1999 two American psychologists, Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris, published an experiment in the journal Perception that went on to become world-famous. They asked participants to watch a short video in which two teams pass a basketball, and gave them the task of counting how many passes the team in white made. Halfway through, a person in a gorilla suit walks slowly into the very centre of the frame, stops, beats its chest, and walks slowly out again — about nine seconds in all. And the result? Around half of the participants never saw the gorilla at all. When the video was replayed, they couldn’t believe their own eyes.

Psychologists call this “inattentional blindness”. Brothers and sisters, isn’t this exactly what the Lord Jesus said? “Seeing you will see, and will in no way perceive.” The eyes are fine, the light is good enough, the thing is right in the middle of the picture — but the heart isn’t prepared, and so people simply don’t see.

In fact our eyes have a blind spot built in. On the retina of each eye, at the point where the optic nerve passes out, there are no light-sensitive cells, so that small patch sees nothing at all. Yet we’re normally completely unaware of it, because the brain automatically fills in the surrounding pattern and lets us believe we’re seeing a complete world. Brothers and sisters, what an exact picture that is: our hearts have blind spots too, and the most frightening thing is this — our hearts automatically “fill in” the gap for us, so that we think we already understand.

Here is another comparison. A man has memorised an entire musical score; he knows every note and every rest. But he has never once heard the piece performed. One day he sits in a concert hall, the orchestra strikes its first chord, and suddenly tears are running down his face. Brothers and sisters, not a single note of the score has changed. What has changed is that he has heard it. Information is the score; revelation is the moment the music actually sounds.

The sixteenth-century Reformer John Calvin, in Book One, Chapter Six of his Institutes of the Christian Religion, used a famous comparison: the Word of God is like a pair of spectacles. A person with blurred sight, even holding a book right before his eyes, sees only a confused mass; put on spectacles, and the words become clear. Calvin goes on in Chapter Seven to explain “the inner testimony of the Holy Spirit”: our certainty that the Bible is God’s Word rests in the end not on human argument but on the Holy Spirit bearing witness in our hearts. Brothers and sisters, the Bible is the spectacles; the Holy Spirit is the eyesight. With spectacles but no eyesight, you still can’t see.

Paul puts the difference between the two as plainly as it can be put: “For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Corinthians 3:6). And he says, “But whenever someone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away” (2 Corinthians 3:16). Brothers and sisters, the veil isn’t over the Bible; the veil is over the human heart.

Brothers and sisters, here we need to make an important distinction. The “revelation” Scripture speaks of works at two levels. The first level is the completion of special revelation: God delivered his plan of salvation to the saints once for all, and it was written down as the Bible. “Every Scripture is God-breathed and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness” (2 Timothy 3:16). Revelation at this level is complete; no one may add to it and no one may take away from it. The second level is the Holy Spirit opening up this already-written Bible to particular people at particular moments, so that their hearts truly understand. The “revelation” we are speaking of today is this second level. Brothers and sisters, the distinction matters a great deal: true revelation never contradicts Scripture; it always brings us back to Scripture. Any “new revelation” that goes beyond the standard of Scripture does not come from the Holy Spirit. The Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide — these two foundations always stand together and never clash.

From the 321 perspective, this is precisely the third of the Three Foundations: the Holy Spirit is my guide. We often stop at the second — the Bible is my standard — and forget the Guide who lights up that standard. 321 reminds us: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll have joy, rely on the brain and you’ll have worry. The wellspring of life flows from the heart, not from the brain. When we do nothing but analyse with our heads, the truth becomes distant, hard to live and heavy with pressure; when we rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, the very same sentence becomes light.

Brothers and sisters, this is the power of revelation: it turns lifeless rules into truth charged with life.

sections.heading: Key Point 2: The Revelation of the Holy Spirit Turns Us from Discouragement to Strength
sections.html:
The lesson says that Jesus’ disciples are the truest example of this. They had followed Jesus for years and heard countless teachings, and still they didn’t understand his words — until, after his resurrection, Jesus appeared to them himself and opened their minds to understand the Scriptures. In that moment their mindset was turned upside down.

Listen once more to our theme verse: “Then he opened their minds, that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24:45).

Brothers and sisters, notice the contrast between the disciples’ lives before and after. It is a watershed, deep and unmistakable.

Before revelation, what state were they in? When the Lord was arrested, “all the disciples left him and fled” (Matthew 26:56). Peter denied the Lord three times and went out and wept bitterly. On the day of the resurrection they dismissed the women’s testimony as nonsense. The two on the Emmaus road, sad-faced, said, “But we were hoping that it was he who would redeem Israel” (Luke 24:21) — “we were hoping”: that is the past tense, a hope that had already gone out. By evening, John records, “the doors were locked where the disciples were assembled, for fear of the Jews” (John 20:19). The doors were shut, and so were their hearts.

But after revelation? On the day of Pentecost, “They were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and began to speak with other languages, as the Spirit gave them the ability to speak” (Acts 2:4). The Peter who had trembled before a servant girl stood up and preached at the top of his voice, and that day about three thousand people turned to the Lord (Acts 2:41). Later, when they were hauled before the Council for trial, Scripture says, “Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and had perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marveled. They recognized that they had been with Jesus” (Acts 4:13).

The word “boldness” in Greek is παρρησία (parrēsia). Its root meaning is “to say everything”, and from that it came to mean openness without fear, speech that holds nothing back. Brothers and sisters, the same group of people, the same surroundings — the Roman soldiers were still there, the power of the Council was still there. What changed wasn’t their circumstances; it was the mindset within them. Before, they had only “known” the truth of Jesus; now they were “living out” the truth of Jesus. Revelation turned them from weakness to strength and from fear to courage, and it brought the first wave of revival in the history of the church.

Let’s look at two true testimonies from church history.

The first is Martin Luther. He was a monk and a professor of the Bible; no one could say he lacked biblical knowledge. Yet he admitted himself that he hated the words “the righteousness of God”, because he thought it meant the righteousness by which God judges sinners. Day and night he wrestled with Romans 1:17: “For in it is revealed God’s righteousness from faith to faith. As it is written, ‘But the righteous shall live by faith.’” In 1545, in the preface he wrote for the complete edition of his Latin works, Luther recalled that suddenly, in one moment, he understood — the righteousness of God is not the righteousness by which God judges us, but the righteousness God gives us freely through faith. He described how he “felt that I was altogether born again and had entered paradise itself through open gates”.

Brothers and sisters, notice this: not one word of that verse had changed. Luther had read it hundreds of times. What changed wasn’t the text; it was that his mind had been opened. And that one opening turned around not only the life of a single monk, but the whole history of the Western church.

The second is John Wesley. He was an Oxford scholar and had served as a missionary; he fasted, he prayed, he gave to the poor — he did it all, yet he never had any assurance of salvation. On the evening of 24 May 1738 he went, very reluctantly, to a small meeting in Aldersgate Street in London. Someone there was reading Martin Luther’s preface to the Epistle to the Romans. Wesley wrote in his journal the words that are still quoted today: he felt his heart “strangely warmed”, and he was assured that Christ had taken away his sins and saved him from the law of sin and death. From that night on, a servant who would bring a great spiritual revival to England was born.

Brothers and sisters, look: Luther was in his study, Wesley was at a small meeting, the disciples were on the road and at the supper table. The lesson is right: the revelation of the Holy Spirit is not bound by time or place. He can enlighten us in prayer, and he can also bring us to a sudden “Now I see it!” in a conversation, at a meeting, even in an ordinary everyday situation.

Psychology has studied this kind of “Now I see it!” too. In 1917 the German psychologist Wolfgang Köhler published The Mentality of Apes, recording his observations on the island of Tenerife. A chimpanzee named Sultan simply could not reach a banana outside his cage. First he gave up and sat motionless; then after a while he suddenly leapt up, fitted two short bamboo sticks together into one long pole, and in one move drew the banana in. Köhler pointed out that this wasn’t learned slowly through trial and error; it was an instant reorganisation — what he called “insight”.

Modern brain science has gone further still. Mark Beeman of Northwestern University in the United States and John Kounios of Drexel University worked together, using brain waves and functional MRI to study people’s “aha moments” as they solved puzzles. In research published in 2004 in PLoS Biology, they found that when someone solves a problem through insight, a specific area of the right temporal lobe shows a burst of high-frequency gamma waves; and in the split second just before that, the brain shows a burst of activity like “shutting out the outside world” — which in their later book The Eureka Factor (2015) they described as the brain’s “blink”.

Brothers and sisters, what a beautiful picture this is: even science tells us that before insight comes, the brain first turns off the light from outside and grows quiet within. Spiritual revelation is all the more like that. Stillness is the prelude to revelation; waiting is the preparation for illumination. No wonder the psalmist says, “Be still, and know that I am God” (Psalm 46:10).

The Old Testament has the same picture. The king of Aram’s troops surrounded the city of Dothan by night. Elisha’s servant got up early, looked out, and saw an army with horses and chariots all around the city. In alarm he cried, “Alas, my master! What shall we do?” Elisha didn’t tell him to count the enemy’s horses and soldiers, nor did he hand him an escape plan. Scripture records: “Elisha prayed, and said, ‘Yahweh, please open his eyes, that he may see.’ Yahweh opened the young man’s eyes; and he saw: and behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire around Elisha” (2 Kings 6:17). Brothers and sisters, notice this: the horses and chariots of fire on the mountain were there all along, from beginning to end; they were there before the servant’s eyes were opened. What changed wasn’t the facts; it was that he saw the facts. That is revelation. The difficulties you and I face today may not disappear by tomorrow morning; but when the Lord opens our eyes, we will see that those who surround us are more than those who besiege us.

From the 321 perspective, the disciples’ change is a complete demonstration of the fivefold change: a change of mindset — their minds were opened; a change of life — from fear to courage; a change of daily living — no longer hiding behind locked doors; a change of relationships — they were of one heart and mind, together in the temple day by day; a change of ministry — the gospel went from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth. Brothers and sisters, this order must not be reversed. 321 stresses it again and again: life first, then relationships, then ministry. We are often in a hurry to do ministry and skip over life; but the disciples were opened first, and only then did they go out.

So it is with us today — only when the Holy Spirit opens the eyes of our hearts does the truth come alive in our lives.

sections.heading: Key Point 3: Humility Is the Door to Revelation
sections.html:
The lesson says that revelation does not come through cleverness; it comes out of humility.

This is how the Lord Jesus prayed: “At that time, Jesus answered, ‘I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you hid these things from the wise and understanding, and revealed them to infants. Yes, Father, for so it was well-pleasing in your sight’” (Matthew 11:25–26).

Notice the context. This prayer comes right after the Lord Jesus rebuked three towns: Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum. Those three towns had seen more miracles than any others, and still they did not repent. Immediately afterwards the Lord lifted his eyes and gave thanks to the Father, because God had hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to infants.

The Greek word for “infants” is νήπιος (nēpios), which literally means “one who cannot yet speak”. A child who can’t yet talk can claim nothing for himself; he depends on others for everything. “The wise and understanding”, on the other hand, is σοφῶν καὶ συνετῶν — the wise, the discerning. Brothers and sisters, it isn’t that God dislikes intelligence; it’s that God cannot make himself known to those who “think they already have enough”.

The lesson puts it with great precision: revelation does not belong to the proud, because pride makes people think, “I already understand”; revelation belongs to the humble, because humility makes people willing to admit, “Lord, I still need your light.”

Let Scripture interpret Scripture. When Peter recognised at Caesarea Philippi that Jesus was the Christ, the Lord immediately said to him, “Blessed are you, Simon Bar Jonah, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 16:17). That confession was not something Peter reasoned his way to; the Father revealed it. Paul likewise says the gospel he preached “came to me through revelation of Jesus Christ” (Galatians 1:12).

Scripture repeats the same sentence in two places: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6; 1 Peter 5:5). Brothers and sisters, the word “resists”, ἀντιτάσσομαι (antitassomai) in Greek, is a military term: to draw up in battle array against. It isn’t merely that the proud fail to receive revelation; it’s that God himself draws up his ranks against them. By contrast, the psalmist says, “The friendship of Yahweh is with those who fear him. He will show them his covenant” (Psalm 25:14).

So true prayer sounds like this: “Open my eyes, that I may see wondrous things out of your law” (Psalm 119:18). And this is how Paul prayed for the church: “that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give to you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him, having the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know what is the hope of his calling, and what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints” (Ephesians 1:17–18). Brothers and sisters, notice that what Paul asks for the believers isn’t new information; it is enlightened eyes of the heart.

Here’s an illustration. A seeker went to visit a teacher, and before the conversation had even begun he was holding forth about how much he knew. The teacher quietly poured him tea, and when the cup was full he kept on pouring, until tea ran all over the table. The seeker cried out, “It’s full! It’s full!” The teacher set down the teapot and said, “You are like this cup. You are already full. How can I pour anything in?” Brothers and sisters, nothing can go into a cup that is already full, however fine the tea. The most frightening thing about pride isn’t that it makes people do wrong; it’s that it makes them think they don’t need the light.

Consider a scientific fact. When our eyes go from a bright place into a dark room, at first we can see nothing at all; full “dark adaptation” takes about twenty to thirty minutes. During that time the rod cells of the retina regenerate their light-sensitive pigment, and their sensitivity can rise to tens of thousands of times what it was, until even the faintest starlight becomes visible. Brothers and sisters, there is a spiritual lesson here: to see a faint light, you must first be still, first wait, first stop lighting yourself up with the glare of your own self. The impatient never see the stars.

The Church Father Augustine has a famous saying, generally thought to come from his sermons: “Believe, so that you may understand” (crede ut intelligas). Later Anselm of Canterbury condensed it into a single phrase: faith seeking understanding. Brothers and sisters, the world says, “I’ll believe it when I see it”; the Bible says, “Believe, and you will see.” The Lord said to Martha, “Didn’t I tell you that if you believed, you would see God’s glory?” (John 11:40).

There’s something else we need to learn: revelation often comes gradually, and humility makes us willing to keep waiting. Mark’s Gospel records the Lord Jesus healing a blind man at Bethsaida — the only healing in the four Gospels completed in two stages. After the Lord first laid his hands on him, “He looked up, and said, ‘I see men; for I see them like trees walking.’” The Lord didn’t rebuke him, nor did he stop there: “Then again he laid his hands on his eyes. He looked intently, and was restored, and saw everyone clearly” (Mark 8:24–25). Brothers and sisters, have you ever been in that stage of “seeing, but seeing blurrily”? You know the Lord is speaking, but you can’t yet make out exactly what he’s saying. Don’t lose heart, and don’t pretend you already see clearly. The humble will come back to the Lord and say, “Lord, please lay your hands on me once more.” The proud will take the blurry half they have and say, “I see.”

The lesson says that every act of humility is a moment when the door of revelation is opened. When we are willing, as we listen to preaching, pray or read the Bible, to lay aside our own preconceptions and rational analysis and simply seek the light of the Holy Spirit, we will experience the grace of everything suddenly coming clear, and the truth will pass from “the letter” into “spirit and life”. The Lord himself said, “The words that I speak to you are spirit, and are life” (John 6:63).

From the 321 perspective, this is the very heart of the whole vision. 321 says that the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. What was the temptation in the Garden of Eden? “You will be like God, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:5). What Satan offered humanity was precisely a shortcut to “knowing” without depending on God. Brothers and sisters, that was the first time humanity tried to “get revelation on its own”, and the result was that their eyes were indeed opened — but what they saw was their own nakedness.

That’s why 321 says: humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. And selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering the boundless and living out the boundless — “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. Brothers and sisters, only a cup that has been emptied can hold the living water that comes from heaven.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: Let the Guide Be Our Teacher
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s look at today’s message once more within the framework of 321.

The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. In today’s lesson the emphasis falls especially on the third foundation. Many brothers and sisters work very hard at the second foundation — reading the Bible, studying it, listening to sermons, taking notes — and that is all excellent; but without the third foundation, we hold a pair of spectacles and have no eyesight. The Lord himself promised, “However when he, the Spirit of truth, has come, he will guide you into all truth” (John 16:13). And again, “But the Counselor, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things, and will remind you of all that I said to you” (John 14:26). Brothers and sisters, we have a Teacher who lives within us.

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. The purpose of revelation isn’t to make our knowledge richer so that we look impressive before others; the purpose of revelation is for Jesus truly to reign as King in our hearts. Paul speaks of “the knowledge of him” (Ephesians 1:17) — not true knowledge of “his teachings”, but true knowledge of “him”. And when he reigns as King, the glory naturally goes to him — because we know perfectly well that none of this was something I thought up; it was something he revealed.

The Goal: establish God’s system. A person who has been enlightened doesn’t stop at being moved himself; he carries that light into his family, into his small group, into his workplace, so that God’s order is established on earth.

A shift of perspective. 321 says: from man’s perspective to God’s perspective, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. The two disciples on the Emmaus road were seeing things from man’s perspective — all they could see was a failed cross and a shattered hope. What the Lord gave them wasn’t new news; it was a new perspective: “Didn’t the Christ have to suffer these things and to enter into his glory?” (Luke 24:26). Brothers and sisters, the same cross, seen from man’s perspective, is defeat; seen from God’s perspective, it is victory. Revelation is seeing the same thing with a new pair of eyes.

The Path of Serving. 321 sets out the order of serving in five words: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God. First comes the guidance of the Holy Spirit (Spirit), and only then true understanding (Understanding); with understanding, life takes shape (Life); with life comes service that pleases God (Service); and the end point of service is glory to God (God). In today’s lesson we are standing between “Spirit” and “Understanding” — and the door from “Spirit” to “Understanding” is called revelation.

The 920 practice. 920 reminds us that every person we have a relationship with is our “2”, and that we are to practise living a selfless (“0”) life that bears the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions. Brothers and sisters, how do you know whether what you’ve received is revelation or just excitement? The most reliable test isn’t feelings; it’s fruit. True revelation always makes a person humbler, with more love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23). If someone claims to have received great revelation yet grows ever prouder, ever more judgemental, ever harder to get along with, it’s most likely not light from heaven.

The 235 relationships. Revelation received by one person alone easily drains away, but revelation received by two or three together can take root. So we are to become a “2” with selfless people — spiritual companions who confirm each other; to establish a “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children, passing on what we’ve received; and finally to become a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. Brothers and sisters, on the Emmaus road there were two people; when the Lord opened their minds, they were together; and they immediately got up, went back to Jerusalem and told the Eleven what had happened. Revelation was never meant to be hidden away and enjoyed alone.

The fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. The first stop revelation changes is our mindset. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. Brothers and sisters, that is exactly where this lesson sits in the eight stages: information brings the fuel in; revelation sets it alight.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Bringing Revelation into Every Day
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices for daily living. Let’s take them one at a time, and then deepen them using the eight stages of changing our mindset in 321 — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

The first practice: in your daily devotions, begin by praying to the Holy Spirit, “Lord, please open the eyes of my heart, so that I understand your word.”

Brothers and sisters, this prayer is short, but it changes the whole nature of Bible reading. Without this prayer, reading the Bible is me studying a book; with this prayer, reading the Bible is God speaking to me. Please put this prayer before you open your Bible, not after. The psalmist prayed the same way: “Open my eyes, that I may see wondrous things out of your law” (Psalm 119:18). I suggest you copy this verse onto the flyleaf of your Bible and read it once every day before anything else.

The second practice: when you listen to a sermon or read the Bible, don’t rush to take notes or analyse; first quiet your heart and wait for the Holy Spirit to show you which sentence is spoken to you.

Brothers and sisters, this one takes a little courage, because we’re so used to “grabbing a bit more”. But remember the picture of dark adaptation: for the eyes to see a faint light, they first have to be still for twenty minutes. Here’s a suggestion: after reading a passage, be quiet for one minute, do no analysis at all, and simply ask the Lord, “Lord, which sentence do you want me to see today?” Then copy that sentence down — just the one sentence. One verse lit up by the Spirit is worth more than ten pages of lifeless notes.

The third practice: after talking with someone, sharing your testimony or serving, learn to ask the Lord, “Lord, what do you want me to understand today?”

Brothers and sisters, revelation doesn’t come only in the quiet of the morning; it also comes in the busyness of the day. An unpleasant conversation, a ministry that went wrong, a look from someone that left you feeling choked up inside — any of these can be the classroom where God wants to teach you a lesson. I suggest you spend three minutes before bed each night recalling the moment today that touched you most or stung you most, and then ask the Lord, “Lord, what do you want me to understand from this?” Write down the Lord’s answer.

Now let’s deepen these three practices with the eight stages.

Stage one, Information. The content of today’s lesson is information. First fix the key points in your mind: information lets us know, revelation lets us see; the Lord explained first and opened their minds afterwards; humility is the door to revelation. I suggest you memorise the theme verse, Luke 24:45.

Stage two, Revelation. Information can only go so far; from here it has to be handed over to the Holy Spirit. After this morning’s devotion, be still for three minutes and ask the Holy Spirit to place one sentence from these three key points into your heart. Don’t ask for all three — one is enough.

Stage three, Conviction. If revelation doesn’t lead to conviction, it stops at being moved. Ask yourself: do I truly believe that without the Holy Spirit’s light, no matter how much I read, I won’t be able to live it? Do I truly believe that humility gains God more than cleverness does? Conviction is the heart saying, “Yes, Lord, this is true.”

Stage four, Implementation. Starting tomorrow morning, for seven days in a row, before you open your Bible pray that one sentence: “Lord, please open the eyes of my heart.” After reading, copy out just one verse.

Stage five, Evaluation. After seven days, look back over those seven verses. Ask yourself: which of them really shaped what I said and did that day? On which days was I just rushing to finish and move on?

Stage six, Correction. If you find you’re always short of time, move your devotions ten minutes earlier; if you find you’re always analysing, close your notebook first; if you find something in your heart is blocking the way, deal with the relationship first and confess your sin first.

Stage seven, Repetition. Revelation isn’t a one-off experience; it’s a lifelong practice. After seven days, do another seven, and let it become a habit. Brothers and sisters, habits become character, and character becomes destiny.

Stage eight, Multiplication. Take the one sentence you’ve received and tell it to one person — your spouse, your children, your spiritual companion. That is 235: first a “2”, then a “3”. When the two disciples at Emmaus received revelation, they got up at once and went back to Jerusalem; they didn’t keep it for themselves.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: From Knowing About God to Knowing God
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, the lesson’s closing words are beautiful: revelation is the extension of information and the beginning of life. Without revelation, truth is only knowledge; with revelation, truth becomes life. When the Holy Spirit opens our hearts, we no longer merely “know about God”; we “know God”.

Between “knowing about God” and “knowing God” stands a door. That door is called humility, and the One who opens it is the Holy Spirit. The prophet Hosea says, “Let’s acknowledge Yahweh. Let’s press on to know Yahweh” (Hosea 6:3). Paul speaks of “the knowledge of him” (Ephesians 1:17). Brothers and sisters, this is the direction of our whole life.

So this morning I want to give you three calls.

First, ask him to open your mind. Stop relying on your own cleverness alone to read the Bible. From today on, every time you open your Bible, bow your head first and say, “Lord, please open the eyes of my heart.” Let Jesus reign as King in your Bible reading.

Second, empty your cup. If there’s a corner of your heart saying, “I already understand this,” please hand it over. Only those willing to be infants can see what the Father wants to reveal. Let Jesus reign as King in your mindset.

Third, pass the light on. If you received a word this morning, don’t keep it for yourself. Pass it on to one person today. Let Jesus receive all the glory through you.

Brothers and sisters, on the day the disciples’ minds were opened, the church was born; on the day Luther’s mind was opened, the Reformation began; on the night Wesley’s heart was warmed, a great revival came. God is still opening people’s minds today. May this light shine into your heart and mine this very morning.

And this revelation will lead us on to the next stage of changing our mindset — “Conviction”.

keyVerses: “Then he opened their minds, that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24:45)
declarations: The lesson has a very important gentle reminder: revelation is not “an increase in learning”; it is “a life lit up by the light”. Don’t rush to “understand more”; learn to “be opened”. Listen humbly, and the truth will become a light in your heart.

Brothers and sisters, this is worth meditating on again and again. In this age of information overload, we have access to more spiritual information than any generation before us; but more information doesn’t mean a deeper life. We need to watch out for one thing: substituting “understanding more” for “being opened” is the spiritual danger that happens most easily and is noticed least.
Now let’s make the lesson’s declaration of faith together:

Lord, thank you for giving us the Holy Spirit, so that I not only hear your words but understand your heart. Please open my mind, so that every time I hear your word and pray, I receive revelation from heaven and live a life of truth!
practices: Before opening your Bible, pray: “Lord, please open the eyes of my heart, so that I understand your word.”
After reading a passage, be quiet for one minute; don’t analyse, just ask the Lord, “Which sentence do you want me to see today?”
Each night before bed, spend three minutes recalling the moment that touched you most today, and ask the Lord, “Lord, what do you want me to understand from this?”
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you.

Lord, we confess that we know far more than we live out. We have heard many sermons and read many verses, but so often they stop in our heads and never reach our hearts. Forgive our complacency, and forgive the pride that says, “I already understand.”

Lord, as you once did on the road to Emmaus, come near to us yourself; as you did on that Easter evening, open our minds, that we may understand the Scriptures. Take away the veil over our hearts and enlighten the eyes of our hearts.

Holy Spirit, we welcome you as our guide. Teach us not to rely on the brain and ourselves, but to rely on the heart and on you. Make every word this morning not just information but revelation; not just a feeling but life.
Lord, from this day on, may we no longer merely know about you, but truly know you. Reign as King in our hearts, and may all the glory be yours.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “Then he opened their minds, that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24:45). Please share: have you had an experience of everything suddenly coming clear — a verse you’d read for a long time, until one day you truly saw it? What change did that opening bring?

“I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you hid these things from the wise and understanding, and revealed them to infants” (Matthew 11:25). Take an honest look: in what area has your heart ever said, “I already understand this”? What concrete steps will you take this week to empty yourself and ask the Lord afresh for his light?
l043.title: From Knowing to Seeing
l043.subtitle: Stage Two of Changing Our Mindset: Revelation
l043.partTitle: Unit 4 · The Prerequisite for Revival — A Change of Mindset

sections.heading: 1. Introduction: From Knowing, to Understanding, to Surrender
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, peace to you this morning. Before we come to today’s message, I’d like you to think back to something very ordinary.

Almost everyone has had this experience. The doctor pushes your test results across the desk, points to a line of numbers and says, “Your blood sugar is over the limit. You must eat less and exercise.” In that moment you nod, you remember the number, you even take a photo of the doctor’s instructions and save it on your phone. That is called “information”.

Some time later, you wake in the middle of the night feeling dizzy, or you hear that an old classmate your own age has been admitted to intensive care with complications, and suddenly your heart jolts: so this really could happen to me. That is called “revelation”. The very same sentence suddenly stands up off the page and becomes words spoken to you.

But will that make you change? Not necessarily. The real watershed is the third step. You walk into the supermarket, your hand is already reaching towards the row of desserts — and then you pull your hand back. What is at work in that moment is no longer knowledge; your will has been persuaded. That is called “conviction”.

Brothers and sisters, change in the spiritual life travels the very same road.

We have already walked together through the first two stages of changing our mindset. The first stage is “Information”: the truth enters our ears and our notebooks. The second stage is “Revelation”: the Holy Spirit lights up a sentence, and we suddenly see that it concerns us. Today we enter the third stage, the most decisive turning point in the whole process of change: “Conviction”.

What is conviction? Conviction is our willingness to let God’s word replace our own ideas, our own emotions and our own judgement, and so to submit to Christ completely. It is a road that runs from “knowing”, to “understanding”, to “surrender”.

Please note that conviction is not the same as being moved. If anything, being moved is what the church has least shortage of. You hear a message, your eyes fill, your heart grows warm — that’s being moved. The next morning the alarm goes off and everything carries on just as before — which shows that being moved hasn’t yet become conviction. Being moved is a ripple of emotion; conviction is a change of ownership of the heart. Conviction is the mind taken back, the life renewed, the place inside us where decisions are made coming under a new Master.

Here’s a picture that may help. When an old house that has been lived in for decades is to be rebuilt, the first step isn’t to move the new furniture in; it’s to demolish. Without demolition there’s nowhere to put the new beams and pillars; and if you force new furniture into the old house, it only becomes more crowded and more chaotic. Our mindset is just the same. If God is to build truth within us, he must first tear down the wrong ideas we have lived in for decades and find so familiar and comfortable. Conviction is when we finally agree to hand over the key and let God come in and do the work.

It’s generally held that the Reformer Martin Luther, at the Imperial Diet of Worms in 1521, under enormous pressure to recant his writings, said these words: “My conscience is captive to the Word of God.” That sentence captures “conviction” with great precision. Conviction isn’t being talked round by people, isn’t being carried along by the atmosphere, and still less is it being crushed into compliance by authority. Conviction is a conscience taken captive by the Word of God, never to go back again.

Brothers and sisters, this morning, may we not merely sit through one more lesson and copy one more page of notes; may at least one part of our mindset truly be taken captive by God’s word.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Background: The Battlefield Is Not the Pulpit but the Mind
sections.html:
Our theme verses come from 2 Corinthians chapter 10. To feel the weight of these words, we first need to know the situation behind the letter.

The author is the apostle Paul. 2 Corinthians is generally dated between AD 55 and 57. Paul had finished his ministry in Ephesus, passed through Troas, and was travelling in the region of Macedonia (see 2 Corinthians 2:12–13; 7:5). The letter was addressed to the church in Corinth.

What kind of city was Corinth? It sat on the isthmus of southern Greece, with a harbour on each side, east and west, linking the Aegean Sea with the Adriatic. Goods passed in and out through it, crowds passed in and out through it, and every kind of philosophy, religion, rhetoric and way of life passed in and out through it too. It was a city that admired eloquence, prized appearances and fawned on the strong. Orators competed in words on the street corners, and crowds applauded fine rhetoric.

It was in exactly this soil that a group calling themselves “the very best apostles” came into the Corinthian church (see 2 Corinthians 11:5). They criticised Paul: “His letters are weighty and strong, but his bodily presence is weak, and his speech is despised” (2 Corinthians 10:10). In their eyes Paul wasn’t impressive enough, wasn’t a good enough speaker, didn’t look enough like a leader.

So chapters 10 to 13 of 2 Corinthians are Paul’s defence of his apostleship. But notice that the way Paul defends himself is completely unexpected. He doesn’t compete on eloquence, or on credentials, or on how many visions he’s had, or on whose meetings draw the biggest crowds. He lifts the whole matter onto an entirely different plane: this is a spiritual war, and the battlefield isn’t the pulpit; it is the human mind.

He begins, “For though we walk in the flesh, we don’t wage war according to the flesh” (2 Corinthians 10:3). Then come our theme verses for today.

Several of the words Paul uses deserve to be savoured slowly.

“Strongholds” in Greek is ochurōma, meaning a fortress, a fortified position. In Roman times a city was taken by piling up earthen ramps, pushing up battering rams and setting up catapults, advancing inch by inch, often in a siege lasting months. Paul says we have weapons from God that are able to bring down fortresses like these.

“Thought” in Greek is noēma, meaning a thought, an idea, whatever the mind produces.

“Bringing into captivity” is aichmalōtizō, which literally means “to capture at spear-point” — that is, to march prisoners of war back under guard. It’s a startling picture: in Paul’s description, the prisoners of war being marched back are not the devil but our own thoughts.

“Obedience” in Greek is hypakoē, whose roots mean “to listen from underneath”. Obedience isn’t being forced to bow your head; it is willingly standing underneath God’s word and listening to him speak.

Brothers and sisters, this is conviction. Paul isn’t telling us to go shadow-boxing; he wants us to face honestly the fortresses of thought inside us, each one built tall and solid. In today’s lesson we’ll look at three things: first, conviction is the central objective of spiritual warfare; second, conviction is a process of being torn down and rebuilt; third, conviction requires repeated meditation, practice and perseverance.

sections.heading: 3. Conviction Is the Central Objective of Spiritual Warfare
sections.html:
“For the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh, but mighty before God to the throwing down of strongholds, throwing down imaginations and every high thing that is exalted against the knowledge of God and bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ” (2 Corinthians 10:4–5).

(1) The War Is Already Won, but the Battlefield Is the Mind

When many people hear the words “spiritual warfare”, the picture that springs to mind is of wrestling with the devil, tugging and grappling, as though the outcome were still undecided and we could only win by shouting loudly enough. But that isn’t what Scripture says.

“Having stripped the principalities and the powers, he made a show of them openly, triumphing over them in it” (Colossians 2:15).

When Jesus said on the cross, “It is finished” (John 19:30), it was not a sigh; it was a proclamation. The outcome was settled long ago. Satan is a defeated enemy whose sentence has been passed and only awaits execution.

So what can he still do? He has only one job left: “engineering thoughts”. He cannot snatch us out of God’s hand, but he can set up strongholds one after another in our thinking, so that though we are saved, we live as if we weren’t; though we have God’s promises, we live as though we had none.

Satan has worked this way from the beginning. The first thing he said to Eve was, “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden’?” (Genesis 3:1). He didn’t lift a hand first; first he shook a mindset — can God’s word be trusted? Is God really good? Paul saw this clearly, which is why he said, “But I am afraid that somehow, as the serpent deceived Eve in his craftiness, so your minds might be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ” (2 Corinthians 11:3).

Brothers and sisters, what is the true objective of spiritual warfare? Not to knock Satan down — Jesus has already done that — but to take our minds back and bring every thought into obedience to Christ.

(2) What Are “Strongholds”?

“Strongholds” are thoughts and mindsets that are deeply rooted and resist the truth. They didn’t move in yesterday. Most of them were built brick by brick out of our childhood, our hurts, our failures and our family’s values — built so solidly that we think they are simply “me”.

The lesson names four common strongholds, and it’s worth holding each one up against our own hearts:

The first is fear. The stronghold of fear says, “What if I fail? What if God doesn’t look after me?” It makes people build their sense of security on control, too afraid to open their hands.

The second is pride. The stronghold of pride says, “I can do it; I don’t need anyone.” It lets people use very spiritual language to cover a heart that refuses to surrender.

The third is control. The stronghold of control says, “If I don’t hold on tight, everything will fall apart.” It makes people move God’s seat over and sit in it themselves, and then wear themselves out living in that seat.

The fourth is self-pity. The stronghold of self-pity says, “No one understands me anyway; this is just the way I am.” It looks humble, but in fact it puts the self at the centre of the world and trades its wounds for an exemption from responsibility.

These four strongholds have one thing in common: they all keep us from trusting God freely.

Paul uses a vivid phrase: “every high thing that is exalted against the knowledge of God”. The Greek for “high thing”, hypsōma, originally means “something towering”, something lifted up high; in ancient astronomical language it could also mean the highest point a heavenly body reaches. In other words, anything raised in our hearts to a position higher than God’s word is a hypsōma.

It may be a body of life experience: “I’ve eaten more salt than you’ve eaten rice.” It may be a professional judgement, a family tradition, an old tape that keeps playing over and over. These things aren’t necessarily bad in themselves; the problem is their “height”. When they sit higher than God’s word, they become strongholds.

(3) A Pair of Glasses Worn Too Long

I often use this comparison. Suppose a man has worn a pair of light grey glasses since childhood — forty years of wearing them. Ask him what colour the sky is, and he will tell you with complete sincerity: the sky is grey. He isn’t lying; he is telling you what he sees. Until one day someone takes the glasses off his face, he looks up, and he is stunned — the sky is blue.

A wrong mindset is a pair of glasses like that. It doesn’t make us feel we are distorting the facts; it simply makes us feel that “this is just how things are”. So the first step of conviction is often not that something is added, but that something is taken off.

Psychology confirms from another angle how hard this is. In 1957 the social psychologist Leon Festinger put forward the theory of “cognitive dissonance”. He showed that when a person’s behaviour and beliefs don’t match, an uncomfortable tension arises inside; and to relieve that tension, people often don’t change their behaviour — they change their story, finding a reasonable explanation for themselves. That is exactly what we most often do before God: we know perfectly well it’s wrong, and instantly produce a whole argument for why it’s “understandable”.

The psychologist and Nobel laureate in economics Daniel Kahneman, in his 2011 book Thinking, Fast and Slow, divides human thinking into two systems: System 1 is fast, automatic and intuitive; System 2 is slow, effortful and logical. He shows that the vast majority of our everyday reactions are System 1 at work. That explains why wrong mindsets are so stubborn — they have sunk to the level of automatic reaction and switch on without any thought at all. To tear them down, a power deeper than they are has to come in.

Thank God, we have that weapon. “For the word of God is living and active, and sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing even to the dividing of soul and spirit, of both joints and marrow, and is able to discern the thoughts and intentions of the heart” (Hebrews 4:12).

(4) As a Man Thinks in His Heart, So Is He

Letting Scripture interpret Scripture, we see the Bible’s consistent position: a person’s outward life is the result of the mindset within.

“For as he thinks in his heart, so is he” (Proverbs 23:7, as the Chinese Union Version renders it).

“Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23).

“Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God” (Romans 12:2).

Notice the order in Romans 12:2: first “be transformed by the renewing of your mind”, and only then “prove the will of God”. Many brothers and sisters seek God’s will earnestly and still get no answer, and often the problem isn’t that God isn’t speaking; it’s that the glasses inside us haven’t come off yet. If the mind isn’t renewed, then even when God sets his will right in front of us, we’ll read it through our old mindset.

So how precisely Paul puts it: the central objective of spiritual warfare is “bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ”.

(5) A 321 Insight: From the Self-Centred Life to Selflessness

In the language of 321, the foundation of every stronghold comes down to one thing — the self-centred life.

The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of every problem. What is pride? Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place. Look at those four strongholds: fear is me wanting to protect myself; pride is me wanting to prove myself; control is me wanting to run everything myself; self-pity is me wanting the whole world to revolve around my wound. Four strongholds, one foundation: “self” sitting on the throne.

And what is humility? Humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

So we say: humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Satan cannot break through a selfless person, because he can find nothing in him to get a grip on. The Lord Jesus said, “the prince of the world comes, and he has nothing in me” (John 14:30).

Remember too that selflessness doesn’t mean erasing yourself and becoming someone of no worth. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering the boundless and living out the boundless. “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me” (Galatians 2:20).

Into whose hands should the mind that has been taken back finally be placed? Into the hands of the King. This is the first of the Two Core Values of 321: let Jesus be King. Conviction, when all is said and done, is a change of king.

sections.heading: 4. Conviction Is a Process of Being Torn Down and Rebuilt
sections.html:
“Behold, I have today set you over the nations and over the kingdoms, to uproot and to tear down, to destroy and to overthrow, to build and to plant” (Jeremiah 1:10).

(1) First Tear Down, Then Build

Conviction isn’t emotional compliance; it is a choice made after both reason and heart have been persuaded by the truth.

God’s way of working has a set order: first he shines his light on us and lets us see our errors — that is “tearing down”; then he rebuilds us with his own word — that is “building”.

When Jeremiah was called, God spoke six verbs to him: uproot, tear down, destroy, overthrow, build, plant. Count them: four are about tearing down, two about building. That isn’t because God enjoys demolition; it’s because you can’t put up a new house on a plot piled high with rubble.

Paul describes the new life in the same order: “that you put away, as concerning your former way of life, the old man that grows corrupt after the lusts of deceit, and that you be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who in the likeness of God has been created in righteousness and holiness of truth” (Ephesians 4:22–24). First put away, then be renewed, then put on — not one of them can be left out.

What happens without “tearing down”? We look at new things through our old framework of thought. The Lord Jesus said, “Neither do people put new wine into old wine skins, or else the skins would burst, and the wine be spilled, and the skins ruined. No, they put new wine into fresh wine skins, and both are preserved” (Matthew 9:17). Many people hear sermons all their lives and their lives don’t change — not because the wine is poor, but because the wineskin hasn’t been changed. Old wineskins can’t hold new wine.

And what happens without “rebuilding”? We fall into an empty void. The Lord Jesus told a sobering parable: “When an unclean spirit has gone out of a man, he passes through waterless places, seeking rest, and doesn’t find it. Then he says, ‘I will return into my house from which I came out,’ and when he has come back, he finds it empty, swept, and put in order. Then he goes, and takes with himself seven other spirits more evil than he is, and they enter in and dwell there. The last state of that man becomes worse than the first” (Matthew 12:43–45).

Notice those three descriptions: empty, swept, put in order. The house is very clean; the problem is that it’s empty. If we only give up old habits without letting the truth move in, sooner or later that empty space will be taken over by something worse. That’s why change that relies on willpower alone never lasts long, while a life rebuilt by the truth can stand firm.

(2) The Lesson of the Caterpillar

God has placed a beautiful picture in the natural world to help us understand tearing down and rebuilding.

For a caterpillar to become a butterfly, it isn’t simply a matter of growing wings. Once it forms its chrysalis, most of the tissue in its body is broken down by enzymes until it is almost a liquid mass; meanwhile, “imaginal discs” that were prepared back in the larval stage begin following a new blueprint, reassembling that material into wings, compound eyes, mouthparts and long slender legs.

What happens inside the chrysalis isn’t patching and mending; it is tearing down and rebuilding. If you cut the chrysalis open halfway through, you wouldn’t find half a butterfly; you’d find a mess.

Brothers and sisters, that is exactly how many people feel in the process of conviction. When God starts tearing us down, we feel confused, disordered, unsure of ourselves — we may even feel worse than before. Don’t be afraid. That isn’t destruction; it’s the work going on inside the chrysalis. God never tears down without building. He tears down because he means to build a larger life, one that can fly. “Being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6).

(3) Moses: Five Excuses, One Surrender

Moses’ experience is the most complete case in Scripture of “being torn down and rebuilt”.

When God called him from the flames of the burning bush at Horeb to lead the Israelites out of Egypt, Moses came up with excuses five times in a row. Let’s look at them one by one, and you’ll notice something remarkable: every time Moses put the focus on himself, God turned the focus back to himself.

The first time, Moses said, “Who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh, and that I should bring the children of Israel out of Egypt?” (Exodus 3:11).

God’s answer wasn’t “Actually, you’re great.” It was this: “Certainly I will be with you. This will be the token to you, that I have sent you: when you have brought the people out of Egypt, you shall serve God on this mountain” (Exodus 3:12). The question was never “Who am I?” but “Who is with me?”

The second time, Moses said, “Behold, when I come to the children of Israel, and tell them, ‘The God of your fathers has sent me to you,’ and they ask me, ‘What is his name?’ what should I tell them?” (Exodus 3:13).

Then God revealed his name: “I AM WHO I AM,” and said, “You shall tell the children of Israel this: ‘I AM has sent me to you’” (Exodus 3:14). The Hebrew is ehyeh asher ehyeh, meaning “I am who I am”, “I will be what I will be”. God didn’t answer Moses with a résumé; he answered him with his own being.

The third time, Moses said, “But, behold, they will not believe me, nor listen to my voice; for they will say, ‘Yahweh has not appeared to you’” (Exodus 4:1).

God didn’t argue with him; he let him experience three signs on the spot: the staff in his hand became a snake, and the snake became a staff again; his hand put inside his cloak came out leprous, and put in again came out restored; and God promised that water from the river poured on dry ground would turn to blood (see Exodus 4:2–9). God turned the most ordinary thing — the shepherd’s staff in his hand — into an instrument of signs.
