The fourth time, Moses said, “O Lord, I am not eloquent, neither before now, nor since you have spoken to your servant; for I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue” (Exodus 4:10).

God answered, “Who made man’s mouth? Or who makes one mute, or deaf, or seeing, or blind? Isn’t it I, Yahweh? Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth, and teach you what you shall speak” (Exodus 4:11–12). God didn’t deny Moses’ weakness; he simply reminded Moses who had made that mouth.

The fifth time, Moses finally said what was really in his heart: “Oh, Lord, please send someone else” (Exodus 4:13).

“Yahweh’s anger burned against Moses” (Exodus 4:14), and yet he still provided Aaron to be his mouthpiece. But look closely: Aaron was a helper; the mission stayed in Moses’ hands — “You shall take this rod in your hand, with which you shall do the signs” (Exodus 4:17). God’s grace will give us companions, but it won’t hand over our calling on our behalf.

So when was Moses truly taken back?

“Yahweh said to Moses in Midian, ‘Go, return into Egypt; for all the men who sought your life are dead’” (Exodus 4:19).

That one sentence dealt directly with a stronghold buried in Moses’ heart for forty years. Forty years earlier he had killed an Egyptian and fled into the wilderness, and from then on he had lived as a wanted man. Underneath all his “I can’t” lay an “I don’t dare”. God said: the men who sought your life are dead. Once that stronghold came down, Moses got up: “Moses took his wife and his sons, and set them on a donkey, and he returned to the land of Egypt. Moses took God’s rod in his hand” (Exodus 4:20).

What happened between “please send someone else” and “took God’s rod in his hand” is what we call conviction.

(4) “I Can’t” Is a Mindset

In her 2006 book Mindset, the Stanford psychologist Carol Dweck distinguishes between a “fixed mindset” and a “growth mindset”. People with a fixed mindset believe ability is fixed, so when they meet a challenge their first thought is “I just can’t”; people with a growth mindset believe ability can be developed through effort, so when they meet a challenge they ask, “What am I still missing?”

At first Moses had a textbook fixed mindset: Who am I? I’m no speaker. I can’t. But what God gave him was higher than a growth mindset — not “Actually, you can,” but “Certainly I will be with you.” True Christian faith isn’t optimism about our own potential; it is certainty of God’s presence.

Psychology can describe our mindset, but it cannot change our heart. Only God’s word and God’s Spirit can change the heart.

(5) A 321 Insight: The Fivefold Change

321 speaks of the fivefold change: when the mindset changes, the life changes; when the life changes, daily living changes; when daily living changes, relationships change; when relationships change, ministry changes. Mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry — this is a road with an order to it.

Moses walked exactly this road. His mindset changed from “Who am I?” to “Who is he?” Once his mindset changed, his life changed: a fugitive became God’s servant. Once his life changed, his daily living changed: from days of shepherding in the wilderness he stepped into days of speaking with God face to face. Once his daily living changed, his relationships changed: his relationships with Aaron, with Miriam and with the whole congregation of Israel were rebuilt. Once his relationships changed, the ministry came — a whole nation brought out of Egypt.

Notice this order, and never reverse it. 321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. If Moses hadn’t been torn down and rebuilt at Horeb, then even if he had led the Israelites out of Egypt, he could never have brought them to the border of Canaan.

And remember the priority of relationships: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. Moses was first reconciled to God, then reconciled to himself — accepting the slow-tongued Moses who had once failed — and only then could he work alongside others, and only last of all accomplish that earth-shaking work.

Brothers and sisters, we often want to skip the tearing down and go straight into ministry. But what God wants isn’t someone who can start work immediately; it’s a vessel that can carry his glory.

sections.heading: 5. Conviction Requires Repeated Meditation, Practice and Perseverance
sections.html:
“So faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Romans 10:17).

(1) Faith Isn’t Filled in One Go; It Is Watered Again and Again

Conviction isn’t a split-second decision; it is a process of meditating again and again and being persuaded by God over and over. Every revelation nurtures faith, and every act of obedience makes faith deeper.

The lesson says that conviction is grounded in faith, and faith comes from meditating on the truth. The biblical basis for this is Romans 10:17. The Chinese Union Version reads: “So faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of Christ.”

The Greek here is fascinating: faith (pistis) comes from “what is heard” (akoē), and “what is heard” comes from “the word of Christ” (rhēma Christou). “Hearing” here doesn’t mean sound waves reaching the ear; it means continually receiving and continually keeping. Faith isn’t a bucket filled in one go; it is a field soaked by the rain again and again.

So in the stage of conviction, what we need to do is very plain: keep meditating on God’s word, let the Holy Spirit remind us again and again, so that faith gradually matures and obedience becomes natural.

(2) What “Meditate” Really Means

“This book of the law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, that you may observe to do according to all that is written in it; for then you shall make your way prosperous, and then you shall have good success” (Joshua 1:8).

“But his delight is in Yahweh’s law. On his law he meditates day and night” (Psalm 1:2).

The Hebrew for “meditate” is hāgāh. Its basic meaning is to murmur in a low voice, to mutter to oneself; Scripture also uses it for the low growl in a lion’s throat as it guards its prey (see Isaiah 31:4). So the meditation the Bible speaks of isn’t emptying your head or sitting in a blank daze. It is like a cow chewing the cud: holding a sentence in your mouth and chewing it over and over until the juice comes out and the nourishment enters your bloodstream.

Notice the order in Joshua 1:8: not departing from the mouth, meditating day and night, being careful to do it — and only then a prosperous way. Mouth, heart, hands: none of them can be left out.

“I have hidden your word in my heart, that I might not sin against you” (Psalm 119:11). Only the word hidden in the heart can step forward and speak up for us in the moment of temptation.

(3) Even the Brain Paves the Way for Truth

The body God created bears witness to the power of “repetition”.

In his 1949 book The Organization of Behavior, the Canadian psychologist Donald Hebb proposed a famous principle that later generations often sum up in one line: neurons that fire together wire together. In other words, every time the same pathway of thought is travelled, that road is widened a little more.

A team led by Eleanor Maguire at University College London published research in 2000 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences showing that London taxi drivers, after years of memorising and mentally rehearsing complex street routes, had a larger volume of grey matter in the rear part of the hippocampus than a control group — and the longer they had been driving, the more marked the difference. Repeated use really does change the structure of the brain.

Also at University College London, a team led by Phillippa Lally published research in 2010 in the European Journal of Social Psychology showing that the median time for a new behaviour to become an automatic habit was about sixty-six days, with very wide individual variation. In other words, it isn’t that you’re not spiritual enough; this road simply takes a good while to walk.

Brothers and sisters, this research isn’t meant to replace the Bible; it simply offers, from the created world, a small testimony to the Bible: God long ago wrote the wisdom of “meditating day and night” into the very nerves of our brains.

Research by the psychologist Anders Ericsson and his colleagues, published in 1993 in Psychological Review, also showed that outstanding performance comes from long-term, goal-directed “deliberate practice” with feedback, not simply from piling up hours. Spiritual practice is just the same: not skimming through the text, but reading with questions, with response, with reflection.

(4) Sometimes Once, Sometimes Many Times

Sometimes a single revelation is enough to change our whole life; sometimes God shines his light on the same thing again and again, until we truly let go of ourselves.

Peter was the second kind. Of the vision God gave him, Scripture says: “This was done three times, and immediately the vessel was received up into heaven” (Acts 10:16). Three times, because the stronghold of “clean and unclean” had been a lifetime in the building.

So was Paul. “Concerning this thing, I begged the Lord three times that it might depart from me. He has said to me, ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness’” (2 Corinthians 12:8–9). Paul didn’t get his answer after asking once; he asked three times before he was persuaded.

So if you find that the same verse has been following you around for months, or the same subject keeps cropping up in different settings, brothers and sisters, that isn’t coincidence. That is God knocking at the same door. He is waiting for you to open it.

(5) Choosing to Believe in the Midst of Struggle

People of conviction aren’t people without struggles; they are people who choose to believe in the midst of struggle. They aren’t people without fear; they are people who still obey in the midst of fear.

The father who brought his demon-possessed child to Jesus prayed the most honest of prayers: “I believe. Help my unbelief!” (Mark 9:24). That sentence holds faith and struggle together, and the Lord received it.

In the Garden of Gethsemane the Lord Jesus himself shows us what conviction truly looks like: “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42). He struggled — so much that “His sweat became like great drops of blood falling down on the ground” (Luke 22:44) — but in the struggle he surrendered. “And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross” (Philippians 2:8).

Brothers and sisters, obedience doesn’t mean not feeling the weight. Obedience means knowing full well the weight is there and still saying, “Your will be done.”

When we are willing to surrender to God’s word, the Holy Spirit gives us power to live it out, and in the doing we experience God’s faithfulness. “For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:13). Notice that even the “willing” is God at work within us. That is grace.

Two scenes from church history put this beautifully.

On the evening of 24 May 1738, John Wesley sat in a small meeting in Aldersgate Street in London, listening to someone read Martin Luther’s preface to the Epistle to the Romans. He wrote in his journal, “I felt my heart strangely warmed.” Before that night he had been an Oxford scholar, an ordained minister, a missionary who had crossed the ocean; he had knowledge enough and to spare. What changed that night was the passage from knowledge into conviction.

In June 1865, on the beach at Brighton in England, Hudson Taylor, after wrestling for a long time under the burden of the unreached people of inland China, finally surrendered. In the margin of his Bible he wrote a prayer asking God to send willing workers into inland China. The China Inland Mission began with that one surrender.

Brothers and sisters, every revival in church history has begun not with a new method but with someone being persuaded by God.

(6) A 321 Insight: Rely on the Heart and the Holy Spirit, Not on the Brain and Ourselves

321 reminds us: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll have joy, rely on the brain and you’ll have worry. The wellspring of life flows from the heart.

This doesn’t mean faith requires no thinking. The whole passage in 2 Corinthians 10 is precisely about a war of thoughts. What 321 means by “not on the brain and ourselves” is not using our own cleverness to calculate God, to second-guess God, or to decide for God how far he can go. Repeated meditation is opening the heart so the Holy Spirit can speak, not revving up the brain to talk ourselves into something.

Among the eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — “Repetition” comes seventh, yet it is the stage where the most people stumble. Because repetition isn’t the least bit romantic. It has none of the shock of first hearing the truth, none of the thrill of first obeying; it is simply coming back, day after day, to the same sentence. But it is in exactly this seemingly dull repetition that the roots of life push down, inch by inch.

“Be strong in the Lord, and in the strength of his might” (Ephesians 6:10).

sections.heading: 6. Integrating the 321 Vision: Conviction Is a Change of King
sections.html:
When we set this lesson within the framework of 321, we see it more clearly still.

(1) The Three Foundations Are the Three Pillars of Conviction

First, Jesus is my role model. Conviction isn’t a one-sided demand God makes of us; it is a road the Lord himself walked first. “Though he was a Son, yet learned obedience by the things which he suffered” (Hebrews 5:8). The One we surrender to surrendered himself all the way to the cross.

Second, the Bible is my standard. What we are convinced of is not a feeling, not an atmosphere, not someone else’s opinion, but God’s word. Conviction without a standard turns into emotional drifting. Whatever you’re persuaded of today, ask: does that sentence have a basis in Scripture?

Third, the Holy Spirit is my guide. Tearing down is the Holy Spirit’s work, and rebuilding is the Holy Spirit’s work too. “However when he, the Spirit of truth, has come, he will guide you into all truth” (John 16:13). We can’t tear down our own strongholds by our own analysis, because those glasses are part of our own face.

(2) The Two Core Values and the Goal

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.

The most direct result of “the mind taken back” is a change of occupant on the throne. Once it was my ideas, my emotions, my judgement, my face that sat on the throne; now it is Christ who sits there. Conviction, when all is said and done, is a change of king.

And when the King takes his throne, the glory naturally goes to him. Someone who has truly been persuaded won’t use the fruit of their obedience to show off their spirituality, because they know better than anyone: if God hadn’t shone his light again and again and waited again and again, they would long ago have gone their own way.

The Goal: establish God’s system. God’s system isn’t an organisational chart; it is a community of people whose minds have been taken back and who have Christ as their King. The problem in the Corinthian church was precisely that it had brought the Worldly system into the church — competing on eloquence, on presence, on whose backer was more powerful. What Paul set out to do was tear down that Worldly system and rebuild God’s system with the cross at its centre.

(3) A Fourfold Shift of Perspective

The process of conviction is really a shift of perspective:

From man’s perspective to God’s perspective — Moses asks, “Who am I?”; God says, “Certainly I will be with you.”

From an earthly perspective to a heavenly perspective — not competing on earthly eloquence and presence, but seeking only heaven’s approval.

From a temporary perspective to an eternal perspective — “while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal” (2 Corinthians 4:18).

From a worldly perspective to a godly perspective — “‘For my thoughts are not your thoughts, and your ways are not my ways,’ says Yahweh. ‘For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways, and my thoughts than your thoughts’” (Isaiah 55:8–9).

(4) 920 and 235: Conviction Must Be Lived Out in Relationships

If conviction stays only in our private prayer room, it easily stalls at being moved by ourselves. The 920 practice of 321 reminds us that every person we have a relationship with is our “2”; before them we are to practise living a selfless (“0”) life and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (“9”) of its expressions.

How do you know a mindset has truly become conviction? Not by what you’ve written in your Bible notes, but by whether, in front of the person at home who most easily makes you angry, you show love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness and self-control (see Galatians 5:22–23). How thoroughly the strongholds have been torn down — your family knows best.

The 235 relationships remind us to become a “2” — spiritual companions — with a selfless person, to establish a “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children — and then to become a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. On the road of conviction we need companions. Moses had Aaron, Paul had Barnabas, Timothy had Paul. Alone you can go fast, but to go the whole way you need someone at your side saying, “What you believe is true. Don’t turn back.”

sections.heading: 7. Putting It into Practice: Deepening It Through the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices for daily living. Let’s set them within the eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — so that they become not just three good suggestions but a road we can keep walking.

Practice 1: Meditate on One Word from God Every Day

Spend time every day meditating on one word from God, asking the Holy Spirit to shine his light on you, so that this word becomes a real conviction rather than a theory.

How to do it: when you read the Bible in the morning, don’t aim to read a lot; aim to carry away one sentence. Write it on a slip of paper or save it on your phone’s home screen, and at least three times during the day say it quietly aloud — before you go out in the morning, in a quiet moment at midday, and before bed at night. As you say it, ask: Lord, if this is true, how am I to live today?

Corresponding stages: this is the practice of moving from “Information” into “Revelation”. Information is me reading it; revelation is it reading me.

Practice 2: Identify the Mindset That Blocks Your Obedience

When you find yourself resisting God’s will in some matter, stop and ask: what mindset is keeping me from obeying?

How to do it: don’t stop at the level of emotion and say, “I just don’t want to.” Dig down three layers. First layer: what am I resisting? Second layer: what am I afraid of? Third layer: what sentence have I believed that makes me this afraid? Write down that third-layer sentence — for example, “If I obey, I’ll lose out,” “If I let go, everything will collapse,” “Someone like me isn’t worthy of being used by God.” Once it’s written down, find a verse of Scripture to confront it with.

Corresponding stages: this is the practice of “Conviction” and “Evaluation”. Once a stronghold has been named, it is already half shaken.

Practice 3: Pray for One Area Not Yet Fully Surrendered

Pray for one area you have not yet fully surrendered, asking the Holy Spirit to help you tear down the old thinking and build up godly faith.

How to do it: honestly choose one area — money, time, marriage, children, career, a broken relationship, someone you have never been willing to forgive. Pray for it for seven days, and each day offer one concrete, small act of obedience in that area.

Corresponding stages: this is the practice of “Implementation”, “Correction” and “Repetition”. “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves” (James 1:22).

Walking Through All Eight Stages

1. Information: take the truth in. A regular morning devotion and regular notes give God’s word a chance to get inside.

2. Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to light it up. As you read the Bible, pray often like this: Lord, please point out to me the one sentence I most need to see today.

3. Conviction: let the truth persuade your will. Stop and ask yourself: am I only agreeing, or do I truly believe it? Am I willing to adjust my decisions according to it?

4. Implementation: turn belief into action. If conviction doesn’t reach implementation, it will slip back. Do one small thing today in response to that sentence.

5. Evaluation: spend three minutes looking back in the evening. At what moment today did I live by the truth? At what moment did I put the old glasses back on?

6. Correction: don’t substitute self-blame for correction. Self-blame circles around the self; correction turns towards God. When you fall, admit it, adjust, and keep walking.

7. Repetition: accept that it takes a long time. Forming a habit takes time, and renewing a life all the more. Don’t draw conclusions because nothing has changed by the tenth day.

8. Multiplication: pass on what you have been convinced of. Find one person and tell them what God has done in you. When you begin passing it on to others, it roots itself even deeper in you.

sections.heading: 8. Closing and Call: True Freedom
sections.html:
The lesson has a gentle reminder that puts it very well: conviction is not repression; it is release.

We often misunderstand obedience as pushing ourselves down and holding back everything we want. It isn’t. Repression is a fire pressed under a pot lid; sooner or later the lid flies off. Release is the fire moved to where it ought to burn, becoming light and warmth. When we stop arguing with God and learn to obey, we experience a peace that flows from the heart.

Conviction is the turning point in changing our mindset, and the key to a life set free. When the Holy Spirit helps us move from information into revelation, and from revelation into conviction, we no longer stay at the level of head knowledge; we live out a life of truth.

The Lord Jesus said, “If you remain in my word, then you are truly my disciples. You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free” (John 8:31–32). Notice the order here: first remaining in his word, then knowing the truth, and only then being made free. Freedom doesn’t come before obedience; freedom comes after obedience.

So true freedom isn’t doing whatever you like; it is being able to act according to God’s heart. If a train envied the freedom of the motorway and jumped its tracks, what it would get isn’t freedom but the scrapyard. The tracks aren’t the train’s limitation; they are the train’s freedom. God’s will is our track.

Brothers and sisters, this morning I want to give you an invitation.

Ask God to show you the strongest stronghold within you — perhaps fear, perhaps pride, perhaps control, perhaps self-pity. Then, before him, hand over the key. You don’t have to wait until you feel good, and you don’t have to wait until you understand completely. When Moses handed it over, he was still the same slow-tongued Moses; he simply stopped saying “please send someone else”, took God’s rod in his hand, and set out for Egypt.

When we learn conviction, revival begins in our hearts. Because revival has never begun in a conference hall; it begins when one person truly surrenders.

Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory. May all that we think, say and do this day be under his reign.

keyVerses: “For though we walk in the flesh, we don’t wage war according to the flesh; for the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh, but mighty before God to the throwing down of strongholds, throwing down imaginations and every high thing that is exalted against the knowledge of God and bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ” (2 Corinthians 10:3–5)
practices: Meditate on one word from God every day
Identify the mindset that blocks your obedience
Pray for one area not yet fully surrendered
prayer: Lord, I am willing for your truth to take my mind back.
Tear down every thought in me that does not please you, and rebuild me with your word, so that I am convinced of you from the heart and gladly obey your will.
Lord, I confess that there is a stronghold in me that was built long ago. I once thought it was simply me, until your word came to me today. I will no longer defend it; I place it in your hands.

Give me strength — not repression, but release; not reluctance, but willingness. When I struggle, help me choose to believe in the midst of the struggle; when I am afraid, help me still obey in the midst of the fear.
Holy Spirit, remind me again and again within, until that word becomes my conviction, my daily living and my life.
May my mind be taken back and brought into obedience to Christ; reign as King in me, and may all the glory be yours.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “Throwing down imaginations and every high thing that is exalted against the knowledge of God and bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ” (2 Corinthians 10:5). Think back over your life: is there a truth you have “known for a long time but never acted on”? What do you think is the mindset blocking your obedience? Where did it come from?

“So faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Romans 10:17). Please share a time when God “shone his light again and again” on you: how long did it take, and how many times, with the same word or the same matter, before he persuaded you? What did you learn from that experience?
l044.title: From Revelation to Conviction
l044.subtitle: Stage Three of Changing Our Mindset
l044.partTitle: Unit 4 · The Prerequisite for Revival — A Change of Mindset

sections.heading: Introduction: That One Step — Why Do You Keep Putting It Off?
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I’d like to begin by asking you to remember something.

Think back. In the past year, was there a morning when you were reading the Bible and a verse suddenly shook you? Was there a meeting where the speaker said one sentence and your eyes filled with tears, and you said to yourself, “Lord, I know you’re speaking to me”?

In that moment the Holy Spirit was shining his light on you. In that moment you didn’t just “hear” — you “saw”.

But brothers and sisters, ask yourself honestly: what became of that verse afterwards?

The person you knew you had to forgive — have you forgiven them? The phone call you knew you had to make — have you made it? The “I’m sorry” you knew you had to say — has it left your lips? The early-morning prayer time you knew you had to restore — have you restored it?

If the answer is “not yet”, then today’s lesson is one God has prepared for you.

On our journey so far we’ve looked at three stages of changing our mindset. Stage one is Information — the truth reaches our ears. Stage two is Revelation — the Holy Spirit drives the truth into our hearts, and suddenly we see. Stage three is Conviction — the resistance inside us crumbles, we are won over heart and mouth, and we are willing to say, “Lord, you are right and I am wrong.”

Brothers and sisters, to come this far is to have come a long way. And yet, if we stop here, it can all still come to nothing.

Because if the renewal of our mindset stays at the level of thoughts and beliefs, a changed life remains a distant dream.

A person can be moved a hundred times and still be the same person. A person can shed tears a hundred times and still live the same way. Tears don’t change a life; action does.

So the fourth stage of changing our mindset is Implementation.

Implementation means moving the truth from our heads down to our feet; implementation means letting an invisible faith become a visible life.

There is a phenomenon in psychology many of us know well, called the “intention–behaviour gap”. The psychologist Peter M. Gollwitzer, in research published in 1999 in the journal American Psychologist, showed that between “I want to” and actually doing it there still lies a deep valley. In 2006 he and Paschal Sheeran pooled more than ninety studies and found something fascinating: simply turning “I will do it” into “I will do it at this time, in this place, in this way” sharply raises the rate of success — the meta-analysis found a medium-to-large effect size (d of about 0.65).

Brothers and sisters, even the world’s psychology has found it out: vague feelings get nothing done; concrete action does.

God’s intention is clearer than psychology’s. He has never wanted us simply to “feel moved”; he wants us to “get up and act”.

The Lord Jesus said, “If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them” (John 13:17). Notice how the Lord words it. He didn’t say, “If you know these things, you are blessed.” He said, “Blessed are you if you do them.” Knowing doesn’t bring the blessing; doing does.

This morning we’ll look at three things together:

First, from revelation to action — letting the truth touch the ground.

Second, implementation has a price — from thought to the birth of life.

Third, implementation takes an act of faith — taking the first step.

One is the direction, one is the cost, one is the start. The direction settles “where am I going?”; the cost settles “am I willing to go?”; the start settles “when do I go?” Put the three together, and you have Implementation.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A Brother of the Lord, and a Scattered People
sections.html:
To stand firm in this lesson, let’s first lay out the background to our key passages.

The author of the letter of James is generally held to be James, the brother of the Lord Jesus according to the flesh (Matthew 13:55 names James among Jesus’ brothers). At first this James did not believe. John 7:5 puts it bluntly: “For even his brothers didn’t believe in him.” A man who ate at the same table as Jesus and grew up under the same roof — and he did not believe. That reminds us of something: being close to the truth is not the same as entering into the truth.

So when did James change? 1 Corinthians 15:7 records that the risen Lord appeared to James in particular. That encounter turned an unbelieving younger brother into a pillar of the church in Jerusalem (Galatians 2:9), and it led him to open his own letter by calling himself “James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ” (James 1:1). He no longer called himself “the Lord’s brother”; he called himself “the Lord’s servant”. Brothers and sisters, that is implementation born of revelation; that is a mindset about identity turned completely around.

James was written somewhere between AD 45 and 50, and may well be the earliest book of the New Testament. It is addressed “to the twelve tribes which are in the Dispersion” (James 1:1) — Jewish Christians scattered abroad by the persecution that followed Stephen’s martyrdom (Acts 8:1).

Notice their situation. They were a suffering people, a scattered people, a people living as strangers. In suffering, the easiest thing to do is to “shrink faith down into an inner comfort”. Life is hard anyway, so I’ll just hold on to what I believe in my heart, and that will do.

James won’t let them do that. In a tone that is almost an interrogation he writes, “And if a brother or sister is naked and in lack of daily food, and one of you tells them, ‘Go in peace. Be warmed and filled;’ yet you didn’t give them the things the body needs, what good is it?” (James 2:15–16)

Brothers and sisters, those words are as sharp as a knife. “Go in peace” — how warm, how spiritual, how well-mannered! And yet that person is still cold, still hungry.

Scholars have counted more than fifty verbs in the imperative mood in the 108 verses of James. It is one of the most densely commanding books in the whole New Testament. Why? Because James is dealing with exactly the sickness we are dealing with today — hearing a great deal, doing very little.

As for John 8, the setting is the Feast of Tabernacles, with Jesus teaching in the temple. Many people believed in him at that time. So the Lord said to these “Jews who had believed him”: “If you remain in my word, then you are truly my disciples” (John 8:31). The word translated “remain” (Greek menō) means “to settle in, to stay on in something”. The Lord didn’t say, “If you understand my word,” nor “If you praise my word.” He said, “If you remain in” it — live inside it, keep on doing it.

In other words, the Lord Jesus himself defined what a true disciple is: not someone who has once been moved, but someone who keeps on doing the word.

James says, “Be doers of the word”; the Lord Jesus says, “Remain in my word.” One is the Lord’s brother, the other is the Lord himself; one is a letter to believers driven from their homes, the other is spoken to the crowds in the temple. The settings are different, but they point to the same thing — the truth has to touch the ground.

sections.heading: 1. From Revelation to Action: Letting the Truth Touch the Ground
sections.html:
1. “Doers of the word” and “auditors”

The stage of implementation is the moment when God’s word becomes concrete, becomes action.

If we stay at “knowing” and “understanding”, our faith is still only a change in our thinking; only when we step into implementation do we see real change in our lives.

Scripture says, “For as the body apart from the spirit is dead, even so faith apart from works is dead” (James 2:26).

Notice how startling James’s comparison is. He doesn’t say that faith without works is “rather weak”, or that faith without works is “not yet mature”. What he says is — dead. A corpse can have fine features, be neatly dressed and lie there without a scratch on it, and yet it is dead, because there is no spirit inside. In the same way, a person’s beliefs can be orderly and well-arranged, he can have an answer for everything and recite verses backwards, but if there are no works, it is dead.

A little earlier James had already said the same thing: “Even so faith, if it has no works, is dead in itself” (James 2:17).

And our key verse is more direct still: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves” (James 1:22).

The original wording of this verse repays a closer look. “Doers of the word” in Greek is poiētēs tou logou, meaning “one who carries out, one who makes, the word”; “hearers” is akroatēs. In the Greek world of the time, akroatēs was a rather special word. It meant an “auditor” — someone who walked into the lecture hall, sat in the back row and listened to the famous teacher, but never enrolled, never handed in homework and never sat an exam. They heard a great deal, but they never had to answer for what they heard.

Brothers and sisters, let’s be honest: are there “auditors” in the church? Could we ourselves be the one sitting in the back row, moved for ten years, yet never once handing in our homework?

2. Not doing the word is keeping false accounts in the ledger of our lives

What James says next is more serious still — “deluding your own selves”.

The Greek word for “deluding” is paralogizomai, which was originally a term from commercial bookkeeping, meaning “to miscalculate, to cheat someone with false figures”. In other words, someone who hears the word but doesn’t do it is keeping false accounts in the ledger of his own life: he enters “I’ve heard it” as “I’ve done it”, and “I was moved” as “I’ve changed”. On paper all is prosperous; in reality the storehouse is empty.

So James immediately holds up a mirror: “For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man looking at his natural face in a mirror; for he sees himself, and goes away, and immediately forgets what kind of man he was” (James 1:23–24).

What a vivid picture that is. The point of looking in the mirror in the morning isn’t to “know” that your hair is a mess; it’s to “comb your hair”. If someone sees that he’s dishevelled and unwashed, nods and says, “Yes, it really is a mess,” and then turns and walks away — what use is the mirror to him?

Today we hold in our hands a more perfect mirror — the word of God. Every time we read the Bible, we’re looking in the mirror. The question is: once we’ve looked, do we reach for the comb?

It’s like using satellite navigation when we drive. The sat-nav tells you, “In five hundred metres, turn right.” You heard it, you understood it, you could even recite the whole route — but if you don’t turn the steering wheel, you’ll never reach your destination. Knowing the road isn’t the same as travelling it.

3. True implementation comes from revelation and conviction, not from rules

Brothers and sisters, there’s a very important distinction to make here.

True implementation is driven by “revelation and conviction”, not demanded by external rules.

Implementation without revelation feels forced; implementation without conviction is easily given up.

Implementation without revelation is the religion of the Pharisees: meticulous on the outside, lifeless on the inside. The Lord Jesus said to them, “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you clean the outside of the cup and of the platter, but within they are full of extortion and unrighteousness” (Matthew 23:25). They did a great deal, but none of it came from revelation, so the more they did, the heavier it grew, the more bitter, the more proud.

Implementation without conviction is like a child forced to eat his vegetables: while the grown-up is watching, he eats them; the moment the grown-up turns away, he spits them out.

But with the Holy Spirit’s revelation and the foundation of conviction, implementation becomes a joyful and lasting obedience. Because then we are “willing”, not “forced”.

Paul spells out the secret clearly: “So then, my beloved, even as you have always obeyed, not only in my presence, but now much more in my absence, work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:12–13).

Look closely at the order of these two verses. Verse 12 is “you work out”; verse 13 is “God works in you”. On the surface it’s we who act; in reality it’s God at work within us. So when we’re willing to take the first step, we discover that the Holy Spirit gives strength in it, and implementation becomes a delight rather than a pressure.

The German theologian Dietrich Bonhoeffer left us a famous line in “The Cost of Discipleship” (1937): “Only those who believe obey, and only those who obey believe.” Faith and obedience are not two things; they are two sides of one thing.

4. Applying the 321 vision: the third link in the fivefold change

Brothers and sisters, the 321 vision tells us that life goes through a fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry.

“Information, Revelation, Conviction” change the mindset; Implementation is the door through which the mindset walks into daily living.

Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. If the mindset stays in our heads, the fivefold change is stuck at the first link, and the other four can’t move at all. Implementation is the hand that pushes the jammed gears into motion.

And we must remember: what moves that hand isn’t our willpower; it’s the Holy Spirit. Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves. Rely on the brain, and you worry; rely on the heart, and you rejoice. Doing the word in our own strength is a burden; doing the word by the Holy Spirit is a delight.

sections.heading: 2. Implementation Has a Price: From Thought to the Birth of Life
sections.html:
1. Truth within us is like an embryo

The process of implementation is like giving birth.

The truth within us is like an embryo, conceived by the revelation of the Holy Spirit and nourished by conviction; but if we are unwilling to pay the price of living it out, that life will miscarry.

Paul used exactly the same picture. He said to the believers in Galatia, “My little children, of whom I am again in travail until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians 4:19). The Greek word for “formed” is morphoō, which speaks of the forming of an inner nature, not of make-up on the outside. What Paul wanted wasn’t for them to memorise a few more verses; it was for the life of Christ truly to take shape within them.

And one of the most heartbreaking pictures in Scripture comes from the days of King Hezekiah. With the Assyrian army at the gates, Hezekiah sent word to the prophet Isaiah: “Today is a day of trouble, and of rebuke, and of rejection; for the children have come to the birth, and there is no strength to give birth” (Isaiah 37:3).

Brothers and sisters, what could be more agonising than “the children have come to the birth, and there is no strength to give birth”? The child is already there inside, yet cannot come out. If a woman in labour does not deliver, both mother and child are in danger; in the same way, if we do not put the truth into practice, our spiritual life stalls and may even wither.

How many brothers and sisters carry within them God’s calling, God’s stirring, God’s word — have carried it for three years, five years, ten years — and still have never had the strength to bring it to birth? It isn’t that God hasn’t given; it’s that we won’t push.

2. The struggle out of the chrysalis is necessary

Implementation always comes with challenge and pain, because it requires us to “break free of our old self”.

The natural world gives us a beautiful picture. Inside the chrysalis a caterpillar almost entirely dissolves and is reassembled into the body of a butterfly. When the time comes to emerge, it has to fight its way out through that narrow opening. Biologists long ago discovered that it is precisely this squeezing that pushes fluid from its body into the veins of its wings, so that the wings can unfold, harden and fly.

Someone once, out of pity, took a pair of scissors and cut the chrysalis open for the butterfly. The butterfly came out — but with a swollen body and shrivelled wings, and for the rest of its life it could never fly.

Brothers and sisters, did you hear that? The struggle you spare yourself is paid for with a lifetime of never flying.

If we are content merely to agree in our thoughts and never take a step of action, our faith is still dead, and our spiritual life cannot grow.

The Lord Jesus put it more deeply still: “Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24). A grain of wheat doesn’t find its worth by being eaten; it’s by falling into the ground, being buried and breaking down that new life springs up. Implementation is opening your hand, letting that grain go, and burying it in the soil.

Science offers another wonderful fact: the squeezing a baby undergoes in the birth canal helps to expel fluid from its lungs, so that it can start breathing the moment it is born. That seemingly cruel pressure is in fact a loving preparation.

Brothers and sisters, the pressure you’re feeling right now — “it’s so hard to live this out” — may well be God preparing you with the power to breathe.

3. Knowledge without implementation is a form of self-deception

As Scripture says, “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves” (James 1:22).

Knowledge without implementation is a form of self-deception; faith that acts is true worship.

Paul says, “Therefore I urge you, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service” (Romans 12:1). Notice — what is offered is our “bodies”, not our “ideas”. The worship God wants is worship that moves our hands, our feet and our mouths.

Psychological research has also confirmed that “paying the price” cannot be skipped. Phillippa Lally of University College London and her colleagues, in a study published in 2010 in the European Journal of Social Psychology, followed ninety-six participants and found that for a new behaviour to become an automatic habit took on average sixty-six days, with individuals ranging from eighteen to two hundred and fifty-four days.

Brothers and sisters — sixty-six days. No shortcuts, no crash course. It’s the same with spiritual life: the Lord Jesus himself, “though he was a Son, yet learned obedience by the things which he suffered” (Hebrews 5:8). If even the Son of God learned obedience through suffering, how much more must we?

4. Applying the 321 vision: the old self is self-centred, the new self is selfless

Brothers and sisters, “breaking free of our old self” — this is the very heart of the 321 vision.

The old self lives “the self-centred life”; the new self lives in “selflessness”. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of every problem. And the reason implementation hurts is that it asks us to lay down that “self”.

I don’t want to apologise, because “self” feels it will lose face; I won’t forgive, because “self” feels hard done by; I daren’t step up and serve, because “self” is afraid of failing and being shamed. Behind every refusal to put the truth into practice stands a “self” that has not been dealt with.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

And selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living it out. Paul says, “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me” (Galatians 2:20).

The moment it breaks out of the chrysalis, the butterfly loses the right to be a caterpillar — and gains the whole sky.

sections.heading: 3. Implementation Takes an Act of Faith: Taking the First Step
sections.html:
1. Why won’t we take the first step? Because we’re afraid of failing

Why do so many people understand the truth, and are even convinced by it, yet still stand still?

Because they’re afraid of failing.

Afraid of doing it badly, afraid of being laughed at, afraid of giving up halfway, afraid that “if I can’t live it out, won’t that be even worse?” So they keep waiting — waiting until they’re more certain, until they have more time, until they feel more stirred, until they understand a little better.

But Jesus said, “If you remain in my word, then you are truly my disciples. You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free” (John 8:31–32).

Notice the Lord’s order: first “remain in my word”, then “you will know the truth”.

The Lord’s order is: do first, understand afterwards. We don’t wait until we understand completely before we act; it’s in the course of acting that we truly come to understand. Truth is experienced and confirmed in the practice of obedience.

Elsewhere the Lord Jesus says it even more directly: “If anyone desires to do his will, he will know about the teaching, whether it is from God, or if I am speaking from myself” (John 7:17).

Brothers and sisters, that sentence turns the whole order on its head. We think it’s “understand, then do”; the Lord says it’s “do, then understand”.

2. First steps in the Bible

Of the miracles in the Bible, hardly a single one happened while people stood still.

When were the waters of the Jordan cut off? God’s command was: “It shall be that when the soles of the feet of the priests who bear the ark of Yahweh, the Lord of all the earth, rest in the waters of the Jordan, that the waters of the Jordan will be cut off. The waters that come down from above shall stand in one heap” (Joshua 3:13). And Scripture records: “When those who bore the ark had come to the Jordan, and the feet of the priests who bore the ark had dipped in the edge of the water (for the Jordan overflows … ), the waters which came down from above stood, and rose up in one heap a great way off, at Adam, the city that is beside Zarethan” (Joshua 3:15–16).

Brothers and sisters, look closely: the water didn’t part first so the priests could step in; the priests stepped in first, and then the water parted. And Scripture adds a special note: “for the Jordan overflows all its banks all the time of harvest” (Joshua 3:15). Not the dry season — the flood season. The first step is always a step into a place that looks impossible.

And Naaman the general? The prophet told him to go and wash seven times in the Jordan. He flew into a rage; it was too simple, too humiliating, too unreasonable. But his servants reasoned with him, and so Scripture says: “Then went he down, and dipped himself seven times in the Jordan, according to the saying of the man of God; and his flesh was restored like the flesh of a little child, and he was clean” (2 Kings 5:14).

What if he had only gone down six times? Nothing would have happened. Implementation can’t be done at a discount.

And Peter? He had toiled all night and caught nothing, and now it was daylight — the very worst time to let down the nets. But he said, “Master, we worked all night, and took nothing; but at your word I will let down the net” (Luke 5:5). With that one phrase, “but at your word”, the net was filled.

And Abraham? “By faith, Abraham, when he was called, obeyed to go out to the place which he was to receive for an inheritance. He went out, not knowing where he went” (Hebrews 11:8).

Not knowing where he was going — and he had already gone. That is the action of faith.

3. Failure isn’t the frightening thing — refusing to try is

Learning to drive, learning to swim, learning to play the piano — all of them are learned through trying again and again and getting it wrong; and so is putting the spiritual life into practice.

No one has ever learned to swim by watching a swimming tutorial. You have to get into the water, swallow a few mouthfuls, flail about — and then one day, your body suddenly remembers.

In a classic study published in 1993 in Psychological Review, the psychologist K. Anders Ericsson and his colleagues showed that the key to top performance isn’t aimless repetition but “deliberate practice” — practice with clear goals, immediate feedback and the constant correction of mistakes.

Brothers and sisters, notice that phrase, “the correction of mistakes”. So mistakes are not the enemy of deliberate practice; mistakes are its raw material.

Brain science tells us, too, that every repeated action strengthens the corresponding neural pathways and thickens the myelin sheath around the nerve fibres, so that signals travel faster and more reliably. It’s generally said that neuroscientists have summed this up in one sentence: “Neurons that fire together wire together.” This is one of the wonders of God’s creation — he has written the principle that “repetition gives shape” into our very brains.

So failure isn’t the frightening thing; what’s frightening is being unwilling to try. Falling down and getting up again, getting it wrong and putting it right — that is the road of growth.

Scripture said it long ago: “for a righteous man falls seven times and rises up again; but the wicked are overthrown by calamity” (Proverbs 24:16). The righteous are not people who never fall; the righteous are people who fall and get up again.

The Song dynasty poet Lu You, in a poem written for his son, has this couplet: “What is gained from paper always proves shallow in the end; to truly know a thing, you must do it yourself.” People understood it more than eight hundred years ago: what you read in books is shallow in the end; if you really want to know, you must do it with your own hands.

4. From “discipline” to “longing”: drawing near to God as an example

Let’s take the example closest to home — “drawing near to God”.

If you only know the theory, you will never enjoy the sweetness of being with God; but when you begin each morning to read the Bible quietly, to pray and to worship, keep going — even if at first your mind wanders.

At first your mind will certainly wander. You’ll think of the meeting you’ve got today, the bills you need to pay, that cutting remark from yesterday. Never mind — just draw your heart back again. You’ll find it dry, as though you’re talking to the ceiling. Never mind — come back tomorrow.

Little by little you’ll discover that “drawing near to God” is no longer a discipline but a longing and a delight.

David says, “Oh taste and see that Yahweh is good. Blessed is the man who takes refuge in him” (Psalm 34:8). Notice — first “taste”, and then “see”. If you never taste it, you’ll never know that honey is sweet.

James says too, “Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you” (James 4:8). The initiative lies on our side: we move one step, and God comes to meet us.

Even the Lord Jesus himself lived this way: “Early in the morning, while it was still dark, he rose up and went out, and departed into a deserted place, and prayed there” (Mark 1:35). If the Son of God rose to pray while it was still dark, then our gathering this early morning to read together means we’re already walking in his footsteps.

5. Applying the 321 vision: the focus is on Jesus, the training ground is relationships

Brothers and sisters, the 321 vision says: the focus is on Jesus — not on ourselves, not on other people, not on our circumstances.

Why don’t we dare take the first step? Because our focus is wrong. Focus on yourself, and you see your own inadequacy; focus on other people, and you fear their eyes; focus on your circumstances, and you see a Jordan overflowing all its banks.

Peter could walk on the water because he was looking at Jesus; he began to sink because he saw the wind and the waves (see Matthew 14:29–30).

So the secret of implementation isn’t “try harder”; it’s “change your focus”.

The 321 vision’s shift of perspective is here too: from man’s perspective to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. From man’s perspective, stepping into the water first is too great a risk; from God’s perspective, not stepping in is the greatest risk of all.

sections.heading: 4. Integrating the 321 Vision: Implementation Is Truly Letting Jesus Be King
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s set this lesson back into the whole picture of 321.

1. The Three Foundations: the three pillars of implementation

The Three Foundations are: Jesus is my role model; the Bible is my standard; the Holy Spirit is my guide.

These three pillars answer precisely the three most crucial questions of implementation.

The first question is: “What kind of person am I to become?” The answer — Jesus is my role model. The Lord Jesus was never one to talk without doing. He said we must deny ourselves, and he went to the cross; he spoke of washing feet, and he tied a towel around himself and washed the disciples’ feet with his own hands (John 13:4–5). He is the original pattern of every doer of the word.

The second question is: “What am I to act by?” The answer — the Bible is my standard. Not acting by my feelings, not by other people’s expectations, not by the fashions of the age. David says, “Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path” (Psalm 119:105). Notice: a lamp to my “feet” — God’s light usually shows us only the next step, not the whole road. That’s exactly why we need to walk it step by step.

The third question is: “Where does my strength come from?” The answer — the Holy Spirit is my guide. Implementation in our own strength will surely run dry; implementation by the Holy Spirit has living water. The Lord said, “But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you” (Acts 1:8).

2. The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory

What does it mean to “let Jesus be King”?

Brothers and sisters, a king’s authority isn’t shown in the titles on our lips but in the obedience of our hands and feet. If a king issues a command and his subjects only applaud warmly while no one carries it out, he isn’t really king.

The Lord Jesus himself asked a piercing question: “Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and don’t do the things which I say?” (Luke 6:46)

So “implementation” is the most concrete form of “letting Jesus be King”. Every time we live out his word, we plant one more boundary stone on the territory of our lives that reads, “Jesus is King.”

And when we really live it out, what others see is no longer our doctrine but the life of Jesus. The Lord said, “Even so, let your light shine before men; that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16).

Notice — it is when people “see your good works” that they “glorify your Father”. If nothing is lived out, the glory has no way to go up. Implementation is the very channel through which Jesus receives all the glory.

3. The Goal: establish God’s system

The Goal is to establish God’s system.

A system isn’t established by holding meetings; it’s lived out day after day by a body of people willing to do the word. The Worldly system is held together by institutions; God’s system is held together by life. And life grows only through implementation.

4. Life first, then relationships, then ministry

The order in the 321 vision is: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

So when we talk about implementation, we’re not asking anyone to dive headlong into “doing a bit more ministry”. If the life hasn’t changed, the more ministry there is, the bigger that “self” will grow.

The first arena of implementation is relationships. The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things.

First with God — this morning, have you truly quietened your heart?

Then with yourself — are you willing to face honestly the self that won’t do the word?

Then with others — is there a phone call you should make, an “I’m sorry” you should say?

Last of all with things — only then come the work and the service in your hands.

5. The 920 practice: living out the “0” before every “2”

Brothers and sisters, this is where the 920 practice gets most practical.

Everyone we’re in relationship with is our “2” — spouse, children, parents, colleagues, neighbours, that brother in your small group who gives you headaches. Practising a life of selflessness in front of them is the “0”; and what it bears is the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23).

Notice that not one fruit of the Spirit can grow in a vacuum. Patience only grows when someone provokes you; forgiveness can only be practised when someone hurts you; gentleness only shows when someone talks back to you.

So God hasn’t placed that “2” beside you to torment you, but so that you can live the truth out.

6. 235 relationships: doing the word together, going further

What does implementation fear most? Walking alone.

That’s why the 321 vision speaks of 235 relationships: to become a “2” with someone selfless — a spiritual companion; to build a “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children; to become a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.

Scripture says, “Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls, and doesn’t have another to lift him up” (Ecclesiastes 4:9–10).

Brothers and sisters, this morning, please find yourself a “2”. Tell them the thing you’re going to put into practice and ask them to check in with you once a week. One person’s resolve cools; two people’s agreement lasts.

7. A shift of perspective

Finally, the power to implement comes from a shift of perspective: from man’s perspective to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly.

From man’s perspective, apologising means losing face; from God’s perspective, apologising means gaining life.

From an earthly perspective, forgiving means losing out; from a heavenly perspective, forgiving means gaining freedom.

From a temporary perspective, getting up early to read the Bible costs you half an hour’s sleep; from an eternal perspective, that half hour is changing your whole life.

sections.heading: 5. Practice for Daily Living: Going Deeper with the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, the lesson gives us three practices. We want to place these three practices within the eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — so that they really take root.

Practice one: write down one revelation and ask, “How will I put it into practice concretely?”

Take a pen and paper, write down a revelation you’ve recently received from God, and ask yourself: “How will I put it into practice concretely?”

Don’t write “I’m going to love the Lord more” — that’s too vague. Write it as a sentence with a time, a place and an action. For example: “This Wednesday at eight in the evening I’m going to ring my brother and apologise to him.”

This is exactly the psychological finding we mentioned earlier: turn “I want to” into “when, where and how”, and the rate of action rises sharply. Human beings, as God made them, simply work this way.

Within the eight stages, this step pins down the “Information” and the “Revelation” so they aren’t scattered by the wind. Once it’s written down, it can’t run away.

Practice two: this week, choose one small thing, do it concretely, and record what you learn

Some time this week, choose one small thing — forgiving, giving thanks, drawing near to God, serving someone — do it concretely, and record what you learn.

Notice the word “small”. One of Satan’s favourite tricks is to get us to set our goals so high that we can never even begin, and then give up in a sense of helplessness.

The Lord Jesus said, “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much. He who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much” (Luke 16:10). The arithmetic of God’s kingdom never starts big; it starts small.

Forgiving someone is too hard? Then begin by praying for them once.

Giving thanks to God, but don’t know where to start? Then write down three things every night before you go to bed.

Drawing near to God, but no time? Then get up ten minutes earlier.

Serving others, but no gifting? Then offer to carry a chair, wash a cup.

And the step of “recording what you learn” corresponds to Evaluation in the eight stages. Without a record there is no evaluation; without evaluation there is no correction. Many people fail not because they won’t act, but because once they’ve acted they forget all about it and never look back even once.

Practice three: when difficulties come, don’t give up; let the Holy Spirit lead you to correct course again and again

If you meet difficulty or setback as you put things into practice, don’t give up; hand the process over to the Lord and let the Holy Spirit lead you to correct course again and again.

This is stage six of the eight, Correction, and stage seven, Repetition.

Brothers and sisters, please keep “correction” separate from “condemnation”. Satan’s voice says, “See? You’ve failed again. You’ll never manage it.” The Holy Spirit’s voice says, “It’s all right. Let’s try again — a different way this time.” One tells you to stop; the other helps you keep going.

Scripture says, “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).

And Repetition is the delivery room of the spiritual life. The sixty-six-day study tells us that repetition is the only way to engrave a behaviour into our lives. Spiritually it’s the same — Paul says, “Exercise yourself toward godliness” (1 Timothy 4:7). The Greek word for “exercise” is gymnazō, the root of the word gymnasium, and it refers to the endless, repeated training of an athlete.

Last comes stage eight, Multiplication. When you really have lived it out, go and take someone with you. Tell them honestly about your struggles, your falls and your getting up again, and then walk part of the road beside them.

The Lord’s Great Commission puts it plainly: “teaching them to observe all things that I commanded you” (Matthew 28:20). Notice — not “teaching them to understand” but “teaching them to observe”. The finishing line of discipleship is always living it out.

A Gentle Reminder

Don’t wait until you’re fully ready before you act.

Obedience isn’t about being perfect; it’s about being willing.

God’s word isn’t too hard to do — Moses said, “For this commandment which I command you today is not too hard for you or too distant” (Deuteronomy 30:11). “But the word is very near to you, in your mouth and in your heart, that you may do it” (Deuteronomy 30:14).

God doesn’t require you to “be able to do it”; he requires you to “be willing to begin”.

sections.heading: 6. Closing and Call: Letting Our Lives Blossom into the Likeness of Jesus Through Implementation
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, we’re coming to a close.

Implementation is the fruit of revelation and conviction; faith without action is only empty knowledge.

When we’re willing to take the first step of faith, God’s word moves from thought to the testimony of a life.

Growth in life doesn’t lie in how much we know, but in how much we’ve done.

This morning God doesn’t want us to know a little more. What he wants is that step.

The step you’ve known about for a long time but keep putting off.

That phone call, that “I’m sorry”, that forgiveness, that offering, that early alarm, that elderly relative you promised to visit but keep putting off.

If the priests hadn’t set their feet in the water, the Jordan would never have parted. If Naaman hadn’t gone down the seventh time, his leprosy would never have been cleansed. If Peter hadn’t let down that net, he would never have seen a boat full of fish.

And you — if you don’t take that step, you’ll never know what God has prepared for you.

Let’s let the truth touch the ground, respond to God with action, and let our lives no longer stay stuck in our thoughts but blossom, through implementation, into the likeness of Jesus.

May we be not people who are moved, but people who do the word.

May we be not people who have heard a great deal, but people who live it out.

May every step we take let Jesus be King; may every step we take let Jesus receive all the glory.

keyVerses: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.” (James 1:22)
“For as the body apart from the spirit is dead, even so faith apart from works is dead.” (James 2:26)
“Jesus therefore said to those Jews who had believed him, ‘If you remain in my word, then you are truly my disciples. You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.’” (John 8:31–32)
declarations: Brothers and sisters, please declare with me:

Lord, thank you that your word is taking root in my heart. Help me not only to hear, but to be willing to live out your word. Even with weakness and fear, I will rely on the Holy Spirit to take the step of faith, letting the truth take shape in my life and become my daily practice.
practices: Write down one revelation and ask, “How will I put it into practice concretely?”
This week, choose one small thing, do it concretely, and record what you learn
When difficulties come, don’t give up; let the Holy Spirit lead you to correct course again and again
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,

Thank you for speaking to us once again this morning. Lord, we confess that we have heard a great deal yet done very little; we have been moved many times yet changed very few. Forgive us for the self-deception of counting “I’ve heard it” as “I’ve done it”.

Lord, may your Holy Spirit shine on us right now, so that we see clearly the one thing you want us to do. Take away our fear, take away our concern for face, take away the “self” within us that holds us back.

Give us strength to set our feet in the water, to let down that net, to make that phone call. Even when we are weak, even when we fall, lift us up, and let us correct course time and again, and begin anew time and again.
Lord, may your word take shape in us; may the life of Christ grow up within us. May every small thing we do today be a sign that you reign as King, and give all the glory to you.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: James 1:22 says, “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.” Looking back over the past six months, is there a stirring or revelation God gave you that you still haven’t lived out? What has held you back — fear, face, feeling it’s too hard, or simply forgetting?

John 7:17 says, “If anyone desires to do his will, he will know about the teaching, whether it is from God, or if I am speaking from myself.” Share a time when you “obeyed first and understood later”: you didn’t fully understand at the time, yet you went ahead and did it — what did God later show you?
l045.title: Bringing Truth Down to Earth
l045.subtitle: Stage Four of Changing Our Mindset: Implementation
l045.partTitle: Unit 4 · The Prerequisite for Revival — A Change of Mindset

sections.heading: Introduction: Without the Courage to Look Back, There Is No Strength to Move Forward
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I’d like to begin by asking you to remember a small thing.

Have you ever had this experience? You’re driving on the motorway, the traffic is flowing, the music is just right and you’re in a good mood — until at some point you suddenly notice that the sign by the road shows a place name you don’t recognise. With a jolt, you realise you took the wrong exit thirty kilometres back. At that moment you have two choices. One is to keep driving forward and reassure yourself, “I must be nearly there anyway.” The other is to pull over, open the map, admit honestly, “I’ve gone the wrong way,” and turn round.

The first choice is more comfortable; the second is more humble. But only the second will get you home.

In life we often come to the same kind of fork in the road. Having come this far in the 321 Morning Devotion course, we have already learned the first four stages of changing our mindset together: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation. We heard the truth (Information); the Holy Spirit lit up the truth in our hearts (Revelation); we were won over, heart and mouth, and said, “Lord, this is right” (Conviction); and we plucked up courage to take the first step (Implementation). By rights, change should now simply follow, like water flowing into a channel. Yet strangely, many people stall at Implementation. Keen in the first week, forcing it in the second, cooling off in the third, back where they started in the fourth.

Why? The problem isn’t that they aren’t keen enough; it’s that they’re missing one crucial move: looking back.

That is the fifth stage we’re learning today — Evaluation.

What is evaluation? Evaluation is, after acting, growing quiet and honestly asking three questions: What did I do? How did it turn out? What does God want me to adjust? Evaluation isn’t fault-finding, it isn’t raking up the past, and it certainly isn’t self-accusation. Evaluation is for seeing the truth and adjusting our direction, so that the truth moves from a one-off action to a lifelong habit.

It’s generally held that the Greek philosopher Socrates, at his trial, said something that has echoed down history: “The unexamined life is not worth living” (recorded in Plato’s “Apology”). If a pagan philosopher knew the value of self-examination, how much more should we — God’s children, indwelt by the Holy Spirit and illuminated by the truth?

The Reformer John Calvin put it more deeply still at the opening of his “Institutes of the Christian Religion”: nearly all the true and sound wisdom we possess consists of two parts — the knowledge of God and the knowledge of ourselves. The two are bound together. Every time we honestly evaluate ourselves, we come to know God more deeply; every time we know God more deeply, we see ourselves more clearly.

Brothers and sisters, this morning may the Holy Spirit give us a heart that isn’t afraid to look back. Because true humility isn’t never taking a wrong turn; it’s being willing, when we find we’ve gone wrong, to turn round bravely.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: An Evaluation Meeting Led by the Lord Jesus Himself
sections.html:
1. The Author, Date and Readers of Luke’s Gospel

Luke, the author of Luke’s Gospel, was a Gentile, a physician, and a faithful co-worker of the apostle Paul. Writing from prison, Paul mentions him warmly: “Luke the beloved physician and Demas greet you” (Colossians 4:14). At the very end of Paul’s life, when everyone else had deserted him, Luke was still at his side: “Only Luke is with me” (2 Timothy 4:11).

Luke wrote this Gospel to a man named Theophilus: “It seemed good to me also, having traced the course of all things accurately from the first, to write to you in order, most excellent Theophilus; that you might know the certainty concerning the things in which you were instructed” (Luke 1:3–4). The word “traced” is παρακολουθέω (parakoloutheo) in Greek, which originally means “to follow closely, to track all the way”. In other words, the very birth of Luke’s Gospel was an exceptionally rigorous “evaluation report” — he interviewed eyewitnesses, checked his sources and set things in order, so that his readers could be certain that what they believed was true.

As for its date, most evangelical scholars place it around the AD 60s, written for educated Gentile readers in the Greco-Roman world. That is why Luke takes special care to stress that salvation is for all peoples, and the gospel must go to the ends of the earth.

2. The Sending and Return of the Seventy

Our key passage today comes from Luke chapter 10. Its background begins at Luke 9:51: “It came to pass, when the days were near that he should be taken up, he intently set his face to go to Jerusalem.” From this verse on, the Lord Jesus is on the road to the cross.

Before this, the Lord had already sent out the twelve apostles (Luke 9:1–6). Now in chapter 10 he sends out another group: “Now after these things, the Lord also appointed seventy others, and sent them two by two ahead of him into every city and place where he was about to come” (Luke 10:1).

Notice that the Chinese Union Version reads “seventy”. Some ancient manuscripts read “seventy-two”; this is a difference between manuscripts and does not affect the truth, and in our sharing we follow the Chinese Union Version (as does the World English Bible) and say “seventy” throughout. The number very likely echoes the count of the nations in Genesis 10, a sign that the gospel is to reach every family on earth.

They went, and they came back. “The seventy returned with joy, saying, ‘Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name!’” (Luke 10:17) Then the Lord Jesus said three things:

“I saw Satan having fallen like lightning from heaven.” (Luke 10:18)

“Behold, I give you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy. Nothing will in any way hurt you.” (Luke 10:19)

“Nevertheless, don’t rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.” (Luke 10:20)

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? This is an evaluation meeting. The disciples went out and put things into practice, came back and reported, and the Lord Jesus led them through an evaluation. First the Lord affirms (Satan really has fallen; authority really has been given), then he adjusts (nevertheless, don’t rejoice in this … but rejoice that …). That is exactly the healthiest order for an evaluation: first see what God has done, then adjust the focus of our hearts.

Even more striking is the passage that follows. After the evaluation, “In that same hour Jesus rejoiced in the Holy Spirit” (Luke 10:21). Then comes the parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:25–37), and after that the story of Martha and Mary (Luke 10:38–42) — Martha, distracted with much serving, her heart in a whirl; Mary, sitting at the Lord’s feet listening to his word, and the Lord says she has chosen the good part. For the whole chapter the Lord Jesus is doing one and the same thing: drawing his disciples’ focus back from “ministry” to “life”.

3. The Background to Proverbs 27:17

“Iron sharpens iron; so a man sharpens his friend’s countenance.” (Proverbs 27:17) This verse belongs to the second collection of Solomon’s proverbs: “These also are proverbs of Solomon, which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied out” (Proverbs 25:1). When King Hezekiah led a religious reform in the eighth century BC, he had these ancient sayings of wisdom collected and copied.

The word “sharpens” is חָדַד (chadad) in Hebrew, meaning “to make keen”. The Chinese Union Version renders the second line loosely and adds a small note beside it: “literally, sharpens his friend’s face” — which is just what WEB’s “countenance” preserves. In Hebrew, “face” (פָּנִים, panim) means more than a person’s features; it speaks of their expression, their bearing and the state of their life.

It’s a vivid picture. For an iron blade to be sharp, it needs another piece of iron to grind it. As it’s ground there is friction, there are sparks, there is noise, and some iron filings are even worn away. But once the grinding is done, the edge appears. God has designed human growth the same way — he doesn’t let us become holy on our own; he has us sharpen one another in relationships.

sections.heading: Key Point 1: Evaluation Turns Action into a Habit of Life
sections.html:
1. Implementation is only the beginning; evaluation makes change last

The eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — are not eight separate boxes but a single road of life. Of these, Evaluation, Correction and Repetition form an ever-ascending cycle. Implementation gets us moving; evaluation helps us see clearly; correction puts us on the right path; repetition makes our steps steady.

A single action doesn’t turn a mindset into life. Getting up early to pray once today doesn’t make you a person of prayer; being gentle with your spouse once today doesn’t mean your home has changed. Only through the cycle of evaluation, correction and repetition does truth move from “something I’ve done” to “who I am”.
