In a classic study published in 1993 in Psychological Review, the psychologist Anders Ericsson and his colleagues put forward the idea of “deliberate practice”. They found that what makes top musicians and athletes excel isn’t only the “hours” of practice but its “quality” — and the one indispensable element is immediate, specific “feedback”. Repetition without feedback simply makes you better at your mistakes; repetition with feedback is what brings progress.

Brothers and sisters, that is precisely the role of evaluation in the spiritual life. Service without evaluation may only make us more practised at our old faults; service with evaluation makes us more like Jesus each time.

The educational psychologist David Kolb’s “experiential learning cycle”, put forward in 1984, says the same thing: real learning is a cycle — concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualisation, active experimentation, and then back to experience. Take away reflective observation, and the cycle is broken: experience stays just experience and never becomes ability.

As the saying goes, we don’t learn from experience; we learn from reflecting on experience.

2. From “what they did” back to “who they are”

When the seventy came back, they came back “with joy”. They hadn’t sinned, hadn’t failed, hadn’t done anything wrong. They had cast out demons in the Lord’s name, and the demons really had submitted to them — a real, solid victory. The Lord Jesus confirmed it with his own lips: “I saw Satan having fallen like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10:18).

And yet the Lord Jesus still led them through an evaluation. That tells us something extremely important: evaluation isn’t only for after failure; it’s also for after success. Evaluation after failure rescues us from discouragement; evaluation after success rescues us from pride. And the latter is often the more dangerous.

What did the Lord Jesus adjust? Their focus. He said, “Don’t rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20). “The spirits are subject to you” is the result — “what I’ve accomplished”; “your names are written in heaven” is identity — “who I am in God’s eyes”.

Here “written” is, in Greek, the perfect passive ἐγγέγραπται (engegraptai), meaning “has been written, and remains in force”. Brothers and sisters, what a comfort that is! Your name is written in heaven not because of how many demons you cast out today, how many sermons you preached or how many people you led to faith, but because the Lord’s grace has already written it there — and that ink will never fade.

Why did the Lord make this adjustment? Because people whose focus is on results will sooner or later fall. When the results are good, they exalt themselves; when the results are poor, they reject themselves. Their emotions rise and fall with the numbers; their worth is built on other people’s applause. But people whose focus is on identity are different — they know who they are, so whatever the results, they can give the glory to God.

This is just what the 321 vision says: the focus is on Jesus — not on ourselves, not on other people, not on our circumstances. Pay attention only to results, and we easily exalt ourselves; pay attention to identity, and we glorify God.

3. One degree off, sixty miles astray

In navigation at sea and in the air there is a well-known rule of thumb called the “one-in-sixty rule”: if your heading is one degree off, then for every sixty nautical miles you travel you drift about one nautical mile off course. One degree is so small you can barely see it on the instruments; but after a thousand nautical miles you’re more than sixteen nautical miles off — enough to miss the airport altogether.

Life is like that. A little self today, a little pride, a little craving for applause — it looks trivial at the time, but ten years on it may have carried us somewhere completely unfamiliar. That’s why pilots correct their heading at regular intervals — not because the plane is broken, but because drift is inevitable.

Evaluation is course correction for the spiritual life. You don’t need it because you’ve failed; you need it because you’re still flying.

4. Applying the 321 vision: life first, then relationships, then ministry

Luke 10 shows us a clear order. The disciples came back with news of victory in “ministry”, but the Lord Jesus brought them back to the foundation of “life”. This is exactly what the 321 vision emphasises: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

Many who serve walk it backwards: ministry first, then relationships, and only at the end do they discover their life has gone empty. They take “how much I’ve achieved” to mean “how much I’m worth”, and so the more they serve, the drier their hearts; the greater the results, the hollower they are inside. In this evaluation meeting the Lord Jesus was pulling his disciples back off that road.

So in every evaluation, the first question to ask is not “Was it a success this time?” but “Did I become more like Jesus this time?” Not “How many people came?” but “Where was my heart?”

sections.heading: Key Point 2: Evaluation Is Not Criticism but Building Up
sections.html:
1. Why we’re afraid of evaluation

For many people, just hearing the word “evaluation” makes their stomach knot. Because in our experience growing up, evaluation often meant being told off. At home, it was parents raking up the past; at school, it was the teacher calling out your name; at work, it’s the boss looking for someone to blame. Over time our bodies learned to get defensive first, and then our hearts learned to shut the door.

But “examining ourselves” in the Bible means nothing of the sort. The apostle Paul says, “Examine your own selves, whether you are in the faith. Test your own selves” (2 Corinthians 13:5). The word “test” here is δοκιμάζω (dokimazo) in Greek, originally a term from metalworking, meaning to assay metal in the fire. Notice that the purpose of refining gold is not to throw the gold away, but to prove it genuine and to remove the dross, making it purer.

Paul also says, “For if we discerned ourselves, we wouldn’t be judged” (1 Corinthians 11:31). “Discern” (διακρίνω, diakrino) means to separate things that are mixed together and see them clearly. So biblical evaluation is discerning, it is refining, it is for keeping the true gold — not for condemning.

The Lord Jesus himself used an even lovelier picture: “Every branch in me that doesn’t bear fruit, he takes away. Every branch that bears fruit, he prunes, that it may bear more fruit” (John 15:2). The Greek for “prunes” is καθαίρω (kathairo), from the same root as “clean” (καθαροί) in the next verse: “You are already pruned clean”. Pruning is cleansing. The shears in the gardener’s hand are not an instrument of punishment but an instrument of grace.

The writer to the Hebrews says too: “All chastening seems for the present to be not joyous but grievous; yet afterward it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it” (Hebrews 12:11). Brothers and sisters, remember these two time-words: “for the present” it isn’t joyful; “afterward” it bears fruit. The pain of evaluation is temporary; the fruit of evaluation lasts.

2. When we are evaluated, learn to listen humbly

The lesson reminds us: when we are evaluated, we should learn to listen humbly, without justifying ourselves and without refusing because it’s uncomfortable. That’s easy to say, but doing it comes at a price.

The management thinker Chris Argyris, in his famous 1991 Harvard Business Review article “Teaching Smart People How to Learn”, pointed to an unsettling finding: the more professional and accomplished people are, the harder they find it to learn from failure. Because they have so rarely experienced failure, the moment someone points out a mistake they switch on “defensive reasoning” — pushing the problem outward onto other people, onto circumstances, onto the system, anywhere but themselves.

Brothers and sisters, isn’t that a portrait of us? When others point out our shortcomings, our first reaction is often not “Is he right?” but “Who is he to say that about me?” We’re busy explaining our motives, adding background, describing our difficulties — and so that reminder, which may well have come from the Holy Spirit, slips away between our fingers.

Scripture says, “Don’t reprove a scoffer, lest he hate you. Reprove a wise person, and he will love you” (Proverbs 9:8). And again, “The ear that listens to reproof lives, and will be at home among the wise” (Proverbs 15:31). The difference between the scoffer and the wise isn’t which of them gets reproved, but how they respond afterwards.

King David’s attitude is one we should learn from: “Let the righteous strike me, it is kindness; let him reprove me, it is like oil on the head; don’t let my head refuse it” (Psalm 141:5). “Don’t let my head refuse it” — what a powerful line! When you’re being sharpened, don’t pull your head back.

The lesson puts it exactly: even if the other person’s opinion isn’t entirely correct, we can still receive revelation from it and see a new angle. That is great wisdom. We don’t need to wait until someone is a hundred per cent right before we’ll listen; as long as there is one per cent of truth in what they say, we’ve gained one per cent of growth.

3. The one who raises an evaluation also needs courage

The lesson reminds us of the other side too: whoever is willing to raise an honest evaluation also has to pluck up courage. That sentence is worth reading again.

In real relationships, silence is always the safest option. Pointing out someone else’s shortcomings means risking being misunderstood, being kept at arm’s length, being hit back. So when someone is willing to take that risk to tell you the truth, it’s usually not because they don’t love you — it’s precisely because they do.

How penetrating Scripture is here: “Better is open rebuke than hidden love. The wounds of a friend are faithful, although the kisses of an enemy are profuse” (Proverbs 27:5–6). Brothers and sisters, be clear about this: words that make you comfortable aren’t necessarily love, and words that hurt aren’t necessarily harm.

Of course, the one raising an evaluation must go about it the right way. Paul says, “Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness; looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted” (Galatians 6:1). The word “restore” (καταρτίζω, katartizo) was used in the medical language of the day for setting a dislocated bone back in place. The aim is to “set it back”, not to “knock him down”.

Paul also says, “but speaking truth in love, we may grow up in all things into him who is the head, Christ” (Ephesians 4:15). Love and truth — neither can be missing. Love without truth is indulgence; truth without love is injury. And remember: “Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear” (Ephesians 4:29). Building up is the purpose of evaluation.

4. Psychological safety: a biblical truth confirmed by modern management science

Harvard Business School professor Amy Edmondson is known for her work on “psychological safety”, a concept she set out formally in a 1999 paper in Administrative Science Quarterly; its starting point was a study of hospital nursing teams that she published in 1996. Her original hypothesis was that the better a medical team performed, the fewer mistakes it would make. But the data showed the opposite — the best-performing teams actually “reported” the most errors.

On closer study she discovered that the difference wasn’t in the number of errors but in whether people dared to speak up. In teams with high psychological safety, people dare to admit mistakes and raise questions, so errors are seen, dealt with and learned from; in teams with low psychological safety, errors are hidden — and then erupt at a worse moment.

Google’s “Project Aristotle”, carried out between 2012 and 2016, analysed data from a great many teams within the company, and its first conclusion was the same: psychological safety is the most important characteristic of highly effective teams.

Brothers and sisters, can you hear it? Isn’t this exactly what the church was always meant to be? A community where it’s safe to say, “I was wrong”; a community where no one has to pretend to be perfect; a community that will “confess your offenses to one another, and pray for one another” (James 5:16). What the world took decades of research to discover, the Bible said long ago.

In 2008 the World Health Organization introduced its “Surgical Safety Checklist”, and a study by Haynes and colleagues published in 2009 in the New England Journal of Medicine showed that after this simple checklist was introduced in eight hospitals, in-hospital deaths fell from 1.5% to 0.8% and post-operative complications from 11% to 7%. One sheet of paper, a few questions, a short pause to check with one another — and countless lives were saved. That’s how concrete the power of evaluation is.

5. Applying the 321 vision: humility overcomes pride, selflessness overcomes Satan

Why is being evaluated so hard? The root of it comes down to one word: “self”. The old self is self-centred, so the moment it’s touched, it leaps up; the new self is selfless, so it can listen quietly, and even give thanks.

The 321 vision tells us that the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. When it comes to evaluation, pride says, “I don’t need anyone to tell me” — that is wanting to take God’s place as the One who knows all things; humility says, “Lord, please remind me through my brother” — that is returning to our originally intended position as creatures.

And remember: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. When someone gets defensive the moment they’re evaluated, the person raising it will be harder next time, and the more the two rub against each other, the more they wound each other. But when someone being evaluated sincerely says, “Thank you for telling me,” the other person’s heart softens too, and next time they’ll speak more gently. That’s the two-way blessing the lesson speaks of — the one evaluated is helped, and the one raising the evaluation also learns to build up in love.

Paul says, “doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself” (Philippians 2:3). “Counting others better than himself” is a heart already prepared in advance for evaluation.

sections.heading: Key Point 3: A Suggestion Is Not a Decision but a Contribution
sections.html:
1. I am not the final decision-maker

The lesson reminds those who raise an evaluation of one extremely important mindset: a suggestion is not a decision.

When we offer a suggestion, we need to understand that we are not the final decision-maker. Our view isn’t necessarily the most perfect, but it can become an opening for discussion and for seeking God’s will together. If the other person doesn’t take it up, that doesn’t mean we’ve been rejected; it simply means the situation didn’t suit it.

Why is this hard? Because when our suggestion is turned down, what we feel has been turned down isn’t the suggestion but “me”. Which brings us back to the same root — “self”. A self-centred person ties the suggestion to himself, so having his suggestion refused means being refused himself; a selfless person lays the suggestion before God, so if it’s taken up he’s grateful, and if it isn’t he’s at peace.

Scripture gives us a beautiful example. At the Council of Jerusalem the church was debating whether Gentile believers had to be circumcised. “The apostles and the elders were gathered together to see about this matter” (Acts 15:6). Peter spoke, Barnabas and Paul recounted signs and wonders, and finally James put forward a proposal. What was their conclusion? “For it seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us, to lay no greater burden on you” (Acts 15:28).

Notice the order: the Holy Spirit first, and us after. Everyone put forward what they had seen, but the final decision belonged to no single person — it belonged to the Holy Spirit. This is exactly the third of the Three Foundations in the 321 vision: the Holy Spirit is my guide.

2. Not defensive, not comparing — because many perspectives help us see more fully

The lesson also says that when others raise different views on our suggestions, we must learn not to be defensive and not to compare, because many perspectives can help us see more fully.

Why do we need many perspectives? Because human vision is limited by nature. This isn’t a question of being spiritual or unspiritual; it’s a fact of how we were made. Our eyes have a blind spot — where the optic nerve passes through the retina there are no light-sensitive cells, and that small patch we simply cannot see. The brain is very clever and automatically “fills it in”, so we think we’re seeing everything. Brothers and sisters, what a profound parable that is! Our hearts have blind spots too, and our hearts are also very good at “auto-completing”, making us think we see the whole picture.

That’s why God has put us in a body and not on a desert island. “The eye can’t tell the hand, ‘I have no need for you,’ or again the head to the feet, ‘I have no need for you’” (1 Corinthians 12:21). What others can see is precisely the patch I can’t.

Proverbs says, “The way of a fool is right in his own eyes, but he who is wise listens to counsel” (Proverbs 12:15). And again, “Where there is no wise guidance, the nation falls, but in the multitude of counselors there is victory” (Proverbs 11:14). The psalmist David went further and placed his own blind spots in God’s hands: “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way” (Psalm 139:23–24).

The psychologists Daniel Kahneman & Gary Klein, in a dialogue-style paper published in 2009 in American Psychologist, pointed out that whether expert intuition can be trusted depends on two conditions — whether the environment is regular enough, and whether the individual receives good-quality feedback. In fields without feedback, no number of years of experience guarantees sound judgement.

That gives us a gentle reminder: seniority is not wisdom, and experience is not correctness. Someone who has served for thirty years but never accepted evaluation may simply have repeated the same one year of experience thirty times.

3. Iron sharpening iron makes sparks — and an edge

Let’s go back to our key verse: “Iron sharpens iron; so a man sharpens his friend’s countenance” (Proverbs 27:17).

Notice that the verse says “iron sharpens iron”, not “cotton sharpens iron”. When two pieces of iron grind against each other there will always be heat, noise and sparks. If two people can discuss something with no tension whatsoever, it’s usually not because they’re especially spiritual; it’s because someone isn’t telling the truth.

But notice too that the aim of iron sharpening iron isn’t to grind the other flat, but to “bring out an edge”. The relationship between whetstone and blade is that the whetstone quietly wears itself away so that the blade grows sharp. In the church we are one another’s whetstones. Being willing to spend time, take risks and take trouble to sharpen another person — that is love.

An old carpenter once said that for a piece of timber to become furniture, it has to go through three things — the cut of the saw, the smoothing of the plane and the polish of the sandpaper. Cutting gives it shape, planing removes the excess, sanding brings out the sheen. The spiritual life is the same: implementation is picking up the tools, evaluation is measuring, correction is planing, repetition is sanding. Leave out any one of them and you’ll never make good furniture.

4. Applying the 321 vision: sharpening one another in 235 relationships

The “235 relationships” of the 321 vision are designed for exactly this kind of mutual sharpening: to become a “2” with someone selfless — a spiritual companion; to build a “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children; and then to become a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.

Why become a 2 “with someone selfless”? Because when two self-centred people are together, what the grinding produces is temper; only when a selfless person is together with another selfless person does it produce an edge. Your “2” is the person who can tell you the truth and to whom you’re willing to open up. If there’s no such person beside you, this morning ask the Lord to provide one for you.

And in the 920 practice, everyone we’re in relationship with is our “2”. As we practise living out a selfless (“0”) life before them, the nine graces of the fruit of the Spirit grow: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23). Brothers and sisters, think about it: at the moment you’re being evaluated, which fruits do you need most? Patience, gentleness, self-control. At the moment you’re raising an evaluation, which do you need most? Love, kindness, goodness. So every occasion of evaluation is a practical class in the nine graces.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: Seeing the Whole Road of Life in One Evaluation
sections.html:
1. The Three Foundations: The Measuring Lines of Evaluation

Evaluation without a measuring line turns into everyone talking past one another. The Three Foundations of the 321 vision are the three rulers of evaluation.

Jesus is my role model — the first question of evaluation is: how would Jesus do this? Not “how do other people do it”, not “how was it done before”, but how would Jesus do it.

The Bible is my standard — the second question of evaluation is: what does the Bible say about this? Our feelings change, other people’s opinions change, the fashions of the age change; only God’s word never changes. “Every Scripture is God-breathed and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness” (2 Timothy 3:16). Notice that this verse contains a complete process of evaluation: teaching (information), reproof (seeing where we’ve drifted), correction (putting it right), instruction in righteousness (making it a habit).

The Holy Spirit is my guide — the third question of evaluation is: what is the Holy Spirit reminding me of in this? “However when he, the Spirit of truth, has come, he will guide you into all truth” (John 16:13). Evaluation doesn’t rest on self-analysis but on the Holy Spirit’s light.

2. The Two Core Values: The Purpose of Evaluation

Let Jesus be King — when we evaluate, we hand the throne back to Jesus. The disciples rejoiced that “the demons are subject to us” — that was putting themselves at the centre; the Lord Jesus adjusted them so that God’s name would be lifted high. Every evaluation is a small coronation: I step down, the Lord goes up.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — evaluation isn’t so that I can be more successful, but so that the Lord can be more clearly seen. If after evaluating all we think is “next time I’ll perform better”, we’re still self-centred; if after evaluating we think “next time let people see Jesus more clearly”, that is true renewal.

3. The Goal: Establish God’s System

Only a church that evaluates is a church that can grow. In Revelation, the Lord Jesus speaks to seven churches, and almost every letter is an evaluation report: first the affirmation, “I know your works”, then the pointing out, “But I have this against you”. To the church in Ephesus the Lord says, “But I have this against you, that you left your first love” (Revelation 2:4).

The Lord Jesus personally evaluates his church because he wants to establish God’s system. God’s system is not a system without problems, but a system with the capacity to face problems, deal with them and grow through them.

4. The Fivefold Change and a Shift of Perspective

The 321 vision says the fivefold change is mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. Evaluation is the hinge of this whole chain — it lets us look back after Implementation and check: Has my mindset really changed? Has my life really been transformed? Can it be seen in my daily living? Are my relationships better? Is my ministry bringing God more glory?

Evaluation is also a shift of perspective: from man’s perspective to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. The disciples saw things from an earthly perspective: the demons submitted to us — what a success! The Lord Jesus reminded them from a heavenly perspective: your names are written in heaven — that is what is eternal.

And the key to it all is to rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves. Evaluate with the brain, and the more you evaluate, the more you worry, because the brain only knows how to tally accounts; evaluate with the heart, and the more you evaluate, the more joyful you become, because the heart meets God. “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23).

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Going Deeper with the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. Let’s put them into the eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — so that they aren’t just three things to do but a road we can walk all our lives.

Practice one: set aside time each week to evaluate your daily living and service honestly

The lesson’s practice: set aside time each week to evaluate your daily living and service honestly — are you still walking within “3-2-1”, that is, Jesus as your role model, the Bible as your standard, the Holy Spirit as your guide?

Information: set yourself a definite time and place. We suggest a fixed thirty minutes each week — better short and steady than long and broken off.

Revelation: pray before you begin: “Search me, God, and know my heart” (Psalm 139:23). Don’t dig into yourself on your own; let the Holy Spirit shine his light. Digging into yourself brings accusation; the Holy Spirit’s light brings freedom.

Conviction: admit that you need to evaluate — not because you’re especially bad, but because you’re still on the road. “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8).

Implementation: take a pen and paper and write it down, foundation by foundation. This week, did I take Jesus as my role model? Did I take the Bible as my standard? Did I obey the Holy Spirit’s guidance? For each one write down one concrete thing — no reflections, only facts.

Evaluation: ask yourself quietly: what did I get right, so that I can thank God? Where did I drift, so that I need to adjust?

Correction: pick just the one most crucial thing to change. Try to change ten things and you usually change none; change one thing and ten others often move with it.

Repetition: keep it up for twelve weeks in a row. Psychological research reminds us that forming a habit takes far longer than we imagine; a study by Phillippa Lally and colleagues at University College London, published in 2010 in the European Journal of Social Psychology, found that for a new behaviour to become automatic took on average about sixty-six days, with wide individual differences, from eighteen days to more than two hundred. So don’t give up after three days.

Multiplication: share your evaluation sheet with a brother or sister and invite them to do it with you. Truth is only complete when it’s passed on.

Practice two: take the initiative to invite others to give you feedback

The lesson’s practice: in your small group or family, take the initiative to invite others to give you feedback, and learn to listen with a grateful heart rather than a defensive one.

Information: notice the words “take the initiative”. Accepting evaluation passively is patience; inviting evaluation actively is wisdom.

Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to show you your defence mechanisms. When you’re corrected, how does your body react? Do you speak faster? Louder? Or fall silent? That reaction is the evidence that your “self” is still alive.

Conviction: believe from the heart that “he who listens to reproof gets understanding” (Proverbs 15:32).

Implementation: this week, find the person who knows you best and ask them one specific question. Don’t ask, “What do you think of me?” — that’s too big; no one will dare answer it. Ask, “When I speak in our small group, is there anything that makes people uncomfortable?” The more specific the question, the more genuine the gift you’ll receive.

Evaluation: when you’ve heard them out, don’t explain yourself yet. Say only this: “Thank you.” Then go home and pray, bring what they said before God, and ask the Lord, “How much of this is what you want to say to me?”

Correction: from what they said, pick out the smallest, most doable change, and do it straight away.

Repetition: do this once a month. And deliberately go to different people — what your family sees, what your co-workers see and what younger people see are all different.

Multiplication: once this becomes a habit, you’ll become a source of safety in your small group. Your openness will give others the courage to open up too.

Practice three: before offering your view, pray and seek the Holy Spirit’s wisdom

The lesson’s practice: if you are going to offer your view, first pray and seek the Holy Spirit’s wisdom, so that your words carry grace and build up, rather than pass judgement.

Information: remember three checkpoints — motive (is this for his good, or to vent my feelings?), timing (say it now, or wait a while?), manner (in public, or in private?).

Revelation: ask the Lord first to show you the beam in your own eye. “Why do you see the speck that is in your brother’s eye, but don’t consider the beam that is in your own eye?” (Matthew 7:3)

Conviction: believe that “speaking truth in love, we may grow up in all things into him who is the head, Christ” (Ephesians 4:15) is God’s way.

Implementation: when you speak, affirm first and then adjust, just as the Lord Jesus did with the seventy. And use “What I’ve noticed is … how I feel is … what I’d suggest is …”, not “You always … you never …”.

Evaluation: once you’ve spoken, watch the other person’s response. Did they take it in? Were they built up? If they were hurt, have the courage to go and apologise.

Correction: adjust your tone and your words until what you say really does build people up.

Repetition: don’t stop telling the truth for good because of one setback, and don’t go around correcting everyone because of one success.

Multiplication: when the two sayings “evaluation is not criticism” and “a suggestion is not a decision” become the shared language of your family and small group, you’re taking part in establishing God’s system.

A Gentle Reminder: being pruned is the process of bearing more fruit

The lesson has a precious gentle reminder: the truly humble aren’t afraid of being evaluated, because they know that being pruned is the process of bearing more fruit. Don’t be afraid of having your mistakes seen, because mistakes are exactly where God begins to correct and rebuild.

Every fruit grower knows that an unpruned fruit tree grows lush with branches and leaves, but its fruit is small and sparse — because the nourishment all goes into the branches and leaves. Pruning looks like loss; in fact it’s concentration. The Lord Jesus said, “Every branch that bears fruit, he prunes, that it may bear more fruit” (John 15:2). Notice that it isn’t the bad branches that get pruned; it’s precisely the ones “that bear fruit”.

Brothers and sisters, if lately you’ve felt that God is taking the shears to you, don’t be afraid. Those shears are held in nail-scarred hands. He prunes you not because he has rejected you, but because he sees that you can still bear more fruit.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: To Learn to Evaluate Is to Learn to Be Renewed
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, today we’ve seen together that evaluation is the key link by which a change of mindset grows towards maturity.

It helps us move from “action” into “life” — no longer content with what we’ve done, but longing to become a certain kind of person.

It helps us return from “service” to “identity” — no longer proving ourselves by results, but rejoicing because our names are written in heaven.

When we face evaluation with the right attitude, the truth can shape us more deeply, so that we’re no longer afraid of having our shortcomings seen, but bear more fruit because we’ve been pruned.

To learn to evaluate is to learn to be renewed. This is God’s way of helping us keep growing and become more and more like Jesus.

So this morning I want to give you three invitations.

First, let Jesus be King in your evaluation. Don’t be your own judge; give the throne to him. His evaluation always comes with grace, because he has already borne the punishment for you on the cross.

Second, let Jesus receive all the glory. When you’ve made progress after evaluating, don’t say, “I finally managed it”; say, “Lord, this is your work.”

Third, let evaluation become a blessing between you and others. Today, go to someone and say, “Thank you for reminding me last time.” And say to someone else, “May I offer you a suggestion? It’s only a suggestion — the decision is yours.”

Paul says, “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). Brothers and sisters, selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living it out. When “I” grow smaller, Christ grows greater; when I no longer need to prove myself, I am free.

May we all become iron that isn’t afraid to be sharpened, branches that aren’t afraid to be pruned, disciples who aren’t afraid to look back. Because our names are already written in heaven.

keyVerses: Key Verses (World English Bible)
“Nevertheless, don’t rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.” (Luke 10:20)
“Iron sharpens iron; so a man sharpens his friend’s countenance.” (Proverbs 27:17)
declarations: Lord, thank you for letting me be imperfect, because in every evaluation I can become more like you. Give me a humble, teachable heart, unafraid of being reminded and unafraid of being pruned. Let me learn to adjust as I evaluate, and keep growing as I adjust, so that my life matches your heart more and more.
practices: Set aside time each week to evaluate your daily living and service honestly
Take the initiative to invite others to give you feedback
Before offering your view, pray and seek the Holy Spirit’s wisdom
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we thank you for shining your light on us through your word this morning.

Lord, we confess that we are often afraid of evaluation. When our shortcomings are pointed out, we rush to justify ourselves; when our suggestions are turned down, we are quietly hurt. Forgive the “self” within us that leaps up at the slightest touch.

Lord Jesus, you are our role model. When your disciples were at their most elated, you gently turned their focus back to heaven; after Peter fell, you received him again by the lakeside and entrusted him with your sheep. Please treat us in the same way.
Holy Spirit, please be our guide. When we evaluate ourselves, do not let us fall into self-accusation, nor let us excuse ourselves. Shine on us with truth, and hold us up with love.

Give us humble, teachable hearts, give us the courage to speak the truth, and give us gentleness when we speak. Let “evaluation is not criticism, and a suggestion is not a decision” become the shared language of our families and our church.
Prune us, so that we bear more fruit; sharpen us, so that we become vessels fit for use.
May you reign as King in our lives, and may all the glory be yours.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Question 1: The Lord Jesus said to the seventy, “Nevertheless, don’t rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20). Think of the last time you were pleased with the results of your service. Was your joy built on “results” or on “identity”? How does the Lord want to adjust your focus today?

Question 2: “Iron sharpens iron; so a man sharpens his friend’s countenance” (Proverbs 27:17). In your life, who is the iron willing to sharpen you? How did you react the last time you were evaluated? This week, how will you concretely open up to someone and invite them to give you feedback?
l046.title: Evaluation Brings Life to Maturity
l046.subtitle: Stage Five of Changing Our Mindset — Evaluation
l046.partTitle: Unit 4 · The Prerequisite for Revival — A Change of Mindset

sections.heading: Introduction: One Degree Off, and a Hundred Thousand Heartbeats
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning.

This morning, let’s begin with two numbers.

The first number is “one degree”. Suppose a plane takes off from Taipei and its heading is off by one degree. The pilot doesn’t notice and doesn’t correct it. After a hundred kilometres, how far off its intended course will it be? Work it out with a little trigonometry: a hundred kilometres times the tangent of one degree comes to roughly 1.7 kilometres. That doesn’t sound like much. But if the plane has ten thousand kilometres to fly, by the time it reaches its destination it will be more than 170 kilometres off course — that isn’t landing on the wrong runway any more; that is landing in a different city.

One degree is so small you can hardly see it. But add time, and one degree is enough to take you somewhere you never meant to go.

The second number is “a hundred thousand”. A healthy adult heart beats about seventy times a minute at rest; over twenty-four hours, that comes to around a hundred thousand beats. We breathe roughly twenty thousand times a day. From the moment we were born, the heart has not gone on strike for a single day, and the lungs have not taken a single day off. They do one and the same thing — over, and over, and over again. And precisely because of that unceasing repetition, we are alive.

Brothers and sisters, these two numbers are exactly the two themes of today’s lesson: correction, and repetition.

Correction deals with that “one degree” of deviation; repetition builds that rhythm of “a hundred thousand beats”.

We have already walked step by step through the eight stages of changing our mindset. The first stage is Information — the truth reaches our ears. The second is Revelation — the Holy Spirit opens up the truth so that we “see” it. The third is Conviction — in our hearts we say, “Amen, this is true.” The fourth is Implementation — we begin to act on it. The fifth is Evaluation — we look back and honestly face how well we have done.

Today we step into the sixth and seventh stages: Correction and Repetition.

Why are these two stages so important? Because if the first five stop here, the most we are likely to get is a moving experience, a page of notes, a week of zeal — and then everything goes back to how it was. So many brothers and sisters know this from experience: in the meeting, tears are streaming down their faces; three days after they get home, they are right back where they started. Where is the problem? Not that they weren’t moved enough, but that after being moved there was no correction, and after correction there was no repetition.

The lesson text puts it with great precision: Evaluation lets us see the problem, Correction lines us up with the right direction, and Repetition lets the change sink in until it becomes habit. Without correction there is no growth; without repetition, life never sets into shape.

I love that phrase, “sets into shape”. When concrete is poured, it flows; it takes time before it sets. Once it has set, it can bear weight. Our lives are like that too. When a new mindset first comes in, it is fluid, unstable, liable to be washed away by our surroundings at any moment. Correction is setting the formwork straight; repetition is waiting for it to harden. You can’t do without either.

Brothers and sisters, please ask yourself a question this morning: is there a “one degree of deviation” in my life that I have known about for a long time, yet have never corrected? And is there something I know I should be doing every day, yet have never kept on doing, again and again?

In this lesson, God wants to meet us in these two things.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: An Old Apostle, Two Letters and an Athletic Arena
sections.html:
To understand “correction” and “repetition”, we first need to understand the situations in which today’s two theme passages were written.

The first is Paul’s letter to Timothy.

First Timothy is generally thought to have been written between AD 62 and 64. It comes from the apostle Paul’s later years and belongs to the Pastoral Epistles. Its recipient, Timothy, was the spiritual son whom Paul took under his wing at Lystra on his second missionary journey and kept at his side for many years. Paul calls him “Timothy, my true child in faith” (1 Timothy 1:2). At the time, Paul had left Timothy in Ephesus to shepherd a church that was large, rich in gifts — and full of problems.

What kind of city was Ephesus? It was the capital of the Roman province of Asia, populous and thriving in trade, and home to the temple of the goddess Artemis, one of the Seven Wonders of the World. The city had not only its temple but also a huge theatre and a stadium, where athletic contests were held regularly. Athletes of the Greco-Roman world underwent long and rigorous training under the eye of a trainer, repeating the same movements day after day and receiving the coach’s constant correction.

When Paul wrote to Timothy, he used exactly this picture, one every person in that city would understand. He said: “Exercise yourself toward godliness” (1 Timothy 4:7). The word for “exercise” here is the Greek gymnazō, from the same root as our word “gymnasium”; its original sense was of an athlete stripping off his outer garments to train unclad. In the original, this verb is a present imperative. What it expresses is not “do it once”, but “keep on doing it, continually”.

Brothers and sisters, hear clearly what Paul means: maturity of spiritual life is not the fruit of a single evangelistic rally; it is the work of the gym. No one grows muscle by watching one workout video; and no one grows into the likeness of Christ by hearing one sermon.

Paul goes on: “For bodily exercise has some value, but godliness has value in all things, having the promise of the life which is now, and of that which is to come” (1 Timothy 4:8). Notice that Paul does not say physical training is worthless. He says it has “some value”. He is drawing a comparison: the benefit of bodily training is confined to this life, to this perishable body; the benefit of training in godliness reaches across this life and the life to come.

More importantly, a few verses later in the same chapter Paul describes this training more fully: “Be diligent in these things. Give yourself wholly to them, that your progress may be revealed to all. Pay attention to yourself and to your teaching. Continue in these things, for in doing this you will save both yourself and those who hear you” (1 Timothy 4:15–16).

Brothers and sisters, look at the order: training (verse 7), diligence and wholehearted devotion (verse 15), perseverance (verse 16), and finally “you will save both yourself and those who hear you” (verse 16). Isn’t this exactly the three key points we will cover today — correction, repetition, and finally the multiplication they bring? Two thousand years ago, Paul had already walked this whole road.

The second theme passage comes from Paul’s words to the churches of Galatia.

Galatians is generally regarded as one of Paul’s earliest letters, written around AD 48–49. A group of Judaizing false teachers had come into Galatia, insisting that Gentile believers must be circumcised and keep the law before they could truly be saved. For the sake of the purity of the gospel, Paul wrote this, the most fiery of all his letters.

But when he reaches chapter 6, Paul’s pen turns from argument to exhortation. First he speaks of spiritual order: “Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness; looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted” (Galatians 6:1). Then he speaks of sowing and reaping: “Don’t be deceived. God is not mocked, for whatever a man sows, that he will also reap” (Galatians 6:7). Only then does he give us today’s theme verse: “Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season, if we don’t give up” (Galatians 6:9).

The word for “be weary” is the Greek enkakeō: to lose heart, to grow discouraged, to give up halfway. Paul knew that the greatest enemy of spiritual training is not failure but weariness — that voice which, on the morning of day thirty-seven, says to you, “Forget it. Nothing’s changing anyway.”

That is why Paul says, “We will reap in due season.” After a farmer sows his seed, he doesn’t dig it up every day to check whether it has sprouted. What he needs is waiting, the turning of the seasons, and repeated watering.

Brothers and sisters, the introduction to today’s lesson text cites Galatians 6:10. This is what it says: “So then, as we have opportunity, let’s do what is good toward all men, and especially toward those who are of the household of the faith.” This verse follows straight after “let’s not be weary”, and its meaning is very plain — don’t wait for some great opportunity before you do good; whenever a small opportunity comes, act on it. Repetition is built precisely out of countless small opportunities piled one on another.

One letter is an old man’s charge to his spiritual son; the other is an early battle for the truth of the gospel. More than a decade apart, yet Paul is saying the same thing: keep up the training, and don’t grow weary in doing good.

This is correction and repetition.

sections.heading: Key Point 1: Correction — Adjusted in Our Mistakes, Strengthened in Our Successes
sections.html:
The lesson text says: if Evaluation does not lead to Correction, it remains mere theory. Correction is the action that follows Evaluation; it is the key that turns “knowing” into “renewal”.

Brothers and sisters, this sentence deserves to be chewed over again and again. Evaluation is “seeing”; correction is “getting your hands dirty”. A person can see his own problem for twenty years and in twenty years never lift a finger about it. Seeing is not the same as changing. And knowing is not the same as being renewed.

Scripture says: “Every Scripture is God-breathed and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness” (2 Timothy 3:16).

Notice the four terms here. “Teaching” tells you what is right; “reproof” points out where you went wrong; “correction” helps you back onto the right path; “instruction in righteousness” trains you to keep walking it. The word for “correction” is the Greek epanorthōsis, built from the ideas of “again” and “straight”; literally it means “to make straight once more”. Picture a young tree bent over by a strong wind. The gardener comes along, stands it upright and ties it to a stake. That action is correction.

So correction is not punishment. Correction is setting upright. When God corrects us, he isn’t trying to knock us down; he is setting us back up into the shape he designed us for in the first place.

sections.heading: 1. The First Direction of Correction: Confirm What Is Right, and Keep Strengthening It
sections.html:
The lesson text points out that correction runs in two directions. The first direction is to confirm what is right and keep strengthening it.

We often overlook this. The moment we hear the word “correction”, our instinct is to think, “Where did I go wrong?” But the lesson text reminds us: when Evaluation shows that what we have put into practice is right, we should give affirmation and encouragement, so that the right direction can be repeated again and again until it becomes second nature.

Brothers and sisters, affirmation is a kind of correction too — it corrects that lie in our hearts that says, “I’ll probably never get this right.”

This is how the Lord Jesus himself led people. In his letters to the seven churches in Revelation, he says to the church in Ephesus: “I know your works, and your toil and perseverance, and that you can’t tolerate evil men” (Revelation 2:2). He affirms first, and only then says: “But I have this against you, that you left your first love” (Revelation 2:4). To the church in Thyatira he says: “I know your works, your love, faith, service, patient endurance, and that your last works are more than the first” (Revelation 2:19).

First see what is right, then point out what is wrong. This is the Lord’s way.

Psychological research confirms this order. The psychologists Avraham Kluger and Angelo DeNisi published a large meta-analysis in Psychological Bulletin in 1996, pulling together hundreds of studies on “feedback”. They found that, on average, feedback does improve performance — but in roughly a third of cases, feedback actually made performance worse. What made the difference? Whether the feedback was aimed at “the task” or at “the person”. When feedback points to specific behaviours and methods, people improve; when feedback points to a person’s worth and identity, people shrink back, become defensive and may even give up.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly what Scripture taught us long ago — “restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness” (Galatians 6:1). Address the issue, not the person: this is not just good management; it is spiritual wisdom.

The research of the Stanford psychologist Carol Dweck takes this a step further. In a study published with Claudia Mueller in 1998 in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, she found that children praised with “You’re so clever” were later quick to give up when they hit a hard problem, while children praised with “You worked really hard” were later more willing to take on difficult problems. The first kind of praise ties worth to “who I am”; the second puts the focus on “how I go about it”.

So when we speak words of encouragement to brothers and sisters, to our children, to our co-workers, say: “You were willing to apologise first this time — that was really well done.” Not a vague “You’re amazing.” Only specific affirmation can become a direction that can be repeated.

sections.heading: 2. The Second Direction of Correction: Find What Is Wrong, and Put It Right at Once
sections.html:
The lesson text says: when Evaluation exposes wrong behaviour or wrong motives, we must have the courage to adjust, so that we don’t get caught in a cycle of repeated mistakes. True growth is not “never being wrong” but “being willing to change”.

That sentence ought to be framed and hung on the wall of every Christian: true growth is not “never being wrong” but “being willing to change”.

Scripture says: “For a righteous man falls seven times and rises up again; but the wicked are overthrown by calamity” (Proverbs 24:16).

Brothers and sisters, notice that the righteous fall too — and not just once, but seven times. The difference between the righteous and the wicked is not whether they fall, but whether they get up after they fall. The word for “rises up” is the Hebrew qum, simply “to stand up”. The righteous person is the one who stands up again, and again, and again.

That is why the Reformer Martin Luther, at the very beginning of his Ninety-five Theses in 1517, said: when our Lord and Master Jesus Christ said “Repent”, he willed the entire life of believers to be one of repentance. Repentance is not a single act on the day we come to faith; it is the posture of a whole lifetime.

The word “repentance” is the Greek metanoia, made up of “change” and “mind”; literally, it means “a change of mindset”. Brothers and sisters, isn’t this exactly what our 321 vision says? The fivefold change begins with the mindset: change the mindset and the life changes; change the life and daily living changes; change daily living and relationships change; change relationships and ministry changes. Repentance is a change of mindset; and correction is working that changed mindset out concretely, one action at a time.

Why must we put things right “at once”? Because mistakes compound.

Neuroscience offers us an interesting confirmation. As early as the early 1990s, the German researcher Michael Falkenstein and the American researcher William Gehring independently discovered that at the very instant we make a mistake, the brain produces a specific brainwave, called the “error-related negativity” (ERN). It appears extremely quickly — within about a tenth of a second of the error. In other words, when God made us, he placed an “error-detection system” inside us. Very often, in the very instant we go wrong, we already know we’ve gone wrong.

The problem has never been that we don’t know. The problem is that once we know, we push it down.

Brothers and sisters, that gentle nudge of the Holy Spirit, that little jolt you feel in your heart — that is the Lord saying, “You’re one degree off here. Come back.” If we correct it right then, the cost is small. If we let it drag on for three months, that one degree of deviation has already carried us 170 kilometres off course.

sections.heading: 3. Encouragement Before Correction: Jesus and Peter’s Breakfast
sections.html:
The lesson text reminds us of something enormously important: if, before correcting someone, we find that they are struggling or discouraged in putting things into practice, then all the more we must encourage them first. Encouragement rebuilds confidence and gives people the strength to try again.

For this part, we need to read John chapter 21 slowly.

After denying the Lord three times, Peter went back to fishing. They toiled all night and caught nothing. As day was breaking, Jesus stood on the shore. He had lit a charcoal fire for them, cooked the fish and got the bread ready. Brothers and sisters, notice this — the first thing the risen Lord did for a disciple who had failed was not to interrogate him. It was to make him breakfast.

Scripture records: “So when they had eaten their breakfast, Jesus said to Simon Peter, ‘Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me more than these?’ He said to him, ‘Yes, Lord; you know that I have affection for you.’ He said to him, ‘Feed my lambs’” (John 21:15).

The Lord asked three times. Of the third time, Scripture says: “He said to him the third time, ‘Simon, son of Jonah, do you have affection for me?’ Peter was grieved because he asked him the third time, ‘Do you have affection for me?’ He said to him, ‘Lord, you know everything. You know that I have affection for you.’ Jesus said to him, ‘Feed my sheep’” (John 21:17).

Three denials, matched by three questions. The Lord did not say, “Why did you betray me?” The Lord only asked, “Do you love me?”

Brothers and sisters, this is what the lesson text means: not correction that condemns, but restoration in love.

And we need to see that the Lord’s correction comes with a commission. Each time Peter answered, the Lord gave him a fresh charge: feed my lambs, tend my sheep, feed my sheep. The Lord was not demoting Peter; he was reinstating him. In fact, long before Peter fell, the Lord had already prepared the road to his correction: “But I prayed for you, that your faith wouldn’t fail. You, when once you have turned again, establish your brothers” (Luke 22:32).

“When once you have turned again” — the Lord knew all along that he would fall. “Establish your brothers” — the Lord had also prepared, all along, how he would use him after his fall.

This is our Lord. When he corrects us, it is never to humiliate us, but to restore us — and through us to strengthen others. Scripture says: “All chastening seems for the present to be not joyous but grievous; yet afterward it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it” (Hebrews 12:11).

Correction and 321: Only the Selfless Can Be Corrected

Brothers and sisters, why do some people go their whole lives unable to be corrected?

Because of the self-centred life.

Our 321 vision says it very clearly: the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take the place of God; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.

When a self-centred person hears words of correction, his first reaction is to defend himself: “You don’t understand my situation.” “He was wrong too.” “I’ve already tried really hard.” And so pride stirs up pride, and both sides lose. When a selfless person hears words of correction, his first reaction is to come back before God: “Lord, is this word from you?” And so humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. The power to be corrected has never been a matter of willpower. It is a matter of the “self”.

So when it comes to correction, not one of the Three Foundations can be missing. The Bible is my standard — the measure of correction is not my feelings, nor other people’s expectations, but the word of God. The Holy Spirit is my guide — what drives correction is not self-reproach but the Holy Spirit’s light. Jesus is my role model — the way of correction is not condemnation but restoration in love, just as the Lord dealt with Peter.

Brothers and sisters, this morning, if the Holy Spirit is putting his finger on something in your heart, please don’t argue with him. Say to him: “Lord, I am willing.”

sections.heading: Key Point 2: Repetition — Letting Change Become the Natural Overflow of Life
sections.html:
The lesson text says: the stage of Repetition is the key to letting a mindset “set”. If change is not repeated, it fades with time.

Brothers and sisters, this is a deeply honest observation. Our being moved fades; our resolutions fade; even our most heartfelt repentance, if it isn’t repeated, fades too.

Scripture says: “But his delight is in Yahweh’s law. On his law he meditates day and night” (Psalm 1:2). “Day and night” — not thinking about it once in a while, but by day and by night.

sections.heading: 1. Repetition Is Not Mechanical; It Is Persevering with the Heart
sections.html:
The lesson text draws a very clear distinction: repetition is not “doing the same thing mechanically” but acting “persistently, with the heart engaged”. It is the process by which truth is transformed from “behaviour” into “character”.

This distinction is vital. For there is a kind of repetition that is dead, and a kind of repetition that is alive.

The Pharisees repeated their prayers every day too; they fasted twice a week; their tithes were exact to the last coin. Yet the Lord Jesus said: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you clean the outside of the cup and of the platter, but within they are full of extortion and unrighteousness” (Matthew 23:25). Their repetition produced a shell, but never a heart.

Our 321 vision says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and you worry, rely on the heart and you rejoice. The wellspring of life flows from the heart. If repetition is only a matter of the brain, what it produces is religion; if repetition comes from the heart, what it produces is life.

Interestingly, psychological research has arrived at the very same conclusion. In a classic 1993 study published in Psychological Review, the psychologist K. Anders Ericsson and his colleagues put forward the idea of “deliberate practice”. Comparing violin students of different levels at a music academy, they found that what truly set them apart was not “how long they practised” but “how they practised”. Deliberate practice has several elements: a clear goal, full concentration, immediate feedback, and deliberately working on the very things you can’t yet do well.

In other words, simply playing the same piece a thousand times won’t make you a pianist; if there is no correction in those thousand times, all you do is make your mistakes more fluent.

Brothers and sisters, do you hear it? Correction and repetition were always twins. Repetition without correction trains our deviations into habits; correction without repetition leaves our being moved in a notebook. God placed these two stages side by side for a reason.

sections.heading: 2. From Deliberate to Natural: The Lesson Text’s Two Everyday Illustrations
sections.html:
The lesson text gives two illustrations very close to everyday life.

The first is a child learning maths or the piano. At first it takes deliberate practice; once it is mastered, the sums or the music come naturally.

Think about ourselves. The first time you learned to ride a bicycle, you had to keep your eyes on the front wheel, think about your balance, remember to pedal — palms sweating, nervous as anything. But twenty years on, what are you thinking about when you ride? You’re thinking about what to cook for dinner. A movement that once demanded every ounce of your attention has sunk beneath your awareness and become part of your body.

Science tells us there is a real physiological change behind this. When the same neural circuit is used over and over, the “myelin sheath” wrapped around the nerve axons gradually thickens. In myelinated nerve fibres, signals can travel at more than a hundred metres per second, while in unmyelinated fibres they travel at only about one metre per second. That is a hundredfold difference. When God made us, he wrote this principle — that repetition makes us quicker, steadier and more natural — into our very bodies.

On the psychology side, Phillippa Lally and her colleagues at University College London published a study in 2010 in the European Journal of Social Psychology that followed ninety-six participants as they formed a new daily habit. They found that it took an average of sixty-six days for a behaviour to move from “deliberate” to “automatic”, with wide individual differences — anywhere from eighteen to two hundred and fifty-four days.

Brothers and sisters, sixty-six days. Not six days, and not six weeks. No wonder we often give up on day ten — because we assumed change ought to come faster.

The lesson text puts it well: if “humility”, “forgiveness” and “loving others” are to become our life, we must keep practising them and putting them into action again and again in daily living.

It is generally held that the American writer Will Durant, in his book The Story of Philosophy, summed up Aristotle’s ethics in these words: we are what we repeatedly do; excellence, then, is not an act but a habit. The saying is often wrongly attributed to Aristotle himself, but it is actually Durant’s interpretation. Yet Scripture said the same thing long ago.

sections.heading: 3. The Power of Repetition Lies in Consistency, Not Intensity
sections.html:
The lesson text’s second illustration cuts even closer: just as someone who works out only once a month will never have a strong body.

Brothers and sisters, exercising once a month for four hours, and exercising fifteen minutes a day thirty times a month, add up to roughly the same total hours. But the results are worlds apart. Why? Because the body doesn’t respond to the total; it responds to frequency. Not to intensity, but to regularity.

Spiritual life is the same. One retreat a year cannot compare with three hundred and sixty-five quiet mornings. One tearful confession cannot compare with daily self-examination.

The lesson text speaks of training in godliness “daily”, citing 1 Timothy 4:7. Here we need to be clear: in the Chinese Union Version, 1 Timothy 4:7 reads, “But refuse profane and old wives’ fables. Exercise yourself toward godliness.” The verse itself does not contain the word “daily”. “Daily” is the sense of continuity carried by the Greek present imperative, and it is also the plain teaching of Scripture elsewhere.

Where does Scripture say “daily”? The Lord Jesus said: “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke 9:23) — and the Chinese Union Version reads “take up his cross daily”. When Luke writes of the Bereans he says: “Now these were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, examining the Scriptures daily to see whether these things were so” (Acts 17:11). Paul says: “I die daily” (1 Corinthians 15:31).

Brothers and sisters, “daily” is the rhythm of the Bible.

Scripture also uses a few other words to express the same thing: “as was his custom”, “as his custom was”, “as he did before”.

Luke’s Gospel records of the Lord Jesus: “He came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up. He entered, as was his custom, into the synagogue on the Sabbath day, and stood up to read” (Luke 4:16). Of that night in Gethsemane, Scripture says: “He came out and went, as his custom was, to the Mount of Olives. His disciples also followed him” (Luke 22:39).

Notice the setting of that verse: it was the night the Lord was betrayed, the hardest night of his life on earth. And on such a night, what the Lord did was what he always did. He didn’t change his habit of prayer because the pressure was too great — rather, the very habit he had built up by repetition held him up through that darkest of nights.

Daniel was the same. “When Daniel knew that the writing was signed, he went into his house (now his windows were open in his room toward Jerusalem) and he kneeled on his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did before” (Daniel 6:10).

Brothers and sisters, look at those words: “as he did before”. With the threat of the lions’ den hanging over him, Daniel didn’t double his prayers, nor did he cut them back — he did what he always did. Because that was how he always prayed. How a person responds in a crisis is the sum of what he has repeated in ordinary days.

Church history gives us a beautiful testimony too. In 1729, John Wesley and his brother Charles formed a small fellowship with a few fellow students at Oxford University. They read Scripture, prayed and took Communion at set times, visited prisoners and helped the poor, and lived lives of strict regularity. Their fellow students mocked them for being far too “methodical” and gave them a nickname: “Methodists”. In time, that mocking nickname became the name of a great spiritual revival that swept across Britain and America.

Brothers and sisters, repetition is never glamorous. Repetition is often laughed at. Yet it is precisely in those early mornings when no one is applauding that God, little by little, engraves the shape of Christ within us.

Scripture says: “But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord, the Spirit” (2 Corinthians 3:18). “From glory to glory” — layer upon layer, day upon day.

Repetition and 321: Life First, Then Relationships, Then Ministry

Brothers and sisters, our 321 vision says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. Repetition is precisely the work done at the level of life.

Many people rush ahead to ministry but won’t do the repetition at the level of life. The result is that they do a great deal, yet no life grows; they teach a great deal of doctrine, yet they themselves don’t change.

The most concrete way to put the training of repetition into practice is 920. Every person we have a relationship with is our “2” — spouse, children, parents, colleagues, co-workers, that neighbour who is hardest to get along with. Before every “2”, we practise living out the “0” — a selfless life, letting the Holy Spirit bear his fruit in all nine of its expressions: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23).

The nine graces are not nine performances; they are nine traits of character. And where does character come from? From repetition.

Being patient once today doesn’t make you patient. Being patient today, and tomorrow, and the day after when he says that very same thing again, and still being patient — that is when patience becomes your life.

A change of mindset that stays only in the head is information; when it is worked out in daily actions, that is life. This is the road of the fivefold change: change the mindset and the life changes; change the life and daily living changes; change daily living and relationships change; change relationships and ministry changes.

sections.heading: Key Point 3: From Repetition to Multiplication — Letting Life Influence Life
sections.html:
The lesson text says: the ultimate aim of repetition is not just to change ourselves but to bring influence. As we keep putting God’s mindset into practice in our lives, again and again, these values will overflow naturally and touch the people around us.

Brothers and sisters, a key phrase appears here: “overflow naturally”.

A deliberate performance wears you out; a natural overflow doesn’t. If a person still has to strain to be gentle, he can’t keep it up for long. But once gentleness has been repeated until it is part of his character, he doesn’t need to strain — gentleness simply flows out of him. And it is what flows out that touches others.

sections.heading: 1. The Lord Jesus Taught by Repetition for Three and a Half Years
sections.html:
The lesson text says: for three and a half years on earth, Jesus taught his disciples love, forgiveness, service and humility, again and again; in the end, these disciples learned to follow his example and pass that life on.

When we read the Gospels, it sometimes strikes us as strange: why does the Lord say the same things over and over? The disciples argue about who is the greatest, and the Lord teaches them humility. A little later they argue again about who is the greatest, and again the Lord teaches them humility. And at the Last Supper they are still arguing about who is the greatest — so the Lord gets up, takes off his outer garment, wraps a towel around his waist, and washes their feet one by one.

Scripture says: “If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet. For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you” (John 13:14–15).

The Lord didn’t give up on them because they were slow to learn. For three and a half years the Lord showed them again and again, taught them again and again, forgave them again and again.

And the result? That same Peter who once argued about who was the greatest later wrote to the churches: “Yes, all of you clothe yourselves with humility, to subject yourselves to one another; for ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble’” (1 Peter 5:5). In the Chinese Union Version that is “gird yourselves with humility” — he still remembered that night, and the sight of the Lord tying the towel around his waist.

Brothers and sisters, whatever is repeated into a person’s life is what flows out of that person’s life.

This is exactly what the 321 vision means by “Jesus is my role model”. A role model is not there for us to admire, but for us to follow. Paul says: “Be imitators of me, even as I also am of Christ” (1 Corinthians 11:1).

sections.heading: 2. The Influence of a Life Is Real and Measurable
sections.html:
Science, too, shows us that the influence people have on one another is far greater than we imagine.

In the 1990s, Giacomo Rizzolatti’s research team at the University of Parma in Italy discovered “mirror neurons”: when we watch someone else perform an action, the neurons in our own brain responsible for that action fire as well. In other words, when God made human beings, he wrote “imitation” into our brains. We are designed to follow one another’s example.

Another study is more specific still. In a study published in 2008 in the British Medical Journal (BMJ), the American researchers James Fowler and Nicholas Christakis analysed twenty years of social-network data from the Framingham Heart Study. They found that “happiness” spreads through networks of people and can travel as far as three degrees of separation — that is, your friend’s friend’s friend may be happier because of you.

Brothers and sisters, if even emotions can travel three steps out, how much more the fruit borne by the Holy Spirit? How much more a life that God has corrected and shaped again and again?

You think no one sees your quiet time each early morning, but your children see it. You think no one notices the words you held back in the office, but your colleagues noticed. You think your change is too small to matter, but that seeker who has been watching you all along is thinking afresh about this God because of you.

sections.heading: 3. Multiplication Is the Last of the Eight Stages
sections.html:
The eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — end with Multiplication.

Correction and Repetition are the very bridge that leads to Multiplication.

What does Paul say? “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also” (2 Timothy 2:2). There are four generations in this verse: Paul, Timothy, faithful men, and others. One generation passing it on to the next — that is multiplication.

What does the Lord say? “Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all things that I commanded you. Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:19–20). “Teaching them to observe” — not teaching them to know, but teaching them to obey. To obey is to do it again and again.

Brothers and sisters, let’s come back to 1 Timothy 4:16: “Pay attention to yourself and to your teaching. Continue in these things, for in doing this you will save both yourself and those who hear you.”

First save yourself, then those who hear you. The order can’t be reversed. A person who has not been corrected cannot correct others; and a person who does not repeat cannot multiply life.

This is also our 321 vision’s “235 relationships”: first become a “2” with one selfless person, supporting one another, evaluating one another, correcting one another; then build the “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children, passing life on from one generation to the next; and finally become the “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades, building together.

And all of this has only one goal: to establish God’s system, to let Jesus reign as King, and to let Jesus receive all the glory.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: Two Stages, One Road
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s set today’s lesson back into the big picture of 321.

First, Correction and Repetition are built on the Three Foundations.

Jesus is my role model — for three and a half years he taught by repetition, and he corrected Peter in love. The Bible is my standard — the ruler we correct by is the word of God, not my emotions, nor other people’s opinions. The Holy Spirit is my guide — it is the Holy Spirit who shines his light so that we see our deviations, and it is the Holy Spirit who gives us the strength to repeat day after day. Without the Holy Spirit, repetition becomes law; with the Holy Spirit, repetition becomes walking with the Lord.

Second, Correction and Repetition point to the Two Core Values.

Let Jesus be King — to be corrected is to hand the throne back to him. The reason we resist correction is that we still want to sit on the throne ourselves. Let Jesus receive all the glory — when an old temper is truly done away with, when a relationship broken for years is truly restored, what people see is not how impressive we are, but the work of God.

Third, Correction and Repetition accomplish the Goal: to establish God’s system.

God’s system is not established by one big conference; it is established by a company of people who have been shaped again and again.

Fourth, the heart of this lesson is moving from the self-centred life to selflessness.

Refusing to be corrected is the self-centred life; refusing to repeat is the self-centred life too — because repetition means denying of self; it means staying faithful through days when there is no applause. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living out that fullness; “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me.

Fifth, what this lesson brings is a shift of perspective.

From the human perspective to God’s perspective — people see failure; God sees an opportunity for correction. From the earthly to the heavenly — earth chases quick results; heaven values what endures. From the temporary to the eternal — one act of patience today will bear fruit in eternity. From the worldly to the godly — the world says “be yourself”; God says “be like Christ”.

Brothers and sisters, this is how the fivefold change unfolds: change the mindset and the life changes; change the life and daily living changes; change daily living and relationships change; change relationships and ministry changes. Correction and Repetition are the very bridge that carries “mindset” over into “life” and “daily living” — the hardest stretch of the road, and the most crucial.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Walking All Eight Stages
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, the lesson text has prepared three exercises for us, and I will add a fourth. Let’s take them one at a time, and deepen them with the eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Exercise 1: Write Down Your Evaluation and Correction

Write down what you found when you evaluated your most recent experience of serving or of dealing with people: what needs correcting? What is worth holding on to?

Don’t just think it over in your head; really write it down. Writing is a form of honesty; writing is also a form of surrender.

Divide your page into two columns. On the left, write “Worth holding on to”; on the right, “Needs correcting”. And please fill in the left column first — remember? When the Lord spoke to the seven churches, he too affirmed first and rebuked second.
