When you’ve finished, bring it before God and pray: “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way” (Psalm 139:23–24).

This step walks through “Information, Revelation, Conviction”. Information is the truth the lesson teaches; Revelation is the moment, as you write, when the Holy Spirit lets you see the problem you have always stepped around; Conviction is when you say to God: Lord, you are right, and I was wrong.

Exercise 2: Set a Goal for Repeated Practice

Set yourself a goal for “repeated practice”. The lesson text gives three excellent examples: pray a prayer of thanksgiving every morning; choose to forgive every day; bless your family every day with one word of love.

Please keep three principles in mind.

First, keep it small. Small enough that on your busiest, most exhausted, least-willing day, you can still do it. A prayer of thanks takes thirty seconds; a word of blessing takes five. A goal that is too big will be dead by day four.

Second, make it specific. Don’t write, “I will love my family more.” Write, “Every evening when I get home, the first thing I’ll say to my wife is a word of thanks.” Only what is specific can be repeated; what is vague can only move you.

Third, give it an anchor in time and place. “Every morning after I brush my teeth, I’ll sit in that chair in the living room and give thanks for three things.” Tie the new practice to an old fixed routine, and your chance of success goes up dramatically.

This step walks through “Implementation”. James says: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves” (James 1:22).

Exercise 3: Review Weekly and Ask the Lord to Establish You

Review once a week, record your progress in change, and pray, asking the Lord to establish you, so that good habits become the natural response of your life.

This step walks through “Evaluation, Correction, Repetition”.

When you review, ask three questions: How many days did I manage this week? On the days I didn’t, what happened? What will I adjust next week?

Notice: it’s “what will I adjust”, not “why am I so hopeless”. If you find you managed only three days out of seven, please don’t condemn yourself — correct the plan. Perhaps the time was wrong; perhaps the goal was too big. Remember what that meta-analysis reminded us: feedback aimed at the task helps people improve; feedback aimed at the person makes them shrink back. Treat yourself the same way.

Then pray. Ask the Lord to establish you. For Scripture says: “For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:13).

Repetition was never about gritting your teeth in your own strength. Repetition is working together with God.

Exercise 4: Go On to Multiplication — Find a Spiritual Companion

Finally, please take one more step forward — the eighth stage, Multiplication.

Find a spiritual companion, your “2”. Share with each other what you wrote on that page, and once a week ask each other: “How many days did you manage this week? Is there anything that needs correcting?”

Scripture says: “Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls, and doesn’t have another to lift him up” (Ecclesiastes 4:9–10).

Brothers and sisters, one person’s repetition breaks off easily; two people repeating together can go a very long way. When you have been lifted up, you are able to lift others. This is “when once you have turned again, establish your brothers” (Luke 22:32).

The lesson text gives us a gentle reminder: don’t be afraid of repetition, for repetition is the secret of growth. Every repetition puts down a deeper root; every correction lifts us a step higher.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: A Rhythm Like Breathing
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, the lesson text’s conclusion puts it beautifully: “Correction” keeps us from repeating our old mistakes; “Repetition” keeps us growing. These two stages are like breathing — the rhythm of a maturing life.

What is breathing? Breathing in brings the new in; breathing out sends the old out. Correction straightens what is crooked; repetition keeps what is straight. In and out, correct and repeat — that is how life goes on living and growing.

No one is proud of having breathed twenty thousand times today, and no one stops breathing because breathing is too ordinary. The training of spiritual life is like that — it is ordinary, it is repetitive, it draws no attention, but it is the evidence that we are alive.

Scripture says: “But the path of the righteous is like the dawning light that shines more and more until the perfect day” (Proverbs 4:18).

Brothers and sisters, notice: it “shines more and more”, not “blazes into full daylight all at once”. The light of dawn grows brighter minute by minute. If you sit and watch the sunrise, you can’t even say at which second it became day. That is exactly how God works in us.

Paul says: “Brothers, I don’t regard myself as yet having taken hold, but one thing I do: forgetting the things which are behind, and stretching forward to the things which are before, I press on toward the goal for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 3:13–14).

“Forgetting the things which are behind” — that is correction. “Stretching forward to the things which are before” — that is repetition. “I press on toward the goal” — that is the direction of a whole lifetime.

So this morning I want to extend an invitation to you:

If you are willing to be corrected, say “yes” to the Lord in your heart. Don’t argue with the Holy Spirit; don’t defend yourself. To let Jesus be King is to give him the authority to adjust us.

If you are willing to begin repeating, please start today — don’t wait until tomorrow, don’t wait until the first of next month. Start with one word of thanks today, one act of forgiveness, one word of blessing.

If you are willing to multiply, bring one name to mind — someone you will begin to walk alongside and support.

Brothers and sisters, this is our hope: “being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6).

He is the one who begins the work, and he is the one who completes it. All we need to do is come back every day, be corrected every day, and repeat every day. The glory doesn’t go to us; the glory goes to Jesus.

keyVerses: “But refuse profane and old wives’ fables. Exercise yourself toward godliness. For bodily exercise has some value, but godliness has value in all things, having the promise of the life which is now, and of that which is to come.” (1 Timothy 4:7–8)

“Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season, if we don’t give up. So then, as we have opportunity, let’s do what is good toward all men, and especially toward those who are of the household of the faith.” (Galatians 6:9–10)
practices: Write down your evaluation and correction
Set a goal for repeated practice
Review weekly and ask the Lord to establish you
Go on to multiplication: find a spiritual companion
prayer: Lord, thank you for continually correcting me in my life, making me more like you.

Give me a humble and teachable heart, willing to be adjusted in the light of the Holy Spirit. When you point out where I have strayed, give me the courage not to defend myself, not to run away, but to turn back at once. When you affirm what I have done, give me faith too, that I may keep being strengthened and not give up halfway.

Lord, give me also a persevering resolve, so that through repeated practice I may form the habits of a godly life. Help me not to grow weary because I can’t see results right away, for you have said that if we don’t give up, we will reap in due season.
Make every change in my life a testimony that glorifies you; so that I am not only corrected and built up, but also able to support the brothers and sisters around me.
Reign as King within me; may all the glory be yours.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “For a righteous man falls seven times and rises up again; but the wicked are overthrown by calamity.” (Proverbs 24:16) Think back to the last time someone pointed out a mistake of yours. What was your immediate reaction? Did you defend yourself, or come back before God? In moving from the self-centred life to selflessness, what do you most need to break through in this matter of being corrected?

“But refuse profane and old wives’ fables. Exercise yourself toward godliness.” (1 Timothy 4:7) Which spiritual practice are you doing “daily” at the moment? If there isn’t one yet, which repeated practice — small enough that you can’t fail — are you willing to begin this week? Whom will you invite to be your spiritual companion, so that you remind each other every week?
l047.title: Correction and Repetition
l047.subtitle: Stages Six and Seven of Changing Our Mindset
l047.partTitle: Unit 4 · The Prerequisite for Revival — A Change of Mindset

sections.heading: Introduction: If Change Stops with Me, It Ends with Me
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Before we come to today’s message, I’d like you to picture a scene.

A farmer brought in a granary full of wheat one autumn. He picked out the plumpest, finest batch, washed it carefully, dried it, poured it into a clear glass jar and set it on the most prominent shelf in his living room. Whenever a guest came, he would take the jar down and show it off: “Look, this is the wheat I harvested this year — every grain plump and full.” Ten years went by, and that jar of wheat was still on the shelf. Not one grain fewer, not one grain more.

His neighbour brought in wheat too. But the neighbour didn’t put his wheat in a jar. He scattered it in his field. Those grains fell into the soil and disappeared from sight; they swelled and split, they rotted, they died. Yet the following spring, the whole field turned green. Ten years later, that neighbour’s wheat was feeding a whole village.

Brothers and sisters, the two farmers harvested the same kind of wheat. The difference wasn’t in the wheat. The difference was this: one kept his wheat in a jar; the other put his wheat into the ground.

Together we have already walked through seven stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition. Having come this far, many people assume they’ve reached the finish line. I’ve heard the truth — that’s Information. I’ve been enlightened by the Holy Spirit — that’s Revelation. I’m convinced in heart and in word — that’s Conviction. I’ve gone and done it — that’s Implementation. I’ve looked back and examined myself — that’s Evaluation. I’ve adjusted where I’d strayed — that’s Correction. And I keep practising, again and again — that’s Repetition. Surely that’s enough?

No, it isn’t. There is an eighth stage. It is called “Multiplication”.

Why do so many people stop at stage seven? Because every one of the first seven stages is about “me”: my understanding, my seeing, my obedience, my self-examination, my practice. Walk through those seven, and you do come away with a sense of achievement. But the eighth stage is different. The eighth stage requires you to step away from yourself and turn your eyes towards another person. The eighth stage costs time; it means bearing disappointment; it means watching a life grow slowly — and what grows won’t necessarily look like me. That’s why the eighth stage is the hardest, and also the most like the Lord.

For the life God gives was never meant to be stored in a jar; the life God gives is meant to be sown in the soil. If a renewed mindset stops with me, it is only my private collector’s item; if a renewed mindset multiplies out from me, it becomes the revival of a family, a church, a generation.

The introduction to the lesson text puts it very precisely: true change does not stop at “my” growth; it reaches out to the renewal of “others”. When a person’s life is changed by the truth, he can become a seed, carrying that changed mindset into the lives of others. Multiplication is not merely the continuation of life; it is the fulfilment of God’s purpose. The Lord Jesus said: “Go and make disciples of all nations” (Matthew 28:19). The multiplication of a mindset is the multiplication of the disciple’s life; it is the starting point of spiritual revival.

Today we’ll look at four things together. First, multiplication moves from being changed ourselves to influencing others. Second, the heart of multiplication is the influence of a life. Third, a real example of how one becomes many. Fourth, not settling at any stage, but pressing on towards maturity.

If I had to sum up today’s message in one sentence, it would be this: a changed life must become a seed that changes others.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Two Passages, a Single Purpose
sections.html:
Let’s begin with the background of our theme passages.

The first is John 12:24.

John’s Gospel was written by the apostle John, the disciple whom the Lord loved. It is generally thought to have been written around AD 90, to believers already scattered far and wide, “that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name” (John 20:31).

The setting of chapter 12 is the last Passover before Jesus’ suffering. He has just ridden into Jerusalem on a young donkey, and the crowds have come out to meet him with palm branches, shouting “Hosanna!” Right at that peak of popular acclaim, some Greeks who had come up for the feast found Philip and said: “Sir, we want to see Jesus” (John 12:21).

This was a turning point: even the Gentiles were beginning to seek him. By human reckoning, this was the moment for his fame to spread, the moment to scale things up. But Jesus’ answer was completely unexpected. He said: “The time has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.” And then he said those words — unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.

Brothers and sisters, notice the order. Jesus told the parable of the grain of wheat in answer to the question of how the nations would be won. He didn’t say, “Let’s hold bigger meetings.” He didn’t say, “Let’s organise a stronger team.” He said: “Die.” A grain of wheat must first fall into the earth and die before it bears much fruit. The road of multiplication is the road of the cross.

The word translated “fruit” here is the Greek καρπός (karpos) — the same word as in John 15, “that you bear much fruit”. The Lord Jesus himself is that first grain of wheat: he fell into the earth and died, rose again on the third day, and bore fruit by the thousands upon thousands — and we are that fruit. And he sets the same road before us: “He who loves his life will lose it. He who hates his life in this world will keep it to eternal life” (John 12:25).

The second passage is Matthew 28:18–20, the familiar Great Commission.

Matthew’s Gospel was written by the apostle Matthew, once a tax collector in Capernaum, whom the Lord called to leave his tax booth and follow him. This Gospel was written mainly for believers from a Jewish background and is generally thought to date from between AD 50 and 70. Throughout, it shows again and again that Jesus is the King, the Messiah promised in the Old Testament. And the book’s final summit is on a mountain in Galilee: the risen Lord appears to the eleven disciples, first declaring, “All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth,” and only then sending them out.

In the original, this passage has only one main verb: “make disciples” (μαθητεύσατε, mathēteusate). “Go”, “baptising” and “teaching” are all participles gathered around that main verb. In other words, the heart of the Great Commission is not “going”, nor “running events”, but “making disciples” — life building life, disciples multiplying disciples.

Brothers and sisters, what a wonderful contrast this is. John’s Gospel tells us the “cost” of multiplication — we must die. Matthew’s Gospel tells us the “content” of multiplication — make disciples. One is the root, the other the fruit; one speaks of denying of self, the other of entrusting. Put the two passages together, and you have the whole picture of spiritual multiplication.

There is one more background passage we can’t leave out: Genesis 1:28. “God blessed them. God said to them, ‘Be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth, and subdue it …’” God’s very first blessing and charge to humanity was to multiply. From the Garden of Eden to the mountain in Galilee, from Genesis to Matthew, God’s purpose has never changed: he wants his image, his life and his kingdom to fill the whole earth.

sections.heading: 1. Multiplication: From Being Changed Ourselves to Influencing Others
sections.html:
The lesson text says: if a change of mindset remains only at the personal level, life stagnates. The stage of Multiplication is sharing the change God has brought about in our lives, so that the lives of others are renewed as well.

The Lord Jesus’ three and a half years of ministry on earth are the most perfect example of “life multiplying life”.

Look at Mark 3:14: “He appointed twelve, that they might be with him, and that he might send them out to preach.”

Brothers and sisters, notice the two parts of this verse, and their order. First, “that they might be with him”; only second, “that he might send them out to preach”. Presence first, then sending; life first, then ministry. The Lord didn’t first run a discipleship training camp, hand out a set of notes, give a written exam and then send people off. For three and a half years he walked with the twelve, ate with them, sailed with them, faced the storms with them, was rejected alongside them. He did not only proclaim the truth; he walked with his disciples with his own life, so that bit by bit they were shaped by the truth.

Look at how the Lord led people. Peter denied the Lord three times, but the Lord didn’t strike him off the list. On the shore of the Sea of Tiberias, the Lord lit a charcoal fire, cooked fish, and then asked him three times, “Do you love me?” (John 21:15–17). James and John jostled for the top positions, but the Lord didn’t send them away. He said: “Whoever desires to become great among you shall be your servant” (Matthew 20:26). As for doubting Thomas, the Lord let him touch the nail marks. Brothers and sisters, the Lord’s discipleship didn’t wait until people were cleaned up before teaching them; he kept on walking with them even when they were at their most unpresentable.

This is exactly the order the 321 vision speaks of: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. One of the greatest dangers in the church today is turning that order upside down — ministry first, then relationships, and only last of all, life. The result is that the ministry grows bigger and bigger while life grows drier and drier; the crowds grow larger while the disciples grow fewer.

After Jesus ascended, what became of the twelve? Because of lives changed by the Lord, they kept proclaiming the gospel, multiplying the mindset of the truth again and again; they established the church and extended the kingdom of God.

Scripture leaves us a clear record. On the day of Pentecost, “there were added that day about three thousand souls” (Acts 2:41). Not long after, “The word of God increased and the number of the disciples greatly multiplied in Jerusalem” (Acts 6:7). In Ephesus, Paul reasoned daily in the lecture hall of Tyrannus: “This continued for two years, so that all those who lived in Asia heard the word of the Lord Jesus, both Jews and Greeks” (Acts 19:10).

Brothers and sisters — two years, one whole province. No internet, no printing press, no great arenas. What did it rest on? On changed lives influencing other lives.

This kind of multiplication even gave the church its name. Acts 11 records how some disciples, scattered by persecution, came to Antioch and preached the Lord Jesus to the Greeks, and “The hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number believed and turned to the Lord.” Barnabas went and saw the grace of God, then went to Tarsus to look for Saul. The two of them taught there for a whole year, and “The disciples were first called Christians in Antioch” (Acts 11:26). Brothers and sisters, look at the chain: the Lord won Barnabas, Barnabas won Saul, Barnabas and Paul together won Antioch, and the mission teams Antioch sent out won the whole Mediterranean world. Link by link, generation to generation — that is multiplication.

The American evangelist Robert E. Coleman, in his 1963 book The Master Plan of Evangelism, points out that Jesus’ method of evangelism was not to win the crowds first, but to win a few men first and pour his life completely into them, so that those few could win the crowds. This is spiritual multiplication — not by events, strategies or organisation, but by changed lives influencing other lives.

This is exactly what 321’s “235 relationships” sets out to build: becoming a “2” with a selfless person, spiritual companions supporting one another; going on to build the “3”, a passing-on of life with spiritual parents and spiritual children; and finally becoming the “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades working together. Brothers and sisters, is there a “2” beside you? Do you have a spiritual child? If not, today is the day to begin.

sections.heading: 2. The Heart of Multiplication: The Influence of a Life
sections.html:
The lesson text says: from the very beginning, God’s purpose commanded humanity to be fruitful, multiply and fill the earth. This is not only physical reproduction; it is a spiritual calling. Whatever has life can multiply; a life that cannot multiply is a life that has lost its vitality.

In Genesis 1:28, “be fruitful, multiply” is two verbs in Hebrew: “be fruitful” (פָּרָה, parah) means to bear fruit, to be abundantly fruitful; “multiply” (רָבָה, ravah) means to increase, to grow in number. From the very beginning, God’s blessing carried this power to expand: the life he gives is, by its very nature, a life that bears fruit and increases.

Turn it the other way round: what does Scripture call a life that cannot multiply? The Lord Jesus said: “Every branch in me that doesn’t bear fruit, he takes away” (John 15:2). And again: “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). Bearing fruit is not a bonus question for extra credit; bearing fruit is the inevitable evidence that the branch is joined to the vine.

So what kind of life has the power to multiply?

The lesson text gives us a sentence that cuts deep: if our faith stays at the level of theory, and we do not let our mindset transform our life, we cannot influence anyone. On the other hand, when God’s word becomes the reality of our lives, our words, attitudes and reactions will naturally carry influence. This kind of influence is not taught; it is lived.

I often say that when people hear you preach, they believe half of it at most; when they watch how you live, they believe all of it. When our lives have love, truth, humility and obedience, these qualities of godly life are seen by others and longed for by others, and then the same life is multiplied in them. Paul said to the church in Thessalonica: “For from you the word of the Lord has been declared” (1 Thessalonians 1:8). Notice, it isn’t “you sent the word out”, but “from you the word has been declared” — the word had become their life, and life speaks for itself.

Psychology confirms this spiritual principle too. In his famous “Bobo doll” experiment in 1961, the Stanford psychologist Albert Bandura found that children didn’t need to be taught or rewarded: simply seeing an adult act violently towards the doll was enough for them to imitate the same behaviour quite naturally. From this he developed “social learning theory”, showing that a great deal of human learning comes from “observation and imitation” rather than from lecturing.

Brothers and sisters, this is a solemn reminder: your children won’t do as you “say”; they will do as you “live”. The same goes for your colleagues and the members of your small group.

The power of multiplication lies in example. As Paul said: “Be imitators of me, even as I also am of Christ” (1 Corinthians 11:1). Most of us wouldn’t dare say that, because we’re afraid. But Paul dared to say it — not because he was perfect, but because he knew that the one he was imitating was perfect. He also said: “The things which you learned, received, heard, and saw in me: do these things” (Philippians 4:9). What is seen matters just as much as what is heard.

The most moving multiplication often happens at home. When Paul wrote to Timothy, he said: “having been reminded of the sincere faith that is in you, which lived first in your grandmother Lois, and your mother Eunice, and, I am persuaded, in you also” (2 Timothy 1:5). Grandmother, mother, son — faith handed down through three generations. Brothers and sisters, Lois never stood in a pulpit, and Eunice never wrote an epistle. But through their daily lives, through their prayers, through meal after meal and night after night of watching and waiting, they multiplied faith into the third generation. And the name of that third generation was Timothy — Paul’s trusted co-worker and the pastor of the church in Ephesus.

I know quite a few brothers and sisters who have never had a chance to share the gospel openly at work. Yet when a colleague is in trouble, he is the first person they think of; when someone in the department has been treated unfairly, they come to his desk and cry; on the day the company lays people off, he is the one who walks with a colleague out of the building. A few years later, that colleague walks into church on his own and says: “I want to know the one you believe in.” Brothers and sisters, when did that brother begin to multiply? Not on that day — but in all those days no one saw.

Don’t say, “I don’t have the gift; I can’t lead people.” If you can cook a meal, if you can keep someone company, if you can weep and pray for someone, then you can multiply.

Influence spreads much further than we imagine. Nicholas Christakis of Harvard and James Fowler of the University of California, drawing on data from the Framingham Heart Study, published research in 2007 in the New England Journal of Medicine showing that a person’s lifestyle spreads through social networks and can even affect “friends of friends of friends”. They call it “three degrees of influence”.

If even lifestyle habits can travel three steps out, how much more a life renewed by the Holy Spirit?

Nature is telling us the same thing. In Fishlake National Forest in Utah, in the United States, there is a grove of quaking aspen called “Pando”. Its roughly forty-seven thousand trees look independent of one another, but in fact they all belong to one root system, one living organism, continually sending up new stems from the same source. It is one of the largest known living things on earth.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly the church God wants: not forty-seven thousand trees each going its own way, but one life, one root, one source, one stem springing from another, one life multiplying into another. This is what 321’s “the Goal” is about — to establish God’s system. A system is not an organisational chart; a system is a living root system.

sections.heading: 3. An Example of Multiplication: From One Person to Many
sections.html:
The lesson text gives us a very true-to-life example. Let’s go through it slowly together.

Imagine a brother — we’ll call him Brother A. One day in a meeting he hears a saying: “It is more blessed to give than to receive.” The words come from Acts 20:35, spoken by Paul at Miletus to the elders of Ephesus: “In all things I gave you an example, that so laboring you ought to help the weak, and to remember the words of the Lord Jesus, that he himself said, ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’”

The occasion of those words is itself a lesson in multiplication. Paul was on his way up to Jerusalem, knowing that what lay ahead was full of danger, and he deliberately asked the Ephesian elders to come to Miletus to see him one last time. As he said goodbye, he gave no instructions about finances or about organisation. His charge was: take heed, and shepherd the church of God. His reminder was: in all things I gave you an example. A spiritual father, at the moment of parting, entrusting his own life once more. That is multiplication.

Stage one: Information. He heard it. The saying entered his ears.

Stage two: Revelation. The Holy Spirit worked in his heart, moving him to give his car to the church. In that moment, the saying was no longer a piece of doctrine; it was a needle piercing into his life.

Stage three: Conviction. He went through struggle, reflection and confirmation. There were two voices in his heart. One said, “I worked hard for that car.” The other said, “Lord, all of this was yours in the first place.” In the end he was convinced.

Stage four: Implementation. He obeyed and gave the car.

Stage five: Evaluation. After giving it, he experienced a joy he had never known before. Looking back and examining it, he found that what he had lost was a car, and what he had gained was a whole new self.

Stage six: Correction. As he went on giving, he gradually corrected his attitude in giving and whom he gave to — no longer giving in order to be praised, but giving out of love for God and for people; no longer giving by feeling, but giving by the guidance of the Holy Spirit.

Stage seven: Repetition. He kept on giving, time after time, until giving became his habit and his very nature.

Later, the Lord called him to lay down his career and go into mission full time. He shared his testimony everywhere he went and moved many people — some gave money, some committed to support him in prayer, some resolved to walk the same road with him.

Brothers and sisters, this is stage eight: Multiplication. One changed life sets off the renewal of many more.

There is a detail here that is often overlooked, and I want to point it out: Brother A’s multiplication didn’t begin when he became a missionary. It began with that one genuine act of obedience. Multiplication isn’t something that happens after you become a spiritual giant; multiplication begins with your act of obedience today.

The Lord Jesus’ words, “It is more blessed to give than to receive,” have also been borne out by psychological research. In 2008, Elizabeth Dunn, Lara Aknin and Michael Norton published a study in the journal Science. They gave participants money: one group was told to spend it on themselves, the other to spend it on someone else. They found that the group who spent the money on others were noticeably happier that day.

Brothers and sisters, it isn’t that God’s word needs science to prove it; it’s that science must in the end come back to God’s word. For the laws of the universe were set by him, and the make-up of the human heart was made by him. God made human beings the kind of creatures who are happy only when they give, because he himself is the God who never stops giving.

There is one more detail worth noticing: after Brother A shared his testimony, some gave money, some committed to support him in prayer, some resolved to walk the road with him. Three kinds of response, three kinds of fruit, each different. Brothers and sisters, the fruit that multiplication produces won’t necessarily look exactly like you. God isn’t trying to clone a batch of Brother As; God wants, through Brother A, to multiply the life of Christ into each person, each according to his own calling. We sow the seed, but we don’t have to dictate what shape it grows into; it is God who gives the increase (1 Corinthians 3:6–7).

Paul states this principle most clearly: “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also” (2 Timothy 2:2). There are four generations in this verse: Paul, Timothy, faithful men, and others. Four generations under one roof — this is the blueprint of spiritual multiplication.

This is also exactly 321’s “920 practice”. Every person we have a relationship with is our “2”; before every “2”, we practise living out the “0” — a selfless life, bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23). Brothers and sisters, you don’t need a pulpit before you can multiply; the one person beside you is the harvest field God is entrusting to you today.

sections.heading: 4. Not Settling at Any Stage, but Pressing On Towards Maturity
sections.html:
Finally, the lesson text reminds us: the eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — are not a one-off process but the path of a life that grows in an unending cycle.

This is a very important mindset. The eight stages are not a straight line that ends once you reach the end; they are a spiral rising round and round. Today I may have reached Multiplication in the matter of “money”, while tomorrow, in the matter of “words”, I may still be at Information. This year I may already be practising “forgiveness” again and again, while next year, in the matter of “time”, I may only just have received Revelation.

So we need to keep asking ourselves two questions. First, which stage am I at now? Second, have I stayed here too long?

The lesson text puts it superbly: what matters most is not working out which stage you are at, but not stopping. A mindset that stands still regresses; a life that does not multiply dries up.

Here I need to add a word of comfort: multiplication takes time. The Lord Jesus said: “God’s Kingdom is as if a man should cast seed on the earth, and should sleep and rise night and day, and the seed should spring up and grow, though he doesn’t know how” (Mark 4:26–27). The sower can’t dig the seed up to see whether it has grown. You may have prayed for someone for three years and seen no sign of anything happening — don’t lose heart. What happens under the soil, God himself will do. Our part is to sow and to water; “God gave the increase” (1 Corinthians 3:6).

Where are we most likely to get stuck? From many years of observation, there are three places where most people stop.

The first stopping point is between “Information” and “Revelation”. People hear stacks of teaching and fill whole notebooks, yet never grow quiet enough to let the Holy Spirit say, “This sentence is for you.” The higher the pile of knowledge, the further away the heart may drift.

The second stopping point is between “Conviction” and “Implementation”. The heart is convinced, the mouth agrees, but nothing moves. James says: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves” (James 1:22). Between “I know” and “I’ll go and do it”, what stands in the way is usually not ability but will.

The third stopping point is between “Repetition” and “Multiplication”. This is the saddest stop of all. We ourselves are well on our way; meetings, Bible reading, giving and serving are all on track — yet we have never thought of bringing one other person along this road with us. And so a lifetime of growth brings only one person to maturity — ourselves.

Israel has two lakes fed by the water of the same river, the Jordan. In the north, the Sea of Galilee: the river flows in and flows out again. The lake teems with fish, the villages on its shores flourish, and most of Jesus’ ministry took place there. In the south, the Dead Sea: the river flows in but never flows out. Its salt content is around thirty per cent, nearly ten times that of seawater, and no fish can live in it.

The same source of water, different outcomes. There is only one difference: one is willing to let the water flow out; the other only wants to keep it.

Brothers and sisters, our spiritual lives are like that too. A faith that only takes in and never gives out will sooner or later become a Dead Sea — plenty of scripture heard, plenty of meetings attended, plenty of notes copied, yet the life grows saltier and saltier, harder and harder, with less and less alive in it.

In the theory of psychosocial development he put forward in 1950, the psychologist Erik Erikson pointed out that in midlife the crucial developmental task is the choice between “generativity” and “stagnation”. Those who can invest what they have learned, what they have and who they are in the next generation experience the fullness of life; those who live only for themselves sink into stagnation and emptiness.

A secular psychologist, of all people, has sketched out for us the spiritual divide between “multiplication” and “drying up”.

Paul’s attitude is one we should follow. He said: “Brothers, I don’t regard myself as yet having taken hold, but one thing I do: forgetting the things which are behind, and stretching forward to the things which are before, I press on toward the goal for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 3:13–14). The writer of Hebrews also says: “Therefore leaving the teaching of the first principles of Christ, let’s press on to perfection” (Hebrews 6:1).

Keep on walking, until the truth takes root in us and bears fruit through us, becoming a blessing to others.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, when we set today’s message within the framework of 321, we see it even more clearly.

The Three Foundations. Jesus is my role model — he is that first grain of wheat that fell into the earth and died, and he is the Lord who spent three and a half years walking with twelve men. The Bible is my standard — multiplication doesn’t run on my enthusiasm; it follows the instructions of the Great Commission. The Holy Spirit is my guide — without the Holy Spirit, all we multiply is our own shadow, not the life of Christ.

The Two Core Values. Let Jesus be King — multiplication is not expanding my influence; it is expanding his kingdom. Let Jesus receive all the glory — when others are changed through me, I must point them to Jesus at once and never keep the glory for myself. The Lord said: “In this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit” (John 15:8).

The Goal: to establish God’s system. Like that grove of quaking aspen at Pando — one root system, one life, passed on from generation to generation.

What is the greatest obstacle to multiplication? The self-centred life. Self-centred people don’t dare to multiply, because they’re afraid others will overtake them; self-centred people can’t multiply, because what they pass on is themselves, not Christ. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take the place of God; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God. Pride stirs up pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

So the secret of multiplication is selflessness. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living out that fullness. Paul says: “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). Brothers and sisters, if a grain of wheat does not die, it can only ever remain one grain; if a grain of wheat dies, it enters into fullness without limit. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.

Here too the fivefold change comes full circle: change the mindset and the life changes; change the life and daily living changes; change daily living and relationships change; change relationships and ministry comes forth. Brothers and sisters, notice — ministry comes fifth, not first. True ministry is the fruit that flows naturally from a changed life, not a performance record propped up by sheer effort.

Then there is the shift of perspective. Multiplication means turning from the human perspective to God’s perspective: no longer asking “What do I gain?” but “What does God gain?” From the earthly to the heavenly: no longer counting the losses in front of us, but seeing the harvest in heaven. From the temporary to the eternal: a car is temporary; a soul won is eternal. From the worldly to the godly: I am not managing my network of contacts; I am establishing God’s system.

One more thing must be said: in multiplication we must rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves. Those who rely on the brain start calculating: Is this person worth investing in? I’ve been discipling him for three months — why is there no result yet? Why is someone else’s small group bigger than mine? Once you start calculating, you start worrying; once you start worrying, you give up. Those who rely on the heart ask only one thing: Lord, whom do you want me to love today? Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23).

Finally, the Path of Serving: Spirit → Understanding → Life → Service → God. The Holy Spirit guides me, the Bible is my standard, Jesus becomes my life; and so I rise up to serve, and in the end Jesus receives all the glory. Multiplication walks along this very path.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice
sections.html:
The lesson text has prepared three exercises for us. Let’s deepen them using the eight stages of changing our mindset.

Exercise 1: Identify one mindset in your life that God has already changed, and write down how that change has affected your daily living.

This is the work of “Evaluation” and “Information”. This very morning, please take out pen and paper and write down three specific things. First, what my old mindset was. Second, which verse or which event God used to change me. Third, what visible mark this change has left on my daily living. If you can’t write it down, that may mean the change is still stuck in your head and hasn’t yet entered your life.

Exercise 2: Pray and ask the Lord to open the way for you to share this mindset with one person, whether a brother or sister at church, a colleague or a family member.

This is the work of “Implementation”. Notice: “one person”, not a group. Ask the Lord to put that one name on your heart, then write it down. When you share, don’t preach doctrine; tell a story — tell what God has really done in you. People can argue with your opinions, but it is very hard to argue with your experience.

Exercise 3: If the other person is moved, keep walking alongside them on this “journey of changing the mindset”, from Information to Multiplication, experiencing the renewal of life together.

This is the work of “Repetition” and “Multiplication”, and it is the step that most needs patience. Paul says: “My little children, of whom I am again in travail until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians 4:19). Giving birth involves pain; walking alongside someone has a cost. But brothers and sisters, this is exactly what the Lord Jesus has done for us, and it is what he wants us to do for others.

As you walk alongside someone, pay special attention to three things. First, don’t rush to give answers; listen first. People are often willing to be changed because they have first been heard. Second, don’t shape them into you; bring them before Jesus. John the Baptist put it best: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30). Third, don’t walk alongside them alone; bring them into the community. One log on its own goes out; a pile of logs burns bright. This is what the “5” in the 235 relationships means — a team of spiritual comrades.

Walk through all eight stages, and your practice will touch the ground. Information — write down what you heard today. Revelation — be still and ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light: where in me is this word meant to deal with? Conviction — say before the Lord, “Lord, I yield.” Implementation — do one concrete thing today. Evaluation — in the evening, look back: where was God’s presence, and where was it my own flesh? Correction — set right any wrong motives or methods. Repetition — not doing it once, but for a season, for a lifetime. Multiplication — walk this road again, bringing another person with you.

sections.heading: Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, the lesson text leaves us with a gentle reminder: never underestimate one changed life.

“Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” (John 12:24)

A grain of wheat sown in the soil grows into a plant and sends up an ear, and one ear usually bears thirty to fifty grains. One grain becomes thirty; when those thirty each fall into the ground, they become nine hundred; when those nine hundred fall into the ground, they become twenty-seven thousand. Brothers and sisters, this is what the Lord meant: “some one hundred times as much, some sixty, and some thirty” (Matthew 13:8).

Your change may well be the starting point of someone else’s revival.

It is generally held that the nineteenth-century evangelist D. L. Moody was deeply shaped all his life by one sentence: “The world has yet to see what God can do with a man fully consecrated to him.” When Moody heard it, he said: by God’s help, I will be that man. And God truly used him — and the countless thousands set ablaze through him.

This morning the Lord is asking us the same question: are you willing to be that grain of wheat that falls into the earth?

Brothers and sisters, perhaps you’ll say: I’m too ordinary; my change is too small. But think about it: the Lord Jesus had only twelve men in his hands, and one of them betrayed him. He had no media, no funding, no venue. Two thousand years later, there are people worshipping him all over the earth. His method was to put life into life.

That method still works today — and the one God wants to use is you, this one grain of wheat.

Multiplication is the ultimate goal of a change of mindset and the continuation of God’s purpose. A changed life is not only a life that bears fruit; it is a life that can multiply. As we keep letting God renew our thinking and shape our lives, he can use us as channels of blessing, so that the truth is passed on through us from generation to generation, until revival comes to the whole earth.

May we not be wheat in a glass jar, but wheat in the field. May we not be a Dead Sea, but a Sea of Galilee. May Jesus reign as King in our families, reign as King in our workplaces, reign as King in our churches; and may all the glory go to him.

keyVerses: “Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” (John 12:24)

“All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth. Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all things that I commanded you. Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age.” (Matthew 28:18–20)
practices: Identify one mindset God has already changed in your life, and write down how that change has affected your daily living
Pray for the Lord to open the way for you to share this mindset with one person — a brother or sister at church, a colleague or a family member
If they are moved, keep walking with them on this “journey of changing the mindset”, from Information to Multiplication, experiencing the renewal of life together
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we worship you.

Lord, thank you for changing my life and calling me to be someone who influences others. Let me not stop at my own renewal, but be willing for your life to multiply through me, so that more people are drawn by your love and changed by your truth, until your kingdom comes.

Lord, forgive me for storing your grace away, like wheat in a glass jar. Today I am willing to fall into the ground, willing for my pride, my face and my self-centred life to die. Holy Spirit, put a name on my heart; give me courage to share, and patience to walk alongside.

Fill me with love, with truth, with humility and with obedience, so that people see you in me. May what I multiply be not my own shadow, but the life of Christ. Reign as King among us, and may all the glory be yours.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.” (2 Timothy 2:2) Share: in your life, who was the person who entrusted the truth to you? And whom has God now placed before you as the one you are to entrust it to?

“Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” (John 12:24) Examine yourself honestly: what are you clinging to right now that you are still unwilling to let fall into the ground and die? What step are you willing to take this week?
l048.title: Life Multiplies Life
l048.subtitle: Stage Eight of Changing Our Mindset: Multiplication
l048.partTitle: Unit 4 · The Prerequisite for Revival — A Change of Mindset

sections.heading: Introduction: What Holds Us Back Is Seldom Ability — It Is Mindset
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I’d like to begin by asking you to be still for one minute and answer a single question: when was the last time someone corrected you, reminded you, or set you straight? And in that moment, what was the first reaction in your heart? Was it “Thank you for teaching me,” or was it “You don’t understand me”?

The question looks small, but it works like a probe that can take the temperature of the deepest places in our lives. Because how a person responds to being corrected is very often the dividing line that decides how far he will go.

We often assume that a breakthrough in our lives needs a greater gifting, that change in our families needs better circumstances, and that revival in the church needs more resources. So we strain after power, after methods, after opportunities. Yet Scripture and history tell us again and again: the key to revival usually lies not in outward ability but in the mindset within. What blocks breakthrough in our lives, change in our families and revival in the church is very often not a lack of gifting but a wrong pattern of thinking.

Picture a scene. A veteran co-worker who has served in the church for thirty years is approached one day by a young brother who came to faith only two years ago. “Brother,” he says, “I didn’t quite follow that part you taught today — was it maybe a bit too fast?” There is no malice in the words, yet they stir up a wave in the older man’s heart. He thinks to himself, “I’ve been serving longer than you’ve been a believer.” He never says it out loud, but from that moment on, the young brother’s voice can no longer get through into his life.

Brothers and sisters, the door is not shut by someone else; we shut it ourselves, from the inside. Satan’s craftiest scheme is not to make people stumble into sin but to get them to hold on to a wrong mindset. Sin hurts, and pain leads us to turn back; but a wrong mindset doesn’t hurt. It only makes us more and more sure we’re right, more and more alone, and less and less able to hear the voice of God.

In Romans 12:2 Paul says, “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” “Be transformed by the renewing of your mind”: the word for “mind” in the original is nous, the way our thoughts, our mindset and our inner reasoning work; “be transformed” is metamorphoō, the kind of change a caterpillar undergoes when it becomes a butterfly — from the inside out, a complete remaking. When God changes a person, he does not begin with behaviour; he begins with mindset. Once the mindset changes, the life changes; once the life changes, daily living changes; once daily living changes, relationships change; once relationships change, ministry changes. This is what the 321 vision calls the fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry.

So if we do not renew our thinking, then even after many years as believers and endless service, we may still be living in self-centredness and pride without knowing it: good at praying but not at listening; good at teaching but unable to be taught; well versed in the truth but unwilling to be pruned by it.

Today we will look together at the first important mindset: the Concept of Humility. It comes down to a single sentence, very simple, yet it takes a lifetime to learn: let the Holy Spirit be our teacher all our lives, and meet every person we encounter with the attitude, “You are my teacher.”

It is commonly said that the church father Augustine, replying in a letter to a man who had written to him with questions, said that the way to truth is first humility, second humility, and third humility. He wasn’t being coy. He was saying that humility is not one virtue among many; humility is the door through which every other virtue comes in. If that door doesn’t open, nothing gets in.

Brothers and sisters, this morning may the Holy Spirit himself come and open our door.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A Parting Charge, and a Teacher Who Never Leaves
sections.html:
To grasp how much weight lies in the words “the Holy Spirit is our best teacher,” we first need to go back to the scene of John chapter 14.

The Gospel of John was written by John, the disciple whom the Lord Jesus loved. The consistent witness of church history is that in his old age John shepherded the churches around Ephesus, and that he wrote this Gospel sometime between about AD 85 and 95. By then most of the first-generation apostles had been martyred, the second generation of believers had never seen Jesus with their own eyes, and the church was being pushed out by the Jewish synagogues and troubled by early heresies. John’s purpose in writing was crystal clear: “but these are written, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name” (John 20:31).

John 13 to 17 is known as the Upper Room Discourse, the warmest and also the heaviest passage in the whole Bible. The time is the eve of the Passover; the place, a large furnished upper room in Jerusalem. Jesus knows that his hour has come to leave this world and go to the Father, and the first thing he does is not to preach. He takes off his outer garment, wraps a towel around his waist, and stoops to wash the disciples’ feet — including the feet that are about to go out and betray him. That night, the disciples around the table were arguing in their hearts about who was the greatest; the Lord at the table was doing a slave’s work. The first lesson in the Concept of Humility was not something Jesus said; it was something he lived out on his knees.

When he had finished washing their feet, Jesus began his farewell words. The disciples’ hearts were troubled, because the Lord said he was going away. The teacher is leaving and the lessons aren’t finished — what then? The disciples’ greatest fear was losing their teacher. So in John 14:16 Jesus promised, “I will pray to the Father, and he will give you another Counselor, that he may be with you forever.”

The word “another” matters a great deal. In the original, allos means “another of the same kind,” not “another of a different kind.” In other words, the Holy Spirit shares the same nature as Jesus, works as Jesus works, and is present as Jesus was present. Jesus was the first Counselor; the Holy Spirit is another Counselor just like him. The disciples were not losing their teacher; they were gaining a teacher who would never leave, never close up shop, and could live within them.

“Counselor” in the original is paraklētos, literally “the one called alongside.” In the Greek world of the day the word could mean an advocate standing beside the accused in a court of law, or a helper, comforter or intercessor summoned to one’s side in a time of trouble. So the Holy Spirit is not a force, not a feeling, but a personal teacher — one who speaks and who is willing to keep us company.

And so in John 14:26 Jesus spoke today’s theme verse: “But the Counselor, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things, and will remind you of all that I said to you.”

Notice the two verbs in this sentence. “Teach” in the original is didaskō, the way a teacher teaches a pupil, line by line until he has it; “remind” is hypomimnēskō, “to bring up from beneath, to make someone remember again.” The Holy Spirit’s work is, on the one hand, to teach us new light, and on the other, to lift up into our hearts, at the very moment we need it most, the words the Lord has already spoken.

Brothers and sisters, what grace this is. Our teacher is not up on a platform; he is within us. We don’t see him once a week; he is on call twenty-four hours a day. He never forgets our names, because he knows the thoughts and intentions of our hearts.

The other two theme passages need a brief word too. Proverbs 9:9 comes from the wisdom literature of King Solomon. Chapters 1 to 9 are a father’s counsel to his son, and chapter 9 portrays Wisdom and Folly as two women, each laying a feast, each calling out to passers-by; what tells the two apart is simply whether a person is willing to be taught. The letter of James is generally held to be by James, the Lord Jesus’ brother in the flesh and the leader of the Jerusalem church, written around AD 45 to 50 to Jewish believers scattered abroad. The words of James 4:6, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble,” are in fact a quotation of Proverbs 3:34 — on this matter the Old and New Testaments speak with one voice.

A teacher who never leaves, a standard that never goes out of date, a lesson we will never finish learning. That is today’s background.

sections.heading: 1. The Holy Spirit Is Our Best Teacher
sections.html:
Scripture

But the Counselor, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things, and will remind you of all that I said to you. (John 14:26)

However when he, the Spirit of truth, has come, he will guide you into all truth, for he will not speak from himself; but whatever he hears, he will speak. He will declare to you things that are coming. (John 16:13)

Scripture Interpreting Scripture: The Perfect Teacher, Teaching in the Perfect Way

Brothers and sisters, the world has many good teachers, but no teacher is as perfect as the Holy Spirit.

First, he knows the whole curriculum. John 14:26 says he will teach us “all things.” A human teacher can only teach what he himself has learned, but the Holy Spirit searches the deep things of God. 1 Corinthians 2:10 says, “But to us, God revealed them through the Spirit. For the Spirit searches all things, yes, the deep things of God.”

Second, he knows the level of his pupils. In John 16:12 Jesus says to his disciples, “I still have many things to tell you, but you can’t bear them now.” What tender consideration lies in that sentence. The Holy Spirit doesn’t tug at the seedling to make it grow faster; he teaches us step by step, according to what we are able to bear.

Third, he never speaks on his own authority. John 16:13 says that “he will not speak from himself; but whatever he hears, he will speak.” The Holy Spirit’s teaching always agrees with Scripture, always exalts Jesus, and never contradicts the word of God. This is also our most important standard for telling the true from the false: any prompting that conflicts with the Bible is not a prompting of the Holy Spirit.

Fourth, he lives within us. 1 John 2:27 says, “As for you, the anointing which you received from him remains in you, and you don’t need for anyone to teach you. But as his anointing teaches you concerning all things.” This verse is not telling us to reject human teaching — John himself is writing a letter to teach people — but saying that anyone’s teaching must in the end be confirmed and internalised by the teacher who lives within us.

How, then, does the Holy Spirit teach? Through at least three channels.

He teaches through the word. 2 Timothy 3:16 says, “Every Scripture is God-breathed and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness.” A passage you have read a hundred times without feeling a thing suddenly, one day, shoots into your heart like an arrow — the passage hasn’t changed; the Holy Spirit has opened your eyes.

He teaches through circumstances. Every difficulty we meet, every delay, every door that closes may be the Holy Spirit’s classroom. Psalm 119:71 says, “It is good for me that I have been afflicted, that I may learn your statutes.”

He teaches through people. This is the hardest to accept, and the most common. God often puts our lesson in the mouth of someone we look down on. In 2 Kings chapter 5, Naaman, commander of the army of Aram, has leprosy, and the key to his healing is that twice he listens to people beneath him in rank: first a little Israelite girl taken captive, who points him to the man of God; later his own servants, who urge him to go and wash seven times in the Jordan. Had Naaman insisted, “I’m the commander — what do you know?”, he would have gone home with his rage, his pride and his leprosy.

An Illustration from Life: The Closed Window and the Open Window

The Holy Spirit’s teaching is like sunlight; it never stops shining. The problem has never been the sun; it is the window. Pride is drawing the curtains and then complaining that the room is so dark.

Or think of a sponge. Drop a dry sponge into water and it soaks it up at once, because there is room inside it. Drop a stone into the same basin and leave it there all day, and when you lift it out it is still a stone, because it is full inside. Brothers and sisters, the Holy Spirit isn’t looking for clever people; he is looking for people with room inside.

Science offers a lovely confirmation too. The brain does not set hard after a certain age, as we once believed. A well-known study by the team of neuroscientist Eleanor Maguire at University College London, published in 2000, found that London taxi drivers, who must memorise a tangled maze of streets, have a noticeably larger rear portion of the hippocampus — the part of the brain responsible for spatial memory — than other people, and the longer they have been driving, the greater the difference. This is neuroplasticity: whatever you keep learning, your brain grows in that direction. When God made us, he wrote “able to be shaped all life long” into our very design. Stopping learning has never been a biological limit; it is a choice of attitude.

sections.heading: Applying the 321 Vision
sections.html:
The third of the Three Foundations of 321 is “the Holy Spirit is my guide.” If those words are only a slogan, we will still go through our days on the strength of our own cleverness; if they become our mindset, then every morning we will first ask, “Lord, what do you want to teach me today?”

321 also often reminds us: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. Because those who rely on the brain and on themselves have to figure everything out, control everything and carry everything themselves, and the result is anxiety; those who rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit first entrust, first listen, first obey, and the result is rest. Proverbs 4:23 says, “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.”

Brothers and sisters, if we remember only one sentence today, let it be this: the best teacher already lives within you; the only question is whether today you have asked him, and whether you have been quiet enough to hear him.

sections.heading: 2. “You Are My Teacher”: A Life Posture of Humble Learning
sections.html:
Scripture

But don’t you be called ‘Rabbi,’ for one is your teacher, the Christ, and all of you are brothers. (Matthew 23:8)

doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself; (Philippians 2:3)

Two Mindsets, Two Ways of Life

“I am your teacher,” or “You are my teacher”? Brothers and sisters, the difference is only a sentence, yet these are two entirely different ways of living.

If we always treat people with the mindset “I am your teacher,” we will make light of other people’s views and refuse to be reminded or corrected. We will start preparing our rebuttal before the other person has finished speaking, and hear every suggestion as an attack on us. Proverbs 18:13 puts it bluntly: “He who answers before he hears, that is folly and shame to him.”

But if we treat people with the attitude “You are my teacher,” we will keep a learning heart, willing to listen and willing to be shaped. That attitude lets the Holy Spirit speak to us freely through others. James 1:19 says, “So, then, my beloved brothers, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger.” God gave us two ears and one mouth; the proportion was always plain.

Notice especially that this has nothing to do with age, position, education or experience; it is a matter of the posture of the heart. In Matthew 23:8 the Lord Jesus says to his disciples, “But don’t you be called ‘Rabbi,’ for one is your teacher, the Christ, and all of you are brothers.” In the Lord’s church there is only one teacher; everyone else is a classmate. Some classmates came into the classroom earlier and some later, but not one of us is the teacher.

When we truly believe “You are my teacher,” we will respect others and be willing to learn from them. Even if they are young, have little learning, speak poorly or say things we’d rather not hear, God can still use them to say the very sentence that we needed to be reminded of. Numbers 12:3 records, “Now the man Moses was very humble, more than all the men who were on the surface of the earth.” This leader, who brought Israel out of Egypt and spoke with God face to face on Mount Sinai, nevertheless in Exodus chapter 18 quietly heard out the advice of his father-in-law Jethro, a foreign priest, and “Moses listened to the voice of his father-in-law, and did all that he had said” (Exodus 18:24). Israel’s whole system of justice began with one act of willingness to listen.

How the Concept of Humility Changes Our Emotions and Actions

This Concept of Humility will shape our emotions and reactions all the way through. When others correct us, we won’t get angry; instead we’ll be grateful, because a teacher’s rebuke is for the pupil’s growth. Proverbs 27:6 says, “The wounds of a friend are faithful, although the kisses of an enemy are profuse.” The hard words of a true friend are worth more than a hundred flatteries.

It will also shape our actions and strategies. With the heart that says “You are my teacher,” we will serve more humbly, value the team, and know how to learn from and build up one another; we will stop going it alone and stop gathering the credit to ourselves. Proverbs 27:17 says, “Iron sharpens iron; so a man sharpens his friend’s countenance.” A blade doesn’t sharpen itself; it has to be ground against another piece of iron. Being ground hurts, but only being ground makes it sharp.

The New Testament has a beautiful example. In Acts chapter 18 Apollos is a Jew who is “an eloquent man” and “mighty in the Scriptures,” and he preaches boldly in the synagogue. But all he knows is the baptism of John; something is still missing. A proud man, having his gaps pointed out by a tentmaking couple, might well have blown up on the spot. But Scripture says, “when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside, and explained to him the way of God more accurately” (Acts 18:26). Apollos didn’t get defensive; he was teachable. And the result? From the very next verse he becomes a great help to the believers. Brothers and sisters, a teachable preacher has a brighter future than a flawless one.

Confirmation from Psychology: Teachability Sets the Ceiling on Growth

Psychology has made some very clear observations here. Stanford psychologist Carol Dweck, through decades of research, drew the distinction between a “fixed mindset” and a “growth mindset.” People with a fixed mindset believe ability is set in stone, so they take every criticism as a verdict on their self-worth, and they avoid challenges and hide their mistakes. People with a growth mindset believe ability can grow through effort and learning, so they treat criticism as information and failure as feedback. In her 2006 book Mindset she points out that the greatest difference between the two often lies not in intelligence but in how people respond to setbacks.

Another study is just as worth pondering. In 1999 David Dunning and Justin Kruger of Cornell University published research describing what came to be called the Dunning–Kruger effect: the less competent people are in a given field, the more they tend to overestimate their own performance, because they lack precisely the ability to recognise their own shortcomings. Socrates is commonly said to have claimed that the only thing he knew was that he knew nothing. That is exactly where wisdom begins.

Brothers and sisters, put these two studies together and they point to a spiritual truth: pride not only stops us learning, pride also blinds us to our need to learn. That is why David prayed, “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way” (Psalm 139:23–24). We need a mirror that does not lie, and that mirror is the word of God, together with the people God has placed beside us.

sections.heading: Applying the 321 Vision
sections.html:
321 says: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. “I am your teacher” is the self-centred life, because that “I” has to stand up high, has to be seen, has to be right every time; “You are my teacher” is selflessness, because that “I” steps aside so that God can speak through anyone at all.

321 also says: pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. When I insist, “I am your teacher,” I am sitting in the seat only the Holy Spirit may sit in. Philippians 2:3 says, “doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself.” The word for “humility” here is tapeinophrosynē, literally “lowliness of mind” — not low self-esteem, but bringing the mind down low, low enough to hear other people.

Brothers and sisters, selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus. Because when I am no longer the only teacher, the whole world becomes my classroom.

sections.heading: 3. A Culture of Humility Brings Unity and Revival
sections.html:
Scripture

See how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to live together in unity! (Psalm 133:1)

with all lowliness and humility, with patience, bearing with one another in love, being eager to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. (Ephesians 4:2–3)

From One Person’s Mindset to a Group’s Culture

If “You are my teacher” stays with one person, it is a virtue; if it becomes the shared breath of a whole group, it is a culture.

What is culture? Culture is “this is how we do things here.” Culture needs no announcement, yet it is more powerful than any announcement. When everyone in a family, a church or a team treats one another this way, a spiritual atmosphere is created — of respect, of learning, of unity.

In marriage, if husband and wife each treat the other as a teacher, they can respect and appreciate one another in place of quarrelling and criticism. The University of Washington psychologist John Gottman spent many years observing how couples interact and identified four patterns that are most destructive to a marriage, which he called “the Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse”: criticism, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling. Of these, the one he found most predictive of a marriage breaking down is contempt — looking down on the other person from above. Brothers and sisters, notice: contempt is simply the emotional form of “I am your teacher.” When a husband has decided in his heart, “You don’t understand,” when a wife has decided, “There’s no talking to you,” the wall has already been built. Conversely, one sincere “I need to learn from you on this” will often do more to take that wall down than ten arguments.

In the relationship between parents and children, if parents are willing to learn from their children, the children will also be willing to heed their parents’ teaching, and the home will be full of love and understanding. Children never learn from what we say; they learn from who we are. A father who never apologises won’t raise a son who can admit he’s wrong; but a father who can say in front of his child, “Daddy was too impatient just now — I’m sorry,” has taught that child the most important lesson of his life.

In the church, if leaders and co-workers treat one another as “my teacher,” clashes over authority are defused, and in their place come the work of the Holy Spirit and the fruit of unity. 1 Peter 5:5 says, “Likewise, you younger ones, be subject to the elder. Yes, all of you clothe yourselves with humility, to subject yourselves to one another; for ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’” Notice the words “to one another” — it doesn’t run one way only; it runs both ways.

Confirmation from Science and History

In 1999 Amy Edmondson of Harvard Business School put forward the idea of “psychological safety”: when the members of a team believe they will not be humiliated for admitting a mistake, asking a question or voicing disagreement, the team’s learning behaviour clearly increases. Later, Google’s “Project Aristotle,” begun in 2012, analysed well over a hundred of the company’s own teams, and its findings, released in 2015, concluded that the single most important trait shared by high-performing teams was psychological safety — not the members’ seniority or IQ.

Likewise, research by Bradley Owens and colleagues, published in 2013 in the journal Organization Science, found that when leaders show humility — admitting their limits, appreciating others’ strengths, being willing to learn — the whole team’s learning orientation and engagement rise.

Brothers and sisters, these studies are not here to endorse the Bible; the Bible needs no endorsement. They simply let us see that the order God designed has left its traces everywhere in the human world.

Church history shows it even more. The great revival in Pyongyang, Korea, in 1907 began not with a brilliant sermon but with missionaries and church elders publicly confessing their sins before the congregation. When those up high came down low first, the river of the Holy Spirit poured down. Revival has never started at the pulpit; revival starts on the floor.

sections.heading: Applying the 321 Vision
sections.html:
321 says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. Nowhere is this easier to test than at home. “You never listen to me” brings back “You’re the one being unreasonable,” and both people win the argument but together lose the relationship. That is both sides losing. On the other hand, “I was too impatient just now — let me think again about what you said” often brings back a softened “Actually, I was in the wrong too.” That is both sides winning.

321 also says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. Many teams fall apart not because the work can’t be finished but because the relationships broke down first.

This is exactly the soil of the “235 relationships.” Becoming a “2” with a selfless person — a spiritual companion — we can share our hearts and hold each other up; going on to build the “3,” we have spiritual parents and spiritual children, and life is passed on from generation to generation; finally we become the “5,” a team of spiritual comrades, a fivefold-ministry team working in harmony. And the starting point of all of this is one sentence: “You are my teacher.” Because two people who both insist on being the teacher can never be companions.

When everyone learns from one another with a humble heart, the Holy Spirit is free to move. We stop being defensive, stop comparing, and grow together as we learn from each other. A team like that will be full of life and full of witness, and Satan will find no breach in it. Ephesians 4:27 says, “and don’t give place to the devil.” Brothers and sisters, pride is the biggest foothold Satan has among us.

sections.heading: 4. Humility Brings Limitless Learning and Wisdom
sections.html:
Scripture

Instruct a wise person, and he will be still wiser. Teach a righteous person, and he will increase in learning. (Proverbs 9:9)

God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble. (James 4:6)

Why the Wise Grow Ever Wiser

Proverbs 9:9 says, “Instruct a wise person, and he will be still wiser. Teach a righteous person, and he will increase in learning.” The Hebrew of this verse is wonderfully terse; translated literally it reads, “Give to a wise person, and he will be wiser still.” Interestingly, the original doesn’t say what to give him — because anything will do. Praise or rebuke, good times or hard times: a teachable person can take anything at all and turn it into wisdom.

So now we understand: the wise grow ever wiser not because they know a great deal, but because they are willing to keep learning. In the same chapter, Proverbs 9:8 says, “Don’t reprove a scoffer, lest he hate you. Reprove a wise person, and he will love you.” The same words enter the ears of two kinds of people and bear completely opposite fruit. What decides the outcome is not the words; it is the listener.

James 4:6 says, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” The word “resists” in the original is antitassomai, a military term for an army drawing up in battle formation to face an enemy. Brothers and sisters, what a sobering picture this is: when a person is proud, what he faces is not merely difficulty, but God himself drawn up in battle array against him. No wonder Proverbs 16:18 says, “Pride goes before destruction, and an arrogant spirit before a fall.”
