The original word for “humble,” tapeinos, means at root “low, lowly”; in the Old Testament, the Hebrew anav carries the sense of “bowed down, submitted to God.” Isaiah 66:2 says, “but I will look to this man, even to he who is poor and of a contrite spirit, and who trembles at my word.” God’s eyes do not look to the heights; God’s eyes look to the low places. Psalm 25:9 says, “He will guide the humble in justice. He will teach the humble his way.” God’s teaching has an intended audience: he teaches his way to the humble.

So humility is not denying ourselves our worth; it is acknowledging that God still has a higher wisdom. It is not giving up thinking; it is being willing to be illuminated and corrected. 1 Corinthians 8:1 says, “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.” Knowledge without humility underneath it will only blow a person up like a balloon.

An Illustration: The Outlet Decides Whether the Water Lives

Israel has two famous bodies of water, both fed by the Jordan River. In the north, the Sea of Galilee has both an inflow and an outflow; its water is clear, full of fish, its shores green — and most of the Lord Jesus’ ministry happened there. In the south, the Dead Sea has an inflow but no outflow; its salt content reaches about 30 percent, far above ordinary seawater at about 3.5 percent, and almost nothing can live in its waters. Water from the same river, and the whole difference comes down to one thing: whether it is willing to flow on. Brothers and sisters, a life that only takes in and never gives out, only receives and never gives, only speaks and never listens, will sooner or later turn so salty that nothing can grow.

The history of science has a famous saying too. In a letter to Hooke in 1675, Newton wrote that if he had seen further, it was by standing on the shoulders of giants. Those words came from one of the greatest scientists in human history, and they were not mere politeness; they were the plain truth. Those who really stand high know best who it is that lifted them up.

sections.heading: Applying the 321 Vision
sections.html:
321 says: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living it out; it is no longer I, but Christ living in me. Galatians 2:20 says, “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.”

When we live in the mindset “You are my teacher,” we enter into limitless learning, because anyone and anything can become our teacher. For the one who must always be the teacher, the ceiling on his learning is himself; for the one willing to be the pupil, the ceiling is God.

This is also what 321 calls a shift of perspective: from man’s perspective to God’s, from an earthly perspective to a heavenly one, from a temporary perspective to an eternal one, from a worldly perspective to a godly one. From man’s perspective, conceding the point is a loss; from God’s perspective, “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Matthew 23:12). From an earthly perspective, being corrected is a loss of face; from an eternal perspective, it is a free lesson God is giving us.

sections.heading: 5. Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s set today’s lesson back into the big picture of 321.

The Three Foundations. Jesus is my role model — Philippians chapter 2 tells us that, existing in the form of God, he did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant; at the Last Supper he stooped down and washed the disciples’ feet. In Matthew 11:29 the Lord says with his own lips, “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls.” The Bible is my standard — we don’t judge who is right and who is wrong by our feelings; we go back to the word of God. The Holy Spirit is my guide — he is the teacher who never leaves, lifting the Lord’s words into our hearts at the crucial moment.

The Two Core Values. To let Jesus be King is to give up the “I am the teacher” seat on the throne of our lives; to let Jesus receive all the glory is, when I am praised, to know that I am only standing on the shoulders of a giant — and that the giant is the Lord himself.

The Goal: establish God’s system. God’s system is not propped up by one strong man; it is built by a group of people willing to be taught by one another.

The fivefold change begins today with its first link: when the mindset changes, the life changes; when the life changes, daily living changes; when daily living changes, relationships change; when relationships change, ministry changes. Today we are changing just one mindset — from “I am your teacher” to “You are my teacher” — and the next four links will move one after another.

The “920 practice” reminds us that every person we are in relationship with is our “2.” That “2” might be your spouse, your child, a co-worker — or the person whose words are the hardest to hear. Before them we practise the “0” — the selfless life — bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions. Galatians 5:22–23 says, “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.” Notice that not one of these nine graces is grown in solitude; every one of them can only be grown in relationships. And every person who becomes our “2” is a teacher God has sent to teach us.

Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not others, not our circumstances. When the focus is on ourselves, we fight for face; when it’s on others, we compare; when it’s on our circumstances, we complain. Only when Jesus is the focal point can we hear the Lord’s gentle voice inside any word that grates on our ears.

sections.heading: 6. Putting It into Practice
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, a mindset that never touches the ground is just a passing emotion. The lesson gives us three practices, and we will use the eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to drive them deep.

Practice 1: Starting today, say “Thank you for teaching me” to three people around you

Not as a pleasantry, but specifically. Name the one thing you have learned from them. Say it to your spouse, to your children, to your co-workers. One specific word of thanks is worth more than a hundred vague compliments.

Practice 2: When someone reminds or corrects you, don’t argue back straight away

Stop first and pray, “Lord, what do you want me to learn?” Give yourself three seconds. Those three seconds are the dividing line between the old self and the new self.

Practice 3: In your small group, your family or your ministry, live out a culture of “You are my teacher”

Take the initiative to listen, and offer affirmation and respect. Let every group you belong to feel a little safer because you are there.

Going Deeper with the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset

Information: today’s lesson is the information God is giving us. Copy out John 14:26, Proverbs 9:9 and James 4:6 on paper and put them where you will see them.

Revelation: information stays in the head; revelation reaches the heart. Quietly ask the Lord to shine his light on you: the last time I couldn’t take in what someone said, who was it? And why couldn’t I take it in?

Conviction: not “I know,” but “I admit it.” Confess to the Lord: Lord, I have been sitting in the seat only you may sit in.

Implementation: between now and the weekend, carry out the three practices above, without skipping a single one.

Evaluation: every evening, spend three minutes looking back: did I interrupt anyone today? Did I pass judgement on someone in my heart before they’d even spoken?

Correction: wherever you find you’ve gone wrong, turn back at once. If you have wronged someone, go and apologise; if you have looked down on someone, go and thank them.

Repetition: for a mindset to become life, it has to be repeated again and again. Keep up these three practices for forty days in a row.

Multiplication: tell others about your change. Find a “2,” pass on to them the mindset “You are my teacher,” and hold each other accountable. The final proof of life is that it can multiply.

sections.heading: 7. A Gentle Reminder
sections.html:
Humility is not a weakness; it is spiritual strength. Pride isolates us; humility connects us. Pride makes us stagnate; humility makes us grow.

Water flows to the lowest place, and so does grace. The higher you stand, the less rain you catch; the lower you stoop, the more living water gathers around you.

sections.heading: 8. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, humility is the starting point for the renewal of our mindset.

When we learn to treat people with the heart that says “You are my teacher,” we open the door for the Holy Spirit to keep on teaching us throughout our lives. A life like this is not only blessed; it can bring unity and revival.

In our everyday dealings with one another, let us build a culture of humility, so that every conversation and every encounter becomes a classroom in which God changes us.

This morning the Lord extends three invitations to us.

First, give up the teacher’s seat. Only the Holy Spirit fits in that seat; if we climb into it, it will only crush us.

Second, take your seat as a pupil. Only those who sit down can hear; only those who bow low can receive.

Third, hand over the King’s throne. Let Jesus be King — King in your thinking, King in your marriage, King in your service.

May our families, our small groups and our churches all become classrooms where no one scrambles to be the teacher. May the Holy Spirit sit in the middle of every conversation we have. And may all our learning, all our change and all our revival give the glory to Jesus, and to no one else.

keyVerses: But the Counselor, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things, and will remind you of all that I said to you. (John 14:26)
Instruct a wise person, and he will be still wiser. Teach a righteous person, and he will increase in learning. (Proverbs 9:9)
God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble. (James 4:6)
declarations: Lord, I am willing to let you be my teacher all my life, and willing to see every person as a teacher you have sent to teach me. Give me a humble heart, so that I do not lean on my own understanding, and as I listen, learn and am corrected, make me more and more like Christ.
practices: When someone reminds or corrects you, don’t argue back straight away
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you.

You are the King of kings, yet on that night you wrapped a towel around your waist and stooped to wash your disciples’ feet. Lord, we are ashamed, for we so often jostle to be the teacher and so seldom agree to be the pupil.
Forgive our pride — the contempt we never voiced, the rebuttals ready before we had heard half of what was said, the self we have wrapped up in spiritual language.

Holy Spirit, be our teacher all our lives. Teach us through your word, remind us through our circumstances, and shine your light on us through the people you have placed beside us. Give us soft hearts that can hear, and humble ears that can be taught.
Lord, make our families families that learn from one another, and our church a church where we build one another up. May Satan find no breach among us, and may your Spirit move freely in our midst.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Matthew 23:8 says, “But don’t you be called ‘Rabbi,’ for one is your teacher, the Christ, and all of you are brothers.” Share: what is the most recent reminder you found hard to take in? Looking back now, what might God want to teach you through it?

James 4:6 says, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” Name one specific person around you: what do you want to learn from them? How do you plan to say “Thank you for teaching me” to them this week?
l049.title: The Concept of Humility
l049.subtitle: You Are My Teacher
l049.partTitle: Unit 4 · The Prerequisite for Revival — A Change of Mindset

sections.heading: 1. Introduction: No One Signs Up for It, Yet No One Escapes It
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we are going to face together a subject no one wants to sign up for, yet no one can escape — suffering.

Just saying the word “suffering” makes the heart sink a little. We long for ease and pursue smooth sailing, and almost every blessing we have heard since childhood points the same way: a fair wind all the way, everything as you wish, peace and joy. Deep down we carry an invisible blueprint for our lives, with a straight road climbing steadily uphill; we even quietly tape it into our prayers, assuming that God is working from that same blueprint.

Until one day the blueprint is torn to pieces.

Perhaps it is a diagnosis that pulls the word “health” out of your life. Perhaps it is a phone call in the middle of the night that takes someone you love out of this world. Perhaps it is a coldness in your marriage that has built up day after day, until under the same roof you feel lonelier than if you lived alone. Perhaps it is a child who suddenly stops talking to you, shuts the bedroom door, and shuts his heart with it. In that moment the deepest question inside us is not “What do I do?” but “Why?” — Why me? God, where are you? Don’t you love me?

Brothers and sisters, I want to say this very honestly: how a person sees suffering decides how he will live his whole life.

If the formula in our hearts is “smooth going equals God’s blessing, suffering equals God’s punishment,” then every trouble will push us away from God. We will complain, we will doubt, we will bargain, and in the end we will quietly break off relations with God in our hearts. But if we have a godly view of suffering, the very same storm will push us into God’s embrace; we will meet God in suffering, experience God, and in the end glorify God.

The circumstances are exactly the same, yet the outcomes are completely opposite. The difference is not in the circumstances; the difference is in the mindset.

This is exactly what Kingdom 321 Online Fellowship has always said: the fivefold change begins with mindset — when the mindset changes, the life changes; when the life changes, daily living changes; when daily living changes, relationships change; when relationships change, ministry changes. What we want to replace today is the part furthest upstream: our view of suffering.

Scripture has never promised us a road without tears. The Lord Jesus said with his own lips, “In the world you have trouble; but cheer up! I have overcome the world” (John 16:33). He did not say, “You will not have trouble”; he said, “You have trouble.” Nor did he say, “Grit your teeth and get through it”; he said, “Cheer up!” Why can we take heart? Because the one who has overcome has already walked this road ahead of us, and he will walk it with us.

So today’s message is simple, yet it takes a lifetime to learn: suffering is not a curse but a pathway to blessing; not God’s punishment but his tool for shaping our lives. Suffering is a blessing in disguise — it comes to us with its face blackened, and only when we are willing to reach out and lead it in through the door does it slowly take off its disguise and reveal the face of grace.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Background: Two Letters Written out of Affliction
sections.html:
Neither of today’s two theme passages was written in a study. Both were spoken and written in the very thick of affliction.

1. Acts 14: Words from a Man Who Had Just Been Stoned

The author of Acts is Luke, a Gentile physician and Paul’s companion on his missionary journeys. He wrote to a man named Theophilus, and the book was completed around the AD 60s. Acts 14 records the close of Paul’s first missionary journey.

Paul and Barnabas had come to Lystra and healed a man lame from birth. The crowds were so stirred that they actually called Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes, and brought oxen and garlands to offer sacrifices to them. But before long, Jews from Antioch and Iconium came and stirred up the people, and the very same crowd that one moment wanted to worship him the next moment stoned him and dragged him out of the city, thinking he was dead.

Scripture goes on: “But as the disciples stood around him, he rose up, and entered into the city” (Acts 14:20). Only then comes our theme verse for today — he turned back and travelled once more through Lystra, Iconium and Antioch to strengthen the souls of the disciples.

Brothers and sisters, please hold on to this picture: the words “through many afflictions we must enter into God’s Kingdom” are not a fine saying from someone who has never tasted hardship. They were spoken by a man still bearing the wounds of the stones, who went back into the very city that had stoned him and said them to new believers who were still shaken to the core. This is theology written in blood.

And notice the pronoun Paul uses — he says “we,” not “you.” He does not point at the congregation and say, “You must suffer”; he stands among the brothers and says, “We are going to walk this road together.”

2. 1 Peter 4: A Letter to a Church Under Fire

1 Peter was written around AD 64, during the very period when the Roman emperor Nero was persecuting the church. At the end of the letter Peter says he is in “Babylon” (1 Peter 5:13), which is generally understood to be the early church’s code name for Rome.

The letter is addressed “to the chosen ones who are living as foreigners in the Dispersion in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia” (1 Peter 1:1). The phrase “living as foreigners” is crucial — these were second-class people in society, without citizenship, without anyone to back them, and now, because they believed in Jesus, they were slandered by their neighbours, harassed by their employers and shunned by their families. They were asking one question: if God loves us, why has the fire come upon us?

Peter’s answer is not “This is just a temporary misunderstanding,” but “Don’t be astonished.” The original means: don’t treat this as something foreign, something you never saw coming. Because the fiery trial has always been written into a disciple’s calendar.

Interestingly, the Peter who wrote this letter is the very man who, years before, beside the fire in the high priest’s courtyard, denied the Lord three times. Now he writes to teach the churches how to stand firm in the fire — and that in itself is the finest testimony.

Brothers and sisters, these two letters tell us one thing: the New Testament church’s view of suffering was not a theory but the footprints left behind by people who had been through the fire.

sections.heading: 3. Key Point 1: Suffering Is the Necessary Path for the Growth of Faith
sections.html:
Scripture

strengthening the souls of the disciples, exhorting them to continue in the faith, and that through many afflictions we must enter into God’s Kingdom. (Acts 14:22)

though he was a Son, yet learned obedience by the things which he suffered. (Hebrews 5:8)

The Weight of the Original

There are two words in this verse worth chewing over slowly.

The first is “afflictions,” in Greek θλῖψις (thlipsis), whose verb at root means “to press, to squeeze.” When the Romans made olive oil, they pressed the olives again and again under a heavy millstone; the first oil pressed out was the purest, the oil used to light the golden lampstand in the sanctuary. Θλῖψις is that feeling of being pressed — hemmed in on every side, unable to move, unable to breathe.

The second is “must,” in Greek δεῖ (dei). Luke is especially fond of this word in his writings, and he uses it almost always of God’s plan: “I must be in my Father’s house” (Luke 2:49); “The Son of Man must suffer many things” (Luke 9:22). Theologians call it the “divine must.” In other words, suffering is not an accident, not a slip of God’s hand, not the result of prayers that weren’t strong enough; on God’s map it is a stretch of road with a name, with coordinates, and with a way out.

Scripture Interpreting Scripture: Even Jesus Walked This Road

Some say, “If God loves me, how could he let me suffer?” The Bible’s answer is very direct — look at his only beloved Son.

Jesus was the Son of God, yet on earth he knew hunger and weariness; he was misunderstood, betrayed, flogged and crucified. Isaiah described him long beforehand: “He was despised and rejected by men, a man of suffering and acquainted with disease” (Isaiah 53:3). Hebrews says, “though he was a Son, yet learned obedience by the things which he suffered” (Hebrews 5:8).

Notice that Jesus did not suffer because he had sinned; he chose, of his own accord, to walk the way of the cross because he loved us. So suffering is never proof of judgement. Peter says it even more clearly: “For you were called to this, because Christ also suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow his steps” (1 Peter 2:21).

The word “example” is the Greek ὑπογραμμός (hypogrammos), which originally meant the copybook a teacher wrote out at the top of the page for a child learning to write, so that the child could trace over the letters. Brothers and sisters, Jesus’ life is that copybook, and the stroke of the cross he has already traced out for us. Every narrow stretch of road we walk today, we are setting our pen down on his strokes.

So real faith is not escaping suffering but continuing, in the midst of suffering, to believe in the goodness of God. When we understand this, our prayers will change: we will no longer only ask the Lord to take us “out of” suffering, but ask him to “lead us through” it. Psalm 23 does not say, “I will not have to pass through the valley of the shadow of death”; it says, “Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me” (Psalm 23:4). It is “walk through,” not “walk around.”

A Scientific Parable: A Tree Without Wind Cannot Stand

In the 1990s there was a famous experiment in Arizona in the United States — Biosphere 2. Scientists built a huge sealed glass structure containing a rainforest, an ocean and a desert, with every condition carefully controlled, including this one: no wind.

The researchers noticed something strange: the trees inside grew fast and tall, but after reaching a certain height they toppled over one after another. The reason? Trees need wind. As the wind keeps blowing and shaking them, trees grow denser, tougher “stress wood” on the side that takes the strain, and at the same time drive their roots deeper. A tree without wind looks lush on the outside but is hollow within, unable to bear its own weight.

Brothers and sisters, are you being shaken right now? God may not be uprooting you; he may be making you put down roots.

Confirmation from Psychology: Post-Traumatic Growth

In the mid-1990s two psychologists at the University of North Carolina at Charlotte, Richard Tedeschi and Lawrence Calhoun, put forward the concept of “post-traumatic growth” and developed a scale to measure it. Among large numbers of people who had come through major loss and trauma, they found that alongside the pain that follows trauma, many also showed positive change in five areas: a greater appreciation of life, deeper relationships, discovering they were stronger than they had imagined, seeing new possibilities in life, and spiritual growth.

Please note: the findings of psychology are only supporting evidence, not the standard. The Bible said it two thousand years ago: “we also rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces perseverance; and perseverance, proven character; and proven character, hope: and hope doesn’t disappoint us, because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us” (Romans 5:3–5). Psychology measures the phenomenon; Scripture reveals the source — the Holy Spirit, who pours love into our hearts.

Applying the 321 Vision

The first of the Three Foundations is: Jesus is my role model. In suffering, these words carry their greatest power. Because the one we believe in is not a God standing on the clouds who has never felt pain; he became flesh and walked the road we are walking now.

Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not others, not our circumstances. The greatest danger in suffering is not the pain; it is that suffering forcibly drags our focus back onto ourselves — my loss, my grievance, my unfair treatment. Once that “I” is magnified, God shrinks. So in affliction, the first thing to practise is moving our focus from “me” back to “him.”

sections.heading: 4. Key Point 2: Ease Makes Us Fall; Suffering Makes Us Strong
sections.html:
Scripture

Lot lifted up his eyes, and saw all the plain of the Jordan, that it was well-watered everywhere, before Yahweh destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah, like the garden of Yahweh, like the land of Egypt, as you go to Zoar. (Genesis 13:10)

Abram lived in the land of Canaan, and Lot lived in the cities of the plain, and moved his tent as far as Sodom. (Genesis 13:12)

For the backsliding of the simple will kill them. The careless ease of fools will destroy them. (Proverbs 1:32)

Two Men, Two Choices, Two Endings

One of the starkest contrasts in the whole Bible is Abraham and Lot.

When their herdsmen quarrelled and the land could not hold them both, Abraham did something quite unheard of at the time: the elder let the younger choose first. He said, “If you go to the left hand, then I will go to the right. Or if you go to the right hand, then I will go to the left” (Genesis 13:9). That was an act of laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position.

Lot “lifted up his eyes” — Scripture’s wording is frighteningly precise. He chose with his eyes, not with faith. He saw “well-watered,” he saw “like the garden of Yahweh,” but he did not see the footnote that comes straight after: “Now the men of Sodom were exceedingly wicked and sinners against Yahweh” (Genesis 13:13).

Then comes that slow and deadly verb: “moved his tent as far as Sodom.” He didn’t leap in all at once; he shifted a little at a time. First his tent faced that way, then he moved into the city, and later still he was sitting in the city gate. By the day fire and sulphur fell, he had lost his property, lost his wife, and fled into a cave with his two daughters, his household in ruins.

Ease never knocked him down in one blow; ease shaved a slice off him every day.

Abraham, by contrast, lived in tents all his life. Hebrews says, “By faith, he lived as an alien in the land of promise, as in a land not his own, dwelling in tents … For he looked for the city which has the foundations, whose builder and maker is God” (Hebrews 11:9–10). A tent is temporary; the city is eternal. It wasn’t that Abraham lacked the means to build a city; his gaze had already gone beyond every earthly city. He worshipped in tents, built altars and offered sacrifices in the wilderness, was refined through trial after trial, and in the end became the father of faith.

A Glimpse of the Original: The Word Called “Ease”

Hebrew has a word, שַׁאֲנָן (sha’anan), meaning “at ease, carefree, without a worry in the world.” In the prophets it often carries a note of warning.

Jeremiah uses a vivid picture: “Moab has been at ease from his youth, and he has settled on his lees, and has not been emptied from vessel to vessel, neither has he gone into captivity: therefore his taste remains in him, and his scent is not changed” (Jeremiah 48:11).

In ancient winemaking, the wine was poured again and again from one vessel to another so that the dregs would settle and be left behind. Moab had never been poured out, so it had always sat soaking in its own dregs. On the surface “his taste remains in him”; in reality it had never once been made pure.

Brothers and sisters, when God pours you from this vessel into that one — a change of job, a change of city, a change in your health, a change in your relationships — each pouring leaves your head spinning. But what is God doing? He is leaving the dregs behind.

David: Falling in Ease, Singing in Suffering

The same principle shows even more clearly in David.

2 Samuel 11:1 records: “At the return of the year, at the time when kings go out, David sent Joab … But David stayed at Jerusalem.” When he should have gone out to battle, he stayed in the palace; when he should have been on the battlefield, he was cooling off on the rooftop — and then he saw what he should not have seen and went down a road he should never have taken. David’s greatest failure did not happen in a cave in the wilderness; it happened on the roof terrace of the palace.

Yet go and read the Psalms, and the deepest passages, the ones that have comforted millions, were almost all written in his days on the run. The heading of Psalm 57 reads: “when he fled from Saul, in the cave.” In the cave, what did he write? “Be merciful to me, God, be merciful to me, for my soul takes refuge in you. Yes, in the shadow of your wings, I will take refuge, until disaster has passed” (Psalm 57:1).

David in the cave was closer to God than David in the palace.

So ease dulls us and suffering wakes us up; ease draws us away from God and suffering draws us near to him. This does not mean ease is a sin in itself; it means that ease, without watchfulness to guard it, turns into the lukewarm water of the spiritual life.

The Body Speaks: The Lesson of Bones and Muscles

In 1892 the German anatomist Julius Wolff set out what became known as Wolff’s law: bone remodels itself according to the load it bears; where it takes more strain, the bone grows dense and strong; where it bears no load for a long time, bone is lost.

This is not mere theory. NASA’s space-medicine research has long confirmed that in weightlessness astronauts lose roughly 1 to 2 percent of the bone mass in their weight-bearing bones every month. No burdens in space sounds like heaven, but the result is osteoporosis. Muscles are the same: without resistance to work against, they do not grow.

No weight, no strength. Brothers and sisters, this is a sermon God has written into our bodies: only under strain do we become strong.

A Sentence That Rings True

The English writer C. S. Lewis wrote a line in The Problem of Pain that is still quoted today: “God whispers to us in our pleasures, speaks in our conscience, but shouts in our pains: it is His megaphone to rouse a deaf world.”

We often can’t hear God when things are going well — not because God isn’t speaking, but because we are too noisy.

Applying the 321 Vision

Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

Lot lifted up his eyes and picked the best piece of land; that is the self-centred life — centred on one’s own interests. Abraham gave up the right to choose; that is selflessness — not having nothing, but putting himself in God’s hands and entering into God’s limitless fullness. And the result? Lot chose the plain and ended up with nothing; Abraham didn’t choose, yet God said to him, “for I will give all the land which you see to you and to your offspring forever” (Genesis 13:15).

Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. Ease is what best feeds the “self”; and suffering is what best tears that “self” down. So sometimes God allows us to lose our comfort because he wants us to gain himself.

sections.heading: 5. Key Point 3: Suffering Is a Blessing in Disguise That Brings Breakthrough in Life
sections.html:
Scripture

As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to save many people alive, as is happening today. (Genesis 50:20)

They bruised his feet with shackles. His neck was locked in irons, until the time that his word happened, and Yahweh’s word proved him true. (Psalm 105:18–19)

Joseph: God Never Wastes Suffering

Joseph’s life is the fullest picture of a “blessing in disguise” in the whole Bible.

He was his father’s favourite, wore a richly coloured robe, and dreamed two dreams of honour. And then? His brothers stripped him of the robe, threw him into a pit and sold him into slavery in Egypt. Just when everything had finally begun to go well, he was falsely accused for keeping himself pure and thrown into prison. In prison he interpreted the cupbearer’s dream, yet once the cupbearer was released, he “didn’t remember Joseph, but forgot him” (Genesis 40:23). Thirteen whole years, all the way down.

Yet on the two darkest stretches of that road, Scripture sets the same sentence: “Yahweh was with Joseph … He was in the house of his master the Egyptian” (Genesis 39:2); “But Yahweh was with Joseph, and showed kindness to him” (Genesis 39:21).

Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: God did not spare Joseph a single step of that hard road; God walked the hard road with him.

Thirteen years later he stood before Pharaoh and became the governor of Egypt. And many years after that, to his brothers kneeling and trembling on the ground, he spoke the words that have shaken history: “As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good.”

Here the Hebrew uses the same root twice, חָשַׁב (chashav), meaning “to think, to plan, to weave.” The brothers “wove” a scheme to do harm; on the very same cloth God “wove” a plan to save. Man’s thread was black; God’s thread was gold. When the weaving was done, that cloth was called salvation.

Without that pit, there would have been no road; without the prison, no throne; without the tears, no glory.

Psalm 105 offers a deeper commentary: “Yahweh’s word proved him true.” What was tested in that prison was not only Joseph’s situation but Joseph’s heart; God used his word to refine this proud and headstrong young man until he could bear the weight of that dream.

When God gives you a vision and then is slow to fulfil it, it is often not because the vision is too big but because the vessel is still too small.

Paul and Silas: Songs in the Prison

The New Testament has a prison story too.

In Philippi, Paul and Silas were beaten with many rods, thrown into the inner prison and had their feet fastened in the stocks. Scripture says, “But about midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them” (Acts 16:25). Their backs were torn, their feet were locked, the night was black — and they were singing.

“Suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken; and immediately all the doors were opened, and everyone’s bonds were loosened” (Acts 16:26). The jailer thought the prisoners had all escaped and drew his sword to kill himself, but Paul shouted to stop him. That night the jailer fell down and asked, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?” They said, “Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will be saved, you and your household” (Acts 16:31).

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? Suffering did not imprison them; instead, through them it set others free. Years later Paul wrote to the church at Philippi from another prison, and the word that appears most in that letter is “joy.”

If suffering can turn people to God, that is the greatest blessing of all.

The Pearl and the Grain of Sand: A Parable from the Sea

How does a pearl come about? When a grain of sand works its way into an oyster’s mantle and becomes an irritant it cannot expel, the oyster secretes layer upon layer of nacre to wrap that injury up. Year after year, the grain of sand that caused it pain becomes a pearl that shines. Notice: at the heart of every pearl there is always a wound.

Brothers and sisters, you cannot choose when that grain of sand comes in; but you can choose whether to let it fester inside you, or let grace wrap it, layer by layer, into a pearl.

Supporting Data: Moderate Adversity

In 2010, the University at Buffalo psychologist Mark Seery and his colleagues published a longitudinal study in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. Analysing data from several thousand American adults, they found a “U-shaped curve”: people who had experienced a moderate amount of adversity in their lives showed better mental health and ability to cope with stress than those who had experienced very high adversity — and also, which often surprises people, better than those who had experienced almost no adversity at all.

A life that has never been through any storm looks the most enviable, yet it is often the most fragile.

There is a much-quoted saying commonly attributed to Charles H. Spurgeon, the English “Prince of Preachers”: “I have learned to kiss the wave that throws me against the Rock of Ages.” A wave is still a wave, and it still knocks you over; but when it throws you onto Christ, you can kiss it.

Applying the 321 Vision

The order of 321 is: life first, then relationships, then ministry. Joseph’s life is the finest demonstration of that order — thirteen years of pit and prison, in which God was working on his “life”; then reconciliation with his brothers, the healing of “relationships”; and only last, the office of governor, which was “ministry.”

We often want to skip the first two steps and go straight to the third. But ministry with no foundation of life is like the tree without wind: quick to grow, and just as quick to fall.

Our perspective needs to shift: from man’s perspective to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. The brothers’ eyes saw only “we did a wicked thing”; Joseph’s eyes saw “God has brought about what is happening today.” The same stretch of history, through two different lenses. May God lend us his lens this very day.

sections.heading: 6. Key Point 4: The Right View of Suffering — Suffering with Jesus, Glorified with Him
sections.html:
Scripture

But because you are partakers of Christ’s sufferings, rejoice, that at the revelation of his glory you also may rejoice with exceeding joy. (1 Peter 4:13)

and if children, then heirs: heirs of God and joint heirs with Christ, if indeed we suffer with him, that we may also be glorified with him. (Romans 8:17)

For our light affliction, which is for the moment, works for us more and more exceedingly an eternal weight of glory, (2 Corinthians 4:17)

One Word: Sharing In

In 1 Peter 4:13, “partakers of Christ’s sufferings” renders the Greek κοινωνέω (koinōneō), from the same root as “fellowship” (κοινωνία, koinōnia), meaning “to share in, to hold in common, to be joined with.”

So Peter is not telling us to “be glad about suffering.” He is saying that when you suffer for the Lord, the pain you go through is joined with the pain Christ went through; you are not hurting alone — you are hurting as one who “shares” it with him.

Brothers and sisters, this is the summit of the view of suffering: the deepest comfort in suffering is not an answer but a companion.

A truly mature believer is not someone who has no fear of suffering, but someone who knows how to recognise, in the midst of suffering, the Lord who is with him. When Daniel’s three friends were thrown into the blazing furnace, King Nebuchadnezzar said in astonishment, “Look, I see four men loose, walking in the middle of the fire, and they are unharmed. The appearance of the fourth is like a son of the gods” (Daniel 3:25). The fire was not taken away, but in the fire there was a fourth man.

Suffering Leads Us to Experience Three Things

First, Deeper Trust

Paul says, “Yes, we ourselves have had the sentence of death within ourselves, that we should not trust in ourselves, but in God who raises the dead” (2 Corinthians 1:9).

“Not trust in ourselves” — that is usually learned not from a sermon but at the end of our rope. Sometimes God takes away our crutches one by one, until we discover that he has always been our only real support. When people have choices, they choose God as “one of” their options; only when they have no choices do they discover that God is the “only” one.

Second, Purer Faith

“that the proof of your faith, which is more precious than gold that perishes even though it is tested by fire, may be found to result in praise, glory, and honor at the revelation of Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 1:7).

The melting point of gold is about 1,064 degrees Celsius. The refiner has to raise the heat that high before the impurities float to the surface to be skimmed off. If the heat isn’t high enough, the dross won’t come out.

In his darkest hour Job spoke one of the brightest sentences: “But he knows the way that I take. When he has tried me, I will come out like gold” (Job 23:10). He didn’t know what was happening, but he knew that God knew. And that was enough.

Third, Truer Love

When everything is going well, it is hard to tell whether we love God or God’s blessings. That was exactly how Satan challenged God long ago: “Does Job fear God for nothing?” (Job 1:9).

Suffering puts that question in front of us: if all the blessings are taken away and you are still here, do I still want you?

When someone who has lost everything can still say, “I still want you,” that love is real. Paul lists seven things — oppression, anguish, persecution, famine, nakedness, peril and sword — and then says, “No, in all these things, we are more than conquerors through him who loved us” (Romans 8:37).

A Testimony from a Concentration Camp

The Austrian psychiatrist Viktor Frankl survived the Nazi concentration camps; his parents, his wife and his brother all died in the camps. After the war he wrote Man’s Search for Meaning and founded logotherapy. In the book he observes that everything a person has can be taken away except one thing: the freedom to choose one’s attitude in any set of circumstances. He also found that under the same hunger and the same shadow of death, those who survived were often not the physically strongest, but those who still held meaning and hope in their hearts.

Psychology can point to the importance of “meaning”; the gospel goes further and tells us who that meaning is — Jesus Christ, who was crucified and rose from the dead.

Applying the 321 Vision

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.

Suffering is the touchstone of sovereignty. When things go well, it’s easy to say, “Lord, you are King,” while in fact our own hands are still on the steering wheel. Then one day things spin completely out of control, and only then do we truly face the question: if I can’t be in control, am I still willing to let him reign as King?

Selflessness overcomes Satan. What Satan fears most is not a Christian without pain, but a Christian who still worships in pain — because that proves he loves God not for what he gets out of it.

“I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living it out. The cross is not the end; it is the door to glory.

sections.heading: 7. Integrating the 321 Vision: Suffering Is the School Where “Self” Is Exchanged for “Him”
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s take today’s four key points and look at them once more within the framework of 321.

The Three Foundations

Jesus is my role model — he walked the hard road first, and “learned obedience by the things which he suffered” (Hebrews 5:8). So I am not walking a road no one has walked before.

The Bible is my standard — in suffering, our feelings will deceive us, our circumstances will frighten us, and people’s words will shake us. Only the word of God is the standard. The psalmist says, “It is good for me that I have been afflicted, that I may learn your statutes” (Psalm 119:71).

The Holy Spirit is my guide — “because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us” (Romans 5:5). Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. What wears us out most in suffering is often not the thing itself, but the thousand possibilities we keep running through our heads.

The Two Core Values

Let Jesus be King — where I cannot be in control, let him reign.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — the final way out of suffering is not “I’ve become stronger” but “He has been lifted high.”

The Goal

Establish God’s system. God spent thirteen years on Joseph, not only to bring one man to maturity but to save many people alive. The work God is doing in you has never been just for you alone.

From the Self-Centred Life to Selflessness

The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of the problem. And suffering is the tool God uses most often to deal with the “self.” It tears down our sense of control, tears down our sense of superiority, tears down our sense of security, until we stand stripped bare before God and say: Lord, I need you.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. “Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time” (1 Peter 5:6).

The 920 Practice

Every person we are in relationship with is our “2.” When, in suffering, we practise living out the selfless (0) life, the nine graces of the fruit of the Spirit grow in the most unlikely soil — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23).

Have you noticed? Fruits like patience, gentleness and self-control are almost impossible to bear when everything is plain sailing. Good times grow leaves; hard times bear fruit.

The 235 Relationships

No one can walk through the valley alone. So we need a “2” — a selfless spiritual companion we can phone in the middle of the night; we need a “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children, someone ahead to lead us by the hand and someone behind to follow; we need a “5” — a team of spiritual comrades, a fivefold-ministry team.

Even in prison Paul was not alone; Silas was beside him. God seldom sends his servants into prison by themselves.

The Fivefold Change

When the mindset changes, the life changes; when the life changes, daily living changes. What we are replacing today is precisely that mindset furthest upstream: suffering is not a curse; it is a blessing in disguise.

sections.heading: 8. Putting It into Practice: Walking Through Suffering with the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. Let’s walk through them thoroughly, using the eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice 1: Write down three ways this could be a “blessing in disguise”

List one hardship or challenge you are facing right now, and write down three ways it could become a “blessing in disguise.”

Information: first write the situation down as it really is. Don’t exaggerate it and don’t play it down. God isn’t afraid of our honesty.

Revelation: take this sheet of paper with you as you read Genesis 50:20 and Romans 8:28, and ask the Holy Spirit to show you the side that human eyes cannot see.

Conviction: even before you see the outcome, sign one sentence at the bottom of the page: “God meant it for good.”

Implementation: this week, look at that sheet once every day and pray over those three directions.

Evaluation and Correction: at the weekend, ask yourself whether your heart has moved from “Why?” to “What for?”; if all you can write is complaint, ask God to adjust your sight, and write it again.

Repetition: rewrite it once a month, until this mindset has grown into your bones.

Multiplication: teach the method of this sheet of paper to another brother or sister who is suffering.

Practice 2: Change the direction of your prayers

When you pray each day, don’t ask God to “take away” the difficulty; ask him to “reveal his will in the midst of” the difficulty.

This is a tiny adjustment, yet a profound one. The Lord Jesus’ prayer in the Garden of Gethsemane is our copybook: “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42).

Notice that Jesus did not pretend it wasn’t bitter. He asked for the cup to be removed — that is honesty. But he handed the final sovereignty back to the Father — that is obedience. Honesty and obedience: you cannot do without either.

Starting tomorrow morning, try dividing your prayer into two sentences: in the first, tell him your pain exactly as it is; in the second, say, “Nevertheless, may your will be done.” Of the eight stages, Repetition is the most crucial here — once won’t change anything, but forty days will change a person.

Practice 3: Share with a spiritual companion, pray for each other, and learn to praise in suffering

The most dangerous side effect of suffering is isolation. Shame tells us to hide, and those who hide are the easiest for Satan to attack one-on-one.

So this week, take the initiative to find a spiritual companion and tell them about the hardship you’re going through. You don’t need to say it perfectly; just say it honestly. Then pray for each other, and open your mouths to praise together — like Paul and Silas, singing before the chains have come loose.

“who comforts us in all our affliction, that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction, through the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God” (2 Corinthians 1:4).

This is Multiplication — the comfort you have received is meant in the end to become comfort for others. God does not waste suffering, nor does he waste the comfort that comes out of suffering.

sections.heading: 9. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, what we have learned today can be distilled into one sentence: ease is not necessarily a blessing, and suffering is not necessarily a curse; what decides the outcome is not our circumstances but our mindset.

On the same piece of land, Lot saw well-watered plains and headed towards Sodom; Abraham saw the starry sky above his tent and headed towards the promise. In the same prison, the cupbearer forgot Joseph, but God remembered him. In the same midnight hour, others were wailing while Paul and Silas were singing hymns.

Circumstances have never had the final say. If God is in your heart, even the hardest road can lead out into glory.

So here is my call to you today:

Stop asking, “God, why did you let this happen to me?” and start asking, “God, what do you want to accomplish through this?”

Stop asking God to carry the cross away; ask him for the strength to take it up and follow him.

Stop waiting for the wind and waves to die down before you worship; open your mouth and praise him while the boat is still rocking.

Because suffering is not an exception to faith but the necessary path of growth. Without suffering, there is no foundation for faith; without trials, there is no testimony of victory. Every unsettled season is a time when God is cultivating us.

“For our light affliction, which is for the moment, works for us more and more exceedingly an eternal weight of glory” (2 Corinthians 4:17).

May we hand over the throne today and let Jesus be King; and may every valley we walk through end in only one way — with Jesus receiving all the glory. If suffering makes us more like Jesus, that is the greatest blessing of all.

keyVerses: strengthening the souls of the disciples, exhorting them to continue in the faith, and that through many afflictions we must enter into God’s Kingdom. (Acts 14:22)

Beloved, don’t be astonished at the fiery trial which has come upon you to test you, as though a strange thing happened to you. But because you are partakers of Christ’s sufferings, rejoice, that at the revelation of his glory you also may rejoice with exceeding joy. (1 Peter 4:12–13)
practices: Write down three ways this could be a “blessing in disguise”
Change the direction of your prayers
Share with a spiritual companion, pray for each other, and learn to praise in suffering
prayer: Lord, thank you for making suffering a teacher in my life.

I confess that I don’t like to suffer; I often ask you to take away my difficulties, but seldom ask you to make your will known. Forgive me for looking at your eternal work with earthly, temporary eyes.

Lord, let me see your hand in my hardship, and learn not to run away, not to complain, but to keep worshipping you even in suffering. Refine me, and skim away the dross within me; tear down my “self,” and let Christ live in me.
Give me spiritual companions, so that we may hold each other up in the valley; and let the comfort I have received become comfort for others.
I place my circumstances, my unknowns and my pain all in your hands. Reign as King in me, and may all the glory be yours.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Genesis 50:20 says, “As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to save many people alive, as is happening today.” Looking back over your life, is there something that felt like “evil” at the time but that you now see was “good”? How did that experience change your understanding of God?

Acts 16:25 says, “But about midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them.” In your present situation, what would “singing at midnight” look like for you in concrete terms? This week, how will you open your mouth to praise before the difficulty has passed?
l050.title: Suffering Is a Blessing in Disguise
l050.subtitle: An Important Mindset: The Concept of Suffering (Part 1)
l050.partTitle: Unit 4 · The Prerequisite for Revival — A Change of Mindset

sections.heading: 1. Introduction: The Morning No One Wants to Mention Again
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I’d like to ask you first to be still for thirty seconds and call one thing to mind: is there a stretch of your life that, even today, you would rather not talk about? Perhaps it was a diagnosis on a sheet of paper. Perhaps it was a phone call in the middle of the night. Perhaps it was a door someone slammed shut on you. At the time, did a question rise up in your heart — God, why me?

I know a sister whose husband died in an accident at work the year she turned forty. On the first morning after the funeral she sat alone in an empty living room before the sun was up. She told me that she did one thing that day: she opened her Bible, but she couldn’t read a single word of it, so she simply laid her head on it and wept. Three years later I saw her again. She was in a hospice ward, keeping company with another sister who had just lost her husband. Holding that sister’s hand, she said, “I know what you’re feeling right now, because I have walked this road.” Brothers and sisters, in that moment I understood something: her suffering had not been cancelled, but her suffering had been put to use by God.

In our last lesson we looked at the first part of the view of suffering — where suffering comes from and what it means. Today we move into the second part: when suffering is already standing in front of us, what mindset do we face it with? For what decides how our story ends is often not the suffering itself, but the way we look at it.

Suffering is a school of the spirit that every believer must pass through. It is not as cruel as we imagine, and it is not God punishing us; it is a course he invites us into, so that we may learn to trust him more deeply. The Lord Jesus himself put it plainly: “In the world you have trouble; but cheer up! I have overcome the world.” (John 16:33) So suffering is nothing to be terrified of; the key is the mindset with which we meet it. If our mindset is wrong, we will run, we will doubt, we may even fall away. If our mindset is right, we will overcome in suffering, be strengthened in it, and grow in life through it.

The English writer C. S. Lewis (1898–1963), in The Problem of Pain (published 1940), wrote words that are often quoted: God whispers to us in our pleasures, speaks in our conscience, but shouts in our pains; pain is his megaphone to rouse a deaf world. Brothers and sisters, this morning may we stop covering our ears, open the door of our hearts, and listen to what God wants to say to us through suffering.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Background: The Lord Jesus’ Last Word to His Disciples
sections.html:
Our theme verse is John 16:33. The Gospel of John was written by the disciple whom the Lord loved, the apostle John, and is generally thought to have been completed between AD 85 and 95, in Ephesus in Asia Minor. By then most of the first-generation apostles had been martyred. The church held second- and third-generation believers, along with great numbers of Gentile converts. They were under pressure from two sides: on one side, expulsion from the Jewish synagogue; on the other, the rising hostility of the Roman Empire. John wrote this Gospel “that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name” (John 20:31).

As for its setting, 16:33 comes at the very end of the Farewell Discourse. John chapters 13 to 17 are the private teaching the Lord Jesus gave the eleven disciples during and after the Last Supper. He washed their feet, foretold Judas’ betrayal, promised the coming of the Holy Spirit, the Counselor, spoke of the vine and the branches, and warned them that the world would hate them: “They will put you out of the synagogues. Yes, the time comes that whoever kills you will think that he offers service to God.” (John 16:2) Having said all this, the Lord summed it up with verse 33. Straight after it comes chapter 17, his high-priestly prayer for his disciples and for believers of every generation. And after that he walks into the Garden of Gethsemane and on to the cross.

In other words, “In the world you have trouble” is not a slogan shouted by someone standing safe on the shore to a person going under in the water. It is the comfort spoken by a Lord about to be crucified, on the eve of his own suffering, to disciples who were about to scatter and run. These words carry the weight of blood.

Three words in the original deserve our attention. First, “trouble” is the Greek thlipsis, whose root sense is “pressing, crushing under weight” — the kind of pressing a winepress gives the grapes and an olive press gives the olives. Brothers and sisters, hold on to that picture: only when grapes are pressed is there new wine; only when olives are pressed is there pure oil. Second, “cheer up” is the Greek tharseite, an imperative: “Take courage, be bold.” The Lord is not saying, “Try to feel a little better.” He is commanding us to take heart. Third, “I have overcome” uses the perfect tense, nenikēka, describing a victory completed in the past whose force remains in effect to this day. The Lord’s victory is not something yet to happen; it is an accomplished fact that still stands.

So in today’s lesson we are not debating a philosophical question. We are receiving a command issued by a Lord who has already won: do not be afraid, take courage, for the outcome is already decided.

sections.heading: 3. Not Afraid of Suffering: Seeing the Blessing Behind It
sections.html:
(1) Suffering is not the exception but the road we must travel

Again and again the Bible reminds us that suffering is not an accident and not an exception; it is the road every believer must travel. Acts records Paul and Barnabas revisiting the newly planted churches, “strengthening the souls of the disciples, exhorting them to continue in the faith, and that through many afflictions we must enter into God’s Kingdom.” (Acts 14:22)

Notice who said this, and in what circumstances. Just a few verses earlier, the people of Lystra, stirred up by the Jews, “stoned Paul, and dragged him out of the city, supposing that he was dead” (Acts 14:19). Here is a man who had just been stoned until everyone thought he had breathed his last. The disciples gathered round him, and he actually got up and went back into the city. The next day he went on to Derbe, preached the gospel there, and then walked back through Lystra, Iconium and Antioch — the very cities that had just tried to kill him — and told the disciples: through many afflictions we must enter into God’s Kingdom.

The word “must” is the Greek dei, which in the New Testament often carries the sense of a “divine necessity” — the same “must” as when the Lord Jesus said that “the Son of Man must suffer many things” (Mark 8:31). This is not the cruelty of fate; it is a necessity within God’s plan of salvation. The road the Lord himself walked, his disciples will walk too.

Brothers and sisters, many Christians see their spiritual life collapse the moment suffering arrives, not because the suffering is so great, but because their mindset was wrong from the start. They assumed, “Once I believe in the Lord, life will be plain sailing.” So when suffering comes, their first reaction is not, “Lord, what do you want me to learn?” but, “God, you lied to me.” Wrong expectations inevitably produce a broken faith. When we fear suffering, circumstances easily swallow us; when we face suffering with courage, God’s power comes upon us.

(2) God made us eagles, not chickens

The lesson uses a lovely picture: God made us to be eagles, not chickens. When the wind gets up, a chicken runs for the coop; when an eagle sees the wind rising, it spreads its wings into it and rides the current higher.

This is not only a metaphor; it is real aerodynamics. The most effortless way for a large bird of prey to fly is called thermal soaring. Because the sun warms the ground unevenly, columns of warm air rise up one after another. The eagle spreads its wings and, barely needing to flap, is carried up round and round within the current to a height of several hundred or even a thousand metres, then glides on to the next thermal. The power that lifts it is not its own strength but the current bearing it up.

Isaiah wrote this very picture into Scripture long ago: “but those who wait for Yahweh will renew their strength. They will mount up with wings like eagles. They will run, and not be weary. They will walk, and not faint.” (Isaiah 40:31) Notice that the verse does not say, “They are very strong in themselves.” It says, “those who wait for Yahweh will renew their strength.” The secret of strength lies in waiting; the power to rise comes from the God who holds us up.

Brothers and sisters, the same gust of wind is a disaster for the chicken and lift for the eagle. The same trial is a blow to those who rely on the brain and on themselves, and a lifting-up to those who rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit. We don’t need to ask God to stop the wind; we need to ask him to teach us to spread our wings.

(3) God says we are lions, not mice

The lesson also says that the Bible calls us lions, not mice. This too has a scriptural basis: “The wicked flee when no one pursues; but the righteous are as bold as a lion.” (Proverbs 28:1) A mouse runs before anyone is even chasing it, because there is fear inside it. A lion does not shrink back from a challenge, because it knows its place and its authority.

Notice that the boldness of the righteous does not come from their own strength but from a right relationship with God. The wicked flee because their conscience is guilty and they have something to hide; the righteous are bold because their sins are forgiven and they are at peace with God. In Christ, our courage does not come from bravado; it comes from the cross.

Science shows that pressure works on living things in just the same way. In 1892 the nineteenth-century German surgeon Julius Wolff (1836–1902) set out what became known as Wolff’s law: bone remodels itself in response to the load placed on it. When the load increases, the bone grows denser and stronger; when the load decreases, bone is lost. In its research on long-duration space missions, NASA has found that in microgravity astronauts’ weight-bearing bones lose on average about one to one and a half per cent of their density each month — not because space is too hard, but because space is too “easy”: there is no weight pressing on the bones.

Brothers and sisters, this gives us a sober reminder: a life without pressure will not make us stronger; it will only make us more brittle. Suffering is not punishment; it is weight training for our spiritual muscles. God does not mean to crush us; he means to make us solid.

(4) Applying the 321 vision: Jesus is the focal point, not our circumstances

The 321 vision teaches us that Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. The deadliest thing about suffering is often not the suffering itself but the way it snatches our focus away from the Lord. As long as Peter, walking on the water, kept his eyes on the Lord, the water held him up; but “when he saw that the wind was strong, he was afraid, and beginning to sink” (Matthew 14:29–30). The wind had not grown any stronger. What changed was his focus.

This is also a change of perspective: from man’s perspective to God’s, from an earthly perspective to a heavenly one, from the temporary to the eternal, from a worldly perspective to a godly one. That is exactly what Paul says: “For our light affliction, which is for the moment, works for us more and more exceedingly an eternal weight of glory, while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.” (2 Corinthians 4:17–18)

Brothers and sisters, the same event, seen from the ground, is crushing affliction; seen from eternity, it is “light affliction, which is for the moment.” Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. This is where the fivefold change that 321 speaks of begins.

sections.heading: 4. Facing Suffering: Finding Strength in Joy
sections.html:
(1) “Count it all joy” is a decision, not an emotion

Suffering is not meant to rob us of our joy; it is meant to teach us to find joy even in hardship. James opens his letter by saying: “Count it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various temptations, knowing that the testing of your faith produces endurance. Let endurance have its perfect work, that you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing.” (James 1:2–4)

There is a key word here. “Count” is the Greek hēgeomai, which originally means “to reckon, regard, calculate, judge.” It is the word a bookkeeper uses when he settles the accounts — a rational assessment, not an emotional impulse. James is not telling us to pretend to be happy. He is telling us to work the sums again: put “the testing of your faith produces endurance” into the column, put “endurance … that you may be perfect and complete” into the column, and when you have added it all up you will find the account comes out in your favour.

Another word is fascinating. “Various” is the Greek poikilos, which originally means “many-coloured, richly varied.” Trials come in every colour: some are the grey of illness, some the black of financial trouble, some the red of broken relationships. And Peter uses the very same word for the grace of God: in “the grace of God in its various forms” (1 Peter 4:10), “various” is again poikilos. Brothers and sisters, there are as many colours of grace as there are colours of trial. God’s grace arrives already colour-matched to the trial.

(2) Joy is a choice of faith and a source of strength

Joy is not an emotional high; it is a choice of faith. When we choose to give thanks in hardship and to praise in pain, joy becomes our strength. The book of Nehemiah records how Ezra read the Book of the Law to the people who had just returned from exile, and as soon as they heard it they wept, because they discovered how far they had strayed from God. Nehemiah said to them: “Don’t be grieved, for the joy of Yahweh is your strength.” (Nehemiah 8:10)

Look closely: it is not “we have strength, so we are joyful”, but “joy becomes our strength.” Joy comes first; strength follows. And the source of this joy is not our circumstances; it is the joy of Yahweh. Happiness that circumstances give will shift as circumstances shift; the joy that Yahweh gives does not.

Psychology offers a fine piece of supporting evidence here. In 1955 the American psychologist Albert Ellis (1913–2007) founded rational emotive behaviour therapy and proposed his well-known ABC model: A is the activating event; B is our belief about and interpretation of that event; C is the emotional and behavioural consequence. Ellis pointed out that most people assume A directly causes C, when in fact what really determines C is B. In other words, it is not events that make us miserable, but the way we see them.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly what 321 says: change the mindset and you change the life. The Bible said this truth earlier and more deeply than psychology. As the Chinese Union Version renders it, “For as he thinks in his heart, so is he.” (Proverbs 23:7)

As for the power of gratitude, there is solid research behind it too. In a study published in 2003 in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, Robert Emmons of the University of California, Davis, and Michael McCullough of the University of Miami randomly divided participants into groups: one group wrote down five things each week they were grateful for, another five things that annoyed them, and a third simply neutral events. After ten weeks, the gratitude group scored markedly higher than the other two on overall well-being and on optimism about the week ahead. Brothers and sisters, gratitude is not just good manners; gratitude changes people.

(3) Suffering is not poison but tonic

The lesson puts it beautifully: suffering is not poison but a tonic — bitter on the tongue, yet able to heal our hearts and make our lives healthier and more mature. The letter to the Hebrews says exactly this: “All chastening seems for the present to be not joyous but grievous; yet afterward it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.” (Hebrews 12:11)

Notice the two expressions of time: “for the present” and “afterward.” For the present it is grievous; afterward it bears fruit. Our problem is often that we live in the “for the present” and forget the “afterward.” Faith is believing in the fruit of afterward while still in the grief of the present.

The psalmist’s testimony is even more direct: “Before I was afflicted, I went astray; but now I observe your word.” “It is good for me that I have been afflicted, that I may learn your statutes.” (Psalm 119:67, 71) Brothers and sisters, have you noticed? This psalmist doesn’t say, “After I suffered, God made it up to me.” He says that the suffering itself was good for him.

If we learn to take suffering in as our food, we will experience God’s presence and comfort within it. In the wilderness the Israelites ate manna, bread from heaven; they also ate bitter herbs, a dish that had to be on the Passover table (Exodus 12:8). The bitter herbs were eaten together with the lamb, because remembering the night of redemption was never meant to be sweet.

sections.heading: 5. Overcoming Suffering: Turned into a Testimony of Blessing
sections.html:
(1) Only looking back do we see God’s hand

When we look back on the suffering behind us, we are often amazed to find that the moments that once made us weep were the very openings God was preparing for our breakthrough. In the middle of his long debate, Job made this declaration of faith: “But he knows the way that I take. When he has tried me, I will come out like gold.” (Job 23:10)

The picture of gold matters. The refiner puts the ore into a crucible and melts it at great heat; the dross that floats to the top is skimmed off, and what remains is pure gold. How did refiners of old know the fire had done its work? It is said they waited until they could see their own face on the surface of the molten metal. Brothers and sisters, God puts us in the fire not to burn us up, but to see his own image in us.

So suffering often becomes three things. First, suffering is a “door of revelation” that lets us know him better — in the end Job said, “I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you.” (Job 42:5) Second, suffering is a “road to breakthrough” by which we gain new life — “we also rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces perseverance; and perseverance, proven character; and proven character, hope: and hope doesn’t disappoint us, because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us.” (Romans 5:3–5) Third, suffering is a “bridge of blessing” that makes us comforters of others.

(2) Only those who have been comforted can comfort others

Paul puts it this way: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort; who comforts us in all our affliction, that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction, through the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God.” (2 Corinthians 1:3–4)

“Comfort” is the Greek paraklēsis; the verb is parakaleō, which literally means “to be called alongside.” It shares a root with the word the Lord Jesus used for the Holy Spirit, “Counselor” (paraklētos, John 14:16). So God’s comfort is not a quick “Hang in there!” but a Person who comes alongside you. He does not shout encouragement from a distance; he walks over to you and sits with you in the ashes.

Notice how this verse is built: God comforts us “that” we may be able to comfort others. That little word “that” tells us the purpose of God’s comfort. Comfort is not the destination; it is a relay station. God puts comfort in your hands so that you will pass it on. If we only receive comfort and never pass it along, it becomes like the water of the Dead Sea — always flowing in, never flowing out, until at last it turns salt and dead.

In the same farewell discourse, the Lord Jesus himself used the picture of a mother giving birth: “A woman, when she gives birth, has sorrow because her time has come. But when she has delivered the child, she doesn’t remember the anguish any more, for the joy that a human being is born into the world.” (John 16:21) This verse sits just a little before our theme verse. A mother goes through the pain of labour to bring new life into the world; the Lord Jesus went through the suffering of the cross to accomplish salvation for all humankind. In the same way, our wounds, placed in God’s hands, can become healing for others.

(3) What psychology has seen: there can be growth after trauma

In 1995 the psychologists Richard Tedeschi and Lawrence Calhoun of the University of North Carolina at Charlotte introduced the concept of “posttraumatic growth”, and in 1996 they published the Posttraumatic Growth Inventory. In long-term follow-up research they found that many people who had been through major trauma reported, alongside the pain, positive growth in five areas: deeper relationships with others, seeing new possibilities in life, an awareness of inner strength, spiritual change, and a deeper appreciation of life itself.

Please note that these scholars never said trauma is a good thing, nor that everyone will grow. They simply observed, honestly, that after being shaken a person may grow something that wasn’t there before. This can echo what the Bible reveals, but it cannot replace the Bible — for what the Bible tells us is not merely that “people may grow”, but that “God will surely be at work”: “We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, for those who are called according to his purpose.” (Romans 8:28)

Further, in 1965 the sociologist Frank Riessman put forward the “helper therapy principle”, observing that in mutual-help groups the people who give help often benefit more than those who receive it. Brothers and sisters, this is God’s economy: when you give comfort away, you yourself are healed first.

(4) Applying the 321 vision: life first, then relationships, then ministry

The 321 vision says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. The lessons of suffering run in exactly that order.

The first step is life: in suffering God first deals with my self-centred life. The trouble with the old self is that it is self-centred — I want control, I want to save face, I want things done my way. What suffering does best is show us that we can control nothing at all, and then invite the “self” to step down from the throne.

The second step is relationships: when the “self” steps down and selflessness rises up, relationships are restored. 321 teaches that the priority of relationships is first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. Suffering is often the tool God uses to rearrange that order. Ordinarily we put things first; when suffering comes, everything stops, and God at last has a chance to talk with us about himself.

Only the third step is ministry: once our life is right and our relationships are right, a ministry of comforting others flows out naturally. So please don’t rush to serve others out of a wound that is still bleeding. Let the Lord heal you first, then let him use you. God never wastes a single tear — but he is never in a hurry either.

This is the 920 practice too: everyone we are in relationship with is our “2”; we practise living out the selfless life of the “0” and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions — “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23). Brothers and sisters, look at these nine graces: which of them grows in easy times? Patience needs something to be patient with; gentleness needs someone who provokes us; self-control needs something to crave. The fruit of the Spirit grows mostly in the soil of suffering.

sections.heading: 6. Learning from Paul: Change the Mindset and the Life Changes
sections.html:
(1) The thorn he asked the Lord three times to remove

Paul was a servant who went through countless sufferings. He drew up a list himself: imprisonments, beatings, near-death, stoning, shipwreck, perils of rivers, perils of robbers, perils among false brothers, sleeplessness, hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness (2 Corinthians 11:23–27). Yet what troubled him most was a “thorn.”

“By reason of the exceeding greatness of the revelations, that I should not be exalted excessively, a thorn in the flesh was given to me: a messenger of Satan to torment me, that I should not be exalted excessively. Concerning this thing, I begged the Lord three times that it might depart from me. He has said to me, ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.’” (2 Corinthians 12:7–9)

Second Corinthians was written around AD 55–56. It is Paul’s second surviving letter to the church in Corinth, written while he was in Macedonia, grieved because some in the Corinthian church were questioning his apostleship. In this letter he is forced to “boast”, yet he chooses to boast of his weaknesses.
