“Thorn” is the Greek skolops — not a fine needle-like thorn but a “stake, a pointed post.” Interpreters through the centuries have guessed at what it was — an eye disease, malaria, epilepsy, the enemies who persecuted him — but the Holy Spirit deliberately left it unsaid. I think that is God’s grace: because it is not specified, everyone who has a thorn can find themselves in this passage.

Pay special attention to two phrases here. The first: “a messenger of Satan to torment me.” The second: “that I should not be exalted excessively.” With the same thorn, Satan’s purpose was to attack him; God’s purpose was to keep him. Satan meant to destroy Paul with this thorn; God used it to preserve him. Brothers and sisters, this is the truth of spiritual warfare: every weapon Satan hands us, God can turn around and make into a vessel. Joseph said it best: “As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to save many people alive, as is happening today.” (Genesis 50:20)

There is one more detail: Paul says, “I begged the Lord three times.” In the Garden of Gethsemane the Lord Jesus also prayed three times (Matthew 26:44). Asking three times, and then yielding — this is not giving up; this is maturity.

(2) God did not change the circumstances, but he changed the man

The Lord’s answer was: “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” (2 Corinthians 12:9)

“Is sufficient” is the Greek arkei, in the present tense, describing an ongoing state — not “will be enough” but “is always enough.” Grace is not a deposit you draw out all at once; it is manna supplied fresh each day. “Is made perfect” is the Greek teleitai, a passive, meaning “is brought to completion, reaches its goal.” For God’s power to reach its full goal, it needs a vessel — and that vessel is human weakness.

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully: Paul’s suffering did not change. The thorn was never pulled out. What changed was Paul’s mindset. He understood one thing: God may not change our circumstances, but he means to change us through them.

When the mindset changes, the feelings change with it. Paul stopped complaining, and instead he said: “Most gladly therefore I will rather glory in my weaknesses, that the power of Christ may rest on me. Therefore I take pleasure in weaknesses, in injuries, in necessities, in persecutions, and in distresses, for Christ’s sake. For when I am weak, then am I strong.” (2 Corinthians 12:9–10)

The word “rest on” is the Greek episkēnoō, literally “to pitch a tent over”, which calls to mind the glory of the Old Testament tabernacle resting upon the tent. Paul means: my weakness has become an open patch of ground, and Christ pitches his tent on that open ground. Brothers and sisters, if there is not one open patch anywhere in us, where will the Lord’s glory rest?

The Austrian psychiatrist Viktor Frankl (1905–1997), founder of logotherapy, lost his parents, his wife and his brother in the Nazi concentration camps, and after the war wrote Man’s Search for Meaning (published 1946). In it he observed that everything a person has can be taken away except one thing: the freedom to choose one’s attitude in any set of circumstances. Brothers and sisters, this scholar, who was not a believer, saw half the truth from the human side; the Bible gives us the whole truth: we not only have the freedom to choose our attitude, we also have a Lord who gives us strength.

(3) The secret for every situation

In the end Paul learned a spiritual balance. From prison in Rome he wrote to the church in Philippi: “Not that I speak because of lack, for I have learned in whatever state I am, to be content in it. I know how to be humbled, and I also know how to abound. In everything and in all things I have learned the secret both to be filled and to be hungry, both to abound and to be in need. I can do all things through Christ, who strengthens me.” (Philippians 4:11–13)

Philippians was written around AD 61–62, while Paul was under house arrest in Rome. A man in chains wrote a letter known as “the epistle of joy”, in which the word “joy” appears more than ten times. That in itself is the most powerful sermon of all.

Two words here deserve notice. “I have learned” is the Greek emathon, learning that comes from experience. “I have learned the secret” is the Greek memuēmai, a word originally used for initiation into the ancient mystery religions, meaning “I have been brought into this mystery.” In other words, contentment is not an inborn temperament but a lesson learned; balance is not the instinct of clever people but a secret into which the Lord leads us step by step.

Notice especially that many people who quote Philippians 4:13 remember only “I can do all things” and forget the context. Paul says it not about achieving great things but about learning contentment; he is not teaching a gospel of success but how to stand firm whether full or hungry. So what this verse really means is this: through the Lord who strengthens me, I can face even want.

The point is not whether “ease is good” or “suffering is good”, but whether in every situation we can keep from grumbling and from pride, and go on leaning on God. Not proud in good times, not grumbling in hard times — that is spiritual maturity.

After many years of research, the Stanford University psychologist Carol Dweck in 2006 set out the distinction between a “fixed mindset” and a “growth mindset”: people with a fixed mindset take difficulty as a verdict on their ability; people with a growth mindset take difficulty as an opportunity to learn. Faced with the same failure, the first says, “I can’t do it”; the second says, “I haven’t learned it yet.” Brothers and sisters, this helps us understand Paul — he did not change his circumstances; he changed his outlook. More precisely, he changed his mindset, and his mindset was renewed by the word of God.

sections.heading: 7. Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
Let’s set today’s message within the 321 framework and look at it once more.

The Three Foundations. Jesus is my role model — he obeyed in suffering: he “learned obedience by the things which he suffered” (Hebrews 5:8). The Bible is my standard — what decides how I see suffering is not my feelings, nor what others say, but the word of God. The Holy Spirit is my guide — the Counselor has been called to our side, to comfort us and lead us himself in our troubles.

The Two Core Values. Let Jesus be King — in suffering the hardest thing of all is to let him reign as King, and not let myself be king. Let Jesus receive all the glory — we do not suffer to win other people’s sympathy, but so that his name may be glorified.

The Goal: establish God’s system. Through suffering, God refines self-centred people, one by one, into members of the body who can uphold and comfort one another, and so establishes God’s system.

From the self-centred life to selflessness. Brothers and sisters, the deepest lesson of suffering is dealing with the self-centred life. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of every problem. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God. When in suffering we say to God, “Why me?”, there is a hidden sentence inside it: “I don’t think I deserve this.” That is the “self” talking. When we change our words to, “Lord, what do you want me to learn?”, that is the “self” beginning to give way.

Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. In suffering, friction between people is often at its worst, because everyone is hurting. Whoever humbles himself first is the first to overcome. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out. “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me — “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. The thorn was a messenger of Satan, but Paul, with a selfless attitude, boasted of his weaknesses, and Satan’s attack became instead an occasion for the power of Christ to rest on him.

The fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Paul’s testimony is a complete road of fivefold change. His mindset changed — from “Lord, take it away” to “Most gladly I will rather glory in my weaknesses.” His life changed — he found strength in weakness. His daily living changed — he learned the secret whether full or hungry. His relationships changed — he no longer needed people’s praise to prove himself. His ministry changed — he comforted those in any affliction with the comfort he had received from God. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living.

A change of perspective: from man’s to God’s, from earthly to heavenly, from temporary to eternal, from worldly to godly. The same thorn, seen from man’s perspective, is a disaster; from God’s perspective, it is protection. From an earthly perspective it is a loss; from a heavenly perspective it is a deposit. From a temporary perspective it is crushing affliction; from an eternal perspective it is “light affliction, which is for the moment.”

The 235 relationships: in suffering, no one can walk the whole distance alone. Become a “2” with a selfless person, spiritual companions who uphold each other; build the “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children, so that those who have walked the road lead those who have not; and go on to become a “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades, fighting together and overcoming together. Brothers and sisters, when Moses held up his hand, Israel prevailed; when Moses’ hands grew heavy, Aaron and Hur held up his hands, one on each side (Exodus 17:11–12). Where is your “2”? Who is holding up your hands? And whose hands are you holding up?

Finally, rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves. Rely on the brain and you worry; rely on the heart and you rejoice. What wears us out most in suffering is often not the situation itself but our minds endlessly working it through, calculating, imagining what if. “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23)

sections.heading: 8. Putting It into Practice
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. We will place them within the eight stages of changing our mindset and walk through them step by step: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice 1: In your present difficulty, write down three things you can thank God for, and praise him for them

Information: first put today’s truth into your head — suffering is a road we must travel; it is a tonic, not a poison; it is God’s tool for changing me. Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to carry this truth from your head into your heart, so that you truly see God’s hand in your own situation. Conviction: say to God, “I believe this is true, even though I can’t feel it yet.” Implementation: today, take pen and paper and write down three things — and be specific. Don’t write, “Thank God that he loves me”; write, “Thank God that so-and-so sent me a message today.” Evaluation: look at it again in the evening and ask yourself whether you wrote it from the heart or just to get it done. Correction: if it was just to get it done, rewrite it tomorrow from a different angle. Repetition: thirty days in a row, three things a day, no repeats. Multiplication: after thirty days, invite a brother or sister to do it with you, and pass the practice on.

The 2003 study by Emmons and McCullough mentioned earlier used exactly this method: participants recorded things they were grateful for each week, and after ten weeks their well-being and optimism had risen markedly. God’s word said it first; science confirmed it later.

Practice 2: In suffering, don’t rush to ask for escape; first ask to understand what God wants you to learn

Information: remember that Paul asked the Lord three times to remove the thorn, and the Lord did not remove it, but gave him something better — grace and power. Revelation: ask God to shine his light on you, so that you see what this suffering is really meant to deal with — is it pride? insecurity? reliance on money? fear of people? Conviction: accept one fact — God loves me, and he makes no mistakes. Implementation: change your prayer from “Lord, please take this away quickly” to “Lord, please take this away; but if you don’t, teach me to know you right here.” Evaluation: a week later, look back and see whether your heart is more at peace or more anxious. Correction: if more anxious, you have most likely put your focus back on your circumstances; turn your focus back to Jesus. Repetition: keep at it until you can say, “When I am weak, then am I strong.” Multiplication: write up what you have learned through this as a short testimony, ready to share at any time.

Practice 3: Find a brother or sister who is suffering, share your own experience, and support them with prayer and comfort

Information: understand that God comforts us so that we can comfort others (2 Corinthians 1:4). Revelation: ask God to put a name on your heart — someone who is suffering right now. Conviction: believe that the road you have walked was not walked in vain, and that your wounds are of use. Implementation: this week, reach out to them. Don’t rush to give answers; first sit with them. Then tell them about a stretch of road you yourself have walked. Finally, pray for them. Evaluation: after you have talked, ask yourself — was I comforting them, or talking about myself? Correction: next time, say half as much and listen twice as much. Repetition: let this kind of companionship become a settled habit, not a one-off visit. Multiplication: once they have been comforted, encourage them to go and comfort someone else — this is the “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children, and it is how God’s comfort circulates through the church.

Brothers and sisters, remember the lesson’s gentle reminder: God may not remove our suffering, but he will surely be with us. When we are willing to meet the storm with faith, he will turn the storm into the current that lifts us. “When you pass through the waters, I will be with you, and through the rivers, they will not overflow you. When you walk through the fire, you will not be burned, and flame will not scorch you.” (Isaiah 43:2) God has not promised that the waters won’t come or that the fire won’t burn. What he has promised is, “I will be with you.”

sections.heading: 9. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, suffering is the touchstone of faith and the seedbed of grace. God does not let us go around suffering; he takes us through it, so that we may become strong overcomers.

Notice the word “through.” Psalm 23 says: “Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me. Your rod and your staff, they comfort me.” (Psalm 23:4) It is “walk through”, not “live in.” The valley is a road, not a home. God has never promised us a road without valleys; what he has promised is that in the valley he walks with us.

When we stop asking, “Why is there suffering?” and start asking, “Lord, what do you want me to learn?”, in that moment our life begins to mature. To ask “why” is to put ourselves on the judgement seat and sit in judgement on God; to ask “what do you want me to learn” is to take the place of a student and let God be King. The difference between those two questions is the difference between the self-centred life and selflessness.

So this morning I want to issue you three calls.

First, let Jesus be King in your suffering. Take the difficulty you have never been willing to hand over, and today put it in his hands. Not into the hands of fate, but into the hands of the Lord who has already overcome the world.

Second, let Jesus receive the glory from your suffering. One day, when someone asks you, “How did you get through it?”, may your answer not be, “I’m very strong,” but, “His grace was sufficient for me.”

Third, let your suffering become a bridge for others. Not one ounce of the pain God has spent on you is wasted. He is training a comforter who can comfort others.

May we all, like Paul, whether in suffering or in ease, draw our strength from Christ and give the glory to God. For our Lord has already said: “In the world you have trouble; but cheer up! I have overcome the world.” (John 16:33) Brothers and sisters, he has already overcome. We are following a Lord who has won.

keyVerses: “I have told you these things, that in me you may have peace. In the world you have trouble; but cheer up! I have overcome the world.” (John 16:33)
practices: In your present difficulty, write down three things to thank God for, and praise him for them
In suffering, don’t rush to ask for escape; first ask what God wants you to learn
Find a brother or sister who is suffering, share your experience, and support them with prayer and comfort
prayer: Lord, I am still before you.
I confess that I don’t like suffering, and my first reaction is often to run. Forgive me for measuring your plans with a self-centred heart, and forgive me for questioning your goodness in my pain.

Lord, I will no longer be afraid of suffering, because your grace is sufficient for me. Teach me to see your hand in hardship, to hear your voice in pain, and to experience your power in weakness. Turn my focus from my circumstances to you, and turn my perspective from earth to heaven, from the temporary to the eternal.

Make me an eagle, not a chicken; a lion, not a mouse. Let me rejoice even in my sufferings, knowing that suffering produces perseverance, and perseverance, proven character, and proven character, hope.
Lord, place the comfort you have given me in my hands, and make me a comforter of others. I am willing to let you be King in my suffering; I am willing to let you receive all the glory.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Discussion 1: “Through many afflictions we must enter into God’s Kingdom.” (Acts 14:22) Think back to a major time of suffering in your life. Was the question in your heart then, “Why me?” or, “Lord, what do you want me to learn?” If you could go through it again today, what would you ask? How would that change of question have changed the way you responded?

Discussion 2: “who comforts us in all our affliction, that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction, through the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God.” (2 Corinthians 1:4) What kind of comfort have you received from God? Is there someone near you right now who needs that very comfort? What is one concrete thing you could do for them this week?

sections.heading: Introduction: A War Without a Shot Fired
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. For this morning’s devotion, I’d like you first to sketch a picture in your heart.

A bride and groom stand at the front of the hall. A hymn is being sung, candles are burning, family and friends are smiling. The pastor asks, “Will you love her, honour her, comfort her and keep her, in sickness and in health, in riches and in poverty, for as long as you both shall live?” The groom says, “I will.” That is not just a sentence; it is a covenant.

Yet ten or twenty years later, why is it that with the very same vows, some couples grow grey together and never tire of each other, while in other homes the two live like silent islands, or even tear the covenant in two and leave it on a lawyer’s desk?

Brothers and sisters, marriage has never been a romantic holiday. Marriage is a war in which no shot is fired. You hear no gunfire and see no smoke, but the front line runs across your dining table, through your bedroom, over your phone screen — and through the mindsets in your head that you assume are “just the way things are.”

Why does Satan target marriage so deliberately? He knows that humanity’s first social unit was not the nation and not the church, but the family; the first institution God established in the Garden of Eden was marriage. If the family is destroyed, the foundation of the church is loosened, the foundation of the nation crumbles, and the values of the next generation are rewritten wholesale. So he doesn’t need to attack the church building; he only needs to break into marriages. He doesn’t need to overthrow doctrine; he only needs to swap out mindsets.

Notice Satan’s method. In the Garden of Eden he brought no knife and no fire; he asked just one question: “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden’?” (Genesis 3:1) His weapon was a question; his battlefield was the human mindset. From ancient times until now, Satan’s method has never changed — first he changes your mindset, then your life, your daily living, your relationships, and in the end he wrecks your ministry.

This is exactly where the first core truth of 321 lies: change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. It is a ladder leading up to heaven — and it can just as easily be a slide leading down. The watershed that decides the direction is the mindset.

Today’s lesson is called “An Important Mindset — Satan’s View of Marriage.” Please don’t skim past the word “important.” Once a mindset has been swapped, we don’t even know it. A computer infected with a virus still looks fine on the screen; a heart infected with lies still looks fine in daily living. Until one day the system crashes, the family falls apart, and only then do we wake up with a start: all along I have been running on an operating system that was not God’s.

More sobering still, these mindsets no longer circulate only in the world; they are quietly seeping into the church. How many young Christians today go to small group and live with a partner at the same time? How many couples serve in the church while privately calculating that “getting divorced wouldn’t be such a big deal”? Satan doesn’t need you to deny Jesus; he only needs you to listen to him about marriage.

So this morning we are going to take apart, one by one, the five lies Satan has let loose, and see them clearly. Not in order to judge the world, but in order to guard our own hearts. For the Bible says: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23)

We will label these five lies with five words: many, food, commodity, animal, same-sex. They correspond to five distorted forms of marriage: plural marriage, trial marriage, divorce, promiscuous unions and twisted marriage. And at the end we will see that these five poisonous roots all grow out of the same soil — a soil called “self-centredness.”

sections.heading: Scripture Background: The First Institution in Eden
sections.html: To recognise the false, you first have to know the true. When banks train staff to detect counterfeit notes, they don’t have them study forgeries all day; they have them handle genuine notes until they know them by touch. So before we take the five lies apart, we must first go back to God’s original blueprint for marriage.

sections.heading: 1. Genesis: Its Author, Its Readers, Its Setting
sections.html:
According to Jewish tradition and the testimony of the Lord Jesus himself, the author of Genesis is Moses. Its first readers were the people of Israel after the Exodus, making their way through the wilderness towards the land of Canaan. These people had only just come out of four hundred years of slavery in Egypt, and their heads were full of the Egyptian worldview. The land of Canaan they were about to enter was saturated with the fertility cults of Baal and Ashtoreth, where temple prostitution, incest and human sacrifice were commonplace.

The setting in which Moses wrote Genesis is very like our own today: behind us, the bondage of old mindsets; ahead of us, the beckoning of new temptations. God wanted to tell his people: don’t look at the world through Egyptian eyes, and don’t look at marriage through Canaanite eyes; look with the eyes of the beginning, with the eyes of the Creator.

sections.heading: 2. Marriage in the Ancient Near East vs. Marriage in the Bible
sections.html:
In the ancient Near East, marriage was largely a property arrangement between two families: a woman was often treated as a tradeable asset, polygamy was a symbol of power, and divorcing a wife was the husband’s one-sided right. In soil like that, the account in Genesis 2 is nothing short of earth-shaking:

“Yahweh God said, ‘It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make him a helper comparable to him.’” (Genesis 2:18)

“A helper comparable to him” is in Hebrew ezer kenegdo. In the Old Testament ezer is most often used of God himself as the helper of his people; it never means “an inferior servant.” The root of kenegdo carries the sense of “corresponding to, equal to, face to face.” What God prepared for Adam was a partner suited to him, standing face to face with him, the two upholding each other.

“Yahweh God made a woman from the rib which he had taken from the man, and brought her to the man.” (Genesis 2:22) God did not use a bone from Adam’s head, lest she be above him; nor a bone from his foot, lest she be beneath him. God took a rib — close to the heart, under the protection of the arm. The moment Adam saw her, he broke into the first love poem in human history: “This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh. She will be called ‘woman,’ because she was taken out of Man.” (Genesis 2:23)

sections.heading: 3. Genesis 2:24: The Three Pillars of Marriage
sections.html:
Next comes our theme verse for today: “Therefore a man will leave his father and his mother, and will join with his wife, and they will be one flesh.” (Genesis 2:24)

This one short verse sets up the three pillars of marriage. First, “leave” — Hebrew azav, meaning to depart decisively, to break away from former attachments. Marriage requires a person to reorder their emotions and responsibilities: the authority of parents steps back, and the covenant between husband and wife takes first place. In an ancient society built around the clan, what a radical declaration that was.

Second, “join” — Hebrew dabaq, to stick fast, to cling, to refuse to let go. The same word is used in Deuteronomy 10:20: “You shall fear Yahweh your God. You shall serve him. You shall cling to him.” That “cling” is dabaq. In other words, the bond between husband and wife is described as a loyalty like a person clinging tightly to God. Marriage is a covenant, not a contract. A contract says, “I’ll do my part if you do yours”; a covenant says, “Whatever you do, I will keep my word.”

Third, “they will be one flesh” — two, not three; becoming one, not walking side by side for a while. This is a union of the whole person: one in body, mind, spirit and life direction.

So the marriage God established was, from the very first day: one man and one woman, one husband and one wife, for one lifetime. Every lie Satan has released since then tampers with these three lines — plural marriage attacks “two”, trial marriage attacks “join”, divorce attacks “become one”, promiscuous unions attack the holiness of “one flesh”, and twisted marriage attacks the very foundation of “male and female he created them.”

sections.heading: 4. How the Lord Jesus Quoted This Verse
sections.html:
One day the Pharisees came to test Jesus, asking him whether a man may divorce his wife for any reason. At the time there were two main rabbinic schools: the school of Shammai held that only serious unfaithfulness justified divorce, while the school of Hillel was so lenient that a wife burning the dinner was grounds enough. The Pharisees wanted to drag Jesus into this war of words.

How brilliant Jesus’ answer was. He took neither school’s side; he pushed the question back to creation: “Haven’t you read that he who made them from the beginning made them male and female, and said, ‘For this cause a man shall leave his father and mother, and shall be joined to his wife; and the two shall become one flesh?’” (Matthew 19:4–5) Then he added a stunning conclusion: “So that they are no more two, but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, don’t let man tear apart.” (Matthew 19:6)

The Pharisees were not satisfied, and asked again: “Why then did Moses command us to give her a certificate of divorce, and divorce her?” Jesus said: “Moses, because of the hardness of your hearts, allowed you to divorce your wives, but from the beginning it has not been so.” (Matthew 19:8)

Brothers and sisters, please remember these words of the Lord: “but from the beginning it has not been so.” Whenever marriage is discussed, the Lord Jesus’ point of reference is never “what everyone does now” but “how God made it in the beginning.” This is the change of perspective 321 speaks of: from man’s perspective to God’s, from passing trends to eternal standards, from worldly common sense to godly truth.

We have handled the genuine note. Now let’s look at the five counterfeit notes Satan has printed.

sections.heading: 1. Many: The Trap of Plural Marriage
sections.html:
Satan’s first lie is: “The more people, the more blessing.” He makes people think that quantity is happiness.

In ancient times this lie wore the clothes of “many wives and concubines”; today it wears the clothes of “multiple partners” and “open relationships.” The clothes have changed; the lie inside is exactly the same.

What the Bible says

The Bible gives us the most splendid and most tragic case of all — King Solomon.

“He had seven hundred wives, princesses, and three hundred concubines. His wives turned his heart away. When Solomon was old, his wives turned away his heart after other gods; and his heart was not perfect with Yahweh his God, as the heart of David his father was.” (1 Kings 11:3–4)

Notice the wording of the text: “turned his heart away.” The original, natah, means “to cause to turn aside, to tilt.” This was not a fall that happened overnight; it was a drift of one degree after another. Think of a ship whose heading is off by just one degree: at first you can hardly tell, but after a thousand kilometres it is more than ten kilometres from its destination. Solomon did not decide one day out of the blue to worship Molech; he drifted from God amid the whispers of a thousand pillow companions.

And the outcome? “Therefore Yahweh said to Solomon, ‘Because this is done by you, and you have not kept my covenant and my statutes, which I have commanded you, I will surely tear the kingdom from you, and will give it to your servant.’” (1 Kings 11:11) As a result the kingdom of Israel split, north facing south, and in the end both kingdoms fell. One man’s view of marriage cost a nation more than three hundred years of its history.

Sadder still, God had warned of this long before: “He shall not multiply wives to himself, that his heart not turn away.” (Deuteronomy 17:17) Solomon was the wisest man who ever lived; he must have read this verse. Which shows that knowing the truth and obeying the truth are two different things.

Scripture interpreting Scripture

Someone will ask: doesn’t the Old Testament have many examples of men with more than one wife? Abraham, Jacob, David — didn’t God use them all?

We need to make a distinction: the Bible recording something is not the same as the Bible approving it. Notice that wherever the Bible records a man taking several wives, suffering follows hard on its heels. When Abraham added Hagar, his household added weeping. When Jacob married two sisters, his house filled with jealousy and rivalry, and twelve sons turned on one another. When David multiplied wives and concubines, his house saw Amnon’s rape and Absalom’s rebellion. With the most unflinching realism the Bible tells us: plural marriage does not mean multiplied blessing; it means multiplied trouble, multiplied pain, multiplied strife.

So Paul puts it with perfect clarity: “But, because of sexual immoralities, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband.” (1 Corinthians 7:2) “His own” — one husband and one wife, back to the beginning.

Everyday illustration and research

Sheena Iyengar of Columbia University and Mark Lepper of Stanford University published a famous experiment in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology in 2000. They set up a jam-tasting stall in a supermarket, one time offering twenty-four flavours, another time only six. The stall with twenty-four flavours drew more people to stop, but in the end only three per cent actually bought anything; at the stall with six flavours, the purchase rate was as high as thirty per cent.

In The Paradox of Choice (2004), the psychologist Barry Schwartz summed up the phenomenon in one line: the more options, the deeper the anxiety and the shallower the satisfaction.

If that is true of jam, how much more of people? When someone keeps several options open in their heart at once, they can never give their heart away whole. The body may be here, but the heart is always calculating somewhere else. That is the truth about plural marriage: it is not gaining several portions of love; it is cutting one love into fragments, each one too thin to nourish anybody.

The 321 insight

Behind plural marriage lies the self-centred life — the never-satisfied self of the old self: I want more, I want better. 321 puts it penetratingly: the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of every problem. Plural marriage treats a spouse as a resource to satisfy oneself and puts “me” on the throne of the marriage.

God’s way is selflessness. When someone lays down “I want more” and gives themselves wholeheartedly to one person and to God, they discover a depth that “more” can never give. One well a hundred metres deep beats a hundred pits one metre deep. Only single-mindedness digs down to living water.

So the conclusion of the first point is this: true blessing lies not in how many people we possess, but in living faithfully and as one, within God’s will.

sections.heading: 2. Food: The Deception of Trial Marriage
sections.html:
Satan’s second lie is: “How will you know if you’re compatible unless you try it first?”

How practical that sounds. You try shoes on before you buy them; you test-drive a car before you buy it. Surely something as big as marriage deserves a trial run first? And so “trial marriage” and living together have become the norm; many people even think that marrying without living together first is the irresponsible thing to do.

Where the lie gives itself away: treating people as food

Notice the core image of this lie — “try.” What do you “try”? You try a sample, try something on, try something out. The words that follow these verbs are all things, not people.

But the Bible says that man “became a living soul” (Genesis 2:7). A person is not merchandise you can return, not a free sample you can spit out. When you say, “Let’s try it first,” in your heart you have already demoted the other person to a dish on the table.

More crucially still: the essence of marriage is covenant, and the essence of covenant is “commit first, then come to know”, not “know first, then commit.”

When the Israelites at the foot of Mount Sinai said, “All that Yahweh has spoken we will do” (Exodus 19:8), they had not yet read the whole Law. When Christ died for us, we were still sinners (Romans 5:8). The logic of covenant love has always been: I give myself to you first, and then together we walk into the unknown.

The logic of “trying” is the exact opposite: I make sure it’s safe first, and only then do I give myself to you. A relationship like that has an emergency exit built in from day one — and a relationship you can walk out of at any moment will never give anyone a sense of security.

What the research says

In a study published in 2006 in the journal Family Relations, Scott Stanley and Galena Rhoades of the University of Denver proposed the concept of “sliding versus deciding.” They found that many cohabiting couples did not solemnly “decide” one day to be together; they “slid” into it — first staying over often, then a toothbrush left at the other’s place, then splitting the rent, then moving out seemed too much hassle, and then they got married. Only when real conflict came did they discover that what bound them together was not commitment but merely inertia and cost.

This is the biggest difference between “covenant” and “trial”: a covenant is a public, solemn decision made before witnesses; trial marriage is just a string of unthinking slides.

Everyday illustration

A wedding ring is like a climbing rope that ties two people together. If you carry a rope in your pack for abseiling down at any moment, you’ll most likely retreat when fog rolls in halfway up; if two people are tied to the same rope, there is only one option left — to climb on up together. In 1943, in a wedding sermon written from prison for his niece, Dietrich Bonhoeffer wrote a famous line: “It is not your love that sustains the marriage, but from now on, the marriage that sustains your love.” Brothers and sisters, that sentence is worth copying down. Feelings rise and fall, but the covenant holds the feelings up.

That is why the Bible says: “Let marriage be held in honor among all, and let the bed be undefiled; but God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterers.” (Hebrews 13:4)

The 321 insight

321 has a saying: life first, then relationships, then ministry. And the priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things.

People who try out marriage turn that order completely upside down. They want the “things” first — to confirm whether it fits, whether it’s convenient. They skip their relationship with God, skip dealing with their own life, and go straight to managing a relationship with another person. They’re in a hurry to build the first floor before laying the foundation.

Real preparation means first letting Jesus be King in your life. A person who has not yet let Jesus reign as King will certainly want to be king in their marriage; and when two people who both want to be king live under one roof, that isn’t called a home — it’s called a battlefield.

So the conclusion of the second point is this: true love is not “let’s give it a try” but “I am willing to commit.”

sections.heading: 3. Commodity: The Tide of Divorce
sections.html:
Satan’s third lie is: “New is better than old.”

This lie is the child of consumerism. We live in an age of “when it’s old, replace it.” Once that way of thinking creeps into marriage, a spouse becomes a commodity — “upgrading” replaces repairing, “swapping” replaces winning back. And so divorce becomes routine, and marriage loses the dignity of covenant.

What the Bible says

As the Chinese Union Version renders it: “‘I hate divorce, and the one who treats his wife with violence!’ says Yahweh, the God of Israel. ‘Therefore pay attention to your spirit, that you don’t be unfaithful,’ says Yahweh of Armies.” (Malachi 2:16)

The Israelites of that day were offering sacrifices in the temple while divorcing “the wife of their youth” to marry foreign women. They wept as they offered their sacrifices, yet could not understand why God would not accept them. The prophet said: “Yahweh has been witness between you and the wife of your youth, against whom you have dealt treacherously, though she is your companion, and the wife of your covenant.” (Malachi 2:14)

“The wife of your covenant” — the original word is berit, the very word used for the covenant God made with Abraham. God himself stands as witness to this covenant; so divorce is never just a matter between two people. It is tearing up a covenant to which God is the witness.

Scripture interpreting Scripture: “The old is better”

“No man having drunk old wine immediately desires new, for he says, ‘The old is better.’” (Luke 5:39)

There the Lord was speaking of the transition from the old covenant to the new, but the everyday observation itself is true: in human relationships, “the old” often really is better than “the new.” New friends are fresh; old friends are trustworthy. People who have weathered storms together know each other with a knowledge that time has tested.

That is all the more true of husband and wife. A new relationship looks better not because that person is better, but because you haven’t yet seen their faults. The greatest illusion in marriage is to think that if you change partners, the problems will disappear. But the problem isn’t in that person; the problem is the untouched “self” inside both of you.

So the Bible’s prescription is not to “swap” but to “change”: “that you put away, as concerning your former way of life, the old man that grows corrupt after the lusts of deceit, and that you be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who in the likeness of God has been created in righteousness and holiness of truth.” (Ephesians 4:22–24)

What God wants is not to swap a person but to change a person. And the person who needs to change is, more often than not, not the other one — it’s you.

Research and illustration

Psychology has a term called “hedonic adaptation”, also known as the “hedonic treadmill.” A study by Brickman, Coates and Janoff-Bulman, published in 1978 in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, found that after a brief thrill, lottery jackpot winners were not noticeably happier in everyday life than a control group. We adapt to any “new” stimulus. A new house becomes an old house after three months; a new car becomes an old car after six. If what you are chasing is “new”, you have stepped onto a treadmill that never stops — running until you’re out of breath, without moving a single step.

On the other side, the Harvard Study of Adult Development, begun in 1938 and now running for more than eighty years, has followed the health and happiness of several hundred men across their whole lives. Its current director, Robert Waldinger, has distilled decades of data into one sentence: what truly keeps people happy and healthy through life is not wealth, not fame, but good relationships; those who were most satisfied in their relationships at fifty were the healthiest at eighty.

In Genesis 2:18 God said, “It is not good for the man to be alone.” More than three thousand years later, Harvard said the same thing with eighty years of data.

As for how to repair rather than replace, the marriage researcher John Gottman, through long-term observation at the University of Washington, identified four especially destructive patterns in couples’ interactions, which he called “the Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse”: criticism, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling — contempt being the strongest negative predictor. And in healthy relationships, positive and negative interactions stay at a ratio of roughly five to one.

In other words, a marriage rarely breaks because of one big explosion; it is usually worn away by small erosions day after day. And a marriage is rarely repaired by one grand romantic gesture; it is usually repaired by five small kindnesses a day.

The 321 insight

321 says: people are more important than tasks; relationships are more important than things. The tide of divorce does exactly the opposite — it treats people as things and relationships as tasks.

321 also says: Jesus is the focal point, not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. When a marriage runs into trouble, our focus usually falls on ourselves (how much I’ve had to put up with), on the other person (it’s all his fault), or on our circumstances (if only there weren’t this financial pressure). Not one of those three focal points can save a marriage. Only when we turn our focus back to Jesus, and see how he loved the church and gave himself up for it (Ephesians 5:25), is there a way forward for a marriage.

So the conclusion of the third point is this: if people look at marriage with the attitude that “the old is better than the new”, the root of divorce will be pulled up. What God wants is not to swap a person but to change a person.

sections.heading: 4. Animal: The Degradation of Promiscuous Unions
sections.html:
Satan’s fourth lie is: “As long as everyone’s happy.”

This is the most fashionable and the most dangerous saying of our day. Affairs, one-night stands, partner-swapping culture — they all hide behind those few words. As long as both sides agree, as long as everyone’s happy, what could be wrong with it?

The greatest difference between humans and animals

To expose this lie we first have to ask a more fundamental question: what, after all, is a human being?

If a human being is just a cleverer animal, then “as long as everyone’s happy” is indeed beyond reproach, because animal behaviour is governed by nothing more than instinct and pleasure.

But the Bible says: “God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.” (Genesis 1:27) It also says that man “became a living soul” (Genesis 2:7).

Human beings bear the image of God; they have a soul, reason, a conscience and the capacity for self-restraint. That is human dignity. When people give their desires free rein and disregard their responsibilities, they are not freer; they have demoted themselves — living like a beast without a soul.

The Bible describes this condition in the sternest terms: “But these speak evil of whatever things they don’t know. They are destroyed in these things that they understand naturally, like the creatures without reason.” (Jude 10)

A scientific fact to make us blush

The neuroscientists Thomas Insel, Larry Young and others spent years studying a small creature called the prairie vole. Prairie voles form long-term pair bonds with a single partner, and research has found that this is closely linked to the distribution of oxytocin and vasopressin receptors in their brains. Their close relatives, meadow voles, lack this receptor pattern, and their behaviour is promiscuous and unattached.

Even in a vole no bigger than the palm of your hand, God placed a design for faithfulness. Yet human beings, created in God’s image, with a spirit and with reason, cry out, “As long as everyone’s happy,” and end up living like meadow voles.

That is not progress; it is regression.

“As long as everyone’s happy” — is no one really hurt?

“As long as everyone’s happy” hides an even bigger lie: it assumes that pleasure has no consequences.

But Paul says: “Flee sexual immorality! ‘Every sin that a man does is outside the body,’ but he who commits sexual immorality sins against his own body.” (1 Corinthians 6:18)

Notice Paul’s logic: sexual sin wounds your own body. For God designed sex not merely as contact between two bodies but as the bonding together of two lives — the very dabaq of Genesis. Paul even quotes Genesis 2:24 to make his case: “Or don’t you know that he who is joined to a prostitute is one body? For, ‘The two’, he says, ‘will become one flesh.’” (1 Corinthians 6:16)

Every union without covenant is a forced tearing-apart of something that has been bonded together. Tear it once and it leaves a scar; tear it ten times and the surface will no longer bond to anything. That is why so many people, after giving themselves free rein, feel not freedom but an emptiness they cannot put into words.

The letter of James describes this process with great precision: “But each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own lust and enticed. Then the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin. The sin, when it is full grown, produces death.” (James 1:14–15) Lust has a gestation period: today a thought is planted, tomorrow it gives birth to an action, the day after it grows into a habit, and finally it bears death.

So the Bible’s command is: “Or don’t you know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God? You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. Therefore glorify God in your body and in your spirit, which are God’s.” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20)

Your body is not your own playground; it is the temple of the Holy Spirit. What belongs in a temple is worship, not indulgence.

The 321 insight

321 says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you rejoice, rely on the brain and you worry.

The trouble with “as long as everyone’s happy” is not the word “happy”; it is that people have looked for happiness in the wrong place. Trying to produce satisfaction of the soul through stimulation of the flesh is like drinking salt water to quench your thirst — the more you drink, the thirstier you get. Augustine’s famous line at the beginning of his Confessions says it best: “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.”

True happiness is the joy of a heart filled with the Holy Spirit. And no joy that comes through the Holy Spirit needs to be regretted the next morning.

321 also says: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. Promiscuity is the self-centred life at its most naked — my feelings come first, my pleasure comes first. But the selfless person speaks Paul’s words: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20)

So the conclusion of the fourth point is this: only by returning to God’s design — the two becoming one flesh — can marriage recover its dignity and holiness.

sections.heading: 5. Same-Sex: The Distortion of Twisted Marriage
sections.html:
Satan’s fifth lie is: “Love is love; any love is right.”

The legalisation of same-sex marriage is a clear sign of the inverted values of the last days. People no longer take God’s word as their standard; instead they exalt the self and human rights. Satan wraps it all in the most beautiful words — “respect”, “freedom”, “love” — so that people mistakenly believe every form of love deserves affirmation.

What the Bible says

First, the order of creation. “God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.” (Genesis 1:27) The image of God is displayed together in the complementary structure of “male and female.”

Second, the definition of marriage. In Matthew 19:4–5 the Lord Jesus himself quotes Genesis 2:24 and binds it together with “made them male and female.” This is the Lord’s own definition of marriage: one man and one woman, one husband and one wife, for one lifetime.

Third, the teaching of the New Testament. In Romans 1:26–27 Paul points out that when people “exchanged the truth of God for a lie”, God gave them up to vile passions, and they “changed the natural function into that which is against nature.” Natural and against nature mean in keeping with the Creator’s design and in defiance of the Creator’s design.

Fourth, and most important of all — the hope of the gospel. First Corinthians 6:9–10 lists a long line of those who will not inherit God’s Kingdom, among them “male prostitutes” and “homosexuals”, but also thieves, the covetous, drunkards, slanderers and extortionists. Paul places these sins side by side, and goes straight on to say something full of hope: “Some of you were such, but you were washed. But you were sanctified. But you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and in the Spirit of our God.” (1 Corinthians 6:11)

Truth, and love as well

Brothers and sisters, I want to give you a special word of caution here, because this is where it is easiest for both sides to lose.

What we oppose is behaviour and teaching, not people. We must never treat anyone with same-sex attraction with mockery, contempt or rejection. In God’s eyes they are a sinner just as I am, and someone Christ laid down his life to save, just as I am. A church full of pride, judgement and contempt does not please God any more than a self-indulgent world does — for pride, too, is Satan’s territory. 321 says it plainly: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

But love does not mean endorsing everything. True love must be built on truth. A doctor who withholds a diagnosis because he is afraid of upsetting the patient is not being kind; he is failing in his duty. Isaiah warned of this age long ago: “Woe to those who call evil good, and good evil; who put darkness for light, and light for darkness; who put bitter for sweet, and sweet for bitter!” (Isaiah 5:20)

The state of the last days

Paul’s description of the last days reads with special force today. He says that people in the last days will be “lovers of self”, and goes on to list more than a dozen traits — lovers of money, arrogant, without natural affection, without self-control, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God, and more (2 Timothy 3:1–4). Notice the first item on the list: lovers of self. Every other item grows out of that one; and the inversion of our view of marriage is the social symptom of love of self carried to its extreme.

The 321 insight

321 says: pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.

This is the crux. When people say, “I will redefine marriage,” “I will redefine gender,” they are leaving the creature’s originally intended position and sitting in the Creator’s seat. It is the modern version of that ancient temptation in Eden: “you will be like God, knowing good and evil.” (Genesis 3:5)

The Christian response is to return to our originally intended position: let man be man and let God be God. God is the Creator; he has the authority to define. I am the creature; my part is to obey.

So the conclusion of the fifth point is this: love is not indulgence but living by the truth. True love must be built on God’s design and on his truth.

sections.heading: 6. Summing Up: The Root of Satan’s View of Marriage Is Self-Centredness
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, we have now looked at five lies. Now set them side by side and see what they have in common.

Plural marriage says: I want more.

Trial marriage says: I want to be sure I don’t lose out first.

Divorce says: I want to swap for someone who suits me better.

Promiscuity says: I want to be happy.

Twisted marriage says: I want to live by my own definition.

Five sentences, five times “I.”

Whether plural marriage, trial marriage, divorce, promiscuity or twisted marriage, the core problem is “self-centredness.” Satan’s lies take a thousand forms, but they only ever have one recipe: lead people to pursue their own pleasure, satisfy their own desires, and run from responsibility and commitment.

Back to the serpent’s first sentence

Look at Satan’s strategy in the Garden of Eden. He did not tell Eve to kill anyone; he did not tell her to steal. He did only one thing: he moved Eve’s focus off God and onto herself — from “what God says” to “how I feel”, from “God’s standard” to “my rights.”

The Lord Jesus called him “the father of lies” (John 8:44).

From Eden until today, Satan’s script has only one page, and he performs the same play over and over: replace “God” with “me.”

A piercing picture

Marriage is like a house with only one throne.

If the husband sits on it, the wife has to kneel; if the wife sits on it, the husband has to kneel; if the two fight over it, sooner or later the chair gets torn apart — and that is divorce.

The only way out is for both of them to step down and let Jesus sit on it. The husband kneels before him, the wife kneels before him too, and there at his feet the two of you meet. Then you will find that what used to be a face-to-face quarrel has become a side-by-side walk.

That is why, after Ephesians 5 sets out the way of husband and wife, it says: “This mystery is great, but I speak concerning Christ and of the assembly.” (Ephesians 5:32) Marriage was not designed to make you happy; it was designed to make you holy and to bring glory to Christ. Here is the wonder of God: when you pursue holiness and God’s glory, happiness often follows as a by-product; when you pursue only happiness, you often end up with neither.

Supporting evidence from psychology

In the 1990s the psychologist Caryl Rusbult and her colleagues described “the Michelangelo phenomenon”: intimate partners are like sculptors who, through day-after-day interaction, “sculpt” each other into the shape they have in mind. When the sculpting moves in the direction of who that person truly longs to become, both the quality of the relationship and personal growth improve.

Two people in a marriage will certainly sculpt each other. The only question is: whose blueprint is in your hand? If it is a self-centred blueprint, you will carve your spouse into a tool for meeting your needs; if it is God’s blueprint, you will carve your spouse into the likeness of Christ.

Michelangelo is generally said to have remarked that he saw an angel imprisoned in the marble, and carved until he set it free. Brothers and sisters, your words are the chisel; your attitude is the hammer. Are you setting free, or are you destroying?

The 321 insight

The Two Core Values of 321 are: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.

The problems of marriage, in the end, are not problems of communication skills, not problems of compatible personalities, not even problems of the family we grew up in. The problem of marriage is a problem of kingship: who is sitting on the throne?

So the conclusion of the sixth point is this: when “I” becomes the lead character in a marriage, God is shut out. Only when Jesus has first place can a marriage get back on track.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: Rebuilding Marriage from God’s Perspective
sections.html:
The Three Foundations: the foundation of marriage

Jesus is my role model. The hardest thing in marriage is not loving each other; it is denying ourselves — and Jesus has already shown us how: “Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the assembly, and gave himself up for it.” (Ephesians 5:25) The benchmark is not “love her as you love yourself” but “as Christ loved the church.”

The Bible is my standard. The chaos around marriage today is, at bottom, a chaos of standards: people use feelings as their standard, trends as their standard — anything but the Bible. When the standard is confused, the direction is bound to be confused.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. In marriage there are so many moments when we “know what to do but can’t do it”: you know you should forgive, but your heart can’t get past it. What you need then is not more knowledge but the power of the Holy Spirit. The fruit the Spirit bears — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23) — every one of them is a basic necessity of marriage.

The Two Core Values and the Goal

Let Jesus be King: only one can sit on the throne of a marriage. Let Jesus receive all the glory: the purpose of marriage is not my happiness but his glory. When these two things are right, many questions suddenly have answers. Who should listen to whom? Both should listen to the Lord. Who should apologise first? Whoever hears the Holy Spirit first.

The Goal is to establish God’s system. Marriage is not a private affair; it is the first brick in God’s system. What Satan wants to tear down is more than a single household. Brothers and sisters, when you guard your marriage, you are holding a piece of ground for the kingdom of God.

The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless

The root of all five lies is the self-centred life; the way out is selflessness. But please hear this clearly: selflessness does not mean having no sense of self-worth, still less silently swallowing abuse in the face of violence. Selflessness is “‘I’ no longer live, but Christ lives in me.” It is not becoming zero; it is taking away the limited “self” and letting the limitless Christ come to dwell. The selfless person has not become smaller; they have entered into the fullness of Christ.

In marriage, the self-centred person asks, “When is he ever going to change?” The selfless person asks, “Lord, how do you want me to change?” That one change of question is often where a family’s turnaround begins.

The fivefold change and the right order

Mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry — this is the map of today’s lesson. Satan starts with the mindset, and God’s renewal starts with the mindset too: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” (Romans 12:2) Only when the mind is renewed can we discern God’s will. The mindset is the lens; if you don’t change the lens, everything you look at is distorted.

321 also reminds us of the order: life first, then relationships, then ministry; people are more important than tasks, relationships more important than things. Many Christian families work all week and serve all weekend, yet husband and wife haven’t had one real conversation in three months. Your spouse is not just a co-worker; your spouse is the first “2” God has entrusted to you.

The 920 practice and the 235 relationships

The 920 practice: everyone we are in relationship with is our “2”, and with them we practise living out the selfless (0) life and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions. Who is your hardest, and most real, “2”? Most likely the person who eats a meal with you every day. The fruit borne in the pulpit may be put on; the fruit borne in the kitchen is the real thing.

The 235 relationships: become a “2” with a selfless person, build the “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children, and become a “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. Marriage is the most complete “2” of all; when the “2” stands firm, the “3” has roots and the “5” has a home.

Four changes of perspective

From man’s to God’s: marriage is not a human invention but God’s institution. From earthly to heavenly: marriage is not only about the daily grind of household needs; it is a picture of Christ and the church. From the worldly to the godly: the world asks, “What’s in it for me?” God asks, “Are you willing to deny yourself for me?” From the temporary to the eternal: feelings fade, but a covenant made before God endures; whatever you lay down for love today is remembered in eternity.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Walking the Truth into Daily Living
sections.html:
The lesson gives three practices. We will use the 321 eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to take them deeper.

Practice 1: Examine whether your thinking about marriage has been shaped by the world’s trends

Information: this morning you have received five lies — plural marriage, trial marriage, divorce, promiscuity, twisted marriage — and one poisonous root: self-centredness. Write these six terms on the first page of your notebook.

Revelation: information stays in the head; revelation enters the heart. Quietly ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light: which of these five lies has already taken up residence in my thinking?

Conviction: when the Holy Spirit points it out, don’t argue and don’t rationalise. Conviction is saying, “Lord, you are right, and I am wrong.”

Implementation: this week, give your mindset a health check. The series you’ve been watching, the songs you’ve been listening to, the short videos you’ve been scrolling through — what view of marriage are they quietly teaching you? Switch off the most toxic source.

Practice 2: If you are married, express committed love to your spouse, and pray for your family, asking the Lord to be its Lord

Evaluation: how long has it been since you last said “I love you” to your spouse? Since you last laid hands on your spouse and prayed? Since you last sincerely said, “I’m sorry, I was wrong”?

Correction: correct it today; don’t wait for the feeling to come. Gottman’s five-to-one principle reminds us that a relationship is built up from small positive interactions every day. Today, do three small things: say one word of affirmation, give one hug, and pray together once.

Tonight, hold your spouse’s hand and say: “Whatever happens, I will never let go.” Then read Genesis 2:24 aloud together and put your home into the Lord’s hands. If your marriage is in a breach right now, don’t hold on alone; ask the Lord to give you a spiritual companion to walk with you — that is exactly why the 235 relationships exist.

Practice 3: If you are not yet married, ask God to cleanse your heart and build a right view of marriage

Being single is not a second-class status; it is a whole status. You are not waiting for life to begin; you are in the middle of life right now.

First, cleansing: ask the Lord to take away the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life (1 John 2:16). Second, preparation: the way you treat your parents, flatmates and colleagues today is a rehearsal for the way you will treat a spouse. Third, prayer: pray for the person you don’t yet know, and pray too for the self who will one day become a husband or a wife.

Repetition and Multiplication

Repetition: a renewed mindset can’t be completed in one sermon. For thirty days in a row, read Genesis 2:24 once every morning.

Multiplication: once you’ve learned it, pass it on. This week, find one person — a child, a newly married couple, a friend who is struggling — and tell them in your own words what you have received today. When truth is spoken aloud, it takes deeper root in you.

A Gentle Reminder

Marriage is not a place for “choosing happiness” but a school for “learning to love.” Wrong mindsets will destroy a marriage; right truth will restore it.

Everyone who enters this school discovers: I thought I was very good at loving, but in fact I was only very good at being loved. Love has to be learned, and marriage is the course God runs with the highest tuition fees of all.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: Back to the Beginning
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, Satan’s view of marriage is self-centred and leads to ruin and chaos; God’s view of marriage is Christ-centred and brings restoration and blessing. Five lies, one poisonous root; one Saviour, one way out.

This morning I want to issue three calls.

First, reject the lies. Ask the Lord to drive out, one by one, the worldly mindsets that have quietly moved into your heart. Stop saying, “Everyone does it”; say instead, “But from the beginning it has not been so.”

Second, go back to the beginning. Return to the principles of Genesis — one man and one woman, one heart and one mind, one lifetime. This isn’t being old-fashioned; these are the Creator’s factory settings. The only way to make a machine run properly is to use it according to the designer’s manual.

Third, let Jesus be King. Hand over the throne. When Jesus reigns as King, what is broken can be mended, what has grown cold can be rekindled, and what has lost hope can hope again.

Perhaps this morning there are brothers and sisters whose hearts are aching: your marriage has come to a very dark place; there are failures in your past you can hardly bring yourself to speak of; you feel you have no right to talk about holiness. Hear these words of Paul: “Some of you were such, but you were washed. But you were sanctified. But you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and in the Spirit of our God.” (1 Corinthians 6:11)

“Some of you were such.” God’s grace always finds a way to write “once upon a time” into a person’s story.

He who sits on the throne says, “Behold, I am making all things new.” (Revelation 21:5) He does not say, “I am replacing all things”; he says, “I am making all things new.” He doesn’t swap out your spouse; he makes the two of you new.

When marriage returns to God’s design, families are healed; when families are healed, the church is built up; when the church is built up, the glory of the kingdom will be revealed. May all the glory go to him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb, for ever and ever.

keyVerses: “Therefore a man will leave his father and his mother, and will join with his wife, and they will be one flesh.” (Genesis 2:24)

“He answered, ‘Haven’t you read that he who made them from the beginning made them male and female, and said, “For this cause a man shall leave his father and mother, and shall be joined to his wife; and the two shall become one flesh?” So that they are no more two, but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, don’t let man tear apart.’” (Matthew 19:4–6)
declarations: Lord, guard my heart, so that I am not deceived by Satan’s lies.
Help me build the foundation of marriage on your truth.
Whether single or married, I will keep you at the centre,
and let my love and my home display your glory.
practices: Examine whether your thinking about marriage has been shaped by the world’s trends
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we worship you. You are the God who established marriage, the God who in the Garden of Eden personally brought the woman to the man; what you established was pure, good and glorious.

Lord, we confess that we live in a generation filled with lies. Forgive us — for reading your word while looking at marriage through the world’s eyes; for calling you Lord with our lips while still wanting to be king in our hearts. Shine the light of your truth into the most hidden corners of our hearts; every mindset that belongs to Satan, remove it, one by one.

We pray for our married brothers and sisters: heal their marriages, take away coldness, bitterness and contempt, and give forgiveness, kindness and hope, so that they move from face-to-face quarrels to walking side by side. We pray for our single brothers and sisters: cleanse their hearts, so that they do not panic as they wait or compromise in their loneliness. And keep our next generation, so that even in this twisted age they can still recognise your design from the beginning.

Lord Jesus, today we hand the throne of our homes back to you; please reign as King. May our marriages and our homes become a testimony to your glory. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Of the five satanic views of marriage — plural marriage, trial marriage, divorce, promiscuity and twisted marriage — which one most easily influences you without your noticing? In what “very reasonable-sounding” words does it usually show up? Answer it in the light of the Lord’s words: “he who made them from the beginning made them male and female, and said, ‘For this cause a man shall leave his father and mother, and shall be joined to his wife; and the two shall become one flesh?’” (Matthew 19:4–5)

The lesson says that what God wants is not to “swap” a person but to “change” a person. In your closest relationship, what is the one area God is asking you to “change”? Share in the light of the Scripture: “that you put away, as concerning your former way of life, the old man that grows corrupt after the lusts of deceit, and that you be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man.” (Ephesians 4:22–24)
l052.title: Satan’s Concept of Marriage
l052.subtitle: An Important Mindset — Exposing Five Lies and Returning to the Covenant God Established
l052.partTitle: Unit 4 · The Prerequisite for Revival — A Change of Mindset

sections.heading: Introduction: A Contract Rewritten
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning.

Let me begin with a question: deep in your heart, what is marriage, really?

If you walked out onto the street today and put that question to a hundred people at random, you would hear every kind of answer. Some would say marriage is a contract — two people agree on terms, spell out rights and duties, and part amicably if it comes to that. Some would say marriage is a high-stakes gamble — you stake most of your youth on it; win, and you call it happiness; lose, and you call it bad luck. Some would say marriage is a form of consumption — you stay together while the love lasts, and when it doesn’t, you trade up, as naturally as changing your phone. And some would say flatly that marriage is an expired ticket for a ship that has already sailed, a relic of the last generation that nobody needs any more.

These answers sound very modern, very free, very “unattached”. But brothers and sisters, notice something: when someone treats marriage as a contract, what he cares about most is “Am I getting short-changed?”; when someone treats marriage as a gamble, what he does most often is “stand ready to cash out”; when someone treats marriage as consumption, what he is best at is “comparing and replacing”.

And so we see a strange thing: this generation has more books on marriage, more relationship courses and more counselling resources than any in history — and also the most fragile marriages in history. We study marriage ever more thoroughly, and live it ever more brokenly.

Where has it gone wrong?

It went wrong at the very start: we picked up the wrong instruction manual.

I often put it this way. Suppose someone gave you a precision instrument, and you operated it by the manual for a different machine. What would happen? Not just a few hiccups — the machine would certainly break. Marriage is the same. Marriage is not an institution humans invented; it is a holy covenant God himself established. The designer is God, and the manual is in the Bible. If we run God’s design using a manual the world has written, how could it not go wrong?

Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: God established marriage before humanity fell.

This matters enormously. Many institutions in human history arose only after sin entered — government is needed because there is evil, law is needed because there is conflict, even sacrifice is needed because there is sin. But not marriage. Marriage was set up by God’s own hand in the Garden of Eden, before anyone had sinned, while the world was still whole and unspoiled. That tells us marriage is not a “remedy” but a “purpose of creation”; it does not exist to solve a problem but to display glory.

The Bible opens with a wedding — God brings Eve to Adam (Genesis 2:22). The Bible closes with a wedding too: “For the wedding of the Lamb has come, and his wife has made herself ready.” (Revelation 19:7) From Genesis to Revelation, from Eden to the New Jerusalem, God uses the picture of marriage to show the unchanging love between himself and his people.

So when Satan sets out to attack God’s glory, he will always attack marriage. To destroy a marriage is to destroy a portrait of God; to destroy a family is to destroy an outpost of God’s system. Satan does not need to persuade you not to believe in God. He only needs to persuade you that marriage can be taken lightly.

In this lesson we are going back to the source together. We will see three things:

First, what was God’s intention in establishing marriage — a man and a woman becoming one.

Second, what “becoming one flesh” truly means — a complete union of spirit, soul and body.

Third, how husband and wife meet each other’s deepest needs — the complementarity of love and respect.

One is the blueprint, one is the substance, one is the practice. The blueprint sets the direction, the substance sets the depth, and the practice sets the fruit.

Brothers and sisters, if you are married, this lesson is meant to help you bring your marriage back to God’s intention. If you are single, it matters just as much — because God wants first to shape you into someone capable of oneness, so that you can enter a marriage of oneness. Marriage will not make an immature person mature; marriage only magnifies an immature person.

Let us receive God’s word together.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Three Passages, Three Settings
sections.html: To understand today’s message rightly, we must first stand where the text originally stood, and hear whom it was first speaking to.

sections.heading: 1. Genesis 2:24: The Charter of Eden
sections.html:
Genesis was written by Moses, around the fifteenth century BC (some say the thirteenth), and its first readers were the Israelites, newly out of Egypt and walking through the wilderness.

This is crucial. These people had just left Egypt — a culture whose view of marriage was in utter confusion — and they were about to enter Canaan, a land where sexual licence was a religious rite. The Canaanites worshipped Baal and Asherah; their temples kept cult prostitutes, and sex and fertility were treated as ways to please the gods. Writing Genesis to them in that setting, Moses was in effect saying: what you saw in Egypt is not the truth, and what you are about to see in Canaan is not the truth either. Let me tell you how God designed it in the beginning.

Genesis 2:24 is the Bible’s first definition of marriage, and it uses three verbs: “leave”, “join” and “become”. These three verbs form the charter of marriage. Notice that this verse comes at a time when Adam and Eve had no parents to leave — Adam was made by God, and Eve was taken from Adam; they had no parents at all. So the verse is not describing an existing fact; it is laying down an eternal rule: from now on, everyone who enters marriage is to do this.

sections.heading: 2. Matthew 19:6: A Debate in the Courtroom
sections.html:
Matthew’s Gospel was written by the apostle Matthew, sometime between AD 50 and 70, chiefly for communities of Jewish believers.

The scene in chapter 19 is a public debate. The Pharisees come to test Jesus and ask him, “Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife for any reason?” (Matthew 19:3) Behind that question lay a famous dispute among the rabbis of the day. Deuteronomy 24:1 says that if a husband finds “some unseemly thing” in his wife, he may write her a certificate of divorce. But what counts as “some unseemly thing”? The school of Shammai held that it meant only serious unfaithfulness; the school of Hillel held that a wife doing anything at all that displeased her husband — including burning the dinner — was grounds for divorce. And what was popular in society then was precisely Hillel’s interpretation, lax to the point of absurdity.

The Pharisees thought Jesus would pick a side between the two schools. But he didn’t. He did something far more fundamental: he took the conversation away from Deuteronomy 24 and back to Genesis 1 and 2. In effect he said: you keep arguing about “when it can be pulled down”, but you have never asked “how it was built in the first place”.

Jesus said, “Haven’t you read…?” (Matthew 19:4) He quoted Genesis 1:27 and 2:24, and then drew his conclusion: “So that they are no more two, but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, don’t let man tear apart.” (Matthew 19:6)

Brothers and sisters, here is a vital mindset: the oneness of marriage is not the product of two people’s efforts but the work of God’s own initiative. The text says “what God has joined together”. The word “joined together” in the original (Greek συζεύγνυμι, suzeugnumi) means “yoked together”, like two oxen put under the same yoke, so that from then on they can only move in the same direction, at the same pace and the same speed. Who put the yoke on? God did. So no human has the right to take it off.
