sections.heading: 3. Ephesians 5:22–25: A Family Letter in a Pagan City
sections.html:
Ephesians was written by the apostle Paul around AD 60–62, from prison in Rome, to the churches of Ephesus and the surrounding region of Asia.

What kind of city was Ephesus? It was home to the temple of the goddess Artemis (whom the Romans called Diana), one of the seven wonders of the ancient world. In that city, religion and lust were tightly bound together; temple and marketplace, worship and debauchery, were all mixed into one. At the same time, Roman society ran on the paterfamilias system: a husband held near-absolute power over his wife, his children and his servants. In a culture like that, Paul hardly needed to tell wives to submit to their husbands — that was common knowledge.

So the truly shocking part of Paul’s letter is not verse 22 but verse 25: “Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the assembly, and gave himself up for it.” (Ephesians 5:25) In a society where a husband could do as he pleased with his wife, Paul required husbands to give themselves up. In that day, this was revolutionary.

What’s more, the whole passage has a governing principle, found in the verse just before: “subjecting yourselves to one another in the fear of Christ.” (Ephesians 5:21) In Paul’s original, verses 21 and 22 are one sentence; verse 22 does not even have its own verb “submit” but borrows it from verse 21. In other words, between husband and wife it is not “one rules and the other obeys”; it is both laying themselves down before Christ and submitting to one another.

Brothers and sisters, remember these three settings: amid the filth of Egypt and Canaan, God says, “From the beginning it was not so”; amid the rabbis’ hair-splitting, Jesus says, “What God has joined together, don’t let man tear apart”; amid the lust of Ephesus, Paul says, “Love your wives as Christ loved the assembly.”

Age after age, the world has kept rewriting the definition of marriage. And God’s word has never changed.

sections.heading: 1. God’s Intention in Establishing Marriage: A Man and a Woman Becoming One
sections.html:
1. Marriage is not a human invention but God’s joining

The Bible says plainly: “Therefore a man will leave his father and his mother, and will join with his wife, and they will be one flesh.” (Genesis 2:24)

Marriage is not a casual human choice but God’s joining: “So that they are no more two, but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, don’t let man tear apart.” (Matthew 19:6)

Brothers and sisters, this is the foundation of the whole message. If the foundation is wrong, however beautiful the house, it will fall.

The world says: I chose this marriage, so I can also un-choose it. God says: I joined this marriage, so no one may tear it apart.

The difference between these two sentences is not in the form of marriage but in whose hands its sovereignty rests. If the sovereignty of my marriage is in my hands, then I stay when I’m happy and leave when I’m not — and who could object? But if the sovereignty of marriage is in God’s hands, then marriage is a holy covenant, a vow I made before God, not terms I negotiated with the other person.

What is the difference between a covenant and a contract?

A contract protects my interests; a covenant fulfils my commitment. A contract asks, “Have you delivered?”; a covenant asks, “Have I kept faith?” The spirit of a contract is “If you break the terms, I’ll end the deal”; the spirit of a covenant is “Even when you are weak, I will keep my vow.” A contract is written on paper; a covenant is made before God.

That is why Scripture says: “Let marriage be held in honor among all, and let the bed be undefiled; but God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterers.” (Hebrews 13:4) The word behind “honour” in the original (Greek τίμιος, timios) means “valuable, precious, worth a high price”. The same word is used of the “precious” blood of the Lord Jesus (1 Peter 1:19). God sees marriage as a costly vessel, not a disposable paper plate.

Let me use a comparison. Two people open a shop together: that is a contractual relationship — the shares are clearly reckoned so that the accounts are easy to settle if they part ways. Parents bring a child into the world: that is a blood relationship — however rebellious the child, he is always your child, and blood cannot be undone. Which kind is marriage? The world treats marriage as the first; the Bible treats it as the second. “They are no more two, but one flesh” — one flesh means bound together in flesh and blood. You don’t cut off your left hand because it won’t do what you want; you bear with it, treat it, and wait for it to heal.

2. One man and one woman, for one lifetime, with one heart

God’s intention in establishing marriage can be summed up in three short phrases: one man and one woman, for one lifetime, with one heart and mind.

“One man and one woman” is who marriage is between. “God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.” (Genesis 1:27) God’s image is not displayed by man alone, nor by woman alone, but by man and woman together in oneness. This is the order God laid down in creation.

“For one lifetime” is how long marriage lasts. When Jesus says, “Don’t let man tear apart,” he means the covenant is valid for life.

“With one heart and mind” is the quality of marriage. God wants not only that two people stay together but that they be of one heart. “Do two walk together, unless they have agreed?” (Amos 3:3) Many marriages have not lost the “one lifetime”, but lost the “one heart” long ago — living under one roof, sleeping in one bed, while their hearts wander off in different directions.

The prophet Malachi puts God’s intention very plainly: “Therefore take heed to your spirit, and let no one deal treacherously against the wife of his youth.” (Malachi 2:15) Notice that God tells us to guard what is within — the Chinese Union Version reads “guard your hearts”. The defensive line of a marriage is not in behaviour but in the heart. The heart leaves first, and then the person leaves; the heart grows cold first, and then the actions betray.

This echoes what we have learned in 321: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23) The fruit of a marriage springs from the hearts of husband and wife.

3. Why did God make Eve? — To complement, not to be subordinate

“Yahweh God said, ‘It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make him a helper comparable to him.’” (Genesis 2:18)

Throughout the first chapter of Genesis, God says “good” six times and “very good” once. The first time he says “not good” is right here — “It is not good for the man to be alone.” While man had not yet sinned and still enjoyed perfect fellowship with God, God still said it was not good for him to be alone. What does that tell us? That the need for oneness is not a result of sin but a design God placed within us.

The phrase “a helper comparable to him” in Hebrew is עֵזֶר כְּנֶגְדּוֹ (ezer kenegdo). Ezer means “helper”, and the word appears twenty-one times in the Old Testament, sixteen of them describing God himself as man’s help — “My help comes from Yahweh, who made heaven and earth.” (Psalm 121:2) So “helper” is never second-class, never subordinate, never a servant; it is the one who brings relief in the hour of need, who steadies you at the critical moment. Kenegdo means “corresponding to him, matching him”, carrying the sense of “face to face, equal, a perfect fit”.

In other words, when God made Eve he was not making a shadow to trail behind Adam, but a partner who could stand face to face with him, the two matching and completing each other.

Adam’s first words on waking were a song: “This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh. She will be called ‘woman,’ because she was taken out of Man.” (Genesis 2:23)

There is a detail here worth noting. God did not make Eve from Adam’s head, lest she rule over him; nor from his foot, lest he trample on her; but from his rib — from his side, close to his heart. This old explanation is often attributed to the Middle Ages and generally thought to come from Jewish and Christian preaching traditions. Scripture does not state it, but it captures the spirit of the text beautifully: standing side by side, heart joined to heart.

4. Satan’s distortion: from “one” to “many”

Satan never creates anything from nothing; he only distorts. For every good thing God makes, Satan tries to produce a counterfeit.

God says “one man and one woman”; Satan markets “many” — affairs, multiple partners, a flood of pornography, diluting faithfulness into consumption.

God says “one lifetime”; Satan markets “trial marriage” — live together and see; stay if it works, leave if it doesn’t, demoting covenant to a free trial.

God says “don’t let man tear apart”; Satan markets “divorce” — calling the breaking of the deal courage, calling the breaking of the vow freedom.

God says “male and female he created them”; Satan markets “same-sex” — blurring at the root the order of the sexes God created.

These four traps share one core: they pull marriage down from a “covenant” and turn it into an “option”. Once marriage is only an option, it must be compared with the other options; and once the comparing begins, the marriage can no longer be held.

Brothers and sisters, look at Genesis 3. Humanity’s first marriage crisis came after the fall. God came and questioned Adam, and how did Adam answer? “The man said, ‘The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it.’” (Genesis 3:12) One sentence, and the blame is passed twice — first onto God, “whom you gave”, and then onto his wife, “she gave me fruit”. In the previous chapter he was singing, “This is now bone of my bones”; in this chapter it has become “the woman whom you gave to be with me”.

What had come in? The self-centred life had come in.

This is exactly what we stress again and again in 321: the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of every problem. The greatest enemy in a marriage is not the other person; it is “me”. When I put “my face, my feelings, my reasons, my rights” first, the marriage begins to crumble. Adam and Eve were originally “both naked, and they were not ashamed” (Genesis 2:25), because there was no covering and no defensiveness between them. After they sinned, the very first thing they did was sew fig leaves together — and people began building walls between each other.

Psychological research also confirms the Bible’s insight. From the 1970s onwards, Professor John Gottman of the University of Washington observed the interactions of thousands of couples in his “Love Lab”, and found that the strongest predictor of divorce was “contempt” — eye-rolling, sneering, mockery, belittling the other person with words. Gottman called contempt, criticism, defensiveness and stonewalling the “Four Horsemen” of marriage. And what is the essence of contempt? It is “I am above you.” Isn’t that pride?

Another of Gottman’s well-known findings is the so-called “magic ratio”: in stable, happy marriages, the ratio of positive to negative interactions during conflict is about five to one. In other words, what holds a marriage together is not never quarrelling, but keeping, even in the middle of a quarrel, a great deal of gentleness, humour, affirmation and acts of repair.

Here the 321 message speaks to marriage: humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride provokes pride, and both are wounded; humility draws out humility, and both win. There is no such thing as “winning” in marriage — win the argument and you lose the relationship; win the debate and you lose the home.

So there is only one road to rebuilding the blessing of marriage: back to God’s original design. Let Jesus be King — let him be Lord in the marriage, rather than letting “me” be lord of the marriage.

sections.heading: 2. The True Meaning of “Becoming One Flesh”: Oneness of Spirit, Soul and Body
sections.html:
Many couples “live together” without ever “becoming one” — their bodies close, their hearts far apart.

I often say: sharing a bed is not the same as sharing a heart; living together is not the same as walking together. In some homes the dinner table is silent, everyone scrolling their own phone; in others plenty is said, yet not one sentence reaches the heart. A marriage like that is “loneliness for two”.

True “oneness” is not an outward union but a complete oneness of spirit, soul and body.

Paul’s prayer for the church in Thessalonica names the three parts of a person: “May your whole spirit, soul, and body be preserved blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.” (1 Thessalonians 5:23) A person is made up of spirit, soul and body, and the oneness of marriage must likewise be a oneness on all three levels.

1. Oneness of spirit: worshipping, seeking and serving with one heart

Oneness of spirit means husband and wife share a common foundation and direction in their spiritual life.

Only when the two worship with one heart, seek God with one heart and serve with one heart can they walk the heavenward road together. If one loves the Lord and the other is cold, a rift opens in the spirit. True oneness of spirit is encouraging, supporting and growing one another in the Lord, and letting God have first place.

The prophet Amos asks a question no one can dodge: “Do two walk together, unless they have agreed?” (Amos 3:3) The verse originally refers to Israel’s relationship with God, but it voices a universal principle: walking together presupposes agreement, and agreement presupposes a shared direction.

Brothers and sisters, there is a secret to two people becoming one: don’t stand face to face pulling against each other; stand side by side looking up to the same Lord.

I often use a triangle to picture it: God at the top, husband and wife at the two ends of the base. As each of them draws nearer to God, the distance between them naturally shrinks. On the other hand, if both drift away from God while trying hard to get closer to each other, the closer they get, the more it hurts — because when two self-centred people press together, the friction only grows.

So the order of oneness in marriage is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others. This is what 321 calls the priority of relationships. Many couples labour hard at the “with others” layer but never deal with the “with God” and “with ourselves” layers, and so they treat the symptoms without touching the root.

Scripture says: “Unless Yahweh builds the house, they who build it labor in vain.” (Psalm 127:1) The Hebrew for “house” (בַּיִת, bayit) means both a building and a family or household. You can build your home with every method the world offers — buy the best house, read the most parenting books, plan the perfect schedule — but unless Yahweh builds it, it is all labour in vain.

When Joshua was old he declared to all Israel: “As for me and my house, we will serve Yahweh.” (Joshua 24:15) Brothers and sisters, that is the moment a family’s spiritual direction is fixed. A family without a spiritual direction will be carried along by the tide of the times.

What is the practical exercise? Very simple, and very hard: pray together.

Not praying together at church, but at home, behind closed doors, holding hands, speaking out loud in prayer for each other. Many couples can travel together, manage money together, raise children together, yet have never once knelt down to pray together. Why is it so hard? Because prayer exposes my true condition; prayer makes me transparent before my spouse. And what a self-centred person fears most is being transparent.

So a couple praying together is in itself a practice of selflessness.

2. Oneness of soul: mindset, emotions and will in step

The soul includes the mind, the emotions and the will.

When a couple share a common mindset and the same values, their emotions resonate and their direction falls into step. This takes constant communication and understanding, learning to replace argument with love and stubbornness with forgiveness.

321 speaks of a fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change the daily living. Change in a marriage also starts with the mindset. If two people’s mindsets differ — about money, about time, about success, about children, about the in-laws on either side — then conflict is not an accident but a certainty.

Notice that oneness of soul is not “one person giving up thinking”; it is two people being renewed together by the truth. Paul says: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” (Romans 12:2) A couple’s mindset is not aligned to each other but aligned together to the truth. If one side simply gives in to the other, that is endurance, not oneness; only when both come back together before God’s word is it oneness.

On the level of the emotions, the hardest lesson is “listening”.

James says: “Let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger.” (James 1:19) When couples quarrel, it is usually the other way round: swift to speak, slow to hear, swift to anger.

Why? Because in conversation we spend most of our time not “understanding” but “preparing a rebuttal”. That is the self-centred life at work. The moment you open your mouth, I am already assembling my case; before you’ve finished, I already know how I’ll knock you down. In the end both people are talking and neither is listening.

The psychologist Carl Rogers proposed “empathic listening”. He pointed out that the greatest barrier to human communication is our habit of evaluating before we understand. He recommended a simple yet difficult exercise: before you respond, restate the other person’s meaning in your own words, and only when they agree that you have really understood may you say your own piece. Brothers and sisters, if couples practised this, many quarrels would stop on the spot.

Because most quarrels are not really about the matter itself; they are about “Do you actually take me seriously?”

On the level of the will, the hardest lesson is “forgiveness”.

Paul says: “And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you.” (Ephesians 4:32) Notice that the standard for forgiveness is not “Do they deserve it?” but “How did God forgive me?”

Remember this passage too: “Love is patient and is kind. Love doesn’t envy. Love doesn’t brag, is not proud, doesn’t behave itself inappropriately, doesn’t seek its own way, is not provoked, takes no account of evil.” (1 Corinthians 13:4–5) “Takes no account of evil” — the original word for “account” (λογίζομαι, logizomai) is a bookkeeping term. Some couples have been married thirty years and kept the ledger for thirty years; every quarrel drags out the old accounts, starting from something said thirty years ago. Brothers and sisters, love’s ledger is meant to be burned.

Replacing argument with love and stubbornness with forgiveness — this is exactly the reminder our lesson gives us, and exactly the lesson of selflessness.

3. Oneness of body: living, walking, working and enjoying together

Husband and wife are not only emotional partners but companions in daily living. The two live together, walk together, work together and enjoy together, and God makes physical intimacy the seal of marriage, deepening the bond between them.

Scripture speaks of the married couple’s bodies in a way that is both holy and frank: “Let the husband give his wife the affection owed her, and likewise also the wife her husband. The wife doesn’t have authority over her own body, but the husband. Likewise also the husband doesn’t have authority over his own body, but the wife.” (1 Corinthians 7:3–4)

Notice how balanced this passage is: it is not that the husband has authority and the wife has none; both give themselves to the other. This is denying of self practised at the most intimate level.

Paul goes on: “Don’t deprive one another, unless it is by consent for a season, that you may give yourselves to fasting and prayer, and may be together again, that Satan doesn’t tempt you because of your lack of self-control.” (1 Corinthians 7:5) Brothers and sisters, notice the words “that Satan doesn’t”. Long-term distance between husband and wife is not only an emotional problem; it is a spiritual breach.

“Living, walking, working and enjoying together” — these four phrases describe oneness in daily living. Living together is sharing space; walking together is sharing direction; working together is sharing responsibility; enjoying together is sharing joy. Many marriages “live together but don’t walk together, work together but don’t enjoy together” — under one roof, yet each going their own way; carrying the load side by side, yet never once enjoying grace together.

Here is an often-overlooked lesson: do the housework together. It sounds terribly ordinary, yet it is deeply spiritual. For “co-worker” is not a word that only applies at church. A husband willing to wash the dishes, a wife willing to show understanding — that is what the cross looks like in everyday life.

The Harvard Study of Adult Development, begun in 1938, has followed hundreds of participants for more than eighty years and is one of the longest-running studies of human happiness in the world. Its current director, Robert Waldinger, has said that its clearest conclusion is this: good relationships make people happier and healthier, and how satisfied people were in their close relationships at age fifty predicted their health at eighty better than their cholesterol levels did.

Brothers and sisters, science spent eighty years and tens of millions of dollars to reach a conclusion the Bible states on its first pages: “It is not good for the man to be alone.” (Genesis 2:18)

4. Personal integration first, then oneness as a couple

To reach “one flesh”, each partner must first come to an integration of spirit, soul and body in their own life — the spirit submitted to God, the soul renewed by the truth, the body restrained by love.

This is one of the most important reminders in this lesson: oneness is not two broken people patching themselves together, but two people restored by God being joined to each other.

If a person’s spirit does not submit to God, the soul takes charge; and if the soul takes charge, the body runs out of control. Conversely, when the spirit submits to God, the soul is renewed by truth and the body is restrained by love, there is order within that person. Two people with order inside them come together and are naturally one; two people without order come together and inevitably clash.

I often use musical instruments as a picture. When two violins are to play together, the first thing is not to tune to each other but for each to tune to the same reference pitch. If each is tuned to that pitch, they will naturally be in harmony when they play; if not, however much the two adjust to each other, the more they adjust, the worse it gets.

Who is the reference pitch in marriage? Jesus.

This is exactly what 321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. Many couples rush to fix the “relationship” but won’t deal with the “life”. If the life has not changed, the relationship will spring back however often you fix it.

The Lord Jesus’ prayer is our highest model: “that they may all be one; even as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be one in us; that the world may believe that you sent me.” (John 17:21) The supreme pattern of oneness is the triune God. The oneness of the Father and the Son is not one conquering the other, but perfect love and perfect submission.

When each person has first been restored and integrated by God, the oneness of the couple will flow out naturally.

sections.heading: 3. Meeting Each Other’s Needs: The Complementarity of Love and Respect
sections.html:
A happy marriage is not something to take for granted; it is the fruit of both partners learning from each other and building each other up.

Scripture shows that husbands and wives have different needs in marriage. God made male and female, and they were different from the start; the difference is not meant for opposition but for complementing each other.

1. A husband’s deepest need is to be respected

So Scripture says: “Wives, be subject to your own husbands, as to the Lord.” (Ephesians 5:22)

Hear this clearly first: submission is not self-abasement; it is respect for the husband’s role and responsibility.

The original word for “be subject” (Greek ὑποτάσσω, hupotassō) is a military term meaning “to be ranked under, to stand in order in one’s own place”. It speaks of order, not worth; of position, not of higher and lower. In the triune God, the Son submits to the Father, and the Son shares equal honour and glory with the Father — submission has never meant being one rung lower.

And the text is perfectly clear: “as to the Lord”. This phrase carries two meanings. First, a wife submits to her husband for the Lord’s sake, not because her husband is perfect. Second, the standard of submission is the Lord — if a husband demands something contrary to God’s word, submitting to the Lord comes before submitting to man.

When a wife is willing to replace control with trust and criticism with gentleness, her husband feels the worth of being respected, and has more strength to love his wife.

Brothers and sisters, look at how Paul sums up this passage: “Nevertheless each of you must also love his own wife even as himself; and let the wife see that she respects her husband.” (Ephesians 5:33) Paul did not say “husbands, respect your wives; wives, love your husbands.” He said husbands are to “love” and wives are to “respect”. That choice of words is no accident. It is the central observation Emerson Eggerichs develops in his book “Love and Respect” (2004): what a wife longs for most is to be loved, and what a husband longs for most is to be respected; yet couples often fall into a “Crazy Cycle” — the wife feels unloved and expresses it through criticism; the husband feels disrespected and responds by withdrawing; so the more she criticises, the more he withdraws, and the more he withdraws, the more she criticises.

This is just what 321 says: pride provokes pride, and both are wounded.

There is only one way to break the cycle: someone has to stop first. And that person need not wait for the other to change first.

2. A wife’s deepest need is to be loved and protected

So Scripture says: “Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the assembly, and gave himself up for it.” (Ephesians 5:25)

If a husband’s love can be like Christ’s — sacrificial, responsible and tender — it gives his wife tremendous security and trust.

Notice how high a standard this verse sets for husbands. God did not say, “Love your wife the way you love your car,” nor “the way the world loves its wives.” God said: “even as Christ also loved the assembly, and gave himself up for it.”

How did Christ love the church? “Who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” (Philippians 2:6–8)

“Emptied himself” — this is the New Testament’s clearest description of selflessness. Christ’s love is a love that lays down its rights, a love that pays the price first, a love that keeps no score of returns.

Brothers and sisters, husbands, before you require your wife to submit, ask yourself first: what have I ever given up for her?

Paul goes on to say that the purpose of Christ’s love for the church was “that he might sanctify it, having cleansed it by the washing of water with the word” (Ephesians 5:26). So a husband’s love is meant to make his wife more and more holy before God, more and more radiant, more and more like the woman God created her to be. A wife who is loved will shine; that is the husband’s responsibility, and also the husband’s glory.

Peter puts it in finer detail: “You husbands, in the same way, live with your wives according to knowledge, giving honor to the woman, as to the weaker vessel, as also being joint heirs of the grace of life, that your prayers may not be hindered.” (1 Peter 3:7) “According to knowledge” is the literal sense of the original — a husband is to give himself to truly knowing his wife. And how solemn that last phrase is: if a husband does not treat his wife well, his prayers will be hindered. God weighs the relationship between husband and wife more heavily than we imagine.

3. Love and respect, like the two sides of breathing

When the husband loves his wife with Christ’s love, and the wife submits to her husband with a respectful heart, the two can live out the order of marriage God designed.

Love and respect are like the two sides of breathing: neither can be missing. The more deeply the husband loves, the more the wife is able to submit; the more the wife respects, the more the husband is able to love. Such a marriage becomes a vessel that bears witness to Christ’s glory.

Why is breathing the best picture? Because breathing in and breathing out cannot argue about which matters more, and no one says, “I’ll breathe in once you’ve breathed out.” Love and respect are the same — not a transaction but a cycle.

That is why Paul builds the whole passage on one governing principle: “subjecting yourselves to one another in the fear of Christ.” (Ephesians 5:21) Before Christ, husband and wife are both people called to lay themselves down.

Paul goes further and reveals the mystery behind it all: “For this cause a man will leave his father and mother, and will be joined to his wife. The two will become one flesh. This mystery is great, but I speak concerning Christ and of the assembly.” (Ephesians 5:31–32)

Brothers and sisters, your marriage is a sermon preached to the world. People may not read the Bible, but they read your home every day.

In May 1943, in a Nazi prison, Dietrich Bonhoeffer wrote a wedding sermon for his niece’s marriage. In it he wrote an often-quoted line: it is not your love that sustains the marriage, but from now on, the marriage that sustains your love. Brothers and sisters, feelings rise and fall, but a covenant does not; the feeling of love may ebb, but the covenant God has made stands firm.

sections.heading: 4. Integrating the 321 Vision: Let Jesus Be King in Your Home
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let us set today’s message back into the framework of 321.

The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model — as he loved the church, so I love my home; the Bible is my standard — the definition of marriage is not set by the times but by God’s word; the Holy Spirit is my guide — the many words husband and wife cannot bring themselves to say, the knots they cannot untie, only the Holy Spirit can open a way through.

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King — there is only one throne, and neither the husband nor the wife sits on it; Jesus does; let Jesus receive all the glory — the purpose of marriage is not my happiness but his glory, and when he receives the glory, we truly receive happiness.

The Goal: establish God’s system. The family is the smallest and most crucial unit of God’s system. A godly home will raise a godly next generation.

The old self is the self-centred life; the new self is selflessness. Marriage is God’s most precise mirror for exposing what we really are, and the most effective cross. While you’re single, “I” can stay well hidden; once you marry, “I” has nowhere to hide. So marriage is not meant to make you comfortable; it is meant to make you like Jesus.

Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness — and living out the fullness — of Jesus. “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20) When the husband’s old self dies, the wife meets Christ; when the wife’s old self dies, the husband meets Christ.

A shift of perspective: from the human to the divine — no longer asking “Has he done right by me?” but “What kind of person does God want me to become in this home?”; from the earthly to the heavenly — no longer measuring marriage by the world’s standards; from the temporary to the eternal — no longer sacrificing a lifelong covenant to a passing emotion; from the worldly to the godly — no longer letting the trends define my home.

The 920 practice: your spouse is the closest “2” you have. It is with those closest to us that selflessness is hardest to live out; yet those closest to us are the truest examination hall for the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions. Love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control — brothers and sisters, if these nine graces cannot grow at home, at church they are only a performance.

The 235 relationships: first let husband and wife become a like-minded “2”, spiritual companions; then build the “3”, spiritual parents and spiritual children; and finally become the “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. The order cannot be reversed. Many people build many spiritual relationships outside, while at home the most important “2” lost connection long ago.

“If a man prevails against one who is alone, two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.” (Ecclesiastes 4:12) Marriage is not two strands but three — husband, wife, and God. Without the third strand, the two will sooner or later come loose.

sections.heading: 5. Putting It into Practice: From Information to Multiplication
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. We will use the 321 “eight stages of changing our mindset” — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to put them firmly into practice.

Practice one: make one expression of love or one act of respect today

If you are married, when was your last “expression of love” or “act of respect”? Go and actually do one today.

Information: I already know that a husband needs to be respected and a wife needs to be loved. Revelation: I ask the Holy Spirit to shine on me today and show me which of the two my spouse has truly been missing lately. Conviction: I believe God’s order is right, even if the other person has not changed yet. Implementation: sometime today, do one concrete thing — a word of affirmation, a hug, a phone call, a household chore quietly done. Evaluation: in the quiet of the evening, ask yourself: when I did it, was my heart willing, or was I just ticking a box? Correction: if there was reluctance in my heart, bring that “reluctance” to God and ask him for a new heart. Repetition: one thing a day, for forty days in a row. Multiplication: once you’ve tasted the fruit, go and bring another couple to practise with you.

Practice two: if you are single, ask God to shape you into someone who can love, submit and build others up

If you are single, ask God to shape you into someone who can love, submit and build others up.

Brothers and sisters, remember: you are not “waiting for the right person”; you are “becoming the right person”. God first trains you through the people around you — parents, flatmates, colleagues, brothers and sisters — because someone who cannot be one with others now will not suddenly learn oneness one day just because of a marriage certificate.

Practice three: pray every day for your marriage (or your future marriage)

Pray every day for your marriage (or your future marriage), asking the Holy Spirit to help you become “someone willing to change first”.

“Someone willing to change first” — these few words are the key to this whole message.

The most common deadlock in marriage is this: both are waiting for the other to move first. The husband says, “When she respects me, I’ll love her”; the wife says, “When he loves me, I’ll respect him.” And so both stand where they are — for a year, ten years, thirty years.

Brothers and sisters, God never waits for us to change first. “But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (Romans 5:8) The Lord moved first, so we too can move first.

A Gentle Reminder

Marriage is not the union of two perfect people, but two people willing to let God change them walking together and building each other up.

Remember — changing yourself does more to bring oneness than changing the other person.

sections.heading: 6. Closing and Call: May My Home Be a Dwelling for God’s Glory
sections.html:
A godly marriage does not pursue “who is right and who is wrong” but “how we can be one”.

Brothers and sisters, arguing over right and wrong in marriage is a war that never has a winner. You may be right in every sentence and still drop the temperature of your home to freezing; you may win every debate and still lose the one who once was willing to weep for you.

When husband and wife are willing to lay down self and return to God’s original design — a complete union of spirit, soul and body — marriage becomes a corner of heaven.

I want to issue a call to three kinds of brothers and sisters.

First, if your marriage is at freezing point right now, God wants to say to you today: don’t first ask, “When will he change?” First ask, “Lord, what do you want me to lay down first?” You don’t need to wait for the other person; you only need to come back to God first.

Second, if your marriage is smooth and settled, God wants to remind you today too: smooth is not the same as one. Tonight, find a moment, take your spouse’s hand, and pray together once.

Third, if you have not yet entered marriage, God wants to say to you today: start being shaped now. The way you treat people today is the way you will one day treat your spouse.

Finally, brothers and sisters, let us hand the throne of our homes back to the Lord. Not the husband as king, not the wife as king, but let Jesus be King; not so that my marriage looks good, but so that Jesus receives all the glory.

May each of our homes become a dwelling place for God’s glory.

keyVerses: “Therefore a man will leave his father and his mother, and will join with his wife, and they will be one flesh.” (Genesis 2:24)
“So that they are no more two, but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, don’t let man tear apart.” (Matthew 19:6)
declarations: Brothers and sisters, please declare with me:

Lord, thank you for establishing marriage, so that I can learn oneness in love and truth. Help me to become someone who submits to you, respects my spouse and lives out the love of Christ. May my marriage glorify your name and be a testimony through which others see your grace.
practices: Make one expression of love or one act of respect today
Pray every day for your marriage (or future marriage)
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we thank you, because marriage is a good gift you established with your own hand before humanity ever sinned. You joined man and woman together, so that they would become one and display your love and glory.

Lord, forgive us. So often we run the marriage you designed by the world’s instruction manual. We treat covenant as contract, commitment as a transaction, and our spouse as an opponent. It is before those closest to us that our self-centred life shows itself most easily.

Lord, take away the pride within us. Help us to stop fighting over who is right and who is wrong, and to seek only how to be one. Make our spirits submit to you, our souls be renewed by the truth, and our bodies be restrained by love; integrate us first in our own lives, so that oneness flows naturally in our marriages.

Lord, teach husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church — willing to give themselves up, to carry responsibility, to be tender. Teach wives to replace control with trust and criticism with gentleness, and to honour the man God has entrusted to them.
Lord, we pray too for our single brothers and sisters. Shape them yourself, so that they become people who can love, submit and build others up.
Lord, we want to be “people willing to change first”. Reign as King in our homes, and may all the glory be yours. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “Therefore a man will leave his father and his mother, and will join with his wife, and they will be one flesh.” (Genesis 2:24) Share: in your mindset, is marriage more like a “contract” or a “covenant”? How has that mindset shaped your attitudes and reactions in your marriage (or future marriage)?

“Nevertheless each of you must also love his own wife even as himself; and let the wife see that she respects her husband.” (Ephesians 5:33) Share: what does your spouse (or the person closest to you) most need right now — to be “loved” or to be “respected”? What first step are you willing to take this week?
l053.title: The Two Become One Flesh
l053.subtitle: God’s Concept of Marriage (Part 1)
l053.partTitle: Unit 4 · The Prerequisite for Revival — A Change of Mindset

sections.heading: Introduction: The Last Page of the Fairy Tale Is the First Page of Marriage
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Let’s begin this morning’s devotion with a line we have all heard: “And they lived happily ever after.”

That is the last line of a fairy tale. The prince and the princess come through every peril and at last join hands in the church; the story ends there, the book closes, the lights go down. But brothers and sisters, allow me to point something out: that line is the last page of the fairy tale, but the first page of marriage. The fairy tale ends at the wedding; marriage begins at the wedding.

I once attended a very beautiful wedding. The bride’s veil trailed long down the red carpet, sunlight streamed through the church’s stained glass, and the officiating pastor asked, “Will you?” The two of them answered as one: “I will.” In that moment, everyone’s eyes were wet. Three years later I saw the same couple again, in a tiny kitchen. This time there was no veil and no sunlight, only an unwashed pot, a sentence left unfinished, and two faces turned back to back. With red eyes the wife said, “Pastor, I thought marriage was the beginning of happiness. How did it turn into the beginning of endurance?”

Many people carry dreamlike expectations of marriage, thinking that once they marry, all loneliness will be filled, all wounds healed, all lack supplied. Yet real marriage often comes with conflict, differences and challenges. Do you squeeze the toothpaste from the middle or the end? Should the air conditioning be set at twenty-four degrees or twenty-seven? Whose family do we visit for Lunar New Year? How do we spend the money? How do we raise the children? These things sound trivial, yet they are enough to turn two people who once gazed at each other with love into two people standing back to back.

If we don’t have the right view of marriage and the right expectations, we will easily give up in disappointment. And that is the saddest thing of all: it is not the marriage itself that collapsed, but our idea of marriage — and then we assume the marriage has collapsed.

Brothers and sisters, a godly marriage does not avoid problems; it learns, in the midst of problems, to love, to deny self, and to build the other up.

John Gottman, a psychologist at the University of Washington, spent many years observing couples’ interactions in his laboratory. In “The Seven Principles for Making Marriage Work”, published in 1999, he pointed out that about sixty-nine per cent of conflicts between couples are “perpetual problems” — differences rooted in personality, upbringing and values that will very likely never go away. Brothers and sisters, hearing that figure, are you discouraged or relieved? I hope you are relieved. Because it means a happy marriage has never been a marriage without problems; a happy marriage is one where two people have learned how to walk with their problems, and how to build each other up in the middle of them.

Today we will look at three things together. First, recognising the reality of marriage — accepting an imperfect spouse. Second, understanding the essence of marriage — self-giving love and a heart that builds the other up. Third, building the defences of marriage — fleeing temptation and guarding purity.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A Letter on Marriage Sent from Prison
sections.html:
Our main text today comes from Ephesians chapter 5. To grasp the weight of these verses, we must first stand where the writer stood.

Ephesians was written by the apostle Paul. In the letter he says: “I therefore, the prisoner in the Lord, beg you to walk worthily of the calling with which you were called.” (Ephesians 4:1) And again: “for which I am an ambassador in chains.” (Ephesians 6:20) The letter is generally thought to have been written between AD 60 and 62, during Paul’s first house arrest in Rome. In other words, this loftiest teaching on marriage did not come from the hand of a happily married husband but from an apostle in chains, imprisoned and alone. He was not talking romance in good times; he was talking covenant in chains.

The letter was addressed to the saints in Ephesus. Ephesus was the capital of the Roman province of Asia, with a population of perhaps 250,000, one of the most prosperous cities on the eastern Mediterranean at the time. Its most famous building was the temple of Artemis, vast in scale and counted among the seven wonders of the ancient world. Acts 19 records that Paul’s preaching in Ephesus set off a riot led by Demetrius the silversmith, and the crowd in the theatre shouted for two hours, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” (Acts 19:34) Paul himself said that “for a period of three years I didn’t cease to admonish everyone night and day with tears” (Acts 20:31).

Brothers and sisters, notice the spiritual climate of that city. The worship of Artemis was bound up with temple prostitution, and sexual licence was dressed up as religious devotion. Speaking of the holiness of marriage in a city like that was like planting a pillar in a flood.

More important still was the structure of marriage in Roman society. A form of household instruction was popular at the time, which scholars call the “household code”; it usually taught the head of the house how to manage his wife, his children and his slaves. The husband held near-absolute authority, and the wife was regarded as subordinate. Paul used this same form — but he turned its content completely upside down.

First, he begins with a governing principle: “subjecting yourselves to one another in the fear of Christ.” (Ephesians 5:21) Before either husband or wife receives any instruction, both stand together before Christ.

Second, his command to husbands is longer and weightier than his command to wives. Wives are told, “be subject to your own husbands, as to the Lord” (Ephesians 5:22) — a single short verse. Husbands, though, are told to “love your wives, even as Christ also loved the assembly, and gave himself up for it” (Ephesians 5:25), and Paul keeps going all the way to verse 33. In an age when a husband could divorce his wife at will, Paul tells husbands to die.

Brothers and sisters, what a revolutionary passage this is. Christianity did not give husbands greater authority; Christianity gave husbands a greater cross.

Our other main text is 1 Corinthians 6:18. Corinth was the capital of the province of Achaia, a port city notorious for its licentiousness. Paul wrote this letter around AD 55 — from Ephesus, as it happens. Chapter 6 deals precisely with believers taking one another to court and with sexual immorality. Straight after “Flee sexual immorality!” Paul gives the reason: “Or don’t you know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God? You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. Therefore glorify God in your body.” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20)

sections.heading: 1. Recognising the Reality of Marriage: Accepting an Imperfect Spouse
sections.html:
The first point of our lesson puts it very plainly: marriage is not a perfect union, but two imperfect people entering a covenant that needs grace.

What does Scripture say? “As it is written, ‘There is no one righteous; no, not one.’” (Romans 3:10) Paul goes on: “for all have sinned, and fall short of the glory of God.” (Romans 3:23)

The word “righteous” in Greek is δίκαιος (dikaios), meaning “meeting the standard, beyond reproach”. Paul says there is not one such person. Not “very few”, not “not many”, but “not one”.

Before marriage, many people see only the other person’s strengths. When we are courting, we wear a special pair of glasses: his stubbornness is called conviction, her fussing is called attentiveness, his silence is called steadiness, her impatience is called getting things done. Once we are married the glasses come off, and the very same traits all get new names: conviction becomes domineering, attentiveness becomes nit-picking, steadiness becomes coldness, getting things done becomes rashness. Brothers and sisters, the person has not changed; our glasses have.

Let’s go back to Genesis. God said: “It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make him a helper comparable to him.” (Genesis 2:18) The phrase “a helper comparable to him” in Hebrew is עֵזֶר כְּנֶגְדּוֹ (ezer kenegdo). Ezer means “helper”, and in the Old Testament the word is used many times of God himself — for example Psalm 33:20: “Our soul has waited for Yahweh. He is our help and our shield.” So “helper” never means second-class. And the root of kenegdo carries the sense of “opposite, corresponding to”.

Brothers and sisters, notice: what God prepared for Adam was not someone “exactly like him” but someone “standing opposite him, corresponding to him”. Only what corresponds can truly match.

This explains one of the most common experiences in marriage: why is your spouse always standing on the opposite side from you? Because that is exactly where God put them. Two identical building blocks won’t stack; a mortise and tenon hold fast precisely because one sticks out and the other is hollowed in. The tenon looks at the mortise and thinks it is missing a piece; the mortise looks at the tenon and thinks it has a piece too many. But the craftsman knows: the missing piece is there precisely to receive the extra one.

So the right view of marriage is not “I’ve found the best person” but “I am willing to love and accept the person in front of me, and believe that he or she can become better.”

Our lesson says something very sharp: conflict in marriage is often not because our spouse is too bad, but because our expectations are too high.

Psychology nods along here too. In 1977 the Stanford social psychologist Lee Ross put forward the “fundamental attribution error”. He pointed out that when we explain other people’s behaviour, we tend to attribute it to their “character” and underestimate the “circumstances” of the moment. Add what psychologists call the “actor–observer bias”, and you get a deep-rooted tendency: when explaining other people’s failures, we attribute them to their “character”; when explaining our own failures, we attribute them to the “circumstances” of the moment.

At home, it sounds like this. He forgets to buy the soy sauce — “You just don’t care about this family.” I forget to buy the soy sauce — “Work was crazy today!” He comes home late — “You don’t value me at all.” I come home late — “The traffic was terrible!” Brothers and sisters, the same thing, two rulers: a strict one for others, a lenient one for ourselves.

The Lord Jesus said the same thing two thousand years ago, and said it more strongly: “Why do you see the speck that is in your brother’s eye, but don’t consider the beam that is in your own eye?” (Matthew 7:3) The “speck” in Greek is a splinter of wood; the “beam” is the main beam of a house. The Lord is saying: we examine other people’s splinters with a magnifying glass, while walking around with a roof beam on our shoulders.

Brothers and sisters, have you ever thought about how a pearl is made? When a grain of sand gets into an oyster’s shell, the oyster can neither spit it out nor destroy it. So the oyster starts doing one thing: layer upon layer, it secretes nacre and wraps the grain of sand. Over time, the grain of sand that once hurt it becomes a smooth, glowing pearl.

Brothers and sisters, a pearl is not the result of the sand disappearing; a pearl is the result of the sand being wrapped. The grain of sand in your marriage that makes you uncomfortable — you can’t spit it out, and you can’t get rid of it; but if you are willing to wrap it in love, layer by layer, one day it will become the most precious treasure in your home.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly what the 321 vision says: the old self is the self-centred life; the new self is selflessness. The self-centred person enters marriage carrying a list filled with “he should…”; the selfless person enters marriage carrying a mirror, and looks into it first. The self-centred person asks, “Why can’t he be more like me?” The selfless person asks, “Lord, what do you want to do in me?”

When we are willing to face real differences and imperfections, we can learn real love — the kind of love that is willing to give, willing to bear with the other, willing to walk alongside them as they grow.

sections.heading: 2. The Essence of Marriage: Self-Giving Love and a Heart That Builds the Other Up
sections.html:
Scripture says: “Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the assembly, and gave himself up for it.” (Ephesians 5:25)

Brothers and sisters, notice the standard Paul uses. He didn’t say, “Love your wives the way you love your parents,” nor “love them the way other husbands do.” He said, “even as Christ also loved the assembly.” This is the highest standard in the universe, and its content can be summed up in one phrase: he gave himself up.

The Greek verb behind “gave himself up” here is παραδίδωμι (paradidōmi), which literally means “to hand over, to deliver up”. Two other uses of this word are well worth noticing. One is Judas Iscariot “betraying” — handing over — Jesus; the other is Romans 8:32: “He who didn’t spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how would he not also with him freely give us all things?” The same action can be a handing over out of betrayal, or a handing over out of love.

So, brothers and sisters, denying of self is not “having something taken from me”; it is “handing it over freely”. It isn’t that my spouse snatched my time away; it is that I willingly handed my time over. A person who has been robbed complains; a person who has given rejoices. The same event tastes completely different depending on which way the heart is facing.

What does Christ’s self-giving actually look like? Paul paints it most clearly in Philippians: “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men.” (Philippians 2:5–7)

“Emptied himself” — poured himself out. Brothers and sisters, this is exactly what 321 calls selflessness. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness of Jesus and living it out. Only an empty cup can be filled; a clenched fist can catch nothing.

Paul also says: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)

So our lesson is right: a godly marriage is not centred on “me” but starts from “you”; it does not demand that the other satisfy me, but works hard to meet the other’s needs.

Brothers and sisters, this is the heart of the 321 vision. What is pride? Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights, and wanting to take God’s place. In marriage, pride looks like this: I want to be the one who’s right, I want to be the one who decides, I want to be the one who is served. What is humility? Humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. In marriage, humility looks like this: let him be him, let God be God, and let me do what I ought to do.

And marriage is the place in all the world that most clearly proves the saying: pride provokes pride, and both are wounded; humility draws out humility, and both win.

Have you noticed that couples’ quarrels follow a law: the volume automatically matches. You raise it a notch, and so does he; you cool by a degree, and so does she. That is pride provoking pride, and in the end both are hurt and nobody wins. But the reverse is also true: when one person softens first and says, “I’m sorry, I was too hasty just now,” you’ll be amazed to see the other person’s shoulders relax too. That is humility drawing out humility, and both win.

In a study published in 1992, John Gottman and Robert Levenson found that in stable marriages, the ratio of positive to negative behaviours in a couple’s interactions was about five to one, while for couples heading for divorce the ratio was markedly lower. Brothers and sisters, this is not about doing arithmetic; it is about understanding one thing: one wounding word takes five kind words to repair. That is why Scripture says: “Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear.” (Ephesians 4:29)

Next our lesson says something very precious: denying of self is the deepest lesson in marriage. When we are willing to set aside “what I want” and think about “what the other person needs”, the marriage begins to mature.

So, the lesson goes on, every accommodation, every bit of understanding and every change is an exercise of love.

C. S. Lewis put it well in “Mere Christianity”. He said that love, as distinct from “being in love”, is not merely a feeling but a deep unity, maintained by the will and deliberately strengthened by habit. Brothers and sisters, feelings ebb like the tide, but the will can grip the seabed like an anchor. And in the sermon Dietrich Bonhoeffer wrote in prison for his niece’s wedding, he said: it is not your love that sustains the marriage, but from now on, the marriage that sustains your love.

Then comes the most crucial sentence in the whole lesson: changing the other person is God’s work; changing ourselves is our responsibility.

The lesson quotes a vivid saying: “The hard things, God does; the easy things, we do.” Changing others is the hard thing — hand it to God; changing ourselves is the easy thing — we are willing to obey and do it.

This is what 321 calls the priority of relationships: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. Many couples get the order backwards — first they deal with things (who washes the dishes, who picks up the kids), then with people (it’s all your fault), then only at the end with themselves; as for God, that can wait until the row is over. No wonder the more they sort it out, the more tangled it gets.

And what is the aim of love? Paul makes it plain: “that he might sanctify it, having cleansed it by the washing of water with the word, that he might present the assembly to himself gloriously, not having spot or wrinkle or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without defect.” (Ephesians 5:26–27)

Brothers and sisters, look: the aim of Christ’s love for the church is that the church be “sanctified” and presented “gloriously”. In other words, Christ’s love has a direction — his love is meant to bring the one he loves to her most beautiful self.

That is what it means to build someone up. Building someone up is not indulging them, nor is it remaking them. Indulging says, “Whatever you do is fine; I’m staying out of it.” Remaking says, “You must live the way I do.” Building up says, “I want to help you become the person God wants you to be.”

So Paul goes on: “Even so husbands also ought to love their own wives as their own bodies. He who loves his own wife loves himself.” (Ephesians 5:28) And Peter says: “You husbands, in the same way, live with your wives according to knowledge, giving honor to the woman, as to the weaker vessel, as also being joint heirs of the grace of life, that your prayers may not be hindered.” (1 Peter 3:7)

This is exactly what 321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. A man who speaks eloquently from the pulpit but won’t apologise when he gets home has a ministry that is hollow at the core.

Finally, bringing the 920 practice into marriage could hardly be more fitting. Everyone we have a relationship with is one of our “2”s; and of all our “2”s, the one closest to us, the most real, and the hardest, is our spouse. We practise living a life of selflessness (the 0), bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (the 9) of its expressions — “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23).

When we learn to deny ourselves and are willing to build the other up, our marriage will be built up in the love of God.

sections.heading: 3. The Defences of Marriage: Fleeing Temptation and Guarding Purity
sections.html:
Our lesson is very practical here: marriage is not a safe zone you secure once and for all; it is a relationship that has to be tended continually.

We often think that getting married puts us in a safe deposit box. It doesn’t. Even after marriage, we may still meet someone who stirs our heart, or someone may show an interest in us. The lesson defines this with two very balanced phrases: it is not “impossible”, but it is never “normal”.

Brothers and sisters, these two phrases deserve to be chewed slowly. To say it is “not impossible” is honesty — we still have the flesh, we still live in the world, and we need not pretend we are immune to everything. To say it is “never normal” is the standard — a stirred heart is not a normal state we may indulge, still less an excuse we may justify. Honest without being indulgent, watchful without being panicked — that is a godly view of marriage.

What does Scripture command? “Flee sexual immorality! ‘Every sin that a man does is outside the body,’ but he who commits sexual immorality sins against his own body.” (1 Corinthians 6:18)

The word “flee” in Greek is φεύγετε (pheugete), the present imperative of the verb φεύγω, meaning “keep fleeing, keep on running”. The English word “fugitive” is related to the same root.

Brothers and sisters, notice how precise Scripture’s wording is. About the devil, Scripture says: “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” (James 4:7) About sexual immorality, Scripture says: “Flee sexual immorality!” One you resist; the other you run from.

Why the difference? Because there are some battlefields where simply standing there means you’ve already lost. Resisting the devil means standing on the foundation of truth; but with the temptation to sexual immorality, there is no safe distance at which you can “stand and negotiate”. You do not resist this temptation by willpower; you get away from it by “fleeing”.

The best example in Scripture is Joseph. In Potiphar’s house he faced his master’s wife’s advances day after day. Scripture records: “She caught him by his garment, saying, ‘Lie with me!’ He left his garment in her hand, and ran outside.” (Genesis 39:12)

And the result? He lost his cloak but kept his character; he went to prison but did not lose God’s presence. Scripture says: “But Yahweh was with Joseph, and showed kindness to him, and gave him favor in the sight of the keeper of the prison.” (Genesis 39:21) Brothers and sisters, only those who can let go of the cloak can keep hold of the crown.

Paul gave Timothy the same instruction: “Flee from youthful lusts; but pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace with those who call on the Lord out of a pure heart.” (2 Timothy 2:22) Notice that this verse has both “flee” and “pursue”; both “leaving” and “with those who call on the Lord out of a pure heart”. Fleeing is not running away alone; it is running into a pure community.

The Lord Jesus draws this line of defence even further forward: “But I tell you that everyone who gazes at a woman to lust after her has committed adultery with her already in his heart.” (Matthew 5:28) The Lord does not mean to drive us to despair; he wants us to understand that the battlefield is not in our actions but in our hearts. The line of defence is not at the bedroom door; it is at the entrance of the eyes and the thoughts.

That is why righteous Job made a covenant long ago: “I made a covenant with my eyes, how then should I look lustfully at a young woman?” (Job 31:1) And Solomon says: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23)

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly what 321 says: the fruit of a whole life springs from the heart. Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and you’ll worry, rely on the heart and you’ll rejoice. Guard your marriage by your own willpower and the guarding grows ever more exhausting; guard your marriage by the guidance of the Holy Spirit and the guarding grows ever more free.

In 1972, the Stanford psychologist Walter Mischel and his colleagues carried out the famous “marshmallow experiment”. The researcher put a marshmallow in front of a child and said: if you can wait until I come back before eating it, you can have two. It turned out that the children who managed to wait did not do it by “staring at the marshmallow and holding out”. They turned their faces away, sang songs, covered their eyes with their hands, or simply imagined the marshmallow was a white cloud. Mischel later pointed out that the key to effective self-control lies in “diverting attention”, not in “confronting the desire head-on”.

Later research went further. A study by Wilhelm Hofmann and colleagues, published in 2012 in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, found that people with high self-control are not better than others at “resisting” temptation; rather, they “encounter” temptation less often than others — because they habitually arrange their lives to stay away from situations that trigger desire.

So allow me to say a few concrete, practical things. Don’t take your phone to bed. Don’t have heart-to-heart talks alone with someone of the opposite sex late at night. Don’t, in the name of “counselling” or “praying together”, build a relationship that only the two of you know about. In private messages on social media, if there is a single line you would not want your spouse to see, that line has already crossed the boundary.

Some say this is too strict. Brothers and sisters, why can a submarine withstand the pressure of the deep sea? Because it has one watertight bulkhead after another. If one compartment floods, the others stay dry. Why do cities keep firebreak lanes? Because fire never sends a warning. Flood banks are not built on the day the flood comes; they are built on sunny days.

As our lesson rightly says: husband and wife must both learn to guard their own hearts and give temptation no opening. When feelings arise, turn immediately to God, go back to your spouse, and seek honest communication and mutual watchfulness.

Paul also reminds married couples: “Don’t deprive one another, unless it is by consent for a season, that you may give yourselves to fasting and prayer, and may be together again, that Satan doesn’t tempt you because of your lack of self-control.” (1 Corinthians 7:5) Brothers and sisters, Satan does take his opportunities. We need not fear him, but neither should we give him a foothold. The writer of Hebrews says: “Let marriage be held in honor among all, and let the bed be undefiled; but God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterers.” (Hebrews 13:4)

This is also the training ground for the 321 “235 relationships”. Become a “2” with someone selfless — a spiritual companion. Brothers and sisters, every married person needs a spiritual companion of the same sex with whom they can speak the truth. When a thought has only just stirred in your heart, do you have someone you can call and say, “I’m in a bit of danger lately”? Scripture says: “If a man prevails against one who is alone, two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.” (Ecclesiastes 4:12) Who are the three strands? The husband, the wife, and the God who has bound you together.

The lesson’s last sentence I want you to read aloud, brothers and sisters, right into your hearts: if both resolve in their hearts — “We belong only to each other, and we both belong to God” — the marriage can become a strong city wall, growing sweeter and deeper with the years.

The prophet Malachi says: “Therefore take heed to your spirit, and let no one deal treacherously against the wife of his youth.” (Malachi 2:15) Brothers and sisters, God cares how you treat the one who walked with you through the years of your youth.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: Let Jesus Be King in Your Home
sections.html:
The Three Foundations are the three piles driven in beneath a marriage.

First, Jesus is my role model. When Paul discusses marriage he quotes no philosopher at all; he says only this: “even as Christ also loved the assembly, and gave himself up for it.” (Ephesians 5:25) The textbook for marriage is not other people’s families; it is the cross.

Second, the Bible is my standard. When feelings say, “I don’t love him any more,” the standard says, “Love is patient and is kind” (1 Corinthians 13:4). Feelings change; the standard does not. Building a marriage on feelings is building a house on sand.

Third, the Holy Spirit is my guide. The hardest thing between husband and wife is not knowing what to do but being unable to do it. The fruit of the Spirit is not squeezed out; it grows. “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23)

The Two Core Values are the two doors of a marriage.

First, let Jesus be King. Brothers and sisters, if a home has two kings, there will be war every day; if a home has one king, and that king is Jesus, both people can rest. What do couples fight over? Often not the issue itself but the throne. When we yield the throne to Jesus, we can both step down, stand before him, and be servants together.

Second, let Jesus receive all the glory. This is exactly where the lesson’s closing points: making marriage a temple that bears witness to God’s glory. Your marriage is a pulpit. How you quarrel, how you make up, how you hold hands through hardship — your children, your neighbours and your colleagues are all watching.

The Goal is to establish God’s system. Brothers and sisters, God’s system does not start with church organisation; it starts at the family dinner table. Marriage is the first system God established, and the smallest church. If this smallest unit is won by God, the whole system has roots.

Now to the self-centred life and selflessness. The root of humanity’s fall is the self-centred life, and the root of our problems is pride. Marriage shows this up with perfect clarity. A self-centred marriage is two people each putting themselves in the middle and pulling against each other; a selfless marriage is two people putting Christ in the middle and drawing closer to each other. Have you noticed a simple fact of geometry? If two lines each head outwards, they only grow further apart; if both head towards the same centre, they must draw ever closer. The closer a couple come to God, the closer they come to each other.

The fivefold change happens here too: the mindset changes — I no longer think marriage exists to satisfy me; the life changes — I begin to have a self-giving heart; daily living changes — I start getting up early to pray for my spouse, and start taking back that wounding word; relationships change — the atmosphere at home changes, and the children laugh; ministry changes — when someone asks, “Why is your family different?”, the gospel has a way out.

The shift of perspective is just as crucial: from the human view to God’s view — marriage is not my right but God’s trust; from the earthly to the heavenly — this relationship is meant to point to Christ and the church; from the temporary to the eternal — not for winning one argument but for the fruit of a lifetime; from the worldly to the godly — not measuring happiness by the world’s standards.

The 920 practice reminds us: your spouse is the “2” closest to you, and the person who most needs you to live out selflessness (the 0). The nine graces are to grow at home, every day.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Turning Mindset into Footsteps
sections.html:
Our lesson gives us four practices. We will take hold of them one by one, and use the “eight stages of changing our mindset” — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to fix them firmly into our daily living.

Practice one: pray for your spouse every day, asking God to show you what in him (or her) is worth giving thanks for.

Brothers and sisters, notice that the focus of this practice is not “asking God to change him” but “asking God to let me see”. The same person, seen with complaining eyes, is full of faults; seen with thankful eyes, is full of grace. I suggest keeping a small notebook and writing down one thing about your spouse to be thankful for each day, for thirty days, with no repeats. The first week will go smoothly, the second week you’ll get stuck, and by the third week you’ll begin to know your spouse all over again.

Practice two: when your spouse disappoints you, don’t rush to change them; first ask God to change your own heart.

This is the central practice of this lesson. Next time a conflict comes, say first in your heart, “Lord, change me first.” Then give yourself a rule: while your emotions are rising, do only three things — close your mouth, drink some water, pray. Speak only once your heart has settled. Remember the saying: changing the other person is God’s work; changing ourselves is our responsibility.

Practice three: list three small things you can do for your spouse, and do them today.

Notice the word “today”. Not “when I have time”, not “when he changes first”. The three small things might be pouring her a glass of water, offering to wash that pot, or sending a message that says, “Thanks for all your hard work today.” Brothers and sisters, a marriage is not held together by one big present a year; it is held together by three hundred and sixty-five small things.

Practice four: if temptation comes, turn away at once, and pray that God will guard your heart and your eyes.

“At once” is the key. Not “when I’ve thought it through”, not “I’m only chatting”. Joseph’s example comes down to three words: ran outside. And set up visible lines of defence for yourself: no phone in the bedroom, no late-night heart-to-hearts alone with someone of the opposite sex, no conversations your spouse is not allowed to see.

Now let’s walk these four practices through the eight stages.

Stage one, Information. This morning’s devotion is information — you now know that marriage is two imperfect people entering a covenant that needs grace; you know that the essence of love is self-giving and building the other up; you know that the way to defend it is to flee. But brothers and sisters, information doesn’t change people; it only opens the door.

Stage two, Revelation. Ask the Holy Spirit to turn information into revelation. Be still for one minute and let God say one thing to you. Perhaps it’s a picture, perhaps it’s a sentence: “It’s been a long time since you really looked at her.” In that moment you are not studying doctrine; you are being touched by God.

Stage three, Conviction. Conviction is saying in your heart, “Yes, Lord, you are right.” Not grudging acceptance but willing surrender. Implementation without conviction lasts only a few days.

Stage four, Implementation. Begin with the smallest thing. When you get home today, be the first to say “I’m sorry”, or the first to say “Thank you.”

Stage five, Evaluation. Each week, set a regular time — perhaps Sunday evening — to be still and ask: this week, how many times did I put the focus on myself? How many times did I choose to deny myself?

Stage six, Correction. After evaluating, don’t condemn yourself; correct course. If you find you always lose your temper when you’re tired, adjust your routine; if you find you always explode over a certain topic, pray first and then talk.

Stage seven, Repetition. Brothers and sisters, no lesson in marriage is passed in one go. Only by repetition does it become life. A habit is not formed by resolve; it is formed by repetition.

Stage eight, Multiplication. When God has done his work in your marriage, pass it on. Walk alongside a younger couple and be their spiritual parents; share honestly in your small group the road you have travelled. Paul says: “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.” (2 Timothy 2:2) Multiplication is the last stage of the practice, and the beginning of the system.

A Gentle Reminder

Our lesson leaves us a beautiful line: marriage is not “I love you, so I’m happy” but “I love you, and I’m willing even when I’m not happy.”

Feelings are like the weather; faithfulness is like the climate. The weather changes every day, but the climate defines a place. A marriage does not live by the weather; a marriage lives by the climate.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: Let Marriage Be a Temple That Bears Witness to Glory
sections.html:
A godly marriage is not a dreamy fairy tale but a journey of faith. A fairy tale is written for you by someone else; a journey you walk yourself. A fairy tale has an ending; a journey has companions.

When we make God the centre and love the starting point, marriage is no longer a relationship that wears each other down, but a blessing in which each builds the other up.

So let us learn to deny ourselves in love, to grow in faith, and to walk together in grace, so that our marriages become temples that bear witness to God’s glory.

What is a “temple”? A temple is where God is present, where people worship, where glory is revealed. Brothers and sisters, your home can be a temple. Not because it is big enough, beautiful enough or whole enough, but because Jesus is King there.

The psalmist says: “Unless Yahweh builds the house, they who build it labor in vain. Unless Yahweh watches over the city, the watchman guards it in vain.” (Psalm 127:1)

This morning I want to issue three calls to you, brothers and sisters.

The first call is a call to our eyes. Ask the Lord to take away our fault-finding glasses and let us see that person afresh — he is not righteous, and neither are you; but you are both people God loves.
