The second call is a call to our hearts. Ask the Lord to give us Christ’s self-giving heart. Choose one thing today: set aside “what I want” and do “what the other person needs”.

The third call is a call to our feet. If you know in your heart that a boundary has already become blurred, ask the Lord to give you Joseph’s courage — drop the cloak, turn and run. Run today, not tomorrow.

And behind these three calls there is only one centre: let Jesus be King in your home, and let Jesus receive all the glory from your marriage.

The Lord says: “What therefore God has joined together, don’t let man tear apart.” (Matthew 19:6) What God has joined together, God himself will take responsibility for keeping.

keyVerses: Ephesians 5:25–27

“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the assembly, and gave himself up for it; that he might sanctify it, having cleansed it by the washing of water with the word, that he might present the assembly to himself gloriously, not having spot or wrinkle or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without defect.”
1 Corinthians 6:18
“Flee sexual immorality! ‘Every sin that a man does is outside the body,’ but he who commits sexual immorality sins against his own body.”
practices: Pray for your spouse every day, asking God to show you what in him (or her) is worth giving thanks for.
When your spouse disappoints you, don’t rush to change them; first ask God to change your own heart.
List three small things you can do for your spouse, and do them today.
If temptation comes, turn away at once, and pray that God will guard your heart and your eyes.
prayer: Lord, we bow before you.

Thank you for letting me learn love and denying of self in marriage. Lord, I confess that I often hope the other person will change, yet I won’t let you change me; I often remember his faults, yet forget how much patience you have shown me.
Renew my eyes, so that I see what is worth giving thanks for in my spouse, and accept his imperfections, just as you accept mine.
Give me the heart of Christ; help me learn to build up, to respect and to forgive; help me set aside “what I want” and see “what he needs”.
Build a hedge around my marriage; guard my heart and guard my eyes. When temptation comes, give me the courage to turn and run; when my feelings are weak, uphold my will by your Spirit.
Lord Jesus, I give my home to you. Reign as King in my home, and receive all the glory. May my marriage reflect your love, so that people see your glory among us.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: 1 Corinthians 13:4–7: “Love is patient and is kind. Love doesn’t envy. Love doesn’t brag, is not proud, doesn’t behave itself inappropriately, doesn’t seek its own way, is not provoked, takes no account of evil; doesn’t rejoice in unrighteousness, but rejoices with the truth; bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, and endures all things.” Read this passage aloud, putting your own name in place of “love”. Which line can you least bring yourself to say? That line is where God wants to work in your marriage today. Share one concrete small thing in which you are willing to “set aside what I want and do what the other person needs”.

Genesis 39:12: “She caught him by his garment, saying, ‘Lie with me!’ He left his garment in her hand, and ran outside.” What Joseph threw away was a cloak; what he kept was his character. In your life right now, is there a “cloak” you need to throw away (perhaps a relationship, a habit, a time of day, a social media app)? Which spiritual companion are you willing to invite to be part of your “threefold cord”, keeping watch with you?

l054.partTitle: Unit 4 · The Prerequisite for Revival — A Change of Mindset

l055.intro:
I. Introduction: Is the Church Really Short of Gifted People?

Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning we are going to think together about a mindset that looks very ordinary, yet quietly decides the future of the church: the concept of developing people.

If you visit churches in different places and chat with pastors and co-workers, you will almost certainly hear the same sigh: “Our church just doesn’t have the people.” The Sunday school is short of teachers, the choir is short of an accompanist, the small groups are short of leaders, and the youth ministry can’t find mentors. Year after year this sigh is handed down from one pastor to the next, like a knot no one can untie, binding the church to the spot where it stands.

But brothers and sisters, allow me to ask a question that may sting a little: is the problem really that there are “not enough gifted people”? Or is the problem that our “mindset about developing people” is wrong?

Many churches have a “list of workers,” and it always carries the same seven or eight names. Wherever there’s a gap, someone is pulled from that list; whenever something goes wrong, someone on that list is sent to patch it. Ten years go by, and the names on the list have hardly changed — only each name has a few more wrinkles and a little more weariness behind it. Brothers and sisters, that isn’t “a shortage of gifted people.” That is “not developing people.”

This is a blind spot many churches share. We think gifted people are “found,” “waited for,” or “picked out.” So, like shoppers picking fruit at the market, we turn things over and over, hoping to find one without a scar, without a bruise, perfect in colour. But brothers and sisters, people are not fruit. People are seeds. A seed left on the shelf will always be a seed; only when it is buried in the soil, passes through the dark and breaks open its shell does it grow into a great tree.

There is a deep principle in the Bible: God never goes looking for “ready-made people”; God “makes people.” When Moses was called, he said: “O Lord, I am not eloquent, neither before now, nor since you have spoken to your servant; for I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue.” (Exodus 4:10) By human standards that is a terrible résumé — a man who cannot speak, sent to speak to Pharaoh. Yet Yahweh said: “Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth, and teach you what you shall speak.” (Exodus 4:12) God did not replace the man; God made the man.

David was the same. He was the youngest in his family, the one out in the fields minding the sheep. The prophet Samuel was looking at appearances, but Yahweh said to Samuel: “Don’t look on his face, or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him; for I don’t see as man sees. For man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.” (1 Samuel 16:7) Brothers and sisters, if even Samuel could misjudge, what makes us believe we can pick out the “gifted” at a glance?

What God wants of us is not to “wait” for gifted people but to “develop” them; not to “pick the most capable” but to “equip those who are willing to learn.” In this lesson we will face together three turns in our mindset:

First, only when we dare to use “people who fall” can we develop “people who walk.”

Second, courses can teach theory, but only practice produces gifted people.

Third, give opportunities, and give encouragement too — help those who fall to stand up again.

Put simply, these three turns are the first step of what the 321 vision calls “the fivefold change”: a change of mindset. Once the mindset changes, the life changes; once the life changes, daily living changes; once daily living changes, relationships change; once relationships change, ministry changes. Today the key is not method but mindset. May the Lord, this morning, personally turn that rusty screw inside us.

II. Scripture Background: Two Passages, One Thread

Before we come to the three key points, let’s stand on the ground of Scripture and put our roots down deep.

sections.heading: 1. The Background of Proverbs 24:16
sections.html:
The bulk of Proverbs comes from Solomon, king of Israel. 1 Kings 4:32 records: “He spoke three thousand proverbs; and his songs numbered one thousand five.” Solomon reigned over Israel in the tenth century BC, and the proverbs he left behind are the high point of Hebrew wisdom literature. Proverbs is not a legal code; it takes the truth of fearing Yahweh and condenses it into one saying after another — wisdom for life that you can put in your pocket and carry with you.

This passage in Proverbs 24 belongs to an appendix of “sayings of the wise,” and its theme is the different outcomes of the righteous and the wicked in times of trouble. Verses 15–16 say: “Don’t lay in wait, wicked man, against the habitation of the righteous. Don’t destroy his resting place; for a righteous man falls seven times and rises up again; but the wicked are overthrown by calamity.”

Notice that the contrast here is not “the righteous never fall; only the wicked fall.” The righteous fall too — “seven times.” In Hebrew, “seven” (שֶׁבַע, sheva) is the number of completeness, meaning “again and again, more times than you can count.” What the Holy Spirit wants us to see through Solomon is not that the righteous are luckier, but that the righteous have something the wicked don’t — he “rises up again.” This “rising” (קוּם, qum) means to stand, to get up, to be set firmly on one’s feet once more.

Brothers and sisters, misread, this verse becomes an excuse for taking sin lightly; read rightly, it becomes the mainstay of everyone who is learning to serve. The difference between the righteous and the wicked is not how many times they fall, but where they go after they fall. The prophet Micah said the same thing: “Don’t rejoice against me, my enemy. When I fall, I will arise. When I sit in darkness, Yahweh will be a light to me.” (Micah 7:8)

This is exactly the first mindset we want to establish today: if the church is to have “people who walk,” it must first welcome “people who fall.”

sections.heading: 2. The Background of John 8:31–32
sections.html:
The Gospel of John was written by the apostle John, the disciple whom the Lord Jesus loved. It is generally thought to have been written around AD 80–90, for believers scattered in many places and for those who did not yet know Christ. Its purpose is stated in John 20:31: “but these are written, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name.”

The setting of chapter 8 is the temple in Jerusalem, at the close of the Feast of Tabernacles. Jesus had just said, “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12), and a fierce debate with the Pharisees followed. The text says “many believed in him” (John 8:30), and the Lord Jesus immediately turned to this group who had only just believed and spoke these words.

Pay special attention to the order of the Lord’s words: “If you remain in my word, then you are truly my disciples. You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.” (John 8:31–32) First “remain,” then “know”; first act, then understand. This order runs completely against our natural way of thinking. We always assume we have to understand first and then act, but the Lord says: go and do it, and you will understand.

The word behind “remain” (the Chinese Union Version: “continually keep”) is μένω (menō), which appears more than forty times in John’s Gospel, meaning “to settle down, to stay inside, to keep on without leaving.” The same word is used in John 15: “Remain in me, and I in you.” (John 15:4) So the disciples the Lord Jesus speaks of are not students who collect a certificate after hearing a single class, but people who live in the Lord’s word over the long haul and act according to it.

Brothers and sisters, put these two passages together and you have the main thread of this lesson: truth is known in the doing, and gifted people are formed through falling. If a church treats service as “a stage for performance,” it will only produce actors; only if a church treats service as “a school for growth” will it produce disciples.

III. Key Point 1: Only When We Dare to Use “People Who Fall” Can We Develop “People Who Walk”

sections.heading: 1. A Simple but Forgotten Spiritual Equation
sections.html:
If a church only uses “people who walk,” no new “people who walk” will ever appear. That sentence is worth chewing over again and again this morning.

Why? Because every “person who walks” began as a “person who falls,” without exception. The preacher who speaks so fluently from the pulpit today had sweaty palms the first time he preached; the steadiest small-group leader today once let an awkward silence drag on longer than the prayer the first time she led a group.

Parents all over the world understand this. No mother says to her one-year-old: “When you’ve learned to walk, then I’ll let you down on the floor.” That would be absurd. It is precisely because children are put down on the floor and fall again and again that they learn to walk. Yet in the church we often forget this spiritual principle and say to those just beginning to serve: “When you’re mature, then I’ll give you a chance.” And the result? They never become mature, because maturity itself requires opportunity.

sections.heading: 2. Falling Is Not Sinning — It Is a Necessary Part of Learning
sections.html:
Here we must make a very important distinction, so that grace isn’t misused.

The Bible speaks of two kinds of “falling.” One is moral and spiritual collapse. That is sin, and it must be confessed, repented of and dealt with. The apostle Paul says: “Therefore let him who thinks he stands be careful that he doesn’t fall.” (1 Corinthians 10:12) The church must not tolerate this kind of falling.

The other is the slips, mistakes, shortcomings and inexperience that come with learning. This is not sin; it is the tuition fee of growth. Slides shown in the wrong order, a sermon that runs ten minutes over, the wrong word said on a pastoral visit, an item left out of the event programme, a hymn started in the wrong key — none of these is sin. This is learning to walk.

When we talk today about “daring to use people who fall,” we mean the second kind. If we treat the second kind as though it were the first and look at learners’ mistakes with the eyes of a judge, the church will turn from “a school for growth” into “a stage for performance.” On a stage, the most important thing is not to make mistakes; in a school, the most important thing is to make progress. A stage needs actors; a school needs students. And what the Lord Jesus wants has always been disciples, not actors.

sections.heading: 3. The Way of Developing People the Lord Jesus Himself Modelled
sections.html:
The Lord Jesus is our supreme role model. The way he led his disciples was precisely to “dare to use people who fall.”

Mark 3:14 says: “He appointed twelve, that they might be with him, and that he might send them out to preach.” Look at the order and the pairing of these two things: being with him, and then being sent out to preach. The Lord didn’t wait until they were mature to send them; he put them out into the harvest field while they were still very rough around the edges.

Let’s look at what kind of people these twelve were.

Peter was impulsive. He walked a few steps on the water and then began to sink: “But when he saw that the wind was strong, he was afraid, and beginning to sink, he cried out, saying, ‘Lord, save me!’” (Matthew 14:30) The Lord Jesus didn’t say, “You don’t qualify; don’t come back next time.” Scripture says: “Immediately Jesus stretched out his hand, took hold of him, and said to him, ‘You of little faith, why did you doubt?’” (Matthew 14:31) Those words, “immediately stretched out his hand,” are the essence of the kingdom’s way of developing people. Support comes first; correction comes after.

James and John competed to be the greatest. They actually said to the Lord: “Grant to us that we may sit, one at your right hand, and one at your left hand, in your glory.” (Mark 10:37) What naked self-centredness! The Lord Jesus didn’t dismiss them; he patiently turned their mindset around: “But it shall not be so among you, but whoever wants to become great among you shall be your servant.” (Mark 10:43)

Mark turned back halfway. Acts 15:38 says: “But Paul didn’t think that it was a good idea to take with them someone who had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia, and didn’t go with them to do the work.” Mark fell, and everyone knew it; it even became the spark that split Paul and Barnabas apart. But the story didn’t stop there. Years later, Paul wrote to Timothy from a Roman prison: “Take Mark, and bring him with you, for he is useful to me for service.” (2 Timothy 4:11) The young man who had once turned back went on to write the first of the Gospels.

Brothers and sisters, if Barnabas hadn’t insisted on giving Mark another chance, our Bible today might be missing the Gospel of Mark. That gives us a sober reminder: the person we so easily give up on today may be the very one God is preparing to write the next “Gospel of Mark.”

Most moving of all are the Lord’s words to Peter: “Simon, Simon, behold, Satan asked to have all of you, that he might sift you as wheat, but I prayed for you, that your faith wouldn’t fail. You, when once you have turned again, establish your brothers.” (Luke 22:31–32) The Lord knew full well that Peter would fall, yet he entrusted him in advance with the task of “establishing his brothers.” The Lord didn’t wait until Peter stopped falling before using him; the Lord was ready to catch him after he fell. After the resurrection, on the shore of the Sea of Tiberias, the Lord asked him three times: “Do you love me?” (John 21:15–17) Three questions to answer three denials; three commissions that put a fallen man back in the place of shepherding.

sections.heading: 4. The Science of Developing People, Seen in a Baby Learning to Walk
sections.html:
Science, too, bears witness to this spiritual principle.

In a study published in 2012 in the journal “Psychological Science,” developmental psychologist Karen Adolph of New York University and her research team observed toddlers who had just learned to walk, and found that on average they took over 2,300 steps and fell about seventeen times an hour. The researchers concluded that a great deal of walking and a great deal of falling are exactly what is needed for motor skills to be mastered.

In other words, falling isn’t a failure in learning to walk; falling is part of learning to walk.

Neuroscience also tells us that when a movement is practised again and again, the myelin sheath wrapped around the nerve fibres gradually thickens, so that signals travel faster and more reliably. Skill isn’t built up by understanding; it’s built up by repetition. Spiritual gifts are the same: they have to be used before they can be honed.

Stanford psychologist Professor Carol Dweck, in her research, distinguished between a “fixed mindset” and a “growth mindset” (see her 2006 book “Mindset”). People with a fixed mindset see failure as proof that “I can’t do it,” and so they avoid challenges; people with a growth mindset see failure as a signal that “I haven’t learned it yet,” and so they rise to meet challenges. Dweck’s research showed that children praised for “working hard” were more willing to choose difficult tasks than children praised for “being clever.”

Brothers and sisters, the culture of a church shapes the mindset of its workers. A church that only applauds “flawless performance” will raise a group of people so afraid of mistakes that they won’t attempt anything; only a church that affirms “faithful giving of oneself” will raise a group of people who dare to learn and grow bolder with every setback. When the Lord Jesus commended his servant, he said: “Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things.” (Matthew 25:21) The Lord looks for faithfulness, not perfection.

sections.heading: 5. Applying the 321 Vision
sections.html:
This key point touches the very heart of the 321 vision: the self-centred life and selflessness.

Why are churches afraid to use “people who fall”? The surface reason is “we’re worried about the quality of the ministry”; the deeper reason is often “we’re afraid of losing face.” We’re afraid people will laugh that our worship isn’t professional, afraid newcomers will think we’re not up to standard, afraid my reputation as a leader will suffer. Brothers and sisters, that is the self-centred life. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.

When a leader clings tightly to every ministry and says, “It’s quicker if I just do it myself,” he is really seizing rights, using his own ability to take the place of God’s work in someone else’s life. And when a leader is willing to step back and let a green young brother go up front, and endure those twenty minutes of halting delivery, he is laying down his rights and returning to his originally intended position — letting God do in that brother what God means to do.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. A church that dares to use people who fall is a humble church; and humility spreads like ripples, bringing forth a whole generation of workers who are willing to learn and willing to let others learn.

The 321 vision says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. When we put “a flawless ministry” above “people’s growth,” the order has been turned upside down. A beautifully run ministry in which no one is built up is a losing deal; a plain, simple ministry in which five people grow up is a kingdom investment.

Jesus is my role model — he dared to use people who fall, and we must dare to use people who fall too.

IV. Key Point 2: Courses Can Teach Theory, but Only Practice Produces Gifted People

sections.heading: 1. The First Reaction We Most Easily Fall Into
sections.html:
When many churches set out to develop people, the first thing they think of is “running a course.”

Short of small-group leaders? Run a “small-group leader training class.” Short of Sunday school teachers? Run a “teacher training course.” Workers not committed enough? Run a “discipleship class.” Of course courses matter; teaching is one of the gifts God has given. But brothers and sisters, if course after course has been run and yet there are no more gifted people than before, we have to ask honestly: has something gone wrong somewhere?

The problem is this: courses can teach theory, but only practice produces gifted people.

It’s like a child learning to walk. You can explain to him the mechanics of walking — how the weight shifts, how the knees bend, how the foot meets the ground. You can give three lectures, hand out notes and even set an exam. But if he is never put down on the floor, he will never learn to walk. In the same way, you can memorise every point of swimming technique until you know it backwards, but if you never get into the water, you will never swim.

sections.heading: 2. The Lord Jesus’ Order: First Remain, Then Know
sections.html:
One of this lesson’s theme passages gives us exactly the kingdom’s law of learning. The Lord Jesus said: “If you remain in my word, then you are truly my disciples. You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.” (John 8:31–32)

Notice this order once again: first “remain,” then “know.” Not knowing first and then keeping his word, but keeping his word and then knowing.

Elsewhere the Lord said the same thing: “If anyone desires to do his will, he will know about the teaching, whether it is from God, or if I am speaking from myself.” (John 7:17) Obedience is the doorway to knowledge. The freedom of truth isn’t grasped in a notebook; it is revealed in action.

James puts it even more directly: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.” (James 1:22) Notice the words “deluding your own selves.” For those who hear but don’t do, the greatest danger isn’t ignorance but illusion — they think they understand. Someone who has sat through ten evangelism classes yet never opened their mouth to a single person will mistakenly think they know how to share the gospel; someone who has read ten books on prayer yet never shed a tear for a lost soul will mistakenly think they know how to pray.

When the Lord Jesus trained his disciples, he never just ran a course. Matthew 10 records how the Lord sent out the twelve disciples; Luke 10 records how the Lord appointed seventy others and sent them out two by two. How much did these people understand at the time? They knew nothing yet of the cross, and the resurrection was a complete mystery to them. But the Lord sent them anyway. And the result? “The seventy returned with joy, saying, ‘Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name!’” (Luke 10:17)

Before they went out, it was theory; when they came back, it was testimony. What stood in between was one word: “practice.”

sections.heading: 3. Every Ability Grows Out of Practice
sections.html:
Let’s make this principle concrete:

Preachers learn to preach by stepping into the pulpit time after time, facing their nerves and their mistakes. No sermon is ever “learned” in the study; sermons are “forged” in the pulpit.

Evangelists learn to share the gospel by opening their mouths time after time and facing rejection. After being turned down ten times, the tone of the eleventh conversation is different; that gentleness wasn’t taught in a classroom — it was ground out by rejection.

Those who serve on a team learn to work together through one flustered scramble after another, stepping on each other’s toes and reviewing it all afterwards. Proverbs 27:17 says: “Iron sharpens iron; so a man sharpens his friend’s countenance.” Sharpening hurts; but without sharpening, the blade will always be blunt.

If a church only stresses “get ready, then serve,” it will forever be “getting ready” and never actually “have served.” Brothers and sisters, let me say this very sincerely: no one in this world began serving once they were “ready.” Paul says: “But we have this treasure in clay vessels, that the exceeding greatness of the power may be of God, and not from ourselves.” (2 Corinthians 4:7) God never intended to wait until the clay jars became golden ones before putting the treasure inside. He means to use clay jars, so that the glory goes to him.

sections.heading: 4. Confirmation from Psychology and Church History
sections.html:
In a classic study published in 1993 in “Psychological Review,” psychologist K. Anders Ericsson and his colleagues put forward the concept of “deliberate practice.” They studied violin students at the Berlin music academy and found that the very best group had, by the age of twenty, accumulated far more hours of solitary practice than the other groups. This research was later widely cited, and is often simplified into the “ten-thousand-hour rule.”

But the study’s more important finding is often overlooked: what makes practice produce experts is not just the number of hours, but three conditions — a clear goal, immediate feedback, and challenge at the edge of one’s ability. Mere repetition doesn’t bring progress; repetition with feedback does.

Brothers and sisters, this is precisely the blueprint for developing people in the church. First, give them a clear serving task, not a vague “help out more.” Second, give them immediate, specific feedback, not a reckoning saved up for the year-end review meeting. Third, give them a challenge slightly beyond their present ability — don’t throw them straight into the hardest situation, but don’t leave them handing out the weekly bulletin for ever either.

Church history confirms this principle again and again. In the eighteenth century John Wesley (1703–1791) set up the “class meeting” system: believers were divided into small groups of about twelve, led by lay people, meeting each week to ask one another about the state of their souls. Most of these class leaders had no theological training, yet in the course of leading they were shaped into the backbone of an entire revival. In nineteenth-century London, Charles H. Spurgeon (1834–1892) founded the Pastors’ College in 1856, and many of the students he took in were young men who were already preaching on the streets and in small meetings and whose gifts had been confirmed. He first saw them “doing it,” and only then gave them “the course.”

Do you see? The order is not “first the course, then the service,” but “take the course while serving, and after the course go back to serving.” The course exists to serve practice; it isn’t the entry ticket to practice.

sections.heading: 5. Applying the 321 Vision
sections.html:
The 321 vision says that changing our mindset has eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Look at where each of these eight stages sits. “Information” is only the first stage — that is what a course can give. But if information doesn’t pass through “Revelation” to become inner sight, and through “Conviction” to become heartfelt surrender, it stays stuck in the head for ever. The truly decisive stage for changing a life is the fourth: “Implementation.” Only after Implementation come “Evaluation” and “Correction,” then “Repetition,” and finally “Multiplication.”

Brothers and sisters, if our system for developing people only goes as far as the first stage, we will never reach the eighth. A church that only runs courses and never gives opportunities to serve is a church stuck at stage one; and Multiplication only happens when you go all the way to stage eight.

Paul said to Timothy: “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.” (2 Timothy 2:2) Paul, Timothy, faithful men, others — four generations handing it on: that is “Multiplication.” And the reason those four generations could pass it on is that Paul didn’t just teach Timothy; he took Timothy along with him — walking together, stoned together, imprisoned together.

The 321 vision also speaks of “the 920 practice”: every person we have a relationship with is our “2”; with them we practise living out a selfless (0) life and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions. “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23) Brothers and sisters, notice: not one of these nine graces can be learned in a classroom. Patience is learned while being made to wait; kindness is learned when facing people who are hard to get along with; gentleness is learned when we are misunderstood. Fruit grows only on the branches of daily living, never on the paper of lecture notes.

Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves. Rely on the brain and you’ll worry; rely on the heart and you’ll rejoice. Developing people by courses and structures alone is relying on the brain; taking people with us to serve together, fall together and pray together is relying on the heart.

V. Key Point 3: Give Opportunities, and Give Encouragement Too — Helping “Those Who Fall” to Stand Up Again

sections.heading: 1. If We Dare to Let People Fall, We Must Be Ready to Reach Out a Hand
sections.html:
The first key point said “dare to use people who fall,” and the second said “build people up through practice.” But if we stop at these two, the church may swing to the other extreme: throwing people out there and then leaving them to it.

That is why the third key point is indispensable: if we dare to let people “fall,” we must be ready to “reach out a hand” when they do.

What many beginners in ministry need most is not criticism but encouragement; not rebuke but companionship. They know better than anyone where they fell short — that night, under the covers, they have already replayed the whole thing three times. At a moment like that, one more criticism only cuts again into a wound that is already bleeding; but one sincere word of encouragement can give them the courage to stand up there again next year.

David understood this God’s character deeply. He said: “A man’s steps are established by Yahweh. He delights in his way. Though he stumble, he shall not fall, for Yahweh holds him up with his hand.” (Psalm 37:23–24) Notice: the text doesn’t say the righteous will never stumble; it says that “he shall not fall,” and the reason is that “Yahweh holds him up with his hand.” Brothers and sisters, God’s way with those who fall is to reach out his hand and hold them up. And the church is the body of Christ; the Lord’s hands today are our hands.

sections.heading: 2. Two Ways of Seeing: The Eyes of Law and the Eyes of Grace
sections.html:
When a new worker makes a mistake while serving, there are two ways of seeing set before us to choose from.

The first is the eyes of law: condemn, reject, exclude. It asks only one thing — “Did you get it wrong?” If the answer is yes, the verdict is “You’re not suitable.” This way of seeing looks very righteous, but it makes the church smaller and smaller, because no one it sweeps over ever dares to come back a second time.

The second is the eyes of grace: accept, guide, support. It asks one more question — “What did you learn from it? How shall we adjust next time?” This way of seeing looks very lax, but it makes the church bigger and bigger, because everyone it has held up later becomes someone who holds others up.

In Galatians 6:1 Paul gives the church a very clear standard: “Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness; looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.”

There are three precious expressions in this verse. First, “you who are spiritual” — the qualification for dealing with another’s fall is being spiritual, not being senior. Second, “in a spirit of gentleness”: the original word, πραΰτης (prautēs), means the gentleness of strength under restraint, like a spirited horse fitted with a bridle — the strength is still there, but it submits to its master’s hand. Gentleness isn’t weakness; it is having strength and not using it to hurt. Third, “restore”: the original word, καταρτίζω (katartizō), is used in Matthew 4:21 for James and John “mending their nets,” and in medical language it was also used for “setting a dislocated bone back in place.” Restoring someone who has fallen is like setting a bone — it hurts a little, but the aim is to get them back in the game.

The prophet Isaiah described the Servant this way: “He won’t break a bruised reed. He won’t quench a dimly burning wick.” (Isaiah 42:3) Brothers and sisters, how many bruised reeds in the church have been snapped by a single word of ours; how many dimly burning wicks have been snuffed out by a single look of ours? Yet the Lord Jesus never does this. “There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus.” (Romans 8:1)

sections.heading: 3. Barnabas: A Man Who Helped People Up
sections.html:
The Bible has a model of “helping people up again,” and his name is Barnabas.

Acts 4:36 introduces him: “Joses, who by the apostles was also called Barnabas (which is, being interpreted, Son of Encouragement), a Levite, a man of Cyprus by race.” In the original, “Son of Encouragement” is υἱὸς παρακλήσεως, literally “son of comfort,” “son of encouragement.” This word παράκλησις shares its root with the title of the Holy Spirit, “the Counsellor” (παράκλητος), meaning “the one called alongside to help.” A true developer of people is someone willing to be “called alongside the one who has fallen.”

Barnabas did two crucial things in his life.

The first: when Saul had just come to faith, and all the disciples in Jerusalem were afraid of him and didn’t believe he was a disciple, “Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles” (Acts 9:27). Without Barnabas, the church might have shut its doors and kept Paul outside.

The second is Mark, whom we mentioned earlier. Paul held that Mark had turned back and should not be taken along again, but Barnabas insisted on giving him another chance — and even parted ways with Paul over it. History proved Barnabas right: the young man who had been given up on wrote the Gospel of Mark; and years later even Paul himself said: “Take Mark, and bring him with you, for he is useful to me for service.” (2 Timothy 4:11)

Brothers and sisters, every healthy church needs a Barnabas. A true leader is not a perfect person, but someone who knows how to “help people up again.” Just as parents, watching their child fall, don’t scold but crouch down, smile and say, “It’s all right — get up and try again.” If the church can have a culture like that, those who fall will grow, and the number of those who walk will increase.

sections.heading: 4. Psychological Safety: A Spiritual Principle Confirmed by Science
sections.html:
In a study published in 1999 in “Administrative Science Quarterly,” Professor Amy Edmondson of Harvard Business School put forward the concept of “psychological safety”: team members believing that they can admit mistakes, ask questions and voice disagreement without being humiliated or punished for it.

As early as 1996 she had published a study of hospital nursing teams. She had expected that “the better the team performs, the fewer the errors,” but the data showed the opposite: the best-performing teams actually reported the most errors. The reason was not that good teams made more mistakes, but that good teams dared to speak up about them. When errors are spoken about, they can be corrected; when errors are hidden, they will be repeated.

Google’s “Project Aristotle,” begun in 2012, analysed nearly two hundred of the company’s own teams and reached the same conclusion: the most important factor in highly effective teams was not how clever the members were, but psychological safety.

Brothers and sisters, isn’t that exactly what the church should be like? In a church where people don’t dare admit they can’t do something, or say “I messed up this time,” mistakes don’t disappear — they just get swept under the carpet. Only a church where people accept one another and can honestly say “I need help” is a church that can truly grow up together.

John put it most clearly of all: “There is no fear in love; but perfect love casts out fear.” (1 John 4:18) A culture of fear breeds hiding; a culture of love breeds growth.

sections.heading: 5. Applying the 321 Vision
sections.html:
The 321 vision speaks of “the 235 relationships”: becoming a “2” with selfless people — that is, spiritual companions; building the “3” — the relationship of spiritual parents and spiritual children; and going on to become a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.

Notice that helping up someone who has fallen depends on exactly this “2” and “3.” Ecclesiastes says: “Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls, and doesn’t have another to lift him up.” (Ecclesiastes 4:9–10)

Woe to him who falls alone — not because falling is so terrible, but because there is no one to lift him up. So in the church we don’t first build structures; we first build relationships. The 321 vision says: life first, then relationships, then ministry; and the priority of relationships is God first, then ourselves, then others, and last of all things. If a new worker falls while serving, what he needs most is a “2” who will sit down and listen until he has said everything, a spiritual parent who will tell him, “Back then I fell much harder than you.”

Ephesians 4:11–12 says: “He gave some to be apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, shepherds and teachers; for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ.” The leader’s office is not “to do everything,” but “the perfecting of the saints.” “Perfecting” (καταρτισμός) shares the same root as “restore” in Galatians 6:1. Brothers and sisters, it turns out that “restoring those who have fallen” and “perfecting the saints” are, in the Holy Spirit’s dictionary, one and the same thing.

And the purpose of it all is to “let Jesus be King and let Jesus receive all the glory.” When we help someone up, it isn’t so that we gain one more capable assistant, but so that the body of Christ is built up and the King’s kingdom can expand.

VI. Integrating the 321 Vision: Developing People Is Establishing God’s System

Brothers and sisters, having come this far, we want to set the three key points back into the big picture of the 321 vision.

sections.heading: 1. The Three Foundations, the Two Core Values, the Goal
sections.html:
The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide.

Jesus is my role model — he dared to use people who fall. Of the twelve disciples he chose, not one was considered gifted by the religious world of the day. He walked with them personally for three years, bore with their jostling for greatness, bore with their doubts, bore with their running away — and then placed the whole church in their hands. If we say Jesus is our role model, we cannot choose our workers the way the world chooses its elite.

The Bible is my standard — not efficiency, not results. The world’s standard says, “Use the strongest people to get the quickest results”; the Bible’s standard says, “for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving” (Ephesians 4:12). When these two standards clash, the one we choose shows what we truly believe.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — developing people is not human-resources management; it is spiritual work. Who should be placed where, and when someone needs a push, must all be received in prayer. Paul says: “For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure.” (Philippians 2:13) It is God who works within people; we are only his co-workers.

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory.

When we don’t dare to use people who fall, it’s often because we ourselves are playing king — afraid of losing face, afraid our reputation will suffer, afraid of losing control. When we let Jesus be King, we can bear “imperfection,” because perfection was never something we could give, and the glory was never something we were meant to take.

The Goal: establish God’s system.

God’s system has one distinguishing mark: it multiplies. The Babylonian system gets things done by using people up; God’s system expands the kingdom by equipping people. A church whose list of workers hasn’t changed in ten years is a system that consumes; a church where every year new people are helped up and sent out is a system that multiplies.

sections.heading: 2. The Old Self Is Self-Centred; the New Self Is Selfless
sections.html:
The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem.

When it comes to developing people, the self-centred life shows up in its most pious guise. It says: “I’m protecting the quality of our meetings; I’m being responsible with the things of God.” But the voice underneath is really saying: “I can’t trust anyone else to do it, because I’m the only one who does it best.”

Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God. When a leader treats himself as the one who is “indispensable,” he has left a servant’s originally intended position and sat down in God’s place. And when he is willing to hand over the microphone, hand over the keys and take his name off the programme, he has returned to his originally intended position.

Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out. Paul says: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20) A selfless leader isn’t unsettled when someone else preaches better than he does; he actually rejoices, because it is no longer he who lives.

Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. When a leader humbly says, “This time I didn’t explain the instructions clearly,” the worker who fell will humbly say, “No, I didn’t prepare well enough” — and both sides win. Conversely, if the leader says, “I warned you long ago,” the worker will say, “You never actually taught me” — and both sides lose.

sections.heading: 3. The Fivefold Change and a Shift in Perspective
sections.html:
The 321 vision says the fivefold change is a change in mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living.

From beginning to end, this lesson has been doing the first thing: changing our mindset. From “the church is short of gifted people” to “the church is short of developing people”; from “waiting for people to mature” to “letting people grow”; from “fearing that people will fall” to “daring to let people fall, and daring to help them up.” Once this one mindset turns, your life will loosen up, your daily living will have room to breathe, your relationships with your co-workers will change, and in the end your ministry will multiply.

Our perspective must shift as well: from man’s perspective to God’s — man sees a clumsy beginner, God sees a future servant; from earthly to heavenly — earth counts today’s results, heaven counts eternal disciples; from temporary to eternal — a beautifully run meeting is temporary, a life built up is eternal; from worldly to godly — the world wants the strongest, God wants the most willing.

The Path of Serving is Spirit → Understanding → Life → Service → God: the Holy Spirit is my guide, the Bible is my standard, Jesus is my role model, let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. Developing people means walking alongside someone, step by step, all the way along this path.

Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not others, not our circumstances. When our focus is on ourselves, we’re afraid of losing face; when it’s on others, we find fault; when it’s on our circumstances, we complain that the church has no people. Only when Jesus is the focal point will we see that he has already placed people among us — it’s just that no one has yet reached out a hand to help them up.

VII. Practice for Daily Living

The lesson gives us three practices. We will use the 321 vision’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to take each of them deeper, one by one.

Practice 1: If you are a leader, pray for a brother or sister who is learning to serve and is not yet mature, and give them a real opportunity to serve

Information: This lesson has already set the truth before you — every person who walks began as a person who falls.

Revelation: Be still for five minutes and ask the Holy Spirit to place a name on your heart. Don’t pick the one you like best; let the Holy Spirit pick.

Conviction: Say to God: “Lord, I confess that I’ve never dared to let go, because I’m afraid. I’m willing to lay this fear down.”

Implementation: This week, give them a specific, clearly defined, time-bound piece of service — for example, the Scripture reading next Sunday, the icebreaker at one small-group meeting, or a three-minute testimony. Don’t vaguely say, “Help out more.”

Evaluation: After they have served, take them for a coffee. First ask, “What do you feel you gained most from it?” and then say, “One thing I saw that was really great about you was…”

Correction: Only at the end, mention one thing — just one — that could be adjusted next time, and think it through together with them.

Repetition: Don’t give just one chance. Nerves the first time are normal; only by the third time can you see the gift. Arrange at least three opportunities.

Multiplication: Once they are standing firm, tell them: “Now it’s your turn to find someone and bring them along the way I brought you.”

Practice 2: If you are a co-worker, when you make a mistake while serving, don’t blame yourself or give up — have the courage to stand up again

Information: “For a righteous man falls seven times and rises up again.” (Proverbs 24:16) God’s standard is not that you never fall, but that you are willing to get up.

Revelation: Ask the Lord to help you discern whether the condemning voice in your heart comes from the Holy Spirit’s rebuke or from Satan’s accusation. The Holy Spirit’s rebuke brings repentance and hope; Satan’s accusation brings only despair and retreat.

Conviction: Accept this truth: God values your heart, not your performance. “For I don’t see as man sees. For man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.” (1 Samuel 16:7)

Implementation: The next time an opportunity to serve comes, don’t turn it down. The most important step after falling is the step of getting back up there again.

Evaluation: Write down honestly the real reason for this mistake — was it lack of preparation, unfamiliarity, or being physically and emotionally worn out?

Correction: Adjust according to the cause, rather than condemning yourself. If you weren’t prepared enough, give yourself two more hours; if you weren’t familiar enough, do a run-through first.

Repetition: Keep up this adjustment for three months, and you will see yourself completely changed.

Multiplication: When someone near you makes a mistake, go over and say, “I understand — I’ve fallen too. Let’s do this together.”

Practice 3: Share with a spiritual companion your past experience of “falling” in ministry, and thank God for how he taught you to “walk” through it

Information: Ecclesiastes 4:9–10 says that if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow.

Revelation: Think about it: in your life, who has been the Barnabas who helped you up?

Conviction: Admitting that you need companions is itself an exercise in humility.

Implementation: This week, find your “2” and tell them about the ministry failure you least want to talk about.

Evaluation: Once you’ve said it, notice what changes in your heart — does the shame feel lighter?

Correction: Write down what God did in that experience as three sentences of thanks.

Repetition: Make this kind of sharing a regular monthly rhythm between the two of you.

Multiplication: Tell your story to someone who is falling right now. Your scars will become someone else’s hope.

A Gentle Reminder

There is a fine saying: falling is not failure; giving up is failure. It isn’t a verse of Scripture, but it fits the spirit of Scripture perfectly. God isn’t afraid of your falling; he is only concerned that you might not be willing to get up again. Every fall is his opportunity to shape you into a more mature vessel.

keyVerses: “For a righteous man falls seven times and rises up again; but the wicked are overthrown by calamity.” (Proverbs 24:16)
“Jesus therefore said to those Jews who had believed him, ‘If you remain in my word, then you are truly my disciples. You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.’” (John 8:31–32)
declarations: Lord, thank you for not despising my weakness and for still giving me the chance to learn to serve. Give me courage to face falling, faith to stand up again, and grace to encourage others. May I become more and more like you through practice, a vessel fit for use in your hands.
Brothers and sisters, let’s go back to the question we began with: is the church really short of gifted people?

The church’s truly gifted people are not naturally flawless “people who walk,” but “people learning to walk” who are willing to be trained by God and to get up from their mistakes. They may be clumsy right now, they may be nervous, their sermons may run over, they may start the hymn in the wrong key — but they have a willing heart. And God never despises a willing heart.

When we replace harshness with grace and fear with encouragement, a beautiful cycle will appear in the church — newcomers grow, old hands are renewed, and everyone can be used by the Lord. Paul says: “being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ.” (Philippians 1:6) It is God who begins the work, and God who completes it; our responsibility is simply not to stand in the way.
So this morning I want to issue a call to three kinds of people.

First, a call to leaders: please let go. The piece of ministry you’re clinging to may be the very lesson God wants to use to build up someone else. Letting go isn’t irresponsibility; letting go is trusting that God is better at leading people than you are.

Second, a call to co-workers: please stand up again. Satan wants to use that one mistake to make you quit, but God wants to use it to make you mature. If you don’t give up, that fall will become your qualification for helping others up in the future.

Third, a call to every brother and sister: please be a Barnabas. The church isn’t short of critics; the church is short of encouragers. Go today to the co-worker who has been downcast lately and say to them: “It’s all right — get up and try again.”
May we all become a church that “dares to use people who fall,” so that God’s kingdom is filled with life and revival. May Jesus reign as King among us, and may all the glory go to him.
practices: If you are a leader, pray for a brother or sister who is learning to serve and is not yet mature, and give them a real opportunity to serve
If you are a co-worker, when you make a mistake while serving, don’t blame yourself or give up — have the courage to stand up again
Share with a spiritual companion your past experience of “falling” in ministry, and thank God for how he taught you to “walk” through it
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we thank you.
Lord, you have never cast us aside because we are weak. You chose Peter, who sank; James and John, who jostled for greatness; Mark, who turned back; and you have also chosen us, sitting here today.

Lord, forgive us. So often our lips say the church is short of gifted people, while our hearts refuse to give anyone a chance; so often we look at other people’s mistakes with the eyes of law, forgetting that you look at our mistakes with the eyes of grace. Remove from us the “self” that is afraid of losing face, and make us willing to lay down our rights and return to a servant’s originally intended position.

Lord, give those of us who lead the courage to hand ministry over; give those of us who serve the faith to stand up again after we fall; and give every one of us an encouraging heart, to be a Barnabas in the church.

Lord, raise up among us generation after generation of people learning to walk, and fill your house with a cycle of life. We place our pride, our fears and our calculations in your hands. Be King, Lord, and receive all the glory.
In the victorious name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Proverbs 24:16 says: “For a righteous man falls seven times and rises up again; but the wicked are overthrown by calamity.” Share a time when you “fell” while serving. What made you willing to stand up again at the time? Or have you still not got back up?

Galatians 6:1 says: “Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness; looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.” In your small group or ministry team, who most needs to be “restored” and encouraged right now? What concrete action will you take this week to help them up?
l055.title: Daring to Use People Who Fall
l055.subtitle: An Important Mindset: The Concept of Developing People (Part 1)
l055.partTitle: Unit 4 · The Prerequisite for Revival — A Change of Mindset

sections.heading: 1. Introduction: Those Three Seconds of Silence
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we come together to Lesson 56 of 321 Morning Devotion, titled “God Uses People Who Know They Can’t.” This is the second talk on “the concept of developing people.”

Let me begin by describing a scene almost every church has lived through. It’s the end of the year, and it’s time to nominate the next team of workers. The list is spread out on the table, and everyone naturally starts discussing it. This brother graduated from a top university, speaks well and isn’t nervous on stage; that sister is a company manager and very organised; and there’s someone else who plays the piano, can lead worship and is willing to give their time. The list is settled in no time.

Just then, someone quietly mentions a name: the elderly sister who is first to arrive and last to leave every Sunday, who silently wipes the chairs clean and carries out the rubbish. The room goes silent for three seconds. Then someone says gently: “She… doesn’t really seem to have any gifts.”

Brothers and sisters, I want to ask a question: in those three seconds of silence, whose standard was actually doing the talking?

Was it the Bible’s standard? Or was it a standard we brought into the church from the company, the school and society — one that has never been examined by the cross?

In the last lesson we saw that the church is “a school for growth”, not “a stage for performance”, and that the aim of shepherding is not to get things done but to grow people. Today we want to press further into a more fundamental question: what kind of people does God actually use? If our eye for choosing people is wrong, what we develop will be a crop of people who are very good at getting things done yet don’t know themselves; what we build will be a very efficient organisation without life.

The Bible answered this question long ago. Samuel was sent to Bethlehem to anoint Israel’s new king, and Jesse brought his sons before him one by one. “When they had come, he looked at Eliab, and said, ‘Surely Yahweh’s anointed is before him.’ But Yahweh said to Samuel, ‘Don’t look on his face, or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him; for I don’t see as man sees. For man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.’” (1 Samuel 16:6–7)

Notice that even a prophet like Samuel could get it wrong. He wasn’t a bad man; he simply used human eyes. The one God had chosen wasn’t even in the house that day — “There remains yet the youngest. Behold, he is keeping the sheep.” (1 Samuel 16:11) God’s choice was out in the wilderness where no one could see him, keeping a few sheep that would never applaud him.

Brothers and sisters, the world values outward qualifications: education, ability, eloquence, background; God values the attitude of the heart. He doesn’t look for perfect people; he looks for people willing to be changed by him. He doesn’t use those who think they can; he uses those who know they can’t.

In this lesson, if only our “mindset about choosing people” is changed by God, the way the church develops people will change with it; and once the way we develop people changes, the lives of a whole generation of brothers and sisters will be raised up. This is exactly what 321 calls the fivefold change: change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; change daily living and you change relationships; change relationships and you change ministry. The starting point of it all is mindset.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Background: A City That Worshipped Success, a Letter About the Cross
sections.html:
To grasp the weight of this passage, we need to know who it was written to.

Author, Date and Recipients

The author of 1 Corinthians is the apostle Paul. He wrote this letter while living in Ephesus on his third missionary journey, around AD 55. “But I will stay at Ephesus until Pentecost” (1 Corinthians 16:8) — that sentence reveals where the letter was written. Its recipients were the church in Corinth, which he had planted with his own hands on his second missionary journey (Acts 18:1–11).

Corinth: A Self-Made City

Corinth was the capital of the Roman province of Achaia, sitting on the narrow isthmus that joins the Peloponnese to mainland Greece. Its eastern port, Cenchreae, opened onto the Aegean Sea, and its western port, Lechaeum, onto the Gulf of Corinth; it was a crossroads for people and goods moving between east and west. The city was destroyed by Rome in 146 BC and lay in ruins for a century; in 44 BC Caesar ordered it rebuilt as a Roman colony, and the settlers who moved in were mostly freed slaves, discharged soldiers and traders out to make a living.

This point is crucial. Corinth was not an ancient city with a long aristocratic tradition, but a “self-made,” up-and-coming city. Here no one asked who your ancestors were; they only asked how much you earned now and how high you had climbed. It was a city that worshipped success and was obsessed with moving up. Add the sailors and travellers brought in by its two ports, and its moral corruption was such that “to Corinthianise” became, in the Greek of the day, a byword for a debauched life.

The Wisdom and Eloquence of Greek Culture

Greek culture prized “wisdom” (σοφία, sophia) and eloquence. In those days there were travelling orators who won fame, status and money through polished rhetoric and sharp debate, and audiences followed them the way people follow celebrities today. This spirit blew into the church, and the result was factions and quarrels: “Now I mean this, that each one of you says, ‘I follow Paul,’ ‘I follow Apollos,’ ‘I follow Cephas,’ and, ‘I follow Christ.’” (1 Corinthians 1:12) They were comparing: which teacher was wiser, more eloquent, more weighty.

The Context: From the Cross to You Yourselves

Paul’s answer was not to mediate between personalities but to strike at the root. In 1:18–25 he points out that the message of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God; God used the cross — the thing the world considers weakest and most shameful — to set aside the wisdom of the world.

Having spoken of the cross, Paul immediately turns the camera on his readers: “For you see your calling, brothers…” (1 Corinthians 1:26) The verb at the start of the original is “you see” (βλέπετε, blepete) — look for yourselves, look at what kind of people were called. It is a gentle but powerful wake-up call: you are worshipping wisdom and eloquence, but look back — when God first chose you, this was not the standard he used at all.

Four Key Words

Paul uses four jarring adjectives, each of them heavy in the Greek:

“Foolish” (μωρά, mōra), the source of the English word moron, means what people regard as having no sense and no class.

“Weak” (ἀσθενῆ, asthenē) means without strength, without influence, unable to make anyone afraid.

“Lowly” (ἀγενῆ, agenē), literally “without birth,” means of humble family, with no name worth mentioning.

“Despised” (ἐξουθενημένα, exouthenēmena) means treated as a zero, utterly scorned. Paul even adds “and the things that don’t exist” (τὰ μὴ ὄντα), literally “the things that are not” — people who simply don’t appear on society’s list at all.

God built his kingdom on people like these. Why? Paul gives the only answer: “that no flesh should boast before God.” (1 Corinthians 1:29) Then he says: “Because of him, you are in Christ Jesus, who was made to us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification, and redemption: that, as it is written, ‘He who boasts, let him boast in the Lord.’” (1 Corinthians 1:30–31)

Brothers and sisters, this is the foundation of this lesson. God’s rule for choosing people points from beginning to end to one purpose: that all the glory goes to him. This is exactly 321’s Two Core Values — let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory.

sections.heading: 3. God’s Criteria for Choosing People: Not Ability, but Attitude
sections.html:
The Text

“For you see your calling, brothers, that not many are wise according to the flesh, not many mighty, and not many noble; but God chose the foolish things of the world that he might put to shame those who are wise. God chose the weak things of the world that he might put to shame the things that are strong.” (1 Corinthians 1:26–27)

Scripture Interpreting Scripture: God’s Choosing Was Never Talent Recruitment

Notice that Paul’s word is “not many,” not “none.” God doesn’t reject people who are learned, capable or well placed; Paul himself was a star pupil of Gamaliel. What God rejects is people boasting before him on the strength of these qualifications. The question isn’t what you have in your hands, but what you are relying on in your heart.

From Genesis to Revelation, the Bible keeps saying the same thing. God said to Zerubbabel: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit.” (Zechariah 4:6) When God called Gideon, Gideon answered: “O Lord, how shall I save Israel? Behold, my family is the poorest in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father’s house.” (Judges 6:15) The moment Isaiah saw God’s glory, his first words were not “I’m ready,” but: “Woe is me! For I am undone, because I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell among a people of unclean lips: for my eyes have seen the King, Yahweh of Armies!” (Isaiah 6:5) Yet when God asked, “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” he said: “Here I am. Send me!” (Isaiah 6:8)

Do you see? Only after admitting “I can’t” can we say “Send me.” Between those two sentences lies the turning point of a life.

Moses: Forty Years from “I Can” to “I Can’t”

The life of Moses plays out this principle more clearly than any other.

For his first forty years he was a prince of Egypt. Stephen said: “Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians. He was mighty in his words and works.” (Acts 7:22) For education, he had received the finest the empire could offer; for ability, he was mighty in words and works; for background, he was the son of Pharaoh’s daughter. By today’s standards for nominating workers, he would be at the top of the list.

Then he took action. “But when he was forty years old, it came into his heart to visit his brothers, the children of Israel” (Acts 7:23). He saw an Egyptian mistreating a Hebrew, and “he killed the Egyptian, and hid him in the sand” (Exodus 2:12). His motive was good, his love for his people was real, and he had the ability too — and the result was forty years as a fugitive.

Brothers and sisters, notice: Moses wasn’t a bad man; Moses was a good man doing the wrong thing. His problem wasn’t a lack of zeal, but that inside his zeal there was a “self.” He wanted to save Israel, but by his own methods, on his own timetable, in his own strength. 321 puts it exactly: the root of the old self is the self-centred life. A self-centred person can turn even good deeds into disasters.

For the second forty years, God put this prince in the wilderness of Midian to tend sheep. Forty years with no applause, no title, no progress reports — only sheep. The learning of Egypt was of no use there, and palace eloquence had no audience there. God wasn’t wasting Moses’ time; God was dismantling Moses’ “self.”

As the third forty years began, the call came from the flame in the bush: “Come now therefore, and I will send you to Pharaoh, that you may bring my people, the children of Israel, out of Egypt.” (Exodus 3:10) The Moses who forty years earlier “could,” now answered: “Who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh, and that I should bring the children of Israel out of Egypt?” (Exodus 3:11) He also said: “O Lord, I am not eloquent, neither before now, nor since you have spoken to your servant; for I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue.” (Exodus 4:10)

Interestingly, Acts says he was “mighty in his words and works,” while Exodus says he was “slow of speech, and of a slow tongue.” Had the wilderness made him go backwards? No — the wilderness made him see the truth: once he had thought he could; now he knew he couldn’t. And it was precisely for that moment that God had waited before saying: I will send you.

Later the Bible’s verdict on Moses was: “Now the man Moses was very humble, more than all the men who were on the surface of the earth.” (Numbers 12:3) God took forty years to refine a man who said “I can” into a man who said “I can’t.” For God doesn’t use those who think they can; God uses those who know they can’t.

Confirmation from Psychology: The Less We Know, the More We Think We Know

In 1999, Cornell University psychologists Justin Kruger and David Dunning published a famous study in the “Journal of Personality and Social Psychology.” They tested participants on logical reasoning, grammar and humour, and then asked them to rate themselves. They found that the group who performed worst rated themselves far above their actual scores, while the best performers tended to underestimate themselves. This later became known as the “Dunning–Kruger effect.”

The study points to an unsettling fact: people who lack ability often also lack the ability to recognise that they lack it. In other words, the more ignorant a person is, the less they know their own ignorance; the more of the whole picture they see, the more they know how small they are.

Psychology is only a support; the Bible is the standard. But this research does confirm, from the side, the word of Scripture: “not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think reasonably, as God has apportioned to each person a measure of faith.” (Romans 12:3) Being able to see ourselves accurately is itself a grace.

Applying 321: The Old Self Is Self-Centred; the New Self Is Selfless

The 321 vision says: the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of every problem. Moses’ first forty years were forty years of the self-centred life; the forty years in the wilderness were forty years of moving from the self-centred life towards selflessness.

Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out. Moses didn’t become weaker; he changed his source of strength. “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20) — this is the selfless life.

So when we choose and develop people in the church, the first question to ask isn’t “Can they do it?” but “Has their ‘self’ been dealt with?” Ability that has never been broken down will sooner or later build its own kingdom inside God’s house.

sections.heading: 4. God’s Principle for Using People: Humility Is the Greatest Talent
sections.html:
The Text

“Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.” (Matthew 23:12)

“But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’” (James 4:6)

God Uses Not the Truly Foolish, but Those Who Know Themselves to Be Foolish

Some people read 1 Corinthians 1:27 and misunderstand it, thinking that God prefers people without ability, or even that being spiritual means not making progress. That is a serious misunderstanding. The people God uses are not the “truly foolish,” but those who “acknowledge themselves to be foolish.”

What’s the difference? The truly foolish don’t know they can’t do it, so they never improve; those who acknowledge their foolishness know they can’t, so they are willing to ask, willing to learn, willing to seek, willing to be taught and willing to be corrected. The first are stagnant; the second are growing.

In other words, humility is itself the highest capacity for learning. A humble person keeps growing all their life; a proud person stops growing on the day they think they understand. That is why we say: in God’s hands, humility is the greatest talent.

The Lord Jesus himself said: “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls.” (Matthew 11:29) Notice that the Lord didn’t say, “Come and learn my abilities”; he said, “learn from me” — learn my ways. Jesus is my role model — this is 321’s first foundation. And the first thing Jesus shows us in his ways is that he is gentle and humble.

Pride: The Force That Brought Down the Perfect

Why is God so severe towards pride? Because pride is not one flaw among many; pride is the very essence of rebellion.

Ezekiel 28 is a lament over the king of Tyre, yet its description goes far beyond any earthly king: “You were the seal of full measure, full of wisdom, and perfect in beauty.” (Ezekiel 28:12) Then comes the fatal verdict: “Your heart was lifted up because of your beauty. You have corrupted your wisdom by reason of your splendor. I have cast you to the ground. I have laid you before kings, that they may see you.” (Ezekiel 28:17) Most interpreters through the history of the church have held that these words also point to that created being who was made perfect in wisdom yet fell through pride — the one who became Satan.

Isaiah 14 records the same inner voice, with five “I will”s in a row: “You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north! I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!’” (Isaiah 14:13–14)

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully: there was nothing wrong with the fallen one’s gifts, nothing wrong with his wisdom, nothing wrong with his beauty. What went wrong was those five “I will”s. 321 puts it with piercing clarity: pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.

That is why the Bible says: “Pride goes before destruction, and an arrogant spirit before a fall.” (Proverbs 16:18) However great a person’s gifts, without humility those gifts will only speed up their fall. This is also why, in the church, we would rather use someone with average gifts and a soft heart than dare to use someone with outstanding gifts and a hard heart.

Christ’s Downward Staircase

If pride is a string of upward “I will”s, then salvation is a string of downward steps in which Christ “emptied himself.”

“Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” (Philippians 2:5–8)

“Emptied himself” in the Greek is ἐκένωσεν (ekenōsen), meaning “poured himself out.” The Lord of the universe emptied himself and came down, step by step, all the way to the cross. And then the Bible says: “Therefore God also highly exalted him” (Philippians 2:9).

This is the most perfect commentary on “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.” The way up is the way down.

Confirmation from Management Studies: Level 5 Leadership and the Power of Humility

American management scholar Jim Collins led a team that spent five years analysing long-term company data; the results were published in 2001 as “Good to Great.” They had no intention of studying leaders at first, but the data forced them to admit that every company that leapt from good to great had been led through its critical turning point by the same kind of person. Collins called this “Level 5 Leadership,” marked by two seemingly contradictory traits existing side by side — personal humility combined with professional will. These people didn’t like the limelight; when they succeeded they gave the credit to their colleagues, and when they failed they took the blame on themselves.

Another study is even more direct. Research by Bradley Owens, Michael Johnson and Terence Mitchell, published in 2013 in the journal “Organization Science,” found that the humility leaders display is positively linked with their teams’ willingness to learn, their engagement and their retention. The reason isn’t hard to see: only when the person at the front is willing to say, “I don’t understand this — could you teach me?” will those under them dare to say, “I can’t do this — could you teach me?”

Stanford psychologist Carol Dweck, in her 2006 book “Mindset,” distinguished between a “fixed mindset” and a “growth mindset.” People with a fixed mindset see failure as a denial of their own worth, so they avoid challenges and cover up mistakes; people with a growth mindset see failure as information, so they are willing to adjust and try again. Brothers and sisters, humble people are naturally people with a growth mindset — they don’t need to prove their worth by performance, because their worth has already been settled in Christ.

An Illustration: The Cup and the Jug

To pour water from a jug into a cup, the cup has to be held lower than the jug. If the cup is held higher than the jug, not a drop can get in. Grace is the same. “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (1 Peter 5:5) It isn’t that God is stingy; it’s that the proud have lifted their cup too high.

The ears of rice in the field are the same: the emptier they are, the higher they hold their heads; the fuller they are, the lower they bow. Spiritual maturity has never been about standing taller, but about bowing lower.

Applying 321: Humility Overcomes Pride; Selflessness Overcomes Satan

321 has a saying that is the most practical tactic in spiritual warfare: humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.

Satan fell through pride, and he attacks people with pride. He doesn’t necessarily tempt you into some great sin; all he needs is to make you feel, “I do this better than others,” “The credit for this should be mine,” “What right has he to correct me?” — and that’s enough. The weapon against pride isn’t a stronger will, but the Lord who emptied himself on the cross.

And 321 reminds us: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. Most conflicts in the church aren’t battles over truth; they are two “selves” colliding. As long as one side is willing to bow first, the battlefield becomes an altar. Brothers and sisters, don’t rely on the brain and yourselves; rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit. Rely on the brain and you’ll worry; rely on the heart and you’ll rejoice.

sections.heading: 5. Humility Lets God Lift People Up, and Builds Up the Church
sections.html:
The Text

“God chose the lowly things of the world, and the things that are despised, and the things that don’t exist, that he might bring to nothing the things that exist, that no flesh should boast before God.” (1 Corinthians 1:28–29)

Two Church Cultures

If a church only picks “capable people” to serve, over time a certain culture grows: people begin to compare, begin to put on a front, begin to be afraid of admitting what they can’t do. Those on the platform don’t dare speak of weakness, because weakness means disqualification; those in the pews don’t dare take the first step, because the first step is never pretty.
