On the surface the ministry runs smoothly, but in reality the whole body is depending on talent, not on the Holy Spirit.

On the other hand, if a church learns to use humble people and to give opportunities to those willing to learn, the whole body will be built up. Someone reads the Scripture up front for the first time and gets a word wrong, and everyone smiles and prays for them; someone leads a small group for the first time and stammers all the way through, yet that same week sheds tears for someone else for the first time. Brothers and sisters, the church is not a stage for performance; the church is a garden for growing people. A garden naturally has seedlings, and seedlings naturally grow unevenly.

The Bible defines the responsibility of church leaders very clearly: “He gave some to be apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, shepherds and teachers; for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ” (Ephesians 4:11–12). “Perfecting” means equipping people until they can take the field, not doing everything yourself. Paul also charged Timothy: “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.” (2 Timothy 2:2) Notice that Paul’s first requirement is “faithful,” not “talented.”

Barnabas: A Man Willing to Give People a Chance

The earliest, and most important, act of developing someone in church history came from a man named Barnabas.

After Saul’s conversion, “When Saul had come to Jerusalem, he tried to join himself to the disciples; but they were all afraid of him, not believing that he was a disciple. But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles” (Acts 9:26–27). Everyone assessed him by his past; only Barnabas assessed him by the grace of God.

A few years later, the work in Antioch was flourishing, and Barnabas needed a co-worker. “Barnabas went out to Tarsus to look for Saul. When he had found him, he brought him to Antioch. For a whole year they were gathered together with the assembly, and taught many people. The disciples were first called Christians in Antioch.” (Acts 11:25–26) Barnabas was a senior leader sent by the Jerusalem church; Saul was a newcomer no one dared to use. Later this newcomer became the apostle Paul, whose fame far surpassed that of Barnabas.

Brothers and sisters, let me ask: did Barnabas regret it? A humble person doesn’t regret such things, because he was never developing his own successor; he was developing a worker for Christ. If the church had a few more Barnabases, it would have dozens more Pauls.

Peter and John: Unlearned, Ordinary Men

When the Council questioned the disciples, Luke records a detail: “Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and had perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marveled. They recognized that they had been with Jesus.” (Acts 4:13)

So what amazed them was not learning, but “having been with Jesus.” Brothers and sisters, what we want to develop is not people who preach better, but people who are more like Jesus.

Grace in Weakness

Paul begged the Lord three times to take the thorn away from him, and the Lord’s answer was: “‘My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.’ Most gladly therefore I will rather glory in my weaknesses, that the power of Christ may rest on me.” (2 Corinthians 12:9)

The Lord also said: “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5) The branch doesn’t have to bear fruit on the vine’s behalf; the branch only has to stay joined to the vine. Staying connected is the most important work of our whole lives.

And these words of Paul should be every servant’s reminder each morning: “For who makes you different? And what do you have that you didn’t receive? But if you did receive it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians 4:7) Not one thing you hold in your hands did you earn.

The Witness of Church History

William Carey (1761–1834), the father of modern missions, was originally an English shoemaker. He taught himself Greek and Hebrew, spent forty years in India, and oversaw the translation of the Bible into dozens of Indian languages. Before he died, what he asked to have carved on his gravestone was not his achievements but a line of verse: “A wretched, poor, and helpless worm, on thy kind arms I fall.”

The nineteenth-century evangelist D. L. Moody (1837–1899) had only about a primary-school education. As a young man he worked as a clerk in a shoe shop; his grammar was poor and his speech carried a country accent, yet in both Britain and America he led countless people to the Lord.

John Newton (1725–1807), who wrote “Amazing Grace,” composed his own epitaph during his lifetime, and it begins by calling himself “once an infidel and libertine, a servant of slaves in Africa.”

Brothers and sisters, what the people God has greatly used throughout church history have in common is not overflowing talent, but that they thought very little of themselves and very much of the Lord.

Supporting Evidence from Science: People Who Keep Learning Really Do Change Their Brains

In 2000, Eleanor Maguire’s team at University College London published a study in the “Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences” (PNAS) comparing the brains of London taxi drivers with those of ordinary people. These drivers must pass an extremely demanding test of the city’s streets, spending years memorising tens of thousands of streets. The study found that the rear part of their hippocampus was noticeably larger than that of the control group — and the longer they had been driving, the greater the difference.

This shows that the adult brain is still malleable — if we are willing to learn, its structure really does change. Brothers and sisters, this gives us enormous hope: the sister at the back of the church wiping the chairs, the brother who doesn’t speak well but is willing to learn — they are not without a future; they simply haven’t been given a chance yet.

An Illustration: The Sea of Galilee and the Dead Sea

Israel has two lakes, both fed by the same River Jordan. In the north, the Sea of Galilee has water flowing in and flowing out; it teems with fish, its shores are green with grass, and most of the Lord Jesus’ ministry took place there. In the south, the Dead Sea only takes in and never gives out; its salinity is around 30 per cent, roughly ten times that of ordinary seawater, and nothing can live in it — which is why it is called the Dead Sea.

The same source, different endings, and the difference lies in just one thing: whether or not the water is willing to flow out. Brothers and sisters, a life that only takes and never gives, that only receives development and won’t develop others, will sooner or later become a Dead Sea.

Applying 321: Life First, Then Relationships, Then Ministry

321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. If a church reverses this order — rushing into ministry first, talking about relationships later and only attending to life at the very end — then the bigger the ministry grows, the more deeply people get hurt.

Relationships have an order too: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. If someone’s relationship with God is right, they will dare to face themselves honestly; if they dare to face themselves honestly, they can treat others sincerely; if they can treat others sincerely, the things they do will have life in them.

Here 321’s “920 practice” is very practical: every person we have a relationship with is our “2”; before every “2” we practise living out a selfless (0) life and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23). The most effective way to develop people isn’t to run a course, but to let one selfless life touch another life.

Go a step further, and you come to “the 235 relationships”: becoming a “2” with selfless people, spiritual companions who support one another; building the “3,” becoming spiritual parents and spiritual children, one generation bringing up the next; and finally becoming a “5,” a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades building up the body of Christ together. Barnabas and Paul are the best example of a “2” becoming a “3,” and a “3” growing into a “5.”

sections.heading: 6. Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
Let’s set this lesson back into the whole picture of 321.

The Three Foundations

Jesus is my role model — he is gentle and humble; he emptied himself and took the form of a servant; he is the pattern and the power of all our humility. The Bible is my standard — choosing people, using people and developing people are all measured by God’s word, not by society’s résumé. The Holy Spirit is my guide — not by might, nor by power, but by God’s Spirit is the work accomplished.

The Two Core Values

Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory. This is exactly the purpose of 1 Corinthians 1:29: that no flesh should boast before God. God uses “the things that don’t exist,” so that the glory goes to him beyond any dispute.

The Goal

Establish God’s system. God’s system is not a pyramid held up by a small elite, but every developed life, each in its own role, helping one another and growing up together into maturity.

The Self-Centred Life and Selflessness

The mark of the old self is the self-centred life: I can, I will, my credit, my name. The mark of the new self is selflessness: it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. Selflessness is not becoming nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus — because when I step down, God steps up.

The Fivefold Change

Change the mindset and the life changes; change the life and daily living changes; change daily living and relationships change; change relationships and ministry changes. The mindset this lesson seeks to change comes down to one sentence: God doesn’t use those who think they can; God uses those who know they can’t. If this one mindset truly reaches your heart, the way you see yourself will change, and so will the way you see that brother or sister who “has no gifts.”

A Shift in Perspective

From man’s perspective to God’s — man looks at the outward appearance, God looks at the heart. From earthly to heavenly — earth talks about talent, heaven talks about faithfulness. From temporary to eternal — a beautiful meeting is temporary, a life that is built up is eternal. From worldly to godly — the world uses people to get things done; God uses people in order to perfect those very people.

Jesus Is the Focal Point

The focus is not on ourselves, not on others, not on our circumstances. Look at yourself and you’ll feel either inferior or proud; look at others and you’ll compare or judge; look at your circumstances and you’ll lose heart or grow reckless. Only when we look to Jesus can our hearts be at peace.

The Path of Serving

Spirit → Understanding → Life → Service → God: the Holy Spirit guides me, the Bible enlightens me, the likeness of Jesus takes shape in me, and so my service lets Jesus be King, and in the end all the glory goes to him. Every step of this path needs humility to walk it.

sections.heading: 7. Putting It into Practice
sections.html:
This lesson has three practices, and we will use 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to work them through solidly.

Practice 1: Examine Your Attitude

In my service, do I often think “I can”? Or do I admit “I can’t” and rely on God?

Information: Copy out 1 Corinthians 1:26–31 by hand, and circle in particular “that no flesh should boast before God.”

Revelation: Be still for three minutes and ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light — the last time I felt pleased with myself in my service, what was it about? The last time I wouldn’t ask for help, what was I afraid of?

Conviction: Admit to God that not one of my gifts, opportunities or results is something I did not receive (1 Corinthians 4:7).

Implementation: At least once this week, take the initiative in your service to say, “I don’t know how to do this — please teach me.”

Evaluation: At the weekend, look back: after saying that sentence, did I feel relieved or embarrassed? The place where I felt embarrassed is exactly where the “self” is still alive.

Correction: Bring that point of embarrassment to the cross and hand it over specifically.

Repetition: Practise this for four weeks in a row, until admitting “I can’t” becomes a natural reaction rather than a forced exercise.

Multiplication: Share your experience with a co-worker and invite them to practise it with you.

Practice 2: Learn Humility

Every day, ask the Holy Spirit to remind you to give the glory to God, whether you succeed or fail.

Information: Learn two passages by heart — “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.” (Matthew 23:12) “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (James 4:6)

Revelation: Every night before bed, ask one question: was there anything today that I secretly wanted people to know about?

Conviction: Admit that pride is not a minor fault; it is the force that brought down an angel (Ezekiel 28:17).

Implementation: Form two small habits. First, when you succeed, publicly give the credit to God and your co-workers; second, when you fail, don’t explain — admit your fault first.

Evaluation: Check once a week — how many times did I justify myself this week?

Correction: Take the thing you most wanted to justify and lay it down again before God.

Repetition: Let “giving the glory to God” turn from a slogan into a reflex.

Multiplication: Build this culture in your small group, so that everyone can freely say, “I was wrong.”

Practice 3: Perfect Others

Encourage brothers and sisters who are still learning and not yet mature; give them opportunities, pray for them and grow alongside them.

Information: Read Ephesians 4:11–12 and Acts 11:25–26, and see clearly the model of “perfecting” and “going to look for people.”

Revelation: Ask the Holy Spirit to give you a name — a brother or sister who hasn’t yet been noticed but has a willing heart.

Conviction: Believe that God can use them, just as God once used Moses, who was slow of speech.

Implementation: Do three things this month — give them a real opportunity to serve; pray for them specifically; and when they have finished, affirm them first, then teach.

Evaluation: When they don’t do it perfectly, is my first reaction to take over, or to walk through it with them again?

Correction: If I rush to take over, ask the Lord to remove my anxiety about “results,” so that I value people more than tasks.

Repetition: Walking alongside someone isn’t a one-off; it takes a season, a year.

Multiplication: Once they are on their feet, ask them to go and bring along the next person. That is the “2” becoming a “3,” and the “3” growing into a “5.”

A Gentle Reminder

God doesn’t look for perfect people; he looks for people willing to be shaped. The moment you admit your inadequacy is the starting point of God using you.

sections.heading: 8. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, when God chooses and uses people, he doesn’t look at the outward appearance or at the résumé, but at the heart. He wants to use those who know they can’t, yet are willing to obey him.

Let’s go back to the scene we began with. Those three seconds of silence were actually an opportunity God was giving us — an opportunity to exchange the world’s standard for the kingdom’s. When we change our “mindset about choosing people,” and no longer look only at people’s talents but at their hearts, the church will become a garden for growing people, full of life: here every weak person can be raised up, and every humble person can be greatly used by God.

I want to issue a call to three kinds of brothers and sisters.

First, if today you feel you’re “not good enough” — not educated enough, not a good speaker, someone who has been up front and embarrassed yourself — I want to tell you that where you are standing is exactly where God chooses people. He chose the lowly things of the world, the things that are despised, and the things that don’t exist. You are not someone who was overlooked. Please hand your “I can’t” to the Lord who can do all things.

Second, if today you are someone very capable who has always been relied upon, I want to invite you too — ask the Lord to guard your heart, so that your gifts always follow behind the cross and never run ahead of it. God isn’t against your being capable; it’s just that God cannot share his glory with you.

Third, if today you are someone who leads and develops others, may the Lord give you the heart of a Barnabas: to see other people’s past, yet choose to believe in God’s grace; to give opportunities away, to step aside from the stage, and to give the glory back.

May our church not be a stage for performance but a garden for growing people; not a tower piled up by talent, but a system in which Jesus reigns as King. Let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory — this is the one and only purpose of a lifetime of service.

keyVerses: “For you see your calling, brothers, that not many are wise according to the flesh, not many mighty, and not many noble; but God chose the foolish things of the world that he might put to shame those who are wise. God chose the weak things of the world that he might put to shame the things that are strong. God chose the lowly things of the world, and the things that are despised, and the things that don’t exist, that he might bring to nothing the things that exist, that no flesh should boast before God.” (1 Corinthians 1:26–29)
practices: Examine your attitude
Learn humility
Perfect others
prayer: Lord, thank you that you look not at my ability but at my heart. Today I am willing to lay down my pride, admit my limits and let you be my true strength. Make me a humble vessel, used by you, to glorify your name.

Lord Jesus, you existed in the form of God, yet you emptied yourself and took the form of a servant. Give me your gentle and humble heart. Lord, remove those quiet “I will”s within me, and let me return to my originally intended position before you: let you be God, and let me be man.

Holy Spirit, shine your light into every corner where I boast, and heal every wound where I feel inferior. Let me no longer measure myself with the world’s ruler, nor measure my brothers and sisters with it either.

Lord, give me the heart of a Barnabas, to see those around me who are still learning, to give them opportunities, pray for them and help them grow. May our church become a garden for growing people, where every weak person is raised up and every humble person is used by you.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “For I don’t see as man sees. For man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.” (1 Samuel 16:7) Think back to a time when you assessed someone by outward qualifications and later found you had been wrong. What does that experience say to your mindset today about “choosing and using people”?

“My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” (2 Corinthians 12:9) What is the one “I can’t” you are least willing to admit right now? If you were willing to hand it over to God, how do you think God might use it?
l056.title: God Uses Those Who Know They Can’t
l056.subtitle: An Important Mindset · The Concept of Developing People (Part 2)
l056.partTitle: Unit 4 · The Prerequisite for Revival — A Change of Mindset

sections.heading: Introduction: Not a Shortage of Talent, but a Shortage of Willingness
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I’d like to begin by asking you to be still for thirty seconds and answer one question in your heart: in your church or fellowship, what is the sigh you hear most often?

My guess is that, more often than not, it’s this one: “We just don’t have enough people here.” The Sunday school needs teachers, the worship team needs a pianist, the small groups need leaders, the visitation ministry needs co-workers. Pastors pray about it, the elders and deacons hold meetings about it, the list of co-workers is turned over and over, and the conclusion is always the same: a shortage of talent.

And yet, brothers and sisters, if we bring this whole matter before God and look at it again, we discover something remarkable: the Bible never says that God is short of people. What the Bible says is this: “The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the laborers are few. Pray therefore that the Lord of the harvest will send out laborers into his harvest.” (Matthew 9:37–38) The Lord points out that “the laborers are few”, yet he doesn’t tell us to go and “find talent”; he tells us to “pray that the Lord of the harvest will send out laborers”. Workers don’t come from the labour market; they come from the hand of the Lord of the harvest. And the Lord’s hand is never short of workers.

So where does the problem lie? It lies in two mindsets.

The first wrong mindset belongs to those who are invited to serve: “I haven’t been called yet.” “I need to pray about it some more.” “Let me wait until I’m ready.” These words sound deeply spiritual, yet they often become the most spiritual way of running away. We wait and wait; the prompting of the Holy Spirit is put off, the moment to serve is missed, and the fire that was meant to be kindled in that person’s life slowly, bit by bit, goes cold.

The second wrong mindset belongs to the leaders who invite others to serve: “This person isn’t ready yet.” “He messed it up last time.” And so the church only dares to use the people who “can already walk”. It’s always the same few familiar faces taking turns, worn out to the point of exhaustion, while the great crowd of brothers and sisters who are “still learning to walk” spend their whole lives sitting in the pews watching. Those who can walk grow ever more tired from walking; those who should be learning to walk sit ever longer; and in the end everyone reaches the same conclusion together: our church has a shortage of talent.

Brothers and sisters, let me say it very honestly: the church does not have a shortage of talent. The church has too few people who are “willing to be used”, and too few who are “willing to use people”. This is a problem of mindset, not a problem of manpower.

The 321 message reminds us again and again that fivefold change begins with mindset — change your mindset and you change your life; change your life and you change your daily living; change your daily living and you change your relationships; change your relationships and you change your ministry. If the mindset doesn’t change, no number of methods will help; once the mindset changes, the whole church comes alive. This lesson today is about changing two mindsets: the way we think about “answering the call”, and the way we think about “choosing and using people”. Together we’ll look at four key points: don’t wait to be called, because you have already been called; learn while serving, and pray while learning; move from “using talent” to “developing talent”; and let the church be “a workshop for training”, not “a stage for performance”.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: The Scene Isaiah Saw in the Temple
sections.html:
Let’s first get the background of our theme passages clear, because Isaiah 6:8 is one of the most often quoted — and most often misused — verses in the whole Bible.

Isaiah was a prophet in the kingdom of Judah in the eighth century BC. According to Isaiah 1:1, he served “in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah”. Chapter 6 opens like this: “In the year that king Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting on a throne, high and lifted up; and his train filled the temple.” (Isaiah 6:1) Uzziah reigned for fifty-two years, a rare era of lasting peace and stability in Judah. The moment he died, the nation was plunged into turmoil: to the north the Assyrian empire was on the rise, a powerful enemy was pressing on the border, and people were gripped by fear. At that very moment, when “the earthly throne stood empty”, God let Isaiah see that the heavenly throne had never been empty. The Lord was still seated as King.

What follows is in a very important order, because it sets the direction for this whole message today.

First, Isaiah sees the holiness of God. The seraphim call to one another: “Holy, holy, holy, is Yahweh of Armies! The whole earth is full of his glory!” (Isaiah 6:3)

Second, he sees his own corruption: “Woe is me! For I am undone, because I am a man of unclean lips.” (Isaiah 6:5) He doesn’t first discover how gifted he is; he first discovers that he is finished. Third, God takes the initiative to cleanse him: a seraph touches his mouth with a live coal and says, “your iniquity is taken away, and your sin forgiven.” (Isaiah 6:7) The cleansing isn’t something Isaiah achieved by self-cultivation; it is something God gave.

Only at the fourth step do we come to the words we know so well: “I heard the Lord’s voice, saying, ‘Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?’ Then I said, ‘Here I am. Send me!’” (Isaiah 6:8)

Brothers and sisters, look closely: the Lord’s question isn’t “Who is able to go?” The Lord’s question is “Who will go for us?” In the original, the weight falls on willingness — not qualification, but readiness of heart. And Isaiah doesn’t answer, “I can do it.” He answers, “Here I am.” In Hebrew the phrase is extremely brief, simply “Here I am. Send me.” It is the posture of someone stepping forward, not a CV.

Even more striking: only after Isaiah says yes does God tell him that this people will hear indeed, but not understand (Isaiah 6:9). When he said, “Here I am,” he had no idea what lay ahead. He didn’t see the road clearly first and then agree; he agreed first, and then he was led onto the road.

That is exactly the first lesson we need to learn today: obedience doesn’t act only “after we understand”; obedience responds at once, “in trust”.

The background of our other theme passage, 2 Timothy 2:2, is just as moving. It is the last letter Paul wrote to his spiritual son Timothy, during his second imprisonment in Rome, shortly before his martyrdom. The old apostle, at the end of his life’s road, was not most concerned about his own reputation. He was concerned about one thing: that the word be passed on.

Four generations are hidden in this one verse: Paul, Timothy, faithful men, and others. Paul’s criteria for choosing people come down to just this: “faithful” and “able to teach”. He doesn’t say to look for the eloquent, the highly educated, or those of social standing. The Greek word for “faithful” is pistos, meaning trustworthy, reliable — from the same root as the word for “faith”. What God values is not how capable a person is, but whether that person can be entrusted with something.

Brothers and sisters, our problem is often this: we go looking for people using the world’s specifications, and then complain that God hasn’t given us anyone. In truth, the people God has given have been beside us all along.

sections.heading: 1. Don’t Wait to Be Called, Because You Have Already Been Called
sections.html:
“I heard the Lord’s voice, saying, ‘Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?’ Then I said, ‘Here I am. Send me!’” (Isaiah 6:8)

“Jesus said to them, ‘Come after me, and I will make you into fishers for men.’” (Mark 1:17)

Brothers and sisters, let’s start with a very familiar scene. Your small-group leader comes up to you and says, “Would you lead worship this month?” Or the pastor says, “The Sunday school needs a teacher, and I think you could do it.” What is your first reaction? Nine people out of ten will say the very same thing: “I need to pray about it some more.”

How spiritual that sounds. But let’s be a little more honest. Very often, that “I need to pray about it some more” isn’t followed by prayer at all — only by silence. We aren’t truly seeking God’s will; we want a dignified way out. We use the most spiritual words to do the least spiritual thing: we postpone the Holy Spirit’s prompting, shelve it, and then forget it.

Let me say something that may make you a little uncomfortable this morning: the moment God moves your heart and places an opportunity to serve in front of you — that moment is the call.

In the New Testament, the word for “calling” is the Greek klēsis, and the verb is kaleō, which simply means “to call” or “to invite”. Paul says, “I therefore, the prisoner in the Lord, beg you to walk worthily of the calling with which you were called.” (Ephesians 4:1) He is saying this to the whole church in Ephesus, not to a handful of preachers. In the Bible, being “called” is never a label for a small spiritual elite; it is the identity of every saved person. Peter puts it even more directly: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession.” (1 Peter 2:9) Brothers and sisters, you are already a priest. And priests are there to serve.

So we need to keep two things distinct. The “calling of identity” is something every believer has already received; there’s no need to ask for it again. The “specific sending” — when, in which position, and in what way to serve — is what we are to seek. Our common mistake is to say “I haven’t been called yet” when what we mean is “I’m not yet sure of the specific sending”. The result? The door has long stood wide open, yet we stand at the threshold, year after year, knocking and asking God, “Excuse me, may I come in?”

Let’s look at how the people in the Bible were used by God.

When God was about to send Moses to Pharaoh, Moses said, “I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue.” (Exodus 4:10) He offered his own inability as his reason. God’s answer was: “Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth, and teach you what you shall speak.” (Exodus 4:12) God didn’t hand him eloquence first. God said, “Now therefore go” — and the words were given along the way.

Gideon was hiding in a winepress threshing wheat, frightened half to death. Yet the angel of the Lord appeared to him and said, “Yahweh is with you, you mighty man of valor!” (Judges 6:12) Gideon himself said, “O Lord, how shall I save Israel? Behold, my family is the poorest in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father’s house.” (Judges 6:15) God’s answer was: “Surely I will be with you, and you shall strike the Midianites as one man.” (Judges 6:16) God never says, “Actually, you’re quite impressive.” God always says, “I will be with you.”

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? The logic by which God uses people is not “Because you are useful, I use you”, but “Because I use you, you become useful”.

Paul spells out this logic most clearly: “For you see your calling, brothers, that not many are wise according to the flesh, not many mighty, and not many noble; but God chose the foolish things of the world that he might put to shame those who are wise. God chose the weak things of the world that he might put to shame the things that are strong; … that no flesh should boast before God.” (1 Corinthians 1:26–29) God deliberately chooses those who look unqualified, so that no one can boast and all the glory goes to him.

So the truly biblical attitude is this: “I may be of no use, but God is willing to use me — so I’ll hurry up and let him use me!”

There is a spiritual law here that is strikingly similar to a physiological one: if you don’t use it, it stays useless; the more you use it, the more useful it becomes. Medicine calls it “disuse atrophy” — people who lie bedridden for a long time lose muscle strength rapidly. Conversely, resistance training causes tiny micro-tears in the muscle fibres, and as the body repairs them it builds them back stronger. Muscle isn’t made by protecting it; it is made by using it.

The spiritual life is the same. “If anyone therefore purges himself from these, he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified, and suitable for the master’s use, prepared for every good work.” (2 Timothy 2:21) A bowl that has sat unused for thirty years is, however exquisite, only an ornament; a bowl that is used every day and washed every day is the vessel the household really needs. And we are clay vessels to begin with: “But we have this treasure in clay vessels, that the exceeding greatness of the power may be of God, and not from ourselves.” (2 Corinthians 4:7) God never intended to wait until we became golden vessels before using us.

So why do we still not dare?

Psychological research on procrastination holds up a mirror to us. A meta-analysis by the Canadian scholar Piers Steel, published in Psychological Bulletin in 2007, found that at its core procrastination is not laziness; it is closely linked to “aversion to the task”, “fear of failure” and “doubt about one’s own ability”. In other words, when we hold back from responding, it’s usually not because we are more devout, but because we are more afraid: afraid of not doing it well, afraid of losing face, afraid of being compared, afraid that if we mess it up everyone will be disappointed.

Brothers and sisters, this is precisely what 321 calls the self-centred life. To be self-centred is to have our focus on ourselves: Can I do it? Am I good enough? What will others think of me? Selflessness is to turn our focus to Jesus: Lord, this is yours; you are to be King, and I need only obey. “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20) When “I” am no longer the main character, the question “Can I do it?” simply disappears. 321 reminds us: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. Those days of calculating and recalculating in the face of an invitation to serve, never daring to say yes, are exactly the days when we are “relying on the brain and ourselves”.

It is commonly said that the nineteenth-century British evangelist Henry Varley once told the young D. L. Moody, “The world has yet to see what God can do with a man fully consecrated to him.” When Moody heard it, he said: I will be that man. He never received any formal theological training, and his grammar in the pulpit was often laughed at, yet he led countless people to the Lord. God has never been looking for perfect people; God is looking for willing people.

So, brothers and sisters, if an opportunity to serve comes your way today, please don’t say “I need to pray about it some more” again. Say this instead: “Lord, here I am. Send me!” And then pray as you go.

sections.heading: 2. Learn While Serving, and Pray While Learning
sections.html:
“Continue steadfastly in prayer, watching in it with thanksgiving.” (Colossians 4:2)

“If anyone desires to do his will, he will know about the teaching, whether it is from God, or if I am speaking from myself.” (John 7:17)

At this point some brothers and sisters are bound to feel uneasy: “Are you telling us not to pray — just charge ahead and sort it out later?” Not at all. “Wholeheartedly letting God use us” is never a matter of neglecting prayer. It means moving prayer from being “a checkpoint before action” to being “the breathing within action”.

We often treat prayer like a security gate: once we have prayed it through, the gate opens. But prayer in the Bible is more like oxygen: you don’t take one breath at the door; you keep breathing all the way along. “Always rejoice. Pray without ceasing. In everything give thanks, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus toward you.” (1 Thessalonians 5:16–18) “Pray without ceasing” doesn’t mean “stay on your knees all the time”; it means “without interruption” — like a heartbeat, beating through everything you do.

What we pray needs to change too. Many people pray the same prayer over and over: “Lord, do you actually want me to do this or not?” That treats God like a boss whose instructions need confirming again and again. The biblical prayer is: “Lord, I’m already on the road — please teach me how to do this more after your own heart.” The first kind of prayer leaves people going round in circles; the second kind makes the path grow brighter with every step.

How did the Lord Jesus train his disciples? “He appointed twelve, that they might be with him, and that he might send them out to preach.” (Mark 3:14) “That they might be with him” is life; “that he might send them out to preach” is ministry. The two went on at the same time. He didn’t shut them away in a room for three years of training and only let them out after graduation. The Lord sent out seventy disciples, they came back rejoicing to report, and right then and there the Lord taught them the most important lesson of all: “Nevertheless, don’t rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.” (Luke 10:20) Brothers and sisters, had they not gone out, they would never have learned that lesson.

The Greek word for “disciple” is mathētēs, and its root means simply “a learner”. A disciple is not “a graduate”; a disciple is “someone who learns for a lifetime”. The road of following the Lord is made by walking it, not by thinking about it.

Look again at the Lord’s words: first the desire to do, and then the knowing. We always want to understand first and then act, but the Lord says that many truths you will only understand once you have acted on them.

That’s why the lesson text puts it so precisely: you cannot learn humility from the pulpit; only when you are misunderstood can you practise humility. You cannot learn faith in the classroom; only when there are no resources and you still choose to obey can you live faith out.

You can read a book on humility ten times, but the real exam isn’t in your study. It comes on the day when, after six months of quietly serving, someone else takes the credit. Only at that moment do you find out whether you have humility. You can also know “Now faith is assurance of things hoped for, proof of things not seen” (Hebrews 11:1) off by heart, but real faith shows on the day when the offerings fall short and the co-workers are too few, and you still say, “Lord, I will do as you have said.”

Peter is the best example. That night the Lord said, “Come!” and Peter stepped down from the boat and walked on the water (Matthew 14:29). Then, when he saw that the wind was strong, he was afraid, and beginning to sink, he cried out, “Lord, save me!” (Matthew 14:30) And the Lord reached out and caught him. Brothers and sisters, who learned the lesson that night? Peter, who got out of the boat, took a few steps and nearly sank — or the eleven disciples who sat in the boat and watched the whole thing? Peter may have gone under for a moment, but he was the only one who knew “how quick and how steady the Lord’s hand is”.

Educational psychology confirms this order. The “experiential learning cycle” proposed by the American scholar David Kolb in 1984 shows that learning is a cycle: concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualisation, active experimentation, and then back to concrete experience. Without the step of “concrete experience”, the reflection and growth that follow can never begin. Research by K. Anders Ericsson and colleagues, published in Psychological Review in 1993, likewise found that the key to expertise is not simply the accumulation of time but “deliberate practice” — practice with clear goals, immediate feedback and repeated correction.

Brothers and sisters, isn’t this exactly what 321 calls the eight stages of changing our mindset? Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. The first three — Information, Revelation, Conviction — happen in the heart; if we stop at the third, the mindset will never become life. The fourth, Implementation, is the threshold; only once we cross it do we come to Evaluation, Correction and Repetition, and finally to Multiplication. Many brothers and sisters have been stuck at the station of Conviction for ten years: they understand all the teaching, they’ve been moved before, but they’ve never taken the step of Implementation. Ten years go by, the mindset is still just a mindset, the life hasn’t changed, and ministry is out of the question.

321 says the Path of Serving runs Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God — the Holy Spirit is my guide, the Bible is my standard, Jesus is my role model, let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. This path is meant to be “walked”, not “looked at”. You may know the map by heart, but if you don’t move, you’ll never arrive.

So, brothers and sisters, from today let’s move prayer to a different place: don’t put prayer “in front of” serving as a checkpoint; put prayer “inside” serving as your breath. Stop asking, “Lord, will you use me or not?” and start asking, “Lord, please use me, and teach me how to be used by you more after your own heart.” God isn’t looking for perfect servants; God is looking for servants who are willing to be pruned by him.

sections.heading: 3. From “Using Talent” to “Developing Talent”
sections.html:
“But Yahweh said to Samuel, ‘Don’t look on his face, or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him; for I don’t see as man sees. For man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.’” (1 Samuel 16:7)

“He gave some to be apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, shepherds and teachers; for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ.” (Ephesians 4:11–12)

The first two points were addressed to “those who are invited”; this one is addressed to “those who do the inviting” — especially pastors, small-group leaders and the co-workers in charge of every kind of ministry. Brothers and sisters, we need to admit something together: very often the church’s “shortage of talent” isn’t because there are too few people, but because our “attitude to using people” is wrong.

Listen to the difference between these two sentences. The world’s companies say, “This person is useful, so we use him.” The aim is to make use of people; people are resources — if they perform, they’re given more responsibility; if they don’t, they’re replaced. The church ought to say, “God wants to use this person, so we use him.” The aim is to make people whole; people are not a means — people are the goal. The very reason the church exists is “for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving”.

The word for “perfecting” in Ephesians 4:12 is the Greek katartismos. It can refer to “mending fishing nets”, and also to “setting a dislocated bone back in place”. It means patching up what is torn, straightening what is crooked, joining what has come apart, so that it is restored to working order. Interestingly, when the Lord called James and John, they were “in the boat … mending their nets” (Matthew 4:21) — and “mending” in the original comes from this very root. The Lord called two net-menders so that they would go and mend people.

Brothers and sisters, this is the church’s real business: mending people. Not picking the good ones to use, but mending the ones who aren’t good yet.

Let’s look again at the criteria the Lord Jesus used to choose people. If Jesus had been a human-resources manager, his list of twelve would probably have been sent back by the board.

He chose fishermen. “Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and had perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marveled. They recognized that they had been with Jesus.” (Acts 4:13) “Unlearned and ignorant men” — that was the verdict of Jerusalem’s religious elite on them.

He chose a tax collector. “As Jesus passed by from there, he saw a man called Matthew sitting at the tax collection office. He said to him, ‘Follow me.’ He got up and followed him.” (Matthew 9:9) In those days tax collectors were traitors to their nation, in a profession despised by everyone.

He also chose Simon the Zealot (Luke 6:15), a member of the radical party that called for the armed overthrow of Rome. Just imagine: Matthew, who had collected taxes for Rome, and Simon, who wanted to kill Romans, placed in the same twelve-person small group. Any organisational consultant would tell you that team was going to explode. Yet the Lord not only chose them; he kept them together for three whole years. Because the Lord wasn’t putting together “a capable team”; the Lord was building “a band of changed people”.

Jesus never assessed people by “whether they are useful”; he called people by “whether they are willing”. He didn’t look at the CV; he looked at the heart. When Samuel went to Bethlehem to anoint a king, Jesse brought his seven sons before him one by one, and each time Yahweh said, “Not this one.” Finally the youngest, David — out in the wilderness keeping the sheep, not even called to the table — was fetched, and God said, “This is he.” (1 Samuel 16:12) Brothers and sisters, in your church, is there a David “out keeping the sheep and never called to the table”?

More moving still, the heart of Jesus is a father’s heart: it sees people’s potential and does not give up on their weakness.

Peter denied the Lord three times. That wasn’t a technical slip; it was publicly disowning him at the very moment the Lord most needed him. By the world’s standards, this man’s career was over. But long before Peter fell, the Lord had already said to him: “Simon, Simon, behold, Satan asked to have all of you, that he might sift you as wheat, but I prayed for you, that your faith wouldn’t fail. You, when once you have turned again, establish your brothers.” (Luke 22:31–32) Look at those words: “when once you have turned again”. The Lord knew all along that he would fall, and had already prepared the road for him after the fall. In the Lord’s plan there was never an item called “elimination” — only “when once you have turned again”.

After the resurrection, on the shore of the Sea of Tiberias, the Lord lit a charcoal fire and prepared breakfast, and three times he asked Peter, “Do you love me?” — one question for each denial. Not a word of rebuke, not a word raking up the past; he simply placed the sheep back into Peter’s hands, again and again: “Feed my lambs.” “Tend my sheep.” “Feed my sheep.” (John 21:15–17)

Brothers and sisters, this is what developing people means: not waiting until someone no longer falls before entrusting him with something, but, after he has fallen, lifting him up and entrusting him once more.

Church history has an even more concrete example: Barnabas and Mark. On the first missionary journey, Mark left partway through. Before the second set out, “Barnabas planned to take John, who was called Mark, with them also. But Paul didn’t think that it was a good idea to take with them someone who had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia, and didn’t go with them to do the work. … Barnabas took Mark with him and sailed away to Cyprus.” (Acts 15:37–39)

But look at how it ends. Many years later, the same Paul who had once refused to take Mark wrote in the last letter of his life: “Only Luke is with me. Take Mark, and bring him with you, for he is useful to me for service.” (2 Timothy 4:11) And Mark went on to write the second Gospel of the New Testament. What happened in between? Barnabas happened — a Barnabas willing to stake his own journey on a young man who had once failed. If no one had been willing to give Mark another chance back then, the church would have had one Gospel fewer.

Yet today we so often pick only the person who “can go on right away and will never make a mistake”, because it’s the least trouble and the safest. The result: those few people “who can walk” are used until they run dry, and the crowd of people “still learning to walk” are still sitting in the audience ten years later.

There is a famous study in psychology that shows us the power of “expectation”. In the mid-1960s the American researchers Robert Rosenthal and Lenore Jacobson conducted an experiment in a primary school in California. They told the teachers that tests showed certain pupils were “about to blossom academically”; in fact those pupils had been chosen at random. After one school year, this randomly chosen group showed significantly greater gains on intelligence tests than the other pupils. In their 1968 book, the researchers called this the “Pygmalion effect”. What changed was not the pupils but the way the teachers saw them — and the teachers’ way of seeing really did change the pupils.

Brothers and sisters, how you see a person often determines who that person will become. And this is how God sees us: he called Gideon, hiding in the winepress, “mighty man of valor” (Judges 6:12). He calls us by what we will be, not by what we are now.

321 says: first life, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. Applied to choosing people, it means this: don’t sacrifice people for the sake of getting the job done well; for the sake of building people up, be willing to bear with the job not being done so well. If a worship service is led imperfectly, God’s kingdom will not collapse because of it; but if a brother never dares to stand up there again, a life has been locked away.

321’s “235 relationships” are precisely a blueprint for developing people: become a “2” with a selfless person — spiritual companions supporting one another; build a “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children, where someone leads you and you lead someone else; become a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades, each doing their part to build up the body of Christ. Paul led Timothy, Timothy entrusted the word to faithful men, and the faithful men taught others in turn — four generations handing it on. That is Multiplication.

So our criteria for choosing people must change: not choosing people by ability, but by their heart’s resolve, by their attitude, by whether they are willing to be shaped. A person with ability but no resolve will only last for a while; a person with resolve who is willing to be shaped can be used by God for a lifetime.

sections.heading: 4. Let the Church Be “a Workshop for Training”, Not “a Stage for Performance”
sections.html:
“For a righteous man falls seven times and rises up again; but the wicked are overthrown by calamity.” (Proverbs 24:16)

“Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness; looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted. Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.” (Galatians 6:1–2)

Brothers and sisters, if the first three points are to be put into practice, the church as an “environment” has to change. Because whether a person is willing to step forward depends to a great extent on one thing: what happens if you fall here.

Let’s compare two kinds of places. A stage is a place for “performing”. The rule is that you mustn’t make mistakes; the audience is people, and the ones giving the marks are people too. The person on the stage is thinking, “How well did I perform today?” A workshop is a place for “training”. The rule is that there will certainly be mistakes, and mistakes are part of the process. In a workshop there are master craftsmen, half-finished pieces and failed pieces too; what matters is not whether today’s piece has a flaw, but whether the apprentice’s skill is better each day than the day before. The person in the workshop is thinking, “What did I learn today?”

So let me ask: is our church a stage or a workshop? And our God — is he an audience, or a master craftsman? Brothers and sisters, he is the master craftsman; he is the potter: “When the vessel that he made of the clay was marred in the hand of the potter, he made it again another vessel, as seemed good to the potter to make it.” (Jeremiah 18:4) Notice: when the vessel was marred, the potter didn’t throw the clay away. He made it again.

Perfectionism is a very well-hidden obstacle in the church. It wears the coat of “pursuing excellence”, but underneath it is often “fear of losing face”; fear of losing face is love of face, and love of face is what 321 calls the self-centred life. Pride isn’t only arrogance; it can also be a sense of inferiority — and inferiority is often wounded pride. Either way, the focus is on ourselves, not on Jesus.

The Lord Jesus’ parable of the talents speaks to exactly this. A master entrusted his property to three servants. The first two traded with it and each doubled what he had been given. But the third said, “Lord, … I was afraid, and went away and hid your talent in the earth. Behold, you have what is yours.” (Matthew 25:24–25) Notice his reason: “I was afraid.” He hadn’t lost the money; he hadn’t lost a single coin. Yet his master called him “wicked and slothful” (Matthew 25:26).

Brothers and sisters, what a solemn reminder this is: in the Lord’s accounts, “not moving for fear of making a mistake” is more serious than “making a mistake after moving”. The Lord’s praise for the first two servants was: “Well done, good and faithful servant.” (Matthew 25:21) What the Lord praises is faithfulness, not perfection.

A study of medical teams by Professor Amy Edmondson of Harvard Business School, published in 1996, carries a real lesson for us. Her original hypothesis was that high-performing medical teams would make fewer errors; but the data showed the opposite — the better teams actually had more errors “reported”. It wasn’t that they made more mistakes, but that they dared to speak them out, and so could correct them promptly and learn from one another. In tense teams, errors were hidden, and the same mistakes were made again and again. Later, in a 1999 paper in Administrative Science Quarterly, she called this atmosphere — where telling the truth and admitting a mistake won’t get you humiliated — “psychological safety”.

Brothers and sisters, shouldn’t the church be the place with the highest “psychological safety” in the whole world? We are the one group of people who openly confess that we are sinners living by forgiveness. If even the church can’t allow people to make mistakes, then the gospel of grace among us is reduced to a set of words, not a way of life.

Professor Carol Dweck of Stanford University also points out that people with a “fixed mindset” see failure as a verdict on themselves and so avoid challenges, while people with a “growth mindset” see failure as part of the process and so embrace challenges. And the gospel gives us the firmest foundation of all: our worth is not built on our performance but on Christ’s redemption. Precisely because my identity is secure, I can afford to fail.

So to build “a workshop for training”, three things need to change together.

First, leaders must give people opportunities to train. Not only to the safe pairs of hands, but also to those who are “just learning to walk”. Let them do it first, let them finish, and then go over it with them. Every opportunity you give away is a tree you are planting. Trees take time; fruit comes in its season.

Second, the congregation must be willing to accept training. When the sister leading the songs for the first time sings off key, what is our reaction? A frown, whispering — or going up to her after the meeting, patting her on the shoulder and saying, “Thank you for stepping up”? Brothers and sisters, one word can plant a person, and one look can wreck a person.

Third, the whole community must provide an environment that tolerates mistakes. “Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness.” (Galatians 6:1) The word “restore” is, once again, the Greek katartizō — that same word for “mending nets and setting bones”. Paul also says, “Now we who are strong ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak, and not to please ourselves.” (Romans 15:1) The word “ought” tells us that this is not an option; it is a responsibility.

The 321 practice of 920 makes this very concrete: everyone we are in relationship with is our “2”, and we are to practise living out a selfless (0) life, bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions towards them — “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23) Look how many of these nine graces are made for “tolerating mistakes”: patience, to wait while someone slowly grows; kindness, to keep treating them well when they slip up; gentleness, to say things in a way people can actually hear; self-control, to hold back the word of blame that wants to come out at once.

321 also says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. If a leader corrects someone in a proud tone, the person corrected will respond with a proud heart, and one act of service ends up wounding two hearts. If a leader builds someone up with a humble heart, the one built up learns to serve the next person humbly too. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.

When everyone can accept one another and build one another up, serving is no longer pressure but joyful learning, and mistakes are no longer setbacks but opportunities for progress. Then the church becomes a true “spiritual school” rather than a “spiritual exam hall”. A school is a place where people learn; an exam hall is a place where people are weeded out. Brothers and sisters, our Lord runs a school, not an exam hall.

sections.heading: 5. Integrating the 321 Vision: Exchanging Our Criteria for Choosing People for God’s Criteria
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s set today’s four key points back within the framework of 321 and look at them once more. You’ll find they are really all one and the same thing.

The Three Foundations

Jesus is my role model. The central demonstration in this lesson is the Lord himself: he called fishermen, a tax collector, a Zealot; he taught his disciples as they walked along together; after Peter fell, he placed the sheep back in his hands. If the way we use people differs from the Lord’s, it is we who must change, not the Lord.

The Bible is my standard. We don’t choose people by human eyes but by God’s word: “I don’t see as man sees. For man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.” (1 Samuel 16:7) Paul’s criteria were “faithful” and “able to teach” (2 Timothy 2:2).

The Holy Spirit is my guide. That prompting to step forward and serve is usually not something you thought up yourself; it is something the Holy Spirit put in your heart. 321 says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. When we hold back from moving, it is often because we are calculating with our brain rather than responding with our heart.

The Two Core Values

Let Jesus be King. If Jesus is King, an opportunity to serve isn’t “my business” but “the King’s sending”; and the success or failure of that service isn’t “my face” but “the King’s work”. All we need to say is, “Here I am. Send me.”

Let Jesus receive all the glory. This settles the difficulty for two kinds of people. For those who don’t dare to step forward: since the glory goes to the Lord, you needn’t fear that you aren’t impressive enough. For those who have been stepping forward for a long time: since the glory goes to the Lord, you needn’t fear that others are more impressive than you.

The Goal

Establish God’s system. A system isn’t held up by one person; it is carried on from generation to generation. Paul, Timothy, faithful men, others — four generations handing it on: that is a system. If all we care about is putting on a good service this Sunday, but not a single new person is being raised up, then we are maintaining an event, not establishing a system.

The Self-Centred Life and Selflessness

In today’s lesson, both kinds of people have to face the self-centred life. The one who is invited says, “I’m not ready yet.” On the surface it’s modesty; underneath, it’s often self-centredness — afraid of not being good enough, afraid of taking responsibility. The one doing the inviting says, “He isn’t ready yet.” On the surface it’s responsibility; underneath, it’s often self-centredness too — afraid the programme won’t be perfect, afraid of spending extra time walking with people.

Selflessness is not having nothing; selflessness is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out. “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20) When I am no longer the main character, I dare to go on; when I am no longer the main character, I also dare to let others go on. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.

Fivefold Change and Four Shifts of Perspective

Fivefold change runs: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Today we are changing the first link — mindset: from “waiting for God to use me” to “hurrying to let God use me”, and from “picking talent” to “developing hearts”. Once the mindset changes, life changes; once life changes, daily living changes; once daily living changes, relationships change; once relationships change, ministry follows naturally.

Pay special attention to the order: first life, then relationships, then ministry. When the church is short of workers, the easiest thing to do is to skip life and relationships and go straight to filling the gaps in ministry — and the people brought in that way don’t last long before they collapse.

Our perspective needs to shift in four ways too. From man’s to God’s: man looks at whether someone is useful; God looks at whether someone is willing. From earthly to heavenly: earth looks at whether the meeting was polished; heaven looks at whether a life was built up. From temporary to eternal: letting new people go on today may be a little slower and a little messier, but in ten years you will see a whole generation of workers. From worldly to godly: the world uses people in order to exploit them; God uses people in order to make them whole.

sections.heading: 6. Putting It into Practice: Using the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset to Turn Mindset into Life
sections.html:
The lesson text gives us three very concrete practices. Let’s take them one at a time, and use 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to bring each one down to earth.

Practice 1: When an opportunity comes, respond boldly: “Lord, I am willing to be used by you!”

Information: You have already been called; that prompting, that invitation, is the sending.

Revelation: Ask the Holy Spirit to remind you of a ministry you once turned down. At that moment, what was in the Lord’s heart?

Conviction: Say to the Lord in your heart, “Lord, I believe you really do want to use an imperfect person like me.”

Implementation: Within this week, say one sentence to your small-group leader or pastor: “Whenever there’s a need, please let me have a go.” Say it now; don’t wait for the next opportunity.

Evaluation: After you’ve done it for the first time, be still for ten minutes and ask yourself: Where was the Lord’s grace? Where was my weakness? Where do I need to apologise or say thank you?

Correction: Of the things your evaluation turns up, change one thing concretely — just one.

Repetition: For three months in a row, let this become the norm. Spiritual muscle grows through repetition.

Multiplication: After three months, find a brother or sister newer than you and say, “Next time let’s do it together — you do half.”

Practice 2: Leaders, give one servant who is “just learning to walk” an opportunity to train

Information: The church doesn’t have a shortage of talent; it has too few people “willing to be used”, and too few “willing to use people”.

Revelation: Be still, and let the Lord place a name on your heart — most likely someone you had thought was “not quite ready yet”.

Conviction: Believe that God’s plan for this person is more accurate than your assessment of them. God called Gideon “mighty man of valor” (Judges 6:12).

Implementation: This month, give them a real position — not odd jobs, but a place where they will be seen and might well make mistakes. Help them prepare beforehand, and go over it with them afterwards.

Evaluation: When they slipped up, what was the first thing you said? “See, I told you,” or “Thank you for stepping up”?

Correction: If you said the wrong thing, go and apologise to them. A leader’s apology is one of the most powerful lessons in all of discipleship training.

Repetition: Don’t give just one chance. What Barnabas gave Mark wasn’t one chance; it was a stretch of road walked together.

Multiplication: Once they are standing firm, hand them someone newer: “Now it’s your turn to bring someone along.” This is what it means to “commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also” (2 Timothy 2:2).

Practice 3: Reflect on whether you have ever held back for fear of making mistakes, and ask the Lord to restore your passion to be used

Information: In the Lord’s accounts, “not moving for fear of making a mistake” is more serious than “making a mistake after moving” (Matthew 25:24–26).

Revelation: Ask the Lord to shine his light: after which wound did you bury your talent in the ground? A public mistake? A cutting criticism?

Conviction: Believe that the Lord has never written you off. What he said to Peter was “when once you have turned again” (Luke 22:32), not “you’re finished”.

Implementation: Bring that incident before the Lord and name it specifically, and find a spiritual companion to pray with you. Then dig your talent up out of the ground — start again with one small act of service.

Evaluation: Pay attention to the voice inside. When that “You can’t do it” shows up again, answer it with God’s word.

Correction: Change your self-talk from “I can’t do it” to “I may be of no use, but God is willing to use me — so I’ll hurry up and let him use me.”

Repetition: Every morning, answer the Lord once with Isaiah 6:8: “Here I am. Send me!”

Multiplication: Tell the story of your restoration to another brother or sister who is holding back. Once your weakness has been touched by grace, it becomes a way out for someone else.

A Gentle Reminder

God isn’t afraid of your mistakes; he’s only concerned that you don’t move. True faith isn’t perfect preparation; it is immediate obedience.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: The Lord Is Not Short of People; He Is Waiting for Willing Ones
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s return to the sigh we began with: “We just don’t have enough people here.” Having come this far, I hope we have all seen it: the church does not have a shortage of talent; it has too few people who are “willing to be used”. When we change our mindset about using people — from “waiting for God to use me” to “hurrying to let God use me”, from “picking talent” to “developing hearts” — the church will no longer lack workers. Because God is not short of people; he is only waiting for the willing.

Let me gather up today’s four key points in four sentences. First, don’t wait to be called, because you have already been called — that prompting is the sending. Second, learn while serving, and pray while learning — don’t treat prayer as a checkpoint; treat it as your breath. Third, move from using talent to developing talent — not choosing people by ability, but by their heart’s resolve, their attitude and their willingness to be shaped. Fourth, let the church be a workshop for training, not a stage for performance — God is the master craftsman, not the audience; he runs a school, not an exam hall.

In the end these four sentences all point to the same centre: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. If Jesus is King, then my time, my gifts and my position are all his — if he wants me to step up, I step up; if he wants me to step aside and hold others up, I step aside. If all the glory goes to him, I don’t need to prove myself through serving, nor protect myself by holding on to a position. Then there will be no one in the church jostling to stand up front, and no one hiding to avoid standing up — only a company of clay vessels, joyfully being used by the Lord.

Brothers and sisters, this morning the Lord’s question has not changed. He says, “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” (Isaiah 6:8) He isn’t asking “Who is able?” He is asking “Who will go?”

May we all become vessels like this: mature or still young, willing to say, “Lord, here I am — use me!”

And may we all become leaders like this: however young the other person may be, willing to say, “Come on, I’ll walk with you. This time, you do it.”

keyVerses: “I heard the Lord’s voice, saying, ‘Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?’ Then I said, ‘Here I am. Send me!’” (Isaiah 6:8)
“The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.” (2 Timothy 2:2)
declarations: Lord, thank you that you are willing to use an imperfect person like me. Today I choose to answer your call boldly, no longer waiting, no longer making excuses. As I serve, teach me and prune me, so that I become more and more after your own heart, a vessel that blesses others.
practices: When an opportunity comes, respond boldly: “Lord, I am willing to be used by you!”
Leaders: give one servant who is “just learning to walk” an opportunity to train
Reflect on whether you have held back for fear of mistakes; ask the Lord to restore your passion to be used
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we worship you. You are the King seated on the high throne, and your glory fills the whole earth.

Lord, forgive us. We have used the most spiritual words to put off your prompting, and the most reasonable excuses to refuse your sending; we have so often chosen people with the eyes of the world, instead of developing them with a father’s heart.

Lord, today we are willing to change our mindset. We will no longer wait to be called, because we have already been called. Let us learn while serving and pray while learning; let prayer be not a checkpoint before action, but the breath within it.
Lord, give us the heart of Barnabas, to see people’s potential and not give up on their weakness; make our church a workshop for training, not a stage for performance.
Lord, once again we place these clay vessels of ours into your hands. You are the potter, and we are the clay; when we are marred, please make us again.
Here I am; send me. Reign as King among us, and may all the glory be yours. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Share about a time you said, “I need to pray about it some more,” and the opportunity to serve simply fizzled out. Read Isaiah 6:8 again: “I heard the Lord’s voice, saying, ‘Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?’ Then I said, ‘Here I am. Send me!’” If you could turn back the clock, how would you respond? In what small matter could you take the first step this week?

Each of you, think of a brother or sister who is “just learning to walk”. Read 2 Timothy 2:2: “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.” How will you give them a concrete opportunity to train? When they slip up, what word of encouragement are you ready to say?

l057.subtitle: The Concept of Developing People (Part 3): Changing How We Choose People
l057.partTitle: Unit 4 · The Prerequisite for Revival — A Change of Mindset

sections.heading: Introduction: When One Person Is Willing to Change, a Generation Is Turned Around
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we come together to lesson fifty-eight of 321 Morning Devotion, entitled “Change Begins with Me”.

Let’s begin with a picture. Every year, as winter passes, the snow on the Alps begins to loosen. Geologists tell us that a great avalanche that buries an entire valley usually doesn’t begin with a thunderous crack at the summit, but with one tiny slip beneath a single layer of snow. That slip is too small for the eye to see, yet within seconds it carries the whole mountainside with it. Church history is like that too. On 13 August 1727, in a small village in eastern Germany called Herrnhut — “the Lord’s watch” — a band of refugees who had been driven from their homes for their faith were full of suspicion, rivalry and judgement towards one another. That morning, during a Communion service, the Spirit of God was poured out; one by one they confessed their sins to one another, forgave one another and washed one another’s feet. From that day on they began a round-the-clock prayer meeting that went on for a hundred years, and sent out hundreds of missionaries to the world. Historians call that day the starting point of the Moravian revival. But if we went back to the scene and asked, “Where did the revival begin?”, the answer would be: not from the pulpit, not from an organisation, but from hearts, one after another, that were willing to change.

Brothers and sisters, let me ask a very honest question: how many years have you and I been listening to sermons? We attend meetings, we read the Bible, our notes are neat and tidy — but when we get home, has our temper changed? Has our relationship with our spouse changed? Has the way we react to money, to face, to authority changed? If not, where does the problem lie?

The problem isn’t that the truth doesn’t work. It’s that we have taken “hearing” for “having”, and “being moved” for “being changed”.

The lesson text tells us something extremely important: change is not an overnight miracle but a gradual journey of life. The eight stages of changing our mindset that 321 teaches — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — are the complete process of life change. These eight stages are like a staircase, leading us step by step from the head to the heart, from the heart to the hands, and from ourselves to others.

Today we’ll look at four things together: first, change is a process that begins on the inside and is gradual and all-encompassing; second, why we know the truth and yet haven’t changed; third, the four levels of mindset, from knowing to becoming life; and fourth, the impact of change, reaching out from the individual to the world.

May the Holy Spirit himself speak to each one of us this morning. May we not merely know a little more today, but truly take a step. Because the first prayer of revival is always this one: “Lord, change begins with me.”

sections.heading: Scripture Background: The Turning Point of Romans 12
sections.html:
Our theme passage today is Romans 12:2. To grasp the weight of this verse, we first need to understand its place in the whole book.

The author of Romans is the apostle Paul. The letter is generally thought to have been written around AD 56–57, towards the end of Paul’s third missionary journey. He was then in Corinth, in Greece, preparing to take the contribution of the churches of Macedonia and Achaia to Jerusalem (Romans 15:25–26). The letter was addressed to the church in the city of Rome — a group of believers Paul had never met, made up of both Jews and Gentiles. In AD 49 the Roman emperor Claudius had ordered the Jews expelled from Rome (Acts 18:2); a few years later the ban was relaxed and Jewish believers gradually returned, only to find that the church was now led by Gentile believers. The two groups judged each other over food, festivals and traditions (Romans 14) — and that was the real-life situation in which Paul wrote this letter.

Romans 1–11 is the most complete and rigorous account of salvation in the Bible. Paul begins with the total corruption of humanity and goes on to justification by faith, union with Christ, the indwelling of the Holy Spirit, God’s election and the future of Israel. By the end of chapter 11, Paul cannot help bursting into praise: Oh the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and the knowledge of God! And then the whole book takes an enormous turn.

Chapter 12 verse 1 opens with the word “Therefore”. That word is like the pivot of a door, swinging the truth of the previous eleven chapters round towards the life of the five chapters that follow. Paul says: “Therefore I urge you, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service.” (Romans 12:1) And immediately after comes our theme verse: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” (Romans 12:2)

Brothers and sisters, notice the order. First the truth of chapter 11, then the offering of chapter 12. First “Information” and “Revelation”, then “Conviction” and “Implementation”. Paul doesn’t begin by telling people to change their behaviour; he begins by letting them see the mercies of God. Once we have seen God’s mercies, offering ourselves becomes — as the Chinese Union Version puts it — “only what is fitting”. 321 says: first life, then relationships, then ministry. The very structure of Romans is the best commentary on that saying.

Now look at the original. In “Don’t be conformed to this world”, “conformed” is συσχηματίζω (syschēmatizō); its root, schēma, is “outward form”, and the sense is “being pressed by a mould from outside into the same shape”. The word “transformed” in “be transformed by the renewing of your mind” is μεταμορφόομαι (metamorphoō), whose root morphē means “essential form”. This word appears only four times in the New Testament, one of them in Matthew 17:2, where Jesus on the mountain “was changed” — transfigured — before them. In other words, Paul is drawing an extremely sharp contrast here: the world wants to press you from the outside into its shape; the Holy Spirit wants to change you from the inside into the Lord’s form. One is pressure from without, the other is change from within; one is a mould, the other is a metamorphosis.

“Mind” in the original is νοῦς (nous), the centre of a person’s thinking, judgement and values. “Renewing” is ἀνακαίνωσις (anakainōsis), meaning “new in quality” — not an old thing refurbished, but a change of nature. This is exactly what 321 calls the first level of change: the change of mindset. Change your mindset and you change your life; change your life and you change your daily living; change your daily living and you change your relationships; change your relationships and you change your ministry. In fivefold change, the first domino is mindset.

One more word deserves attention: “prove” is δοκιμάζω (dokimazō), originally a term from metallurgy, meaning to test a metal with fire and approve it only once it had been shown to be genuine. Paul’s point is this: once your mind has been renewed, you have godly discernment, and can tell on the spot what God’s good, well-pleasing and perfect will is. Brothers and sisters, God’s will isn’t found by drawing lots; it is proved by a renewed mind.
