sections.heading: 1. Change Is a Process That Begins on the Inside, Gradual and All-Encompassing
sections.html:
The lesson text says that true change is not merely an adjustment of behaviour; it begins with the renewal of the mind.

The Bible is very clear about this. Through the prophet Ezekiel, God promised: “I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you. I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh.” (Ezekiel 36:26) Notice that God didn’t say, “I will repair your behaviour.” He said, “I will change your heart.” The Hebrew word for “heart” is לֵב (lev), and in the Old Testament it doesn’t refer only to the emotions; it is the centre of thought, will and decision. The operation God intends to perform goes to the deepest place.

Proverbs also says: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23) 321 has a saying that puts it superbly: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. The wellspring of life flows from the heart, not from the brain.

The lesson text divides the eight stages into three levels. This is the skeleton of today’s lesson, so let’s commit it to memory:

The first three stages — Information, Revelation, Conviction — belong to inner change. They are invisible, yet they are the most important foundation.

The fourth stage — Implementation — is the moment change begins to show outwardly; at last other people can see it.

The next stages — Evaluation, Correction, Repetition — make the outward change firm, so that it is no longer a flash in the pan.

The final stage, Multiplication, lets the changed life influence others and produces a multiplying effect.

Brothers and sisters, this order must never be reversed. The mistake we most easily make is either to skip the first three stages and run straight to Implementation, or to stay in the first three stages and never move into Implementation. The first is legalism — gritting our teeth on willpower until we are utterly exhausted. The second is intellectualism — listening to sermons all our lives while our life stays exactly where it was.

Let me give you an illustration. For a tree to grow one metre taller, its roots underground must first push one metre deeper. If you only water and fertilise above ground, forcing the branches and leaves to grow quickly and thickly, one typhoon will tear it out by the roots. There is a leguminous tree of southern Africa, the camelthorn, that grows up to about twenty metres tall, yet its taproot can drill down more than thirty metres to reach the water hidden beneath the desert. The height you can see always depends on the depth you can’t. Inner change is the root; outward change is the branches and leaves.

Science confirms the principle of gradual change too. In a study published in the European Journal of Social Psychology in 2010, a team led by Phillippa Lally at University College London followed ninety-six participants as they formed a new daily habit. They found that it took an average of sixty-six days for a behaviour to become “automatic”, with individual cases ranging from eighteen to two hundred and fifty-four days. This research gives us two reminders. First, change takes time, so don’t condemn yourself because you haven’t changed by day seven. Second, change has a pathway; as long as you keep walking it, the day it becomes automatic will come.

A study by Professor Eleanor Maguire’s team at the same university, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in 2000, is even more surprising. London taxi drivers, in order to pass an extremely difficult test of the city’s routes, spend a long time memorising and practising on the streets; afterwards, the grey-matter volume in the rear part of their hippocampus was clearly larger than that of the control group — and the longer they had been driving, the greater the difference. This is neuroplasticity. When God made human beings, he wrote “able to be changed” into our very brains. Brothers and sisters, you are not a block of concrete that has already set; you are clay still turning on the wheel.

That is why the lesson text says that a true spiritual impact doesn’t begin with large-scale action, but with one heart that is willing to change. When one person is willing to be changed by God, the whole family can be changed; when many people are willing to change together, the whole church — a whole generation — will be turned around.

This is the very core of 321: let Jesus be King. Letting Jesus be King doesn’t mean first making him King of the church or King of the ministry; it means first making him King of this heart of mine. The focus is on Jesus — not on myself, not on others, not on circumstances. When Jesus reigns as King within me, change begins to happen in the deepest place.

sections.heading: 2. Why We Know the Truth Yet Haven’t Changed
sections.html:
The lesson text raises a question that cuts to the heart: many people have heard countless sermons and attended many camps, yet their lives seem to be at a standstill. The problem isn’t that the truth doesn’t work; it’s that we often think we already have a godly mindset when in fact we’ve only got as far as the head.

The Bible doesn’t spare us on this. The writer of Hebrews says: “For indeed we have had good news preached to us, even as they also did, but the word they heard didn’t profit them, because it wasn’t mixed with faith by those who heard.” (Hebrews 4:2) The word “mixed” in the original carries the sense of “blended into one”. The word is like flour, and faith is like water. However much flour you have, without water it stays flour forever; it never becomes bread. Brothers and sisters, our problem usually isn’t too little flour; it’s that the water hasn’t been added.

The Lord Jesus asks it even more directly: “Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and don’t do the things which I say?” (Luke 6:46) And he rebuked the religious leaders of his day: “All things therefore whatever they tell you to observe, observe and do, but don’t do their works; for they say, and don’t do.” (Matthew 23:3) They say, and don’t do — that is what the lesson text calls “the level of the head”.

James puts it most vividly: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.” (James 1:22) Notice the phrase “deluding your own selves”. Those who hear the word and don’t do it aren’t deceiving others; they are deceiving themselves. They mistake “I’ve heard it” for “I have it”, and “I agree with it” for “I’ve done it”. Then James gives an illustration: “For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man looking at his natural face in a mirror; for he sees himself, and goes away, and immediately forgets what kind of man he was.” (James 1:23–24)

Psychology offers good corroboration of this. In 1957 the American psychologist Leon Festinger put forward the “theory of cognitive dissonance”: when a person’s beliefs and behaviour don’t line up, tension arises inside, and to get rid of that discomfort people usually have two roads open to them. One is to change their behaviour so that it fits the truth; the other is to adjust their beliefs and find reasons for their behaviour. Sadly, most people choose the second road, because it takes less effort. We say, “That’s just my personality,” “Once this busy patch is over,” “He wronged me first.” Brothers and sisters, every time we use a reason to get rid of that cut-to-the-heart feeling, we shut the door on change once again.

There is an even more hidden reason. The lesson text says we “think we already have it”. Those few words are the root of every standstill. Educational psychology calls this the “illusion of familiarity”: because we’ve heard it, seen it and copied it into our notes, the brain produces a sense of fluency — “I already understand this” — and that fluency makes people stop learning. The spiritual life is the same. Once someone feels, “I’ve known this for ages,” the words of the Holy Spirit can no longer get in.

Looking deeper still, 321 tells us that the root of all this is the self-centred life. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem. What is pride? Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place. When I know the truth but don’t do it, deep down I’m saying, “I admit this is right, but in this matter I’m still going to be in charge.” In my head I let God be God, but in my daily living I want to be king myself. So the gulf between knowing and doing is not a gulf of knowledge; it is a gulf of kingship.

Humility is exactly the opposite: humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God. That is why 321 says: humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. The moment I am willing to say, “Lord, in this matter I’ll listen to you,” the truth drops from my head into my life.

Paul himself is candid about this struggle: “For desire is present with me, but I don’t find it doing that which is good. For the good which I desire, I don’t do; but the evil which I don’t desire, that I practice.” (Romans 7:18–19) Paul isn’t teaching us to resign ourselves to fate; he is driving us towards the only way out: “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20) Brothers and sisters, relying on our own effort only gets us as far as the despair of Romans 7; it is by the Spirit putting to death the deeds of the body that we enter the victory of Romans 8. Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves.

Dietrich Bonhoeffer, the German pastor and martyr, left us a famous line in “The Cost of Discipleship”: only those who believe obey, and only those who obey believe. That sentence gets to the bottom of the relationship between knowing and doing. Obedience isn’t an optional extra after believing; obedience itself is the evidence of believing.

sections.heading: 3. The Four Levels of Mindset: From Knowing to Becoming Life
sections.html:
The lesson text divides mindset into four levels, and these four levels correspond neatly to the progression of the eight stages of changing our mindset. Brothers and sisters, as you listen, please ask yourself honestly: which level am I on right now?

Level One: Theoretical Mindset

This is the level of “Information”. The lesson text says: we know what is right and can even explain it to others, yet we don’t live it out ourselves; people like this easily become Pharisees, demanding much of others and little of themselves.

The Lord Jesus’ verdict on the Pharisees was: “for they say, and don’t do.” (Matthew 23:3) He also said: “For you tithe mint, dill, and cumin, and have left undone the weightier matters of the law: justice, mercy, and faith.” (Matthew 23:23) The Pharisees didn’t lack knowledge of the Scriptures; they were the people who knew the Scriptures best in their day. Their problem was this: their knowledge grew outwards, but their life didn’t grow inwards.

Paul’s warning is even more direct: “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.” (1 Corinthians 8:1) If knowledge doesn’t walk together with love, it becomes fuel for pride.

Information is of course necessary. The first of the eight stages is Information. Without information, nothing that follows can happen; as Paul says, “So faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.” (Romans 10:17) The problem isn’t information itself; it’s stopping at information.

Let me give you an illustration. A man buys a whole cabinet full of cookbooks. He has leafed through every one, and can even recite the twelve steps of boeuf bourguignon — yet the stove in his kitchen has never once been lit. Does he understand cooking? He understands “information about cooking”, but he can’t cook a meal. The spiritual life is the same. Someone who can expound Romans is not necessarily someone who lives Romans out.

Science offers a good reminder here too. In 1885 the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus put forward his famous “forgetting curve”. Experimenting on himself, he found that newly learned nonsense syllables, if not reviewed, were mostly forgotten within a day. Mere information evaporates. Only what has been fixed in place by Implementation and Repetition will remain.

From the 321 point of view, the attitude most needed at the Information stage is this: the Bible is my standard. Not “the Bible is my knowledge”, but “the Bible is my standard”. A standard is something used to measure me, not to measure others. When every time I read the Bible I first ask, “Lord, which part of me is this passage measuring?”, Information begins to move towards Revelation.

Level Two: Revealed Mindset

This is the level where “the heart is touched”. The lesson text says: under the prompting of the Holy Spirit we begin to understand the truth and even long to act; but if it stays at being moved, without practical action, we are still stuck at the stage of being moved but not moving.

The Greek word for “revelation” is ἀποκάλυψις (apokalypsis), which literally means “taking off the lid”. You may have read the same verse a hundred times and it was only black ink on white paper; then one day the lid is suddenly lifted, and that word seizes you as if it were alive. That is revelation.

The Lord Jesus once said to Peter: “Jesus answered him, ‘Blessed are you, Simon Bar Jonah, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven.’” (Matthew 16:17) Peter recognised Jesus as the Christ not by reasoning but by the revelation of the Father. The Lord Jesus also promised: “However when he, the Spirit of truth, has come, he will guide you into all truth.” (John 16:13) Brothers and sisters, this is precisely the third of 321’s foundations: the Holy Spirit is my guide.

But the lesson text gives a solemn warning: if being moved doesn’t turn into action, we are still standing still. This is exactly what the Lord Jesus said at the end of the Sermon on the Mount —

“Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man, who built his house on a rock. The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat on that house; and it didn’t fall, for it was founded on the rock. Everyone who hears these words of mine, and doesn’t do them will be like a foolish man, who built his house on the sand. The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat on that house; and it fell — and great was its fall.” (Matthew 7:24–27)

Notice that both kinds of people “hear”. The two houses may look exactly alike from the outside, and the two storms are exactly the same. The only difference lies in a few words: “and does them” versus “and doesn’t do them”. Brothers and sisters, the storm won’t inspect our foundations for us; the storm will only expose them.

There is a very important distinction to make here: being moved is a gift, not an achievement. When we weep at a conference or melt in worship, that is God’s grace coming upon us. But tears are not fruit; tears only mean the soil has been loosened. If we mistake being moved for being changed, we will weep year after year and stay exactly where we are year after year. This is what the lesson text calls “the illusion of faith”.

In 1983 the American psychologists James Prochaska and Carlo DiClemente put forward the stages of change in the “transtheoretical model”, later settled as five stages: precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action and maintenance. Their research showed that many people get stuck for a long time in the “contemplation” stage — they know they ought to change, they want to change, yet they never move; some stay stuck for years. How similar this finding is to what the lesson text calls “being moved but not moving”. Psychology merely describes the phenomenon; the Bible gives the way out: we don’t wait until we have the strength before we obey; we receive strength in the act of obeying.

Moving from Information to Revelation is the work of the Holy Spirit; moving from Revelation to Conviction is the surrender of the will. The third of the eight stages, Conviction, corresponds to what Romans calls “obedience of faith” (Romans 1:5). Conviction isn’t “I agree”; conviction is “I surrender”. Brothers and sisters, a person can agree with a thousand things and not change in a single one; but if he truly surrenders in just one thing, that one thing will change his whole life.

Level Three: Practised Mindset

This is the level of “being willing to live it out”. The lesson text says: people begin to respond to the truth with action; though they will stumble and make mistakes, through training they gradually become mature and balanced, and theory turns into a workable way of daily living.

This has always been the Bible’s position. Samuel said to Saul: “Has Yahweh as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying Yahweh’s voice? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams.” (1 Samuel 15:22) The apostle John says: “My little children, let’s not love in word only, or with the tongue only, but in deed and truth.” (1 John 3:18)

Paul uses a word from the sports ground to describe this stage: “Exercise yourself toward godliness. For bodily exercise has some value, but godliness has value in all things, having the promise of the life which is now, and of that which is to come.” (1 Timothy 4:7–8) “Exercise” is γυμνάζω (gymnazō), the root of our word “gymnasium”, referring to the training of athletes, stripped down and drenched in sweat. Brothers and sisters, godliness isn’t a temperament; godliness is trained.

Please pay special attention to a phrase in the lesson text that comes from a true shepherd’s heart: “though they will stumble and make mistakes”. How many perfectionist hearts that phrase sets free! When you first start putting things into practice, you are bound to be unbalanced — to overdo it or underdo it, to be misunderstood, to lose heart. That is normal. A baby learning to walk falls over thousands of times on average before walking steadily, and no parent ever says to a child who falls, “You’re not cut out for walking.” Our Heavenly Father even less so.

This is where we bring in 321’s concrete practice: 920. Everyone we are in relationship with is our “2”; as we practise living out a selfless (0) life in these relationships, we bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions — “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23) Brothers and sisters, notice: fruit isn’t borne in the prayer closet; it is borne in relationships. You can only practise patience when someone provokes you; you can only practise gentleness when someone talks back to you; you can only practise kindness when someone wrongs you. God has placed that difficult person beside you not to torment you, but to bear fruit in you.

In 1977 the Stanford psychologist Albert Bandura put forward his theory of “self-efficacy”. His research found that a person’s belief that they can do something comes mainly not from other people’s encouragement but from “first-hand experience of success”. In other words, you have to do it once before you believe you can. The spiritual life is the same. Every time you obey, your faith in God becomes that much more real. Implementation doesn’t only change your circumstances; it changes you first.

In 321’s language, this level is “Jesus is my role model”. Jesus never wrote a book; in three and a half years of daily life he lived out the Father’s heart before twelve men. “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 2:5) — and what Paul goes on to describe is the Lord’s downward path: he emptied himself, took the form of a servant, humbled himself and became obedient to the point of death (Philippians 2:6–8). The heart of Implementation is following this role model downwards.

Level Four: Living Mindset

This is the level of “living it out naturally”. The lesson text says: through Evaluation, Correction and Repetition the truth becomes part of our life, and flows out naturally without any need for struggle or deliberation; a mindset like this has become a person’s settled position, firm and hard to shake.

The fifth, sixth and seventh of the eight stages are precisely the work of this level.

Evaluation — the Bible calls it self-examination. Paul says: “But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of the bread, and drink of the cup.” (1 Corinthians 11:28) David’s prayer goes deeper: “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.” (Psalm 139:23–24) Notice that David isn’t analysing himself; he is asking God to search him. Self-analysis often slides into self-pity or self-condemnation; only asking God to search us brings light and healing.

Correction means adjusting our direction at once according to what God has pointed out. True repentance, the Greek μετάνοια (metanoia), literally means “a change of mind”. Repentance isn’t feeling sorry; repentance is turning around.

Repetition means walking the same road again and again until that road becomes your instinct. God commanded Joshua: “This book of the law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, that you may observe to do according to all that is written in it.” (Joshua 1:8) Meditating day and night — that is Repetition. Hebrews says: “But solid food is for those who are full grown, who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern good and evil.” (Hebrews 5:14) The word “exercised” speaks precisely of the instinct that grows out of repetition.

I often think of a picture. A pianist is playing on stage, his ten fingers flying, yet he is smiling, even conversing with the music. Is he thinking about which note comes next? No. He no longer needs to think, because the notes have long since passed from the score into his fingers, and from his fingers into his bones. But before that, he played scales for thousands of hours. Research by K. Anders Ericsson’s team at Florida State University in 1993 showed that the greatest difference between top performers and ordinary performers isn’t talent but long-accumulated “deliberate practice” — practice with goals, with feedback and with constant correction. Brothers and sisters, this is simply the secular version of “Evaluation, Correction, Repetition”. God wrote this road into the Bible thousands of years ago.

The most beautiful description of the living mindset is in 2 Corinthians: “But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord, the Spirit.” (2 Corinthians 3:18) Notice that the verb in this verse is passive: “are transformed into the same image” — and in the original it is that very μεταμορφόομαι we saw earlier. We don’t make ourselves better; we are changed as we gaze on the Lord. The focus is on Jesus — not on ourselves, not on others, not on circumstances.

Brothers and sisters, climbing through the four levels: the theoretical mindset is in the head, the revealed mindset is in the heart, the practised mindset is in the hands, and the living mindset is in the bones. The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out — “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20) This is the living mindset.

sections.heading: 4. The Impact of Change: Reaching Out from the Individual to the World
sections.html:
The lesson text says: if a mindset exists only in the head, its influence is limited; but when a mindset becomes life, it can bring about a powerful impact. Change begins with ourselves, but it doesn’t stop with ourselves.

The last of the eight stages is “Multiplication”. It is the outlet of the whole process. If change stops with me, it is a well; when change flows on to others, it becomes a river of living water.

The Lord Jesus said: “Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” (John 12:24) Notice the words “it remains by itself alone”. A grain of wheat that doesn’t die hasn’t gone bad; it simply “remains”. Brothers and sisters, the greatest loss in the spiritual life isn’t falling away; it is simply “remaining”.

How does Multiplication happen? First, through the attraction of a life. The Lord Jesus said: “Even so, let your light shine before men; that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” (Matthew 5:16) Notice that people first see the works, and then give glory to the Father. You don’t need to explain first; live it out first. Second, through deliberate entrusting. Paul said to Timothy: “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.” (2 Timothy 2:2) There are four generations in this one verse: Paul, Timothy, faithful men, and others. Multiplication never depends on numbers; it depends on entrusting, one generation to the next.

This is exactly 321’s 235 relationships: become a “2” with a selfless person, spiritual companions to one another; build a “3”, becoming spiritual parents and spiritual children; and go on to become a “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. Paul voiced the heart of a spiritual parent for the Galatian church: “My little children, of whom I am again in travail until Christ is formed in you.” (Galatians 4:19)

Interestingly, educational research has also found that “teaching others” is itself the most effective way to learn. A study published in 2009 in the Journal of Science Education and Technology described the “protégé effect”: when students were teaching a virtual learning partner, the effort they put in and the learning they achieved were greater than when they were simply learning for themselves. Brothers and sisters, when you begin to bring someone along, you’ll find that the person being built up most is actually you. Multiplication isn’t only giving out; Multiplication in turn roots you deeper.

The lesson text ends by saying: God is looking for people like this — not perfect people, but people willing to change and willing to let the truth come alive.

Throughout the Bible, God’s eyes have been searching for people like this. God promised: “If my people, who are called by my name, will humble themselves, pray, seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then I will hear from heaven, will forgive their sin, and will heal their land.” (2 Chronicles 7:14) Look at the order: first humble themselves, then pray, then seek, then turn — and only then does God heal the land. The order of revival always begins with the human heart, not with circumstances.

Church history proves this again and again. In September 1857, an ordinary city missionary in New York, Jeremiah Lanphier, opened a room during the lunch hour and invited people to come and pray together. At the first meeting only six people turned up, and they trickled in late. Half a year later, tens of thousands of people in New York were praying at midday every day. The movement came to be called the “Layman’s Prayer Revival”, and its influence spread across North America and Britain. Brothers and sisters — six people. God is never short of hands; God is looking for a willing heart.

A saying commonly attributed to the great Russian writer Tolstoy goes: everyone thinks of changing the world, but no one thinks of changing himself. That saying is like a mirror. We pray for the church, we pray for the nation, we pray for the next generation — all of which is right; but without the words “Lord, begin with me”, our prayers are missing the most crucial link.

321 says the Goal is to establish God’s system. A system isn’t an organisation; a system is a body of changed people, joined to one another according to God’s order. And the first stone of that system is you.

sections.heading: 5. Integrating the 321 Vision: Letting Change Follow the Right Order
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s set this lesson within the whole picture of 321.

The Three Foundations correspond neatly to the first half of change. At the Information stage we need “the Bible is my standard” — not going by feelings, not going by trends, but going by God’s word. At the Revelation stage we need “the Holy Spirit is my guide” — because it is the Holy Spirit who lifts the lid, not my cleverness. At the Implementation stage we need “Jesus is my role model” — we don’t act according to our own imagination, but follow in the Lord’s footsteps.

The Two Core Values set the direction of change. Let Jesus be King: every act of Evaluation and Correction is really asking one question — in this matter, who is King? Let Jesus receive all the glory: if change makes people see how much I have grown, that is not yet the finishing line; change should make people “glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16).

The Goal is to establish God’s system. The last of the eight stages is Multiplication, and Multiplication is the building of the system.

Now look at fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. The four levels in this lesson are the first half of that route. The theoretical mindset stays at mindset; the revealed mindset touches life; the practised mindset enters daily living; the living mindset flows naturally into relationships; and Multiplication moves into ministry. First life, then relationships, then ministry — reverse that order and ministry will crush life. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

The priority of relationships is the same: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. Many people can’t change because they skip the checkpoint of “relationship with ourselves” — unwilling to face the truth about themselves honestly, unwilling to admit that they haven’t actually lived it out yet.

Finally, there is the shift of perspective. From man’s perspective to God’s: I see my failures; God sees my future. From earthly to heavenly: earth prizes speed; heaven prizes foundations. From temporary to eternal: a moment of being moved is temporary; a life that has been shaped is eternal. From worldly to godly: the world wants to press me into its mould; the Holy Spirit wants to transform me into the Lord’s form.

Brothers and sisters, the key to all of this is one thing: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred person says, “I know that already”; the selfless person says, “Lord, I obey.” Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. Change begins with me means this: I no longer wait for others to change first; I lay down my rights first and return to my originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.

sections.heading: 6. Putting It into Practice: Deepening This Lesson’s Three Practices with the Eight Stages
sections.html:
The lesson text gives us three practices for daily living. Let’s use the eight stages of changing our mindset to take these three practices deeper.

Practice 1: Reflect on which stage your current response to the truth has stopped at

Information: Reread this lesson’s four levels and write them on the first page of your notebook — theoretical, revealed, practised, living.

Revelation: Be still for five minutes and ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light: “Search me, God, and know my heart” (Psalm 139:23). Don’t rush to judge; wait for God to point out the one thing.

Conviction: Admit what you have seen. No excuses, no comparisons — just say, “Lord, I really am still stuck here.”

Implementation: Write that one thing down, specific down to one person, one situation, one sentence.

Evaluation: Tonight before you sleep, ask yourself: today, did I think I already had it in that matter?

Correction: If so, confess it to the Lord at once, and think of one small action you can take tomorrow.

Repetition: For seven days in a row, examine yourself every evening with the same three questions.

Multiplication: Find a spiritual companion, explain these four levels to them, and invite them to walk this road with you.

Practice 2: Choose one act of obedience to the truth that God brings to mind, and start putting it into practice today

Information: Choose a verse from this lesson’s passages, for example James 1:22: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.”

Revelation: Ask the Lord one question: today, in which matter does this verse want me to live it out?

Conviction: Don’t pick the easiest thing, and don’t pick the most heroic; pick the thing that makes you want to hide a little as soon as you think of it.

Implementation: Do it within twenty-four hours. A phone call, an apology, an act of forgiveness, a gift, some time spent with someone. Of the eight stages, this is the costliest, because it demands that you pay a price.

Evaluation: When you’ve done it, write down three things: what I did, what I felt inside, and how God responded to me.

Correction: If you went about it too hastily or too heavily, adjust the way you do it — rather than giving up the action.

Repetition: Do the same kind of action three more times this week, so that it moves from a decision to a habit. As we mentioned, the 2010 study by Lally’s team at University College London found that a new habit takes an average of sixty-six days to become automatic. Give God time, and give yourself time.

Multiplication: Once it has become your way of daily living, bring a brother or sister along to do the same thing with you.

Practice 3: Share what you experienced in putting it into practice with a spiritual companion; encourage one another and bear witness to one another’s change

Information: Understand what witness means — “You will be witnesses to me” (Acts 1:8) is the Lord’s commission to every disciple.

Revelation: Ask God to give you the right companion — what 321 calls your “2”.

Conviction: Lay down your pride and face. Being willing to speak of your failures is what real companionship is.

Implementation: Meet once this week, and each take ten minutes: what step did I take this week?

Evaluation: Ask each other one question: have I been mistaking being moved for being changed?

Correction: Remind each other, but don’t condemn each other. Remember: humility inspires humility.

Repetition: Set a fixed time, once a week, for a whole quarter.

Multiplication: Once the relationship between the two of you is firm, each bring one more person along, becoming a “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children, and going on towards a “5”, a team of spiritual comrades.

A Gentle Reminder

The lesson text leaves us a sentence to memorise: being moved is not change; action is the breakthrough. If the Holy Spirit’s revelation doesn’t turn into Implementation, it becomes an illusion of faith.

Brothers and sisters, please hold this in your heart: tears will dry, resolutions will fade, but the step you actually take will remain.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: Let Revival Begin with Me
sections.html:
The lesson text closes by saying: revival lies not in outward momentum but in inward renewal. When we are willing to cross over from knowing to doing, from being moved to taking action, God’s power will be released through us. Change is not a distant dream but a daily choice — choosing to let God change me, and to let revival begin with me.

Brothers and sisters, this morning I’m not asking you to do a hundred things. I’m asking you to do just one thing: the one thing you have known about for a long time but have never gone and done.

Perhaps it’s saying sorry to your spouse. Perhaps it’s forgiving the person who hurt you. Perhaps it’s putting your phone down and spending half an hour with your child. Perhaps it’s starting your daily morning reading again. Perhaps it’s taking the initiative to care for the brother you’ve been avoiding all along.

The Lord Jesus said: “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.” (Luke 9:23) In the Chinese Union Version, he says to take up the cross “daily” — please notice that word. Change isn’t a one-time decision; change is a daily choice.

Don’t be afraid that your beginning is too small. God never looks at scale; God looks at obedience. He has already promised: “being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ.” (Philippians 1:6) He is the one who begins the work, and he is the one who completes it; all we have to do is stop resisting, and simply say “yes”.

May our lives be changed — not so that people will praise us for how much we’ve grown, but so that Jesus may reign as King in us and receive all the glory. May our families, our small groups and our churches begin to be different, because one person this morning truly took a step.

Change begins with me.

keyVerses: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” (Romans 12:2)
practices: Reflect on which stage your current response to the truth has stopped at
Choose one act of obedience to the truth that God brings to mind, and start practising it today
Share your experience of putting it into practice with a spiritual companion; encourage one another and bear witness to one another’s change
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you.

Lord, you know how many sermons we have heard, and you know how much of them we have lived out. This morning we will no longer use busyness, or our personality, or other people’s faults to cover ourselves. We confess that we often think we already have it, when in fact it has only stayed in our heads. Please forgive us.

Lord, give us a new heart, and put a new spirit within us. Holy Spirit, carry your word from our heads into our hearts; from our hearts into our hands; from our hands into our very bones, until it becomes our life.

Lord, right now I place into your hands the one thing you have brought to my mind. I am willing to go and do it today. Give me strength; lift me up when I fall, strengthen me when I lose heart, so that I can evaluate, correct and repeat, until this truth becomes my life.

Lord, reign as King within me. May my change not be for my own good name, but so that those who see it will give glory to you. Use me, so that my family, my companions and my church are blessed through this small change in me.
Lord, revival begins with me. In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Matthew 7:24–26: “Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man, who built his house on a rock. … Everyone who hears these words of mine, and doesn’t do them will be like a foolish man, who built his house on the sand.” In your life right now, which truth have you “heard but not yet done”? What has held you back?

2 Timothy 2:2: “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.” Whom has God placed beside you to be your “2”? With what concrete matter could you begin practising together with them, moving towards Multiplication?
l058.title: Change Begins with Me
l058.subtitle: The Eight Stages of Life Change (Part 1)
l058.partTitle: Unit 4 · The Prerequisite for Revival — A Change of Mindset

sections.heading: Introduction: The Notebook Filled to the Margins
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. I’d like you first to picture something in your mind.

A notebook. You open it, and every page is crammed. Sermon outlines copied out, scriptures copied out, memorable sayings copied out, all underlined in three colours of ink. It’s a thick notebook, neat and beautiful. But suppose we close it and ask one question: over this past year, how much has my life actually changed?

That moment is usually a quiet one.

That is the most honest, and the most piercing, starting point for this morning’s devotion. Our generation has no shortage of messages. Open your phone and there are sermons, songs, Bible studies and devotional clips — more than you could ever finish. We may hear more truth in a single week than a believer in the early church heard in a lifetime. But we have to ask: with more truth, has our life grown stronger?

In the last lesson we saw that “change begins with me” — not waiting for others to change first, not waiting for circumstances to change first, but changing myself first. This lesson takes one step further: why does change so often get stuck?

The lesson text puts it with great precision: many people have heard countless messages and studied many scriptures, yet their lives still lack the power to break through. The problem is not that the truth doesn’t work; it’s that we so often stay at the stage of “knowing” and never enter the stage of “living it out.”

Brothers and sisters, “knowing” is not the same as “possessing.” Looking at a menu doesn’t fill you up; reading a book about swimming doesn’t keep you afloat in the water. If truth stays only in the head, it’s like a seed left in your pocket — the seed is real, and its life is real, but as long as it stays in your pocket it will only ever be a seed. It will never grow into a tree.

Jesus himself put it even more directly: “If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.” (John 13:17) He didn’t say, “If you know these things, blessed are you.” He said, “if you do them.” The blessing is not at the knowing end; the blessing is at the doing end.

James says it too: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.” (James 1:22) Notice the words “deluding your own selves.” The greatest danger of hearing the word without doing it is not ignorance but an illusion — I think I already possess it, when in fact I’ve only heard it.

So in this lesson we are going to make a journey: from “I know” to “I’ve grasped it,” from “I’ve grasped it” to “I’m practising it,” and from “I’m practising it” to “I possess it.” And when we truly possess it, that life will touch others, shape the atmosphere around us, form a culture and bring revival.

But on this road there is one obstacle that has to be dealt with first, and the third paragraph of the lesson text names it: we love the wrong thing. So at the end we will come back to 1 John 2:15 and face the most fundamental choice of all: do I love the world, or do I love God?

Change is not a distant dream; it is today’s decision. Let’s go into God’s word together.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A Letter Home from an Old Apostle to Second-Generation Believers
sections.html:
To grasp the weight of 1 John 2:15–17, we need first to stand beside the man who wrote it and take a look.

First, who wrote it. The history of the church consistently testifies that this letter came from the hand of the apostle John — the disciple who leaned on Jesus’ breast at the Last Supper, the disciple who stood at the foot of the cross and received the Lord’s charge. He was no theorist; he was a man who had seen with his own eyes and touched with his own hands. At the very start of his letter he says: “That which was from the beginning, that which we have heard, that which we have seen with our eyes, that which we saw, and our hands touched, concerning the Word of life.” (1 John 1:1) Notice the order: heard, seen, looked upon, touched. From far to near, from the ears to the hands. That is exactly the theme of this lesson — truth must move from being “heard” to being “touched.”

Second, when it was written and to whom. The letter is generally dated between AD 85 and 95, when John was an aged apostle shepherding the churches of Asia Minor around Ephesus. Its readers were not new converts but second- and third-generation believers; most of them had never seen Jesus with their own eyes, and their faith was something they had “heard about.” John was facing precisely a group of believers who “knew a great deal, but might not possess it.” Again and again in the letter he uses the words “know” and “understand,” because he wants to turn a “knowing” that stops in the head into a “knowing” that is truly possessed in life.

Third, the historical and cultural setting. Ephesus was the leading city of the province of Asia, home to the temple of Artemis — one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world — with a busy harbour and a culture of indulgence. At the same time, an early form of Gnostic thought was eating away at the church: it exalted “knowledge,” claimed that salvation came through special secret knowledge, made light of the body and of conduct, and even denied that Christ had truly come in the flesh. John says: “They went out from us, but they didn’t belong to us.” (1 John 2:19) These people are the classic case of those who “know a great deal, yet whose lives have not changed” — knowledge swelled up while love dried up.

Fourth, the context before and after. In 2:12–14, John speaks warmly in turn to the “little children,” the “fathers” and the “young men,” affirming one by one their standing in the Lord: sins forgiven, knowing him who is from the beginning, having overcome the evil one. He establishes identity first, then gives the command — first “who you are,” then “how you should live.” Immediately after, 2:15–17 is that command; and in 2:18 he begins to speak of the antichrist and the last hour. This passage sits between “identity” and “end-times watchfulness,” and it asks a question of direction: since you are a child of God, and since this world is passing away, where will you place your love?

Fifth, two key Greek words. “World” in the original is kosmos, which basically means “order, system, an arranged structure.” John uses it not for the mountains, rivers and lands that God made, nor for the people of the world (it is precisely “the world” of people that God loves, John 3:16), but for a value system that sets itself against God and stands on its own apart from him. The world is not only a place; the world is a system — which is exactly the opposition 321 describes between the Babylonian system and God’s system. The other word is “love.” In 2:15 it is agapaō, which does not mean a passing emotion but a commitment of the will, a direction chosen. What John is dealing with is where we put the weight of our lives.

Brothers and sisters, once the background is clear, we can see that this letter was not written to unbelievers. It was written to us — believers who know a great deal of truth, yet need to be challenged on whether we truly possess it.

sections.heading: Key Point 1: From “Knowing” to “Possessing” — The Four Levels of Mindset
sections.html:
The lesson text says: on the journey of our lives, mindset has four different levels, and each level determines how deep our change goes.

These four levels are not a way of sorting people into four types. They are four stretches of road that the same truth has to travel inside us. If it travels all the way, it becomes life; if it doesn’t, it stops halfway.

Let me give you a picture that runs through the whole lesson: a meal. Level one, I see the menu — I know about the dish. Level two, I smell it and my stomach rumbles — I’m stirred. Level three, I pick up the food with my chopsticks, put it in my mouth and chew — I begin to practise. Level four, the food is digested and becomes my flesh and blood, my strength — I possess it.

Only at level four does the meal truly become mine. Looking at the menu won’t fill you; smelling the aroma won’t fill you; even putting a mouthful in your bowl won’t fill you. Only when it is eaten and digested does it become part of me. Truth is just the same.

Level 1: The Theoretical Mindset — I Know It

The lesson text says: this is the stage of “Information.” We hear, understand, nod in agreement, but have not yet lived it out. A mindset like this exists only in the head; it has no power over our life.

Scripture gives a very stern warning about this level. James 1:22–24 says: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves. For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man looking at his natural face in a mirror; for he sees himself, and goes away, and immediately forgets what kind of man he was.”

Brothers and sisters, notice the picture James uses: looking in a mirror. The man looking in the mirror sees, sees clearly, even sees a smudge on his face — and then he turns and walks away and immediately forgets. It isn’t that he didn’t see; he saw and never lifted a hand to wash his face. That is the classic picture of the “theoretical mindset”: able to see, unwilling to act.

Psychology gives us solid supporting evidence here. In 1885 the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus, using himself as the subject, ran memory experiments with nonsense syllables and plotted his famous “forgetting curve.” He found that material simply memorised, without review or use, is about two-thirds forgotten within a day. For more than a century that curve has been confirmed by study after study.

In other words, if we rely on “hearing” alone, by tomorrow morning only a third of what we received this morning will be left.

Paul also warned of the danger of knowledge: “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.” (1 Corinthians 8:1) Those who stop at the theoretical level face a hidden temptation — to substitute “understanding a lot” for “living like it.” We can explain the difference between grace and law, yet refuse to say sorry to the brother who has wronged us. That is not knowledge’s fault; it’s our fault for treating knowledge as the destination.

Among the 321 eight stages of changing our mindset, this level corresponds to the first: Information. Information is a necessary starting point, so we read the Bible, listen to sermons and take notes. But information is only the doorway, not the home. If we stand in the doorway all our lives, we never actually come home.

Level 2: The Mindset of Revelation — I’ve Grasped It

The lesson text says: when the Holy Spirit himself speaks to us, so that the truth stirs us, gives us light and gives us assurance, we have entered the level of revelation. It is an inner stirring and longing — but if there is only being moved and no action, it still cannot change our life.

The Greek for “revelation” is apokalypsis, which literally means “taking off the covering.” You’ve read the same passage for ten years and felt nothing, and then one day it is as if a veil has been lifted: the words come alive and pierce straight into your heart — that is revelation.

After Peter confessed at Caesarea Philippi, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,” Jesus said: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar Jonah, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven.” (Matthew 16:17) The same sentence, spoken by someone else, might be mere information; spoken by Peter, to whom the Father had revealed it, it is a rock.

Paul’s prayer for the church in Ephesus asks for exactly this: “that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give to you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him, having the eyes of your hearts enlightened.” (Ephesians 1:17–18) “The eyes of your hearts enlightened” — revelation is not one more piece of data in the head; it is one more ray of light in the heart. The disciples on the road to Emmaus said afterwards: “Weren’t our hearts burning within us, while he spoke to us along the way, and while he opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24:32) A burning heart is the mark of revelation.

But brothers and sisters, there is a very important caution here, one the lesson text singles out: being moved is not the same as being changed.

In 1957 the psychologist Leon Festinger put forward the theory of “cognitive dissonance”: when a person’s beliefs and behaviour don’t line up, an uncomfortable tension arises inside, and the person will try to get rid of it. There are two ways to do so: one is to change the behaviour so that it fits the belief; the other is to adjust the belief and find excuses, so as to feel at ease.

That is exactly what goes on inside us after every meeting. The Holy Spirit has moved me, my beliefs and my daily living don’t match, and I feel uncomfortable. At that point there are two roads: one is to obey the Holy Spirit and really change; the other is to shed a few tears, have a good cry, and then tell myself, “I’ve already responded,” so the tension goes away and life carries on as before.

The second road is the most dangerous, because it can make us “addicted to being moved” — chasing the feeling of the meeting, chasing the next emotional high, without ever really taking a single step. Over time, being moved becomes religious consumption rather than a turning point in our life.

Among the 321 eight stages, this level corresponds to the second stage, Revelation, and the third, Conviction. Revelation is the Holy Spirit shining his light in; Conviction is something inside me saying, “Lord, I yield.” Many people have revelation without conviction — the light has come in, but the heart has not surrendered.

Brothers and sisters, the Holy Spirit is my guide. He gives revelation not so that we will be moved but so that we will obey.

Level 3: The Mindset of Practice — I’m Practising It

The lesson text says: when we begin to put God’s word into practice in our daily living, change moves from “theory” into “reality.” We may stumble and get things wrong, but in the practice the truth begins to become concrete and real. The more we practise, the more skilled we become; the more we live it out, the more we experience God.

Paul’s command to Timothy is exactly “practise”: “But refuse profane and old wives’ fables. Exercise yourself toward godliness. For bodily exercise has some value, but godliness has value in all things, having the promise of the life which is now, and of that which is to come.” (1 Timothy 4:7–8)

The Greek word for “exercise” here is gymnazō, the root of the English word gymnasium. It describes the kind of training in which an athlete strips off his outer garment, goes into the arena and trains till he is drenched in sweat. Paul isn’t telling Timothy to “think about godliness”; he’s telling him to “train in godliness.”

Hebrews uses the same root: “But solid food is for those who are full grown, who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern good and evil.” (Hebrews 5:14) Spiritual discernment doesn’t drop from the sky; it is trained.

The two houses Jesus spoke of say the same thing: “Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man, who built his house on a rock.” (Matthew 7:24) Both kinds of people “heard”; the only difference lies in the words “and does them.”

The illustrations from daily life are clear. A child learning to ride a bicycle still falls, even with Dad holding on behind. But one day, suddenly, he can do it — not because he read another book, but because he has fallen enough times.

Science supports this too. In 2010 Phillippa Lally and colleagues at University College London published a study in the European Journal of Social Psychology that tracked how long a new daily habit takes to become “automatic.” The average was about sixty-six days, with individual differences ranging from eighteen to two hundred and fifty-four days. That gives us two lessons: change takes time, so don’t condemn yourself because you missed it for three days; and change takes repetition, because without repetition nothing becomes automatic.

In 1977 the psychologist Albert Bandura put forward the theory of “self-efficacy,” pointing out that the main source of a person’s belief that they can do something is not other people’s encouragement but “their own experience of success.” In other words, confidence is built by doing. The more you practise, the more you believe that God is able to work in you.

Among the 321 eight stages, this level corresponds to the fourth stage, Implementation, the fifth, Evaluation, and the sixth, Correction. After implementation there must be evaluation: did I do it this week? Where did I get stuck? And after evaluation there must be correction: how will I adjust next time? Implementation without evaluation slides into mere form; evaluation without correction brings only frustration.

Brothers and sisters, Jesus is my role model. He didn’t just finish explaining the teaching and leave. He took a towel and wrapped it round his waist, poured water into a basin and washed the disciples’ feet, and only when he had done it did he say: “If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.” (John 13:17)

Level 4: The Mindset of Life — I Possess It

The lesson text says: when a truth has gone through constant implementation, evaluation and repetition, it finally becomes our life’s natural response. At that point we no longer need to remind ourselves to “love others,” “forgive” or “obey”; that kind of life simply flows out of us.

This is the end point of the four levels, and the goal of all change.

Paul describes this kind of life in one sentence: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20) “It is no longer I who live” — this is not Paul reminding himself to be selfless; this is Paul already being selfless.

The psalmist says: “I have hidden your word in my heart, that I might not sin against you.” (Psalm 119:11) Notice: “hidden in my heart,” not “written in my notebook.” Paul also says: “But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord, the Spirit.” (2 Corinthians 3:18) “From glory to glory” is a continuing, gradual transformation brought about by the Holy Spirit.

Here there is a treasure from the original languages worth sharing. The Hebrew word for “know” is yadaʿ, which is never a cold, head-level awareness but a knowing that enters into relationship and experience; Genesis 4:1 says, “The man knew Eve his wife,” and the original uses this very word. Greek has two words for “know”: oida leans towards objective awareness, ginōskō towards knowing through experience. John uses ginōskō again and again for our relationship with God — “This is how we know that we know him: if we keep his commandments.” (1 John 2:3) We come to know God in the keeping.

Brothers and sisters, the very language of the Bible is telling us: true “knowing” has always meant “possessing.”

Science also lets us glimpse the wonder of God’s creation. In 1949 the Canadian psychologist Donald Hebb proposed in his book The Organization of Behavior that when two neurons are repeatedly activated together, the connection between them is strengthened. Later the principle was summed up in one line: “Neurons that fire together wire together.” This is the physiological basis for how “repetition” produces “automaticity.” Every time you choose to forgive, you deepen a pathway of forgiveness in your brain; every time you choose to lose your temper, you deepen a pathway of anger. Over time, whichever road is wider is the one you walk automatically.

When God made us, he wrote into our very bodies the law that “what is repeated becomes character.” This is not telling us to rely on our own effort; it is helping us see that the Holy Spirit means to shape the image of Christ in us through one act of obedience after another.

Let’s go back to the meal. Once a meal is eaten, you won’t remember the taste of that particular mouthful, but it has already become your bones, your blood, the strength in your legs. When truth becomes life, you may not even be able to say which message changed you — because it is no longer outside you; it has become you.

Among the 321 eight stages, this level corresponds to the seventh stage: Repetition.

And at the heart of 321, this level is “selflessness.” Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out; “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. The old self is “self-centred” and asks first of everything, “What’s in it for me?”; the new self is “selfless” and asks first of everything, “Does this bring the Lord glory?” The road from “I know” to “I possess” is the road from the self-centred life to selflessness.

sections.heading: Key Point 2: From Life to Culture — The Spreading Power of a Godly Mindset
sections.html:
The lesson text says: when the mindset of life enters the stage of “Multiplication,” it doesn’t only affect the individual; it can touch others, shape the atmosphere and finally form a godly culture. When such a culture keeps spreading through a community, it becomes a movement, and the movement brings change to society and revival to the kingdom.

This is the eighth of the eight stages: Multiplication.

Paul spells this step out very clearly: “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.” (2 Timothy 2:2) One short verse, four generations: Paul, Timothy, faithful men, others. Once life has taken shape, it has to be passed on.

Jesus said, “You are the salt of the earth, but if the salt has lost its flavor, with what will it be salted?” And he said, “You are the light of the world. A city located on a hill can’t be hidden.” (Matthew 5:13–14) Salt’s work is to permeate; light’s work is to illuminate. Salt doesn’t have to be loud; put it in the soup and the flavour of the whole pot changes. A culture isn’t formed by publicity; it’s formed by permeation.

The most beautiful example in Scripture is Antioch. Acts 11:26 says: “The disciples were first called Christians in Antioch.” Notice that the disciples didn’t give themselves this name; people outside gave it to them. The Gentiles in the city of Antioch saw a group of people whose speech, money, treatment of others and hope were all different, and so they gave them a name: “those who belong to Christ.” That is culture — when godly lives gather together, even unbelievers can tell that there is a different atmosphere here.

Modern science also confirms how influence spreads. In 2007 Nicholas Christakis and James Fowler published a study in the New England Journal of Medicine analysing thirty-two years of social-network data on more than twelve thousand people from the Framingham Heart Study. They found that if a person’s friend became obese during a given period, that person’s own chance of becoming obese rose by fifty-seven per cent; later studies showed that happiness, quitting smoking and other behaviours spread through social networks in the same way.

This is often used to remind people to “choose your friends carefully.” But brothers and sisters, look at it from the other side: if even lifestyle habits can spread through relationships, how far will a life truly changed by God spread through its network of relationships?

This is the foundation of 321’s “920 practice.” Everyone we have a relationship with is our “2.” We don’t set out to change them first; we practise living a selfless (0) life before them and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions — “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23) You don’t need to advertise your change; your change will speak for itself.

One step further is the “235 relationship”: with someone selfless, become a “2,” spiritual companions to one another; build a “3,” as spiritual parents and spiritual children, passing life on; and finally become a “5,” a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades, taking up the charge of God’s kingdom together. This is exactly what the lesson text describes: individual → atmosphere → culture → movement → revival.

Church history bears witness to this road too. In 1904 a young Welsh miner named Evan Roberts began to pray earnestly with a group of young people, seeking the outpouring of the Holy Spirit. The fire was lit in the prayer meeting of a few people and spread across the whole of Wales. According to accounts from the time, within just a few months some hundred thousand people came to the Lord, the taverns stood empty and the courts had no cases to try.

The lesson text puts it well: revival does not begin with outward activity; it begins with one person “letting God’s word become life.”

Brothers and sisters, there is an order here that we must hold on to, the one 321 describes: life first, then relationships, then ministry. Many people turn the order upside down — rushing into ministry first, talking about relationships next, and dealing with life last — so their ministry is busy, their relationships are strained and their life is empty. But God’s order is this: life is established first, and then relationships can be healthy; when relationships are healthy, ministry has a foundation. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

Relationships have an order too: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. When our relationship with God is right, we can be at peace with ourselves; when we are at peace with ourselves, our relationships with others grow roomy; when our relationships with others are roomy, what we do will carry the fragrance of life.

So don’t be in a hurry to change the culture; first let God change you. A person who has truly been changed alters the temperature of every place they walk into.

sections.heading: Key Point 3: The Key to Change — Loving the World, or Loving God
sections.html:
The lesson text brings us to the most central, and the most piercing, passage.

“Don’t love the world or the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the Father’s love isn’t in him.” (1 John 2:15)

The lesson text says: the reason we cannot enter into a changed life is often that we “love the wrong thing.” With our lips we say we love God, but in our actions we love the world; we say we obey the Lord, but in our choices we follow ourselves.

Brothers and sisters, that sentence uncovers the key to the whole lesson. Why do so many people never reach level three or level four? Why do we know perfectly well that we ought to practise, yet stay where we are year after year? Not because we aren’t clever enough, but because our hearts are filled with other things.

Jesus said: “For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.” (Matthew 6:21) The heart doesn’t wander off for no reason; the heart runs after whatever we treasure.

As we said earlier, “world” in the original is kosmos, a system set against God. John goes on to break this system down into three channels: “For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, isn’t the Father’s, but is the world’s.” (1 John 2:16)

First, the lust of the flesh — the craving of the body, wanting the senses satisfied.

Second, the lust of the eyes — the craving of the eyes, wanting to own everything it sees.

Third, the pride of life — in the original, alazoneia, meaning boasting, swagger, showing off what one has. What it wants is to be “seen, exalted, praised.”

We have met these three in Scripture twice.

The first time was in Eden. “When the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took some of its fruit, and ate. Then she gave some to her husband with her, and he ate it, too.” (Genesis 3:6) Good for food — the lust of the flesh; a delight to the eyes — the lust of the eyes; desired to make one wise — the pride of life. Humanity’s first fall was all three succeeding at once.

The second time was in the wilderness. Satan told Jesus to command stones to become bread (the lust of the flesh); showed him the glory of all the kingdoms (the lust of the eyes); and told him to throw himself down from the pinnacle of the temple so that angels would bear him up (the pride of life). The same three, and this time all three came to nothing, because three times Jesus answered: “It is written.” (Matthew 4:4, 7, 10)

Brothers and sisters, see the contrast clearly: Eve failed because she left God’s word; Jesus overcame because he stood on God’s word. The Bible is my standard — not a slogan, but the line between life and death in the wilderness.

And of the three, which is the deepest and hardest to shake off? “The pride of life.”

The 321 vision has always said: the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

The lust of the flesh and the lust of the eyes are fairly easy to spot; the pride of life, though, can put on the clothes of godliness. A person can fast and pray while hoping others will know that he is fasting and praying. This is what the lesson text means: Satan’s greatest scheme is to make us think we love God when in fact we love the world, to keep us at the level of theory, content with an outward religious appearance, without any real change.

That is why Scripture says: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (1 Peter 5:5) Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.

Why is John so absolute — “If anyone loves the world, the Father’s love isn’t in him”? Because love is exclusive. Jesus said: “No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other; or else he will be devoted to one and despise the other. You can’t serve both God and Mammon.” (Matthew 6:24) James puts it even more strongly: “Don’t you know that friendship with the world is hostility toward God?” (James 4:4) He addresses them as “adulterers,” because God’s relationship with his people is a marriage covenant; to give one’s heart to another is unfaithfulness.

The church father Augustine put forward an idea of lasting influence: sin is often not loving what we should not love, but putting our loves in the wrong order. At the opening of his Confessions he left us that famous line: “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.” The problem is not that we love; the problem is that we give to passing things the love that belongs to God.

And this is exactly what John says next: “The world is passing away with its lusts, but he who does God’s will remains forever.” (1 John 2:17)

Brothers and sisters, hear this contrast clearly: on one side, “passing away”; on the other, “remains forever.” This is what 321 calls a shift of perspective — from man’s to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the Worldly to the godly. Seen with temporary eyes, loving the world looks like a bargain, because it is visible, touchable and immediate; seen with eternal eyes, loving the world is the worst deal there is, because you are piling a lifetime’s strength onto a ship that is already sinking.

Notice too: John says, “he who does God’s will remains forever” — he does not say, “he who knows God’s will.” And that brings us back to the theme of this lesson.

So the lesson text says: change has to begin with “the focus of our love.” When we choose to love God above all else, God’s word is no longer just theory; it becomes the power of our life.

Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. For out of the heart flows the wellspring of life.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
Set this lesson inside the framework of 321 and the whole picture becomes clear.

First, the Three Foundations. Jesus is my role model — he washed the disciples’ feet and only then said, “blessed are you if you do them”; he lived it out first. The Bible is my standard — in the wilderness he said three times, “It is written.” The Holy Spirit is my guide — revelation is the Holy Spirit lifting the veil, practice is the Holy Spirit giving strength, and life is the Holy Spirit’s shaping.

Second, the Two Core Values. Let Jesus be King — when truth becomes life, it is Jesus reigning as King within me, not me managing my own religious behaviour. Let Jesus receive all the glory — when others see our change, the glory goes not to our efforts but to the Lord who changed us.

Third, the Goal: establish God’s system. The “culture, movement and revival” the lesson text speaks of are, in the language of 321, coming out of the Babylonian system and being established in God’s system. We are not swaying between two sets of rules; our whole being is meant to be moved across.

Fourth, the fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. The four levels of this lesson are the most detailed breakdown of the stretch “from mindset to life”; the second key point is the spreading into “daily living, relationships and ministry.” Once the order is muddled, the power is scattered.

Fifth, the self-centred life and selflessness. Those who stop at “knowing” are often self-centred people — what really keeps us from living it out is usually not a lack of understanding but an unwillingness to let go: unwilling to let go of face, unwilling to let go of our rights, unwilling to let go of that “I.”

Sixth, 920 and 235. The 920 practice has us bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions with a selfless (0) life before every “2”; the 235 relationship takes us from companions to spiritual parents and spiritual children, and on to a fivefold-ministry team, multiplying life from one generation to the next. This is the concrete roadmap for the “Multiplication” the lesson text speaks of.

Seventh, the Path of Serving: Spirit → Understanding → Life → Service → God. The Holy Spirit guides us into revelation, the Bible brings us understanding of the truth, Jesus’ example makes the truth our life, that life produces service in which Jesus reigns as King, and in the end all the glory goes to God. How closely this path matches the four levels of this lesson!

Brothers and sisters, 321 is not an extra set of homework. It turns the road “from knowing to possessing” into a clear map.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice
sections.html:
The lesson text gives us three practices, and we will deepen them using the eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice 1: Write down one truth you have heard recently and honestly ask yourself, “Is this something I only know, or something I’m already practising?”

Information: Take pen and paper and write down the one truth or verse that has moved you most in the last three months — just one.

Revelation: Be still for three minutes and ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light: Lord, what were you saying to me then?

Conviction: Say to the Lord, “Lord, I yield.” Not bargaining, but surrender.

Implementation: Next to that truth, write one concrete action you can take this week.

Evaluation: At the weekend, look back: how many times did I do it? Where did I get stuck?

Correction: Where you got stuck, cut the goal in half so that it’s something you can do.

Repetition: Keep practising for four weeks in a row. Remember, on average it takes more than two months to become automatic.

Multiplication: Find a “2,” tell them about your practice and what you’ve gained, and invite them to do it with you.

Practice 2: Choose one thing you know you should do but haven’t yet acted on — and start doing it today.

The key to this one is “today.” Being moved is not the end point of change but the starting point of action.

Information: List three things “I know I should do but have never done” — a phone call to apologise, a decision to forgive, a habit to break.

Revelation: Ask the Holy Spirit to show you which one he wants you to do today. Usually the one that makes you most uncomfortable is the one.

Conviction: Admit what the real obstacle is — is it face? Fear of being hurt? Hand that “self” over to the Lord.

Implementation: Take the first action before today is over, even if it’s only pressing the call button. Don’t wait for the mood; act first.

Evaluation: Afterwards, write it down: what was I afraid of before I did it? What did I discover afterwards?

Correction: If you didn’t manage it, don’t condemn yourself; break it into a smaller step and do it tomorrow.

Repetition: Choose one thing each week, for eight weeks.

Multiplication: Share this experience in your small group; your action will become someone else’s courage.

Practice 3: Examine your love for God and for the world: from the way you spend your time, money and thoughts, who has taken hold of your heart? Ask the Holy Spirit to help you readjust your focus.

Information: Keep an honest record for three days. Time: how much of my day goes to God, and how much to entertainment? Money: what were my three biggest expenses this month? Thoughts: what three things do I think about most in a day?

Revelation: Spread the record out before God, read 1 John 2:15–17, and ask the Holy Spirit to enlighten the eyes of your heart.

Conviction: Don’t make excuses. Next to the most honest column, write: “Lord, here I love the world more than you.”

Implementation: Make one concrete adjustment — not a complete overhaul, just one item. For example, swap the thirty minutes on your phone before bed for Bible reading and prayer.

Evaluation: After a week, check: did those thirty minutes really get swapped?

Correction: If thirty minutes is too much, start with ten. Doing it at all matters more than doing it big.

Repetition: Keep it up for a month, and let the new pathway grow wider in your life.

Multiplication: Invite your family or your spiritual companion to make this commitment with you, and remind one another.

Brothers and sisters, let me add the lesson text’s gentle reminder: being moved is not the end point of change but the starting point of action. Don’t stay at “knowing”; go on into “possessing.” If this morning’s devotion leaves you with only one sentence, let it be that one.

sections.heading: Closing and Call
sections.html:
The lesson text closes like this: change begins with me, and it begins with my choices. When we choose to love God more than the world, to choose practice over theory, and life over religion, we will see God’s truth unleash astonishing power in us.
