Brothers and sisters, today we have travelled a road: from “I know it,” to “I’ve grasped it,” to “I’m practising it,” to “I possess it”; from one person’s life, to the atmosphere of a group, to a godly culture, to the revival of the kingdom. And the hinge on which it all turns is one choice: do I love the world, or do I love God?

Remember the contrast in that verse: “The world is passing away with its lusts, but he who does God’s will remains forever.” (1 John 2:17) One side is passing away; the other remains forever. Which side will you stake your life on?

Change doesn’t have to wait until next year, or until circumstances improve, or until someone else moves first. Perhaps what you need to do today is make a phone call, apologise to your child, or loosen your grip on something you can’t bear to let go and hand it to the Lord. That one action looks very small, yet it is the very step by which truth leaves the head and enters life.

Brothers and sisters, let Jesus be King — not only King in our meetings, but King over your diary, King over your wallet, King over your phone screen, King over the relationship you find hardest to forgive.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — and when one day someone asks you, “How did you become so different?”, may you be able to point to the Lord and say: it’s not me; it’s Christ who lives in me.

Starting with you, starting with me, starting right now.

keyVerses: Don’t love the world or the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the Father’s love isn’t in him. For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, isn’t the Father’s, but is the world’s. The world is passing away with its lusts, but he who does God’s will remains forever. (1 John 2:15–17)
practices: Write down one truth you’ve heard recently and honestly ask yourself about it
Choose one thing you know you should do but haven’t acted on — and start today
Examine your love for God and for the world
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you.

Lord, we confess that we have heard too much and done too little. Our notebooks are full, but our lives are empty. Forgive us for letting “knowing” stand in for “possessing,” being moved stand in for obeying, and an outward religious appearance stand in for real change.

Holy Spirit, speak to us yourself; lift the veil and enlighten the eyes of our hearts, so that we not only hear the truth but grasp it. Give us surrendered hearts, so that in your light we can say: Lord, I yield.

Lord, give us the courage to practise, so that we are not afraid of falling or of going slowly. Through every act of implementation, evaluation, correction and repetition, engrave your word into our lives, so that one day we no longer need to remind ourselves to love, to forgive, to obey, because that has already become our life.

Lord, I am no longer content just to hear the truth; I want to live it out. Help me no longer to love the world but to love you alone. Let your word become the foundation of my life, so that from today I live out real change.
Make us seeds of a godly culture, spreading the fragrance of Christ in our families, our workplaces and our communities. Let your kingdom come, and let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.
May all the glory be yours. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: John 13:17: “If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.” Of the four levels — theory, revelation, practice and life — which one do you most often stop at right now? Give a concrete example, and explain what keeps you from taking the next step.

1 John 2:17: “The world is passing away with its lusts, but he who does God’s will remains forever.” Look honestly at your time, money and thoughts: which of them shows most clearly that you still love the world? What one concrete adjustment are you willing to make this week, so that Jesus reigns as King in that area?
l059.title: From Knowing to Possessing
l059.subtitle: Change Begins with Me (Part 2)
l059.partTitle: Unit 4 · The Prerequisite for Revival — A Change of Mindset

sections.heading: Introduction: The Notebook Worn Ragged
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I want to begin by telling you something very real, and very piercing.

I know a brother who never misses a meeting. Sunday worship, midweek Bible study, conferences, retreats — he’s at every one, sitting in the first three rows, taking notes quickly and neatly. Over a dozen or so years his devotional notebooks have filled an entire drawer, every page crammed with speakers’ memorable lines, key points and outlines. One day, while tidying the study, his wife opened one of them at random and saw a line on the flyleaf in his own handwriting — a little scrawled, as if dashed off after some meeting had ended. This is what it said: “What I know is far, far more than what I’ve done.”

Brothers and sisters, could that line be written on the tablet of our hearts too?

Our generation may well be the most “knowing” generation in all of history. Sermons online are inexhaustible; devotional apps push out memorable sayings every day. We know we should forgive, we know we should give, we know we should share the gospel — we can even explain these things to others, and explain them very convincingly. But brothers and sisters, allow me to ask one honest question: has our life really changed because of all this “knowing”?

That is the central question this lesson has to face. Revival does not begin with outward excitement. Revival does not begin with a big conference, or with a stirring song, or with a gifted speaker. Revival begins with a heart willing to be changed by God. And the heart of change is letting God’s word not stay only in our thoughts but become the reality of our life.

When God’s truth is no longer just “theory” but becomes “life,” our actions will bring about a turning of culture, the rise of a movement, even the transformation of society. Every genuine great revival in history has begun with a group of people who no longer just “heard” — they “went and did.”

So this morning I want to state this lesson’s title very plainly: real change begins with me, and it begins with my “action.”

Brothers and sisters, when we finish this lesson this morning, may it be not that we know one more thing, but that we have done one more thing.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A Choice in the Sermon on the Mount
sections.html:
To understand today’s key texts rightly, we must first go back to where they stand.

The words “You can’t serve both God and Mammon” come from the Sermon on the Mount in Matthew chapter 6. The Gospel of Matthew was written by Matthew, the tax collector Levi whom the Lord called; it is generally thought to have been written between AD 50 and 70, chiefly for communities of Jewish Christians. Matthew’s purpose is very clear: to show that Jesus of Nazareth is the Messiah promised in the Old Testament, the King of the kingdom of heaven. And the Sermon on the Mount is the rule of life this King lays down for the people of his kingdom.

If we trace the flow of chapter 6, we find a very clear line. He speaks first about giving, prayer and fasting, warning the disciples not to do these things to be seen by others. Then he turns to the subject of treasure: “Don’t lay up treasures for yourselves on the earth … but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven.” (Matthew 6:19–20) Then he speaks the words that go straight to the heart: “For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.” (Matthew 6:21) And immediately after, verse 24 comes down like a judge’s gavel, delivering the final verdict: “No one can serve two masters … You can’t serve both God and Mammon.”

There is a key word here worth pausing over. The word “Mammon” is mamōnas in Greek, transliterated from Aramaic. The Chinese Union Version adds a small-print note at this point explaining that “Mammon” means “wealth.” Scholars generally think the root of the word is connected with “trusting, relying on” — in other words, Mammon means not merely money but “the thing a person relies on.” This point is vitally important. The Lord Jesus did not say, “You cannot both serve God and have money.” He said “serve.” Money may be in your hand, but money may not sit on the throne of your heart.

Another key word is “serve,” douleuō in Greek, whose root is doulos, “slave.” So the sentence, rendered literally, says: no one can be the slave of two masters. In first-century Roman society a slave’s status was absolute and exclusive: a slave’s time, strength and will belonged entirely to his master, without a shred left for himself. The Lord Jesus uses this social reality, which everyone at the time understood, to tell us: on the throne of your life there is room for only one.

The background to the second key text is grander still. The book of Revelation was written by the apostle John, generally dated around AD 95, when he had been exiled to the island of Patmos for the word of God and the testimony of Jesus; it was addressed to the seven churches of Asia Minor as they faced persecution from the Roman Empire. Chapter 12 describes a war in heaven: the great red dragon is thrown down, the dragon who is the old serpent, called the devil and Satan. Then a loud voice in heaven proclaims: “They overcame him because of the Lamb’s blood, and because of the word of their testimony. They didn’t love their life, even to death.”

Brothers and sisters, look carefully at these three things by which Satan is overcome: the Lamb’s blood — that is the objective redemption; the word of their testimony — that is the subjective living out; not loving their life even to death — that is a thoroughgoing denying of self. The first is what the Lord accomplished for us; the other two are how we respond with our lives. This is precisely the road this lesson means to take us down.

And James 1:22 is the most practical signpost on that road. The author of James is generally thought to be James, the Lord Jesus’ brother in the flesh and the leader of the church in Jerusalem. The letter contains almost no extended theological argument; from beginning to end it is about practice. James is like a stern but deeply loving spiritual father who takes us by the shoulders and says: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.” (James 1:22)

The Greek verb for “delude,” paralogizomai, originally carries the sense of “misleading by false reasoning” — keeping a false set of accounts for yourself. Brothers and sisters, the greatest danger for someone who hears the word but doesn’t do it is not ignorance but feeling good about himself — he thinks he is already living in that truth, when in fact he only knows it.

sections.heading: 1. Loving God or Loving the World: What Sets the Focus of Our Life
sections.html:
Scripture says clearly: “You can’t serve both God and Mammon.” (Matthew 6:24)

These words lay bare a crucial question in our hearts — whom, in the end, are we serving?

To love the world is to let money and material things rule us; to love God is to let him govern our hearts and our choices. Between these two the Lord Jesus left no fuzzy grey area. He didn’t say, “You’d better not,” or, “It’s hard to do both at once.” He said, “You can’t.” This is a statement about the very nature of things, a matter of logic: two absolute sovereignties cannot occupy the same throne at the same time.

Who Controls Whom: The Simplest Test

Measuring whether we love the world is actually very simple. Ask just one question: who controls whom?

Do we control money, or does money control us?

Brothers and sisters, you don’t need a theology degree to answer that question; daily life reveals the answer every day. When overtime pay clashes with dinner with the family, which do I choose first? When the figure in my bank account goes up, my sense of security goes up with it; when it goes down, my peace goes down with it — so who, in the end, holds the power?

Money itself is neutral. Scripture never says money is evil: Abraham was rich, Job was rich, and Joseph of Arimathea was a rich man too. Paul puts it with great precision: “For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. Some have been led astray from the faith in their greed, and have pierced themselves through with many sorrows.” (1 Timothy 6:10) The verse doesn’t say that money is the root of evil but that the love of money is. The problem is not money; it’s the direction of the heart.

But brothers and sisters, once something neutral is no longer managed, it turns round and manages you. Water is neutral: it can irrigate good farmland or burst through a dyke — the key is whether there is a channel and a floodgate. Money is the same: if we cannot manage it, it will become our master.

Giving: Does It Hurt?

When God calls us to give, does our heart “hurt”?

If it does, it means our heart is still bound by the world; if we can give freely and joyfully, it means our heart has already overcome the world — the money is in our hands, rather than we in money’s hands.

Paul says: “Let each man give according as he has determined in his heart, not grudgingly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.” (2 Corinthians 9:7) The Greek for “cheerful” is hilaros, the source of the English word “hilarious,” meaning glad, light-hearted. What God loves is not the person who calculates most precisely but the person who gives most gladly.

The Lord Jesus himself gave us an unforgettable picture. He sat opposite the temple treasury and watched the crowd putting in money. Many rich people put in large sums; then a poor widow came and put in two small coins. “He called his disciples to himself, and said to them, ‘Most certainly I tell you, this poor widow gave more than all those who are giving into the treasury, for they all gave out of their abundance, but she, out of her poverty, gave all that she had to live on.’” (Mark 12:43–44)

Brothers and sisters, look at the Lord’s measuring rod. He doesn’t measure “how much was put in”; he measures “how much was kept back.” The rich gave out of what was left over; the widow gave everything. In human eyes those two small coins wouldn’t even buy a day’s meals; in God’s eyes it was the greatest gift in the world. For behind those two small coins was a heart completely unbound by money.

David was the same. When he wanted to build an altar and offer sacrifice on Araunah’s threshing floor, Araunah was willing to give it to him free, but David said: “No; but I will most certainly buy it from you for a price. I will not offer burnt offerings to Yahweh my God which cost me nothing.” (2 Samuel 24:24) True giving always has weight to it.

Corroboration from Science: Those Who Give Are Happier

Interestingly, even modern psychological research bears out this biblical principle.

In 2008 the psychologists Elizabeth Dunn, Lara Aknin and Michael Norton published a study in the journal Science. They gave participants a sum of money and randomly divided them into two groups: one group spent the money on themselves, the other spent it on others. When happiness was measured again that evening, the result was strikingly consistent — the group that spent the money on others was clearly happier. The size of the amount wasn’t the key; the direction was.

Brothers and sisters, our motive for giving is love for God, not an emotional reward. But this research reminds us that when God made us, he built the circuit “giving brings joy” into us. When we clutch tightly, we go against the nature we were created with; when we open our hands and give, we return to the place God originally designed for us.

As Paul repeated the words of the Lord: “It is more blessed to give than to receive.” (Acts 20:35)

Giving Is Not Taking Away but Setting Free

Loving God is not just talk; it is proved through concrete action. Giving is a test of the heart and a declaration of sovereignty. God does not want to take our things away; he wants to set our hearts free, so that we are not bound by money.

I often use a picture to explain this. A child puts his hand into a narrow-necked sweet jar and grabs a big fistful of sweets — and then he can’t get his hand out. He bursts into tears and says the jar has trapped his hand. But the jar hasn’t trapped him; his own fistful of sweets has trapped him. His father says, “Child, let go.” He isn’t trying to snatch away the sweets; he’s trying to rescue the hand.

Brothers and sisters, when God tells us to give, that is exactly his “Child, let go.”

That is why, in Malachi, God says something he almost never says anywhere else: “Bring the whole tithe into the storehouse, that there may be food in my house, and test me now in this,” says Yahweh of Armies, “if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there will not be room enough for.” (Malachi 3:10) In the whole Bible God almost never permits people to test him — except in this matter of giving, where he says: come and try me. Because he knows all too well that once a person has tasted the freedom of letting go, they will never want to go back to being a slave.

Applying 321: Let Jesus Be King, Starting with Your Wallet

Brothers and sisters, the first of the Two Core Values of the 321 vision is “let Jesus be King.”

Letting Jesus be King sounds very spiritual, but it is actually very concrete. To be King means to have sovereignty; to have sovereignty means that every decision has to go through him. If he can’t change my schedule, can’t touch my decisions about marriage and can’t lay a finger on my bank account, then “let Jesus be King” is just a slogan, and I’m still sitting on my own throne.

321 puts it very directly: pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. Bondage to money is, at its core, a question of power. I hold on tightly to money because I want to be the one responsible for my future; I want to control tomorrow myself. And giving is precisely the moment when I declare: tomorrow is not in my hands; tomorrow is in God’s hands.

This is exactly the shift of perspective 321 speaks of: from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal. Paul says: “while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.” (2 Corinthians 4:18) Only a person who has eternity in view can loosen their grip on earthly treasure.

Brothers and sisters, you don’t have to answer me this morning, but please answer God honestly: in your life, who really controls whom?

sections.heading: 2. The Process from Theory to Life: The Witness of Four Levels
sections.html:
The key to changing our mindset and bringing revival lies in letting theory become life. This process can be divided into four levels.

Brothers and sisters, please notice the word “process.” A changed life never arrives in a single leap. It’s like a tree: from seed to sprout, from sprout to taking root, from taking root to bearing fruit — not one step can be skipped. Many Christians stall not because they don’t love the Lord, but because they get stuck at a certain level and can’t get past it, while imagining they have already finished the course.

This morning I’d like you, as you listen, to mark honestly in your heart: which level am I on right now?

Level 1: The Theoretical Mindset — “Someone Else Tells Me”

This is passive reception. Someone speaks, I listen, I understand, but there is no action. A faith like this has no power, because it is only a pile of knowledge.

Brothers and sisters, this level is not a bad thing; it is a necessary starting point. “So faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.” (Romans 10:17) No one can believe in a God they have never heard of, so the pulpit is precious, and 321 Morning Devotion is precious.

The danger is that many people stay here all their lives. They mistake “having heard” for “having understood,” and “having understood” for “having it.”

Paul says something very weighty: “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.” (1 Corinthians 8:1) This is what 321 calls the self-centred life — when knowledge feeds only my ego, it becomes nourishment for pride.

Let me use an illustration: someone learns a recipe off by heart but has never set foot in the kitchen. What he knows is a recipe, not cooking. This level corresponds to the first of the 321 eight stages of changing our mindset: Information. Information is only raw material, not the finished product; raw material piled up in a warehouse will never turn itself into a house.

Level 2: The Mindset of Revelation — “God Tells Me”

When the Holy Spirit speaks to us, our hearts are stirred, our faith is kindled, and we begin to want to respond. But if we stop at the stage of being moved, the change is still unfinished.

Brothers and sisters, this is an extremely precious level. Between “someone else tells me” and “God tells me” there is a vast gulf, and the one who carries us across it is the Holy Spirit.

Look at Peter. In the region of Caesarea Philippi, the Lord Jesus asked the disciples, “But who do you say that I am?” Simon Peter answered, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” And how did the Lord Jesus respond? “Jesus answered him, ‘Blessed are you, Simon Bar Jonah, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven.’” (Matthew 16:17)

It was the same with Paul: “But I make known to you, brothers, concerning the Good News which was preached by me, that it is not according to man. For I didn’t receive it from man, nor was I taught it, but it came to me through revelation of Jesus Christ.” (Galatians 1:11–12) Paul had received the most thorough training in the law at the feet of Gamaliel, but his real turning point was not in Gamaliel’s school; it was on the road to Damascus.

Brothers and sisters, this is one of the Three Foundations of 321: “the Holy Spirit is my guide.” The Bible is my standard — that is objective truth; the Holy Spirit is my guide — that is subjective illumination. Without the Bible we go astray; without the Holy Spirit we have only the letter. “For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.” (2 Corinthians 3:6)

This level has a well-hidden trap: “mistaking being moved for maturity.”

Brothers and sisters, being moved is not the same as being changed. Being moved is a spark God gives, but if the spark doesn’t land on firewood, it goes out in thirty seconds.

At this point the 321 eight stages list two keys: Revelation, and then Conviction. Revelation is God shining his light on me; Conviction is me saying “Amen” to that light, surrendering with my will. Revelation is God’s work; Conviction is my response. Many people have revelation but no conviction, so they spend their whole lives going round in circles of being moved, without ever taking that step.

Level 3: The Mindset of Practice — “I’ll Live It Out for You to See”

We begin to become role models, so that the truth comes not only from our mouths but is lived out in our actions. This takes courage and perseverance, because practice always brings challenges — but only action can turn truth into power.

Paul dares to say something most of us hardly dare say: “Be imitators of me, even as I also am of Christ.” (1 Corinthians 11:1) And again: “The things which you learned, received, heard, and saw in me: do these things, and the God of peace will be with you.” (Philippians 4:9)

This is the first of the Three Foundations of 321: “Jesus is my role model.” The Lord Jesus himself lived like this. He taught, “Love your enemies,” and then on the cross he said, “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing.” (Luke 23:34) He taught, “Be a servant,” and then he took a towel, wrapped it round his waist and washed the disciples’ feet one by one. He never preached a single word he did not himself live out.

Brothers and sisters, what our generation lacks most is not speakers but role models.

It is generally said that the nineteenth-century British evangelist Henry Varley once said to the young D. L. Moody: “The world has yet to see what God will do with a man fully consecrated to him.” When Moody heard it, he said in his heart: I will be that man. History went on to prove that God really did use that one man to shake two continents.

Psychology also confirms the power of a role model. In 1977 the Stanford psychologist Albert Bandura put forward his “social learning theory,” showing that a great deal of human behaviour is learned not through being lectured but through observing role models: children who see how adults act will naturally imitate them, far more than they follow what they are verbally told to do.

Brothers and sisters, this is why one father who lives it out is worth more than a hundred parenting seminars, and one small-group leader who lives it out is worth more than a hundred sets of small-group materials.

This level corresponds to the fourth of the eight stages: Implementation. It also corresponds to the most crucial stretch of what 321 calls the “fivefold change” — when the mindset changes, the life changes; when the life changes, daily living changes. Daily living is the part other people can see.

Level 4: The Mindset of Life — “I’ll Die for You to See”

This is not physical death but a resolve to be willing to die for the truth and to hold fast for the Lord to the very end. When we live a life of denying of self, the world sees the likeness of Jesus.

Paul distils it into the most powerful sentence in the New Testament: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)

321 says: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem. And selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out; “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me.

Brothers and sisters, please hear this clearly, because it is the most crucial turn in the whole lesson: “I’ll die for you to see” does not mean I become a person of no value; it means I give up the throne and let the Lord of infinite value live out his life through this finite vessel of mine. A drop of water in the palm of your hand soon dries up; a drop of water placed in the ocean never dries up. Selflessness is not disappearing; selflessness is entering into the infinite.

The Lord Jesus used a farmer’s picture: “Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” (John 12:24) The grain of wheat has two roads: stay in the barn, clean and whole, but forever a single grain; or fall into the soil, its husk split open, looking ruined — when in fact it is bearing much fruit.

Brothers and sisters, we often pray for God to give us “abundance,” and God’s answer is often, “First fall into the ground.”

Around AD 155, Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, was brought into the arena, and the proconsul pressed him to deny Christ in order to save his life. This old man of over eighty answered: “Eighty-six years I have served him, and he has done me no wrong. How then can I blaspheme my King who saved me?” Brothers and sisters, that day everyone in the arena heard a sermon — and it was a sermon without a single word preached.

Closer to our own time, in 1956, five young American missionaries were martyred on the banks of the Curaray River in Ecuador. One of them was named Jim Elliot. In his journal in October 1949 he had written a line that has gone round the world: “He is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain what he cannot lose.” Later his wife Elisabeth, together with the sister of one of his companions, went back to that tribe and took the gospel to the very people who had killed Elisabeth’s husband and her companion’s brother, and that people group eventually turned to Christ.

Brothers and sisters, this is the power of “I’ll die for you to see.”

Of course, the great majority of us will not be called to shed our blood for the Lord. But “dying for you to see” is just as real in our everyday life: on the occasion when I could plainly win the argument, I choose to keep quiet; at the moment when I could plainly take advantage, I choose to step back; in the hurt of being plainly misunderstood, I choose not to explain myself, but only to pray. Each time, I am dying. And each time I die, the Lord lives out a little more of himself.

A life like this produces testimony, and “testimony” is precisely the weapon that overcomes Satan: “They overcame him because of the Lamb’s blood, and because of the word of their testimony. They didn’t love their life, even to death.” (Revelation 12:11)

The word “testimony” here is martyria in Greek, the source of the English word “martyr.” Brothers and sisters, in the vocabulary of the early church, “bearing witness” and “laying down one’s life” share the very same root. That tells us something: true testimony costs something. A testimony that costs nothing, Satan doesn’t even notice.

321 says: humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Satan has nothing to get a grip on in a selfless person. He can threaten someone who still has a “self,” because that person still has something to lose; he cannot threaten someone who has already handed over their life.

From Life to Culture, from Culture to Movement

When a life like this touches others, it forms a culture — “you die for others to see.” When families and churches all begin to live this way, and many walk in the truth together, a godly culture will expand into a movement, bringing revival to a region and transformation to the world.

This is the Goal of 321: establish God’s system.

And the book of Acts is a live broadcast of this very process. The Lord said: “But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you. You will be witnesses to me in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth.” (Acts 1:8) From the hundred and twenty in the upper room, to three thousand turning to the Lord at Pentecost, to Antioch, Asia Minor, Europe and Rome — that was no publicity campaign; it was a band of people who “died for others to see,” walking it out all the way.

Paul wrote this principle to Timothy: “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.” (2 Timothy 2:2) There are four generations in this verse: Paul, Timothy, faithful men, others. This is what 321 calls “Multiplication,” the last of the eight stages.

Brothers and sisters, your family is your first arena of movement. Your small group is your first plot of cultural soil. Revival doesn’t have to wait for someone else to start it; revival can start with the one decision you make this morning.

sections.heading: 3. The Key from Mindset to Life: Action
sections.html:
Theory will never turn into life by itself; only practice lets the truth take root.

James uses an extremely vivid picture: “For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man looking at his natural face in a mirror; for he sees himself, and goes away, and immediately forgets what kind of man he was.” (James 1:23–24)

Brothers and sisters, theory never turns into life “automatically.” Hearing the word without doing it is like looking in the mirror without tidying yourself up — you clearly saw, then turned round and forgot. A mirror isn’t there to be admired; it’s there to help you put yourself right. If in the morning you look in the mirror and see your hair is a mess, and all you do is nod and say, “Yes, it certainly is a mess,” and then walk out of the door, that mirror has been no use to you at all. God’s word is that mirror: he lets you see so that you will go and put things right.

James then gives the positive half: “But he who looks into the perfect law of freedom and continues, not being a hearer who forgets, but a doer of the work, this man will be blessed in what he does.” (James 1:25) Notice — “this man will be blessed in what he does.” The blessing is not in the “knowing”; the blessing is in “what he does.”

The Lord Jesus says it just as directly: “If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.” (John 13:17) Between “if you know” and “if you do them” lies a whole lifetime.

So what is the only way for a mindset to move from the inside to the outside, from thought to habit? The Lord’s servant has given us three very practical phrases: do it quickly, do it often, do it constantly.

sections.heading: 1. Do It Quickly — Act as Soon as You Know
sections.html:
As soon as you know, act at once — don’t put it off. Procrastination is the killer of action: it wears down enthusiasm and weakens faith.

The psalmist says: “I will hurry, and not delay, to obey your commandments.” (Psalm 119:60) Look at the two expressions, “hurry” and “not delay” — one positive, one negative, saying the same thing twice, because it matters so much.

Ecclesiastes also reminds us: “He who observes the wind won’t sow; and he who regards the clouds won’t reap.” (Ecclesiastes 11:4) If a farmer keeps waiting for perfect weather, he will never sow. Spiritual things are the same: wait until I’m a bit less busy, wait until my faith is a bit bigger, wait until my finances are a bit more stable — these “waits” are the gentlest killers of the spiritual life.

Why is procrastination so dangerous? Because being moved has a shelf life.

The psychologist Peter Gollwitzer, in a study published in American Psychologist in 1999, put forward the concept of “implementation intentions.” He found that when people set only vague goals (“I’m going to exercise more”), their success rate is very low; but when they make specific “if … then …” plans (“On Monday after work, I’ll go straight to the park and walk for thirty minutes”), their success rate rises markedly. That’s because a specific plan turns the action from “a decision that needs willpower” into “a response triggered automatically by the situation.”

Conversely, action produces faith. “For as the body apart from the spirit is dead, even so faith apart from works is dead.” (James 2:26) Works are not only the fruit of faith; they also feed faith.

It is generally said that the Reformer John Calvin’s seal bore a heart held out in a hand, with these words beside it: “My heart I offer to you, Lord, willingly and gladly, without delay.” Brothers and sisters, “willingly and gladly, without delay” — that is exactly what “do it quickly” means.

In the 321 eight stages, Implementation follows immediately after Revelation and Conviction. Why is the sequence so tight? Because the heat of revelation cools, and the resolve of conviction softens. While the fire is still hot, put the wood on.

sections.heading: 2. Do It Often — Mistakes Aren’t Frightening; Not Doing It Is
sections.html:
Give yourself plenty of opportunities to practise. Mistakes aren’t frightening; not doing it is.

Brothers and sisters, what holds many people back from acting isn’t laziness; it’s fear. Fear of doing it badly, fear of being laughed at, fear of saying the wrong thing, fear that our prayers aren’t spiritual enough, fear of being rejected when we share the gospel. So we choose the safest position — doing nothing. And “doing nothing” looks like zero mistakes, but in fact it is one hundred per cent failure.

The Lord Jesus told the parable of the talents. The one who received one talent went and dug in the ground and hid his master’s money. His reason was: “I was afraid, and went away and hid your talent in the earth.” (Matthew 25:25) This servant didn’t embezzle, didn’t squander; he simply — did nothing. And his master’s verdict on him was: “You wicked and slothful servant.” (Matthew 25:26)

Doing nothing is not neutral. In God’s kingdom, doing nothing is falling short.

The writer of Hebrews says: “But solid food is for those who are full grown, who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern good and evil.” (Hebrews 5:14) The Greek verb for “exercised,” gymnazō, comes from the root that means “arena, gymnasium.” Spiritual discernment isn’t something you read your way into; it’s trained, like a muscle.

Paul uses the same word: “But refuse profane and old wives’ fables. Exercise yourself toward godliness. For bodily exercise has some value, but godliness has value in all things, having the promise of the life which is now, and of that which is to come.” (1 Timothy 4:7–8)

Brothers and sisters, a fitness coach won’t throw you out of the gym because you couldn’t lift the barbell the first time. He’ll say: good, have another go. God is like that too. He isn’t waiting for us to perform perfectly; he’s waiting for us to be willing to try again.

What’s more, practice should start small. The Lord Jesus said: “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much. He who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much.” (Luke 16:10) Don’t begin by resolving to go to Africa as a missionary; first try not raising your voice to your spouse today. Don’t begin by aiming to give a million; first try giving an extra thousand this month. Small faithfulness grows into great faithfulness.

This is also the 920 practice of 321. Everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”; before every “2,” we practise living a selfless (0) life and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions. “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23) Brothers and sisters, fruit isn’t something you get by asking for it; fruit grows in relationships. Whoever you meet today is the training ground God has given you.

sections.heading: 3. Do It Constantly — Only Steady Practice Shows Results
sections.html:
Just as with physical training, only steady practice will show results.

A study by the University College London psychologist Phillippa Lally and her colleagues, published in the European Journal of Social Psychology in 2010, found that for a new behaviour to become an automatic habit takes on average sixty-six days, with wide individual differences, from eighteen to two hundred and fifty-four days. The study also turned up a very comforting result: missing the occasional day does not significantly derail the process of forming a habit.

Brothers and sisters, did you hear that? Missing one day won’t ruin you. What really ruins you is giving up altogether after missing a day.

Neuroscience also gives us a beautiful picture. Repeated practice gradually thickens the myelin sheath around the nerve fibres, and the thicker the myelin, the faster and more steadily the electrical signals travel. In other words, every time you repeat a behaviour, your brain quite literally paves another stretch of road for it. Your first prayer is awkward; your hundredth prayer comes as naturally as breathing — not because you’ve become more spiritual, but because the path has been worn in.

This is exactly “Repetition” among the 321 eight stages. The eight stages are: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Notice that “Implementation” is not followed straight away by “Multiplication”; in between come Evaluation, Correction and Repetition. Because the first attempt is usually imperfect, we need to look back and evaluate, correct our method, and then go again, and again.

Growth in the spiritual life lies not in a single breakthrough but in daily perseverance. Do it quickly, do it often, do it constantly, and your life will be renewed and your faith made strong.

This is also what 321 means by “life first, then relationships, then ministry.” We are often tempted to skip life and go straight to ministry, because ministry is visible and gets applause. But ministry without life is like a flower without roots — stand it in a vase and it will look lovely for three days; on the fourth it withers. Daily practice looks like the slowest road, but it is actually the fastest.

Brothers and sisters, one last reminder: don’t rely on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit. Rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad. “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23) Do it quickly, do it often, do it constantly — not by gritting your teeth on willpower, but by walking with the Lord day by day under the guidance of the Holy Spirit.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: A Road from the Heart to the World
sections.html:
The Three Foundations Map onto the Four Levels

The Three Foundations of 321 are: Jesus is my role model; the Bible is my standard; the Holy Spirit is my guide.

Have you noticed that these Three Foundations and today’s four levels correspond almost one to one?

The theoretical level, “someone else tells me,” must stand on “the Bible is my standard” — not believing whatever anyone says, but going back to Scripture to test everything.

The level of revelation, “God tells me,” is exactly “the Holy Spirit is my guide” — it is the Holy Spirit who turns truth in black and white into living light in my heart.

The level of practice, “I’ll live it out for you to see,” is exactly “Jesus is my role model” — as he lived, so I live.

And the level of life, “I’ll die for you to see,” carries all Three Foundations into the Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. For only when “I” have died can “he” truly reign as King; and only when I stop grabbing the credit will all the glory go to him.

The Old Self Is Self-Centred; the New Self Is Selfless

321 says: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem.

Every section of today’s lesson is, in fact, dealing with the same thing — the “self.”

When it comes to money, the “self” says: this is mine; I’m keeping it for my own future.

When it comes to hearing the word, the “self” says: I already know that; I don’t need reminding.

When it comes to practice, the “self” says: what if I do it badly — what about my face?

And how does the selfless person answer? “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20)

Paul’s description of the Lord Jesus is the most perfect portrait of selflessness: “who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” (Philippians 2:6–8)

321 says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. When one person at home bows their head first, the whole atmosphere of the home changes; when one person in the church admits their fault first, the temperature of the whole team changes. This is how “you die for others to see” becomes a culture.

The Fivefold Change and the Priority of Relationships

321 speaks of the fivefold change — mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living.

Today’s four levels walk exactly this line: theory and revelation are the “mindset” stage; being willing to die for the Lord is the “life” stage; living it out for others to see is the “daily living” stage; touching others to form a culture is the “relationships” stage; spreading into a movement and bringing revival is the “ministry” stage.

321 also reminds us of the priority of relationships: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. “Who controls whom” deals with me and God; “do it quickly, do it often” deals with me and myself; “live it out for you to see, die for you to see” deals with me and others; money and giving are precisely me and things. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

A Shift of Perspective

321 says: from man’s to God’s; from the earthly to the heavenly; from the temporary to the eternal; from the Worldly to the godly.

“Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth.” (Colossians 3:2)

Brothers and sisters, our attitude to money exposes most honestly which perspective we are standing on. Seen with earthly eyes, giving is a loss; seen with heavenly eyes, giving is a transfer to our account in heaven. Seen with temporary eyes, those five missionaries died a pitiful death; seen with eternal eyes, they were the seed of salvation for an entire people group.

The 235 Relationship: Don’t Walk Alone

Finally, the 235 relationship of 321 reminds us: with someone selfless, become a “2,” spiritual companions; build a “3,” spiritual parents and spiritual children; and go on to become a “5,” a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.

Brothers and sisters, with “do it quickly, do it often, do it constantly,” it’s easy to give up when you walk alone; with two of you, you’ll go far. “Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor.” (Ecclesiastes 4:9) So please don’t just make a quiet decision today. Find a “2,” tell them the thing you’re going to do, and ask them to check with you in two weeks’ time.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Let Mindset Become Life
sections.html:
The lesson text gives us three concrete practices. Let’s set them inside the 321 “eight stages of changing our mindset” — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — so that they really take hold on the ground.

Practice 1: Examine Your Attitude to Money and Giving

Ask yourself honestly: when I give, do I give freely, or do I struggle and hold back?

Information: Reread Matthew 6:19–24, and copy “You can’t serve both God and Mammon” onto the first page of your account book.

Revelation: Be still for ten minutes and ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light: Lord, which part of my finances do you not yet reign over as King?

Conviction: Acknowledge that part to God, and say it out loud: Lord, this is yours too.

Implementation: Do one concrete thing this month — resume regular giving, or give an extra gift, or pay off a debt that keeps you from being free.

Evaluation and Correction: At the end of the month, look back: did my heart hurt in that moment? And adjust the order of your budget — give first, then save, and spend last. “Honor Yahweh with your substance, with the first fruits of all your increase.” (Proverbs 3:9)

Repetition: Do this for three months in a row, until it becomes a habit.

Multiplication: Once you’ve tasted the freedom, share the experience with a brother or sister.

Practice 2: Write down one truth God has reminded you to live out, and start practising it today

Not ten truths — one. Not next week — today.

Information: Open this week’s devotional notes and find the one line that keeps going round in your heart.

Revelation: Ask the Holy Spirit: in whom, and in what situation, do you want me to live this out?

Conviction: On paper, write one complete sentence: “At (time), I will do (what) for (whom).”

Implementation: Act straight away. If you can get it done within twenty-four hours, don’t put it off till tomorrow. “I will hurry, and not delay, to obey your commandments.” (Psalm 119:60)

Evaluation and Correction: Write down what I did and how it turned out; if it went badly, don’t condemn yourself — just ask: how will I adjust next time?

Repetition: Do the same practice at least three times this week.

Multiplication: Bring someone along to do it with you, and have them write down their one truth too.

Practice 3: Share Your Action and Testimony in Your Fellowship or Family

Brothers and sisters, testimonies aren’t only for people who have already succeeded; testimonies are for telling to people who are still on the road.

Information: Prepare a three-minute sharing — what I used to be like, what God said, what I did, and what things are like now.

Revelation: Ask the Holy Spirit to remind you which experience he wants to use through you to bless others.

Conviction: Don’t hold back just because “it hasn’t been very successful yet.” Your weakness is part of the testimony too.

Implementation: Share it in your small group or family time this week.

Evaluation and Correction: Notice whose eyes lit up — that may be the person God wants you to follow up; next time you share, use less teaching and more detail.

Repetition: Make it a habit to share at least once a month what God has done in you.

Multiplication: Invite those who heard you to go and do one thing this week too, and next time it’s their turn to share.

A Gentle Reminder

Spiritual growth is not about how much you know but about how much you live out.

Don’t wait until you feel moved before you act; the action itself is the evidence of faith.

Brothers and sisters, we often get the order backwards: we think we must first be moved before we can act. In fact it’s often the other way round — first comes the action, and then the feeling catches up. When the Israelites crossed the Jordan, God didn’t part the waters first and then tell them to walk. The text records that “those who bore the ark had come to the Jordan, and the feet of the priests who bore the ark had dipped in the edge of the water (for the Jordan overflows all its banks all the time of harvest)” (Joshua 3:15), and then “the waters which came down from above stood, and rose up in one heap a great way off” (Joshua 3:16). The priests’ feet went into the water first; then the water parted.

Faith doesn’t wait until the whole road is clear before stepping out; faith puts its foot down when it can see only the first step.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: Revival Begins with This One Person — Me
sections.html:
Revival is not the start of a movement; it is the “start of change” in countless individuals.

And this morning, that one individual can be you.

When we turn from loving the world to loving God, from hearing the word to doing it, from theory to life, we become witnesses of God’s kingdom.

Change begins with me — when I am willing to “die for you, Lord, to see,” Jesus can “live for the world to see” through me.

Brothers and sisters, these are the Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. I die so that he may reign as King; I step back so that he may receive the glory. This is no loss; it is the best exchange in the whole world.

So this morning I want to give you a call that is very simple, yet not at all easy: don’t let this lesson become just one more page in your notebook. Right now, in your heart, choose one thing you can go and do before today is over — perhaps a phone call, a word of apology, a gift, or a prayer.

Do it quickly. Do it often. Do it constantly.

May God’s kingdom, beginning with this one action of yours this morning, come into your family, your church and your city.

keyVerses: “No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other; or else he will be devoted to one and despise the other. You can’t serve both God and Mammon.” (Matthew 6:24)
“They overcame him because of the Lamb’s blood, and because of the word of their testimony. They didn’t love their life, even to death.” (Revelation 12:11)
“But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.” (James 1:22)
practices: Examine your attitude to money and giving
Share your action and testimony in your fellowship or family
prayer: Lord, I no longer want to stay in theory.
Help me overcome the world and overcome the bondage of money, so that before you I am a free person, able to give joyfully and offer willingly.
Lord, make me not only a hearer but a doer; not only moved, but changed. Help me live out your word quickly, no longer putting it off, no longer waiting for a perfect moment.
May your truth become the power of life within me. Take away my “self,” reign as King in me, and let all the glory go to you.
Beginning with me, let revival come to my family, my church and my city.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: The Lord Jesus said: “No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other; or else he will be devoted to one and despise the other. You can’t serve both God and Mammon.” (Matthew 6:24) Share honestly: in your life right now, what is one thing that makes you feel “I’m not controlling it; it’s controlling me”? This week, what one concrete act of letting go are you willing to make in this area?

James says: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.” (James 1:22) Looking back over today’s four levels — theory, revelation, practice and life — which level do you think you are at right now? What is keeping you from moving on to the next? In your small group, name one thing you will “do quickly,” and ask a brother or sister to check on your progress in two weeks.
